text_kjv: The proverbs of Solomon the son of David, king of Israel;

commentary.narrative:
The book opens with a formal attribution to Solomon, son of David, king of Israel. This genealogy and title establish both authority and context—Solomon was famed in ancient Near Eastern tradition as the wise king par excellence, and this connection to David's line carries covenantal weight in Israelite thought. The very first word, 'proverbs' (mishle in Hebrew), is crucial: these are not mere folk sayings or clever observations. The root m-sh-l means 'to rule, to compare, to represent.' A mashal is a governing analogy—a compressed truth that, once received, reorders the hearer's entire perception of reality. It exercises authority over understanding. This is why wisdom literature in Israel was never casual entertainment; it was formative instruction designed to reshape how one perceives and acts in the world.

The attribution to Solomon draws explicitly on the tradition recorded in 1 Kings 4:32, which credits him with composing three thousand proverbs and one thousand five songs. In the ancient Near East, wisdom was a royal prerogative—the king's primary responsibility was to govern justly, and that governance flowed from his wisdom. By opening with Solomon's name, Proverbs claims to offer the compressed wisdom of Israel's greatest wise king. Yet the book's address to the 'simple' and 'youth' (verses 4-5) suggests that while Solomon is the attributed source, the intended audience is not the royal court alone but anyone willing to be formed by these governing analogies.

word_study.meaning: From the root m-sh-l ('to rule, to compare, to represent'). A mashal is far more than a pithy saying or folk wisdom. It is a compressed, authoritative statement that captures reality and exercises power over the hearer's perception. The term encompasses proverbs, parables, allegories, and even prophetic oracles. In Proverbs, a mashal is a governing analogy meant to reshape understanding.
word_study.significance: The KJV 'proverbs' masks the deeper Hebrew concept. A mashal demands active engagement from the hearer—it is not information passively received but a truth that must be internalized and allowed to reorder one's worldview. This is why Proverbs is not merely philosophical but formative; it aims to govern how the reader thinks and acts.

word_study.meaning: Direct genealogical designation. In biblical literature, lineage carries covenantal significance—to be 'son of David' is to be heir to the promises made to David regarding his throne and his seed.
word_study.significance: The phrase ties Solomon not merely to his father's dynasty but to the Davidic covenant itself. Wisdom, in this context, is not an abstract virtue but a kingly responsibility. It flows from the covenant God made with David (2 Samuel 7) and is essential to righteous rule.

cross_references.connection: Explicitly credits Solomon with exceptional wisdom and notes that 'his fame was in all nations round about.' Proverbs 1:1 draws directly on this historical tradition of Solomon as Israel's preeminent wise king.
The covenant promise to David that his seed will be established and will build God's house. Solomon's wisdom is framed as part of the fulfillment of this covenantal promise.

Notes that 'these are also proverbs of Solomon which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out,' indicating that the collection grew and was curated over time, even as it remained attributed to Solomon.
In an LDS context, the Lord speaks of preserving 'the wisdom of the wise' among His people, affirming that divine wisdom—as exemplified by Solomon—is meant to instruct the faithful.

commentary.historical_context: Solomon's reign (approximately 970-930 BCE) was remembered in Israelite tradition as a golden age of prosperity, architectural achievement, and international renown. The attribution of Proverbs to Solomon reflects the ancient Near Eastern pattern of ascribing wisdom literature to great kings—similar collections were attributed to Amenemope in Egypt and to Ahiqar in Aramaic tradition. In the ancient Near East, wisdom was understood as a royal art, essential to just governance. The king was expected to be the source of wise counsel for his people. By attributing Proverbs to Solomon, the book situates itself within this royal wisdom tradition while simultaneously democratizing it—these royal insights are now available to anyone willing to learn, not merely to courtiers.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon frequently invokes Solomon as a type of wisdom and righteousness (e.g., Alma 37:35 uses the image of Nephi as a teacher of wisdom analogous to ancient wise men). The Restoration emphasizes that true wisdom comes through revelation and the Holy Ghost, not merely through human learning—a principle that deepens the call to 'know wisdom' in Proverbs 1:2.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 90:15 counsels that 'it is impossible for a man to be saved in ignorance,' connecting knowledge with salvation in a way that affirms the Proverbs' urgency about acquiring wisdom. D&C 6:7 promises that 'you shall have a knowledge of all things,' suggesting that the kind of wisdom Proverbs pursues—practical, moral, relational—is part of the broader Restoration understanding of knowledge as essential to exaltation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Solomon built the temple, and Proverbs represents the wisdom necessary for righteous governance of God's people. In LDS thought, temple worship itself is an encounter with divine wisdom—the temple teaches through symbol and ceremony in a manner analogous to how Proverbs teaches through compressed, memorable sayings that must be pondered and internalized.

commentary.christological_typology: Solomon himself is often understood in Christian tradition as a type of Christ—the wise king who surpasses all others in understanding. In Matthew 12:42, Jesus claims that 'a greater than Solomon is here,' implying that He embodies and transcends Solomonic wisdom. The governing analogies (meshalim) that Solomon speaks are a foreshadowing of Christ's own use of parables—both compress divine truth into memorable forms that reshape the hearer's understanding. Christ's wisdom, however, is not merely tactical or prudential but redemptive, aimed at transforming not just behavior but the human heart.
commentary.application: Modern readers often approach Proverbs seeking quick life advice—practical tips for success. But verse 1's opening insists on something deeper: these are governing analogies meant to reshape how you perceive reality itself. Before you begin reading Proverbs, settle the question: Are you willing to have your understanding reordered? The proverbs of Solomon demand not just intellectual assent but a willingness to be formed, corrected, and redirected. This is not a book to skim for inspiration but to internalize as a guide to perception. Ask yourself as you begin: What assumptions about money, relationships, time, and success might these ancient wise sayings challenge? Am I prepared to let them govern my understanding?

text_kjv: To know wisdom and instruction; to perceive the words of understanding;

commentary.narrative:
Verse 2 articulates the book's foundational purpose through a paired construction: wisdom paired with discipline, followed by discernment paired with understanding. This is the thesis of Proverbs—the dual agenda that shapes every subsequent verse. The pairing is not accidental. In ancient Hebrew thought, wisdom (chokmah) is not an abstract intellectual quality but embodied competence—the capacity to perceive situations accurately and to act rightly within them. Yet wisdom cannot stand alone; it must be accompanied by musar, which the KJV renders as 'instruction' but which more precisely means 'discipline,' carrying overtones of correction and even painful pruning.

The second line shifts the verb from 'know' to 'perceive' or 'discern' (lehabin), suggesting a deepening. One knows wisdom and discipline; one discerns or penetrates the words of understanding. This is not passive reception but active perception—the capacity to see beneath the surface of what is said and grasp its deeper structure and implication. The 'words of understanding' are not self-explanatory; they require insight to be truly grasped. Together, these two lines establish that the reader of Proverbs is not seeking information but formation—a reordering of perception that will enable wiser living.

word_study.meaning: Chokmah encompasses practical skill (as in Exodus 31:3, where it describes artistic and craft competence), ethical discernment in relationships, and the ability to perceive and navigate complex situations. It is not abstract philosophy or theoretical knowledge but embodied, applied understanding—knowing how to live well.
word_study.significance: Chokmah in Proverbs is fundamentally relational and practical. It is the capacity to read a situation—a person's character, the consequences of actions, the proper time for speech—and to act accordingly. This is why wisdom is never purely intellectual in Proverbs; it always issues in right behavior.

word_study.meaning: From yasar ('to chastise, to correct, to discipline'). Musar is the corrective force that shapes character. It often appears in contexts of physical correction (Proverbs 13:24, 22:15) and carries the implication that formation requires the submission of the learner to correction that may be painful or unwelcome.
word_study.significance: The KJV's 'instruction' softens musar's sharp edge. Wisdom in Proverbs is not a comfortable attainment; it requires the learner to be pruned, corrected, sometimes wounded. The pairing of chokmah and musar at the book's opening signals that wisdom is not for those who wish to remain unchanged but for those willing to be disciplined. This prevents Proverbs from becoming merely about self-improvement; it is about transformation through submission to correction.

word_study.meaning: Binah is the faculty of understanding that penetrates beneath surface appearances. The verb lehabin ('to discern, to distinguish, to gain insight') implies active perception—looking into and seeing through to deeper structure.
word_study.significance: While chokmah and musar are about knowing wisdom and receiving correction, binah is about penetration—seeing beneath what is obvious. The reader of Proverbs is not meant to passively absorb proverbs as mere aphorisms but to 'discern' them—to see how they apply in complex human situations, to grasp their deeper logic.

cross_references.connection: Expands on verse 2's call to seek understanding, emphasizing that wisdom must be actively pursued like treasure, and that it comes from the Lord. The discernment called for in verse 2 is deepened as a kind of spiritual seeking.

Declares that 'the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding.' Connects the fear of the Lord with chokmah and binah, showing that true wisdom in biblical thought is inseparable from reverence toward God.
Paul contrasts worldly wisdom with God's wisdom, suggesting that the wisdom Proverbs pursues—embodied, relational, corrective—is aligned with divine wisdom rather than human cleverness.

Promises that the Holy Ghost 'shall teach you all things that are expedient for you to understand,' aligning knowledge and understanding with the guidance of the Spirit—a principle that enriches the call to perceive understanding in verse 2.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel and the broader ancient Near East, wisdom schools were real institutions where young men (and the intended audience of Proverbs appears to be primarily male youth, though not exclusively) were trained in the skills necessary for scribal, administrative, or diplomatic service. The purpose clause in verses 2-6 reflects this pedagogical context: the book is designed to form individuals for competent living in a complex society. The pairing of wisdom and discipline reflects the actual pedagogy of these schools—learning was not passive instruction but active formation through correction. Students were expected to internalize not just factual knowledge but patterns of discernment that would enable them to navigate ethical dilemmas and social complexities throughout their lives.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly emphasizes the pairing of knowledge with righteousness and correction. Alma 37:35 speaks of making 'all thy doings to be for the welfare of thy soul,' linking practical wisdom with moral and spiritual formation. The Restoration understanding of wisdom, seen in figures like Nephi and Alma, is that true wisdom always includes the willingness to be corrected—Nephi's dream of the tree of life, for instance, is a guided experience meant to reshape his understanding of God's plan.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 101:28 states that the Lord 'sees all things, and all things are manifest before him,' connecting divine perception with wisdom. D&C 121:26-32 emphasizes that influence built on love and kindness—qualities inseparable from true wisdom—endures, while force and coercion do not. This aligns with Proverbs' insistence that wisdom is about understanding how to influence and guide others rightly.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment involves a graduated sequence of instruction and covenants, wherein the participant progresses through understanding—each stage deepening perception and commitment. This mirrors Proverbs' model of wisdom as a deepening discernment rather than a single acquisition. One does not 'complete' the temple; one returns to it repeatedly, each time discerning new layers of meaning and commitment.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is presented in Restoration scripture as the embodiment of both chokmah and musar. In D&C 93:26-28, the Savior is described as one who received grace and truth, and who grew in understanding—suggesting that His wisdom was not merely omniscient knowledge but embodied comprehension of human experience. His teaching through parables and enigmatic sayings (as noted in verse 6) mirrors the method of Proverbs: rather than delivering answers, He poses questions and stories that demand active discernment from the hearer. His willingness to be corrected by the Father (see John 12:49-50) models the kind of submission to discipline that Proverbs insists is central to wisdom.
commentary.application: As you begin reading Proverbs, resist the temptation to approach it as a book of quick tips. The call to 'know wisdom and receive discipline' asks something more demanding: Are you prepared to be corrected? Wisdom in Proverbs is not what you learn; it is who you become through submission to truth that sometimes wounds or redirects you. Identify one area of your life—a relationship, a financial choice, a pattern of speech—where you suspect your current understanding may be incomplete or wrong. Approach Proverbs as a mirror that may show you something you need to see, and commit to the discipline of allowing these ancient sayings to reshape your perception rather than merely confirming what you already believe.

text_kjv: To receive the instruction of wisdom, justice, and judgment, and equity;

commentary.narrative:
Verse 3 specifies the concrete moral outcomes that wisdom produces. The verse is structured as a clarification of verse 2's 'discipline'—to receive musar is specifically to be formed toward righteousness, justice, and uprightness. This is crucial: Proverbs is not teaching wisdom as a neutral skill that might be put to any use. A wise manipulator or a clever thief might be chokmah in the sense of tactical cunning, but this is not the wisdom of Proverbs. True wisdom issues in tsedeq (righteousness—conformity to God's moral standard), mishpat (justice—the right application of that standard in community affairs), and mesharim (uprightness—the personal integrity and straightness that connects principle to practice).

The triad of virtues here is not random but comprehensive. Tsedeq addresses one's standing before God; mishpat addresses one's dealings with others and community; mesharim addresses the internal integrity that must animate both. Together they define what it means to be truly wise: not clever, but righteous; not merely intelligent, but just; not inconsistent, but straight. The repetition of these themes throughout Proverbs (and their prominence in the Psalms, the prophets, and the Torah) indicates that for biblical thought, wisdom divorced from justice is not wisdom at all—it is mere cunning, which leads to destruction. This verse corrects any reader tempted to seek wisdom for selfish advantage.

word_study.meaning: Conformity to God's standard; being in right relationship with the divine order. It encompasses both justification (being declared righteous) and sanctification (becoming righteous in behavior). Tsedeq is fundamentally relational—it means being aligned with God's character and purposes.
word_study.significance: In Proverbs, tsedeq is the foundation. One cannot pursue justice or uprightness without first seeking to be in right standing with God. This is why Proverbs 1:7 will immediately follow with 'the fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge'—wisdom begins with reverence for God and alignment with His righteousness.

word_study.meaning: The right ordering of communal life; the just application of law and principle in specific situations. Mishpat is both the principle of justice and its concrete implementation—the judge's verdict, the ruler's decision, the fair settlement of disputes.
word_study.significance: Mishpat is where righteousness touches the social world. It is not enough to be personally righteous; wisdom demands that one act justly toward others, that one defend the vulnerable, and that one refuse to exploit power or position. Throughout Proverbs, mishpat appears in warnings against oppressing the poor and in affirmations that the righteous judge will prosper.

word_study.meaning: Straightness, integrity, the personal quality of being upright or unbent. Yashar means 'to be straight, to be right, to make straight.' Mesharim is the plural, suggesting multiple dimensions of uprightness—in one's words, one's dealings, one's heart.
word_study.significance: Mesharim connects the inner life to outer action. It suggests that genuine justice and righteousness require an integrated self—not one who is righteous in public but crooked in private, or who speaks justice but acts unjustly. The emphasis on straightness implies that wisdom requires alignment between profession and practice, between heart and deed.

cross_references.connection: Reiterates that wisdom and understanding will cause one to 'understand righteousness, and judgment, and equity'—the same triad of verse 3—confirming that these are the permanent outcomes of wisdom.

Celebrates God's righteousness and justice, affirming that God's testimonies and law produce these virtues in those who embrace them. Connects Proverbs' triad to the broader biblical witness about God's character.

The prophet calls for justice to 'roll down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream,' using the language of mishpat and tsedeq to describe a social order that reflects God's character. Proverbs pursues wisdom precisely so that individuals might act justly and righteously in their communities.
The Lord says that 'the righteousness of the upright shall deliver them,' linking the uprightness of verse 3 with deliverance—suggesting that integrity in conduct has real, protective consequences.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel and the Near East, the king was the chief administrator of justice (mishpat). Wise rulership meant applying God's law (Torah) and principle fairly and impartially, protecting the vulnerable, and maintaining the social order. The phrase 'justice and judgment and equity' would have resonated with anyone familiar with royal inscriptions or law codes from Egypt, Babylon, or Assyria, where kings boasted of administering justice fairly. However, in Proverbs, this call to justice is not limited to kings or judges; it is universalized. Every wise person—whether rich or poor, ruler or subject—is called to seek tsedeq, mishpat, and mesharim. This democratization of virtue is a distinctive mark of Israelite wisdom literature.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon echoes this triad repeatedly. Alma 50:20 notes that Nephite success came when they were 'obedient to the commandments of God, and walking in the ways of his righteousness.' Helaman 13:1-5 emphasizes that righteousness in the people ensures peace and protection. The Restoration consistently teaches that personal virtue is inseparable from justice in community—one cannot be individually righteous while participating in social injustice.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:34-35 teaches that 'light cleaveth unto light' and that when one receives 'truth and light,' this empowers one to 'come unto the Father in my name.' The righteousness, justice, and uprightness of verse 3 are the practical manifestation of receiving truth and light. D&C 121:37 affirms that influence built on 'persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned' endures—these are the relational and moral fruits of wisdom as Proverbs understands it.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant explicitly includes a commitment to 'virtue' and to living according to God's law. The progression of temple instruction moves the participant from individual righteousness toward an understanding of how divine order encompasses all creation. This mirrors Proverbs' movement from personal wisdom to justice in the broader community.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ embodies the triad of tsedeq, mishpat, and mesharim perfectly. His life demonstrated righteousness (alignment with God's will), justice (defense of the vulnerable, refusal to exploit power), and uprightness (absolute integrity between His words and deeds, between His teachings and His life). His teaching consistently linked personal virtue with social justice—the Sermon on the Mount, for instance, begins with internal transformation (blessedness, purity of heart) and extends to social practice (peacemaking, mercy, just speech). In Matthew 23:23, Jesus affirms that 'judgment, mercy, and faith are the weightier matters of the law,' recalling the biblical emphasis on mishpat as central to God's character and ours.
commentary.application: Proverbs 1:3 is a corrective for anyone tempted to view wisdom as merely personal cleverness or success. Wisdom, properly understood, always bends toward justice. Ask yourself: How is my personal pursuit of wisdom reflected in how I treat others? Do I use what I've learned to advantage myself at others' expense, or to serve justly? Identify one situation—at work, in your family, in your community—where you have opportunity to practice justice and uprightness. Wisdom is not proved in private reflection but in public action. What would it mean for you to seek mishpat—right judgment in a specific situation—this week?

text_kjv: To give subtilty to the simple, to the young man knowledge and discretion.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 4 makes a crucial rhetorical and pedagogical move: it names the book's primary audience. The 'simple' (peti in Hebrew) and the 'young man' (naar) are not the wise or the experienced but the untested, the vulnerable, those whose character is still forming. This is radically democratic. Wisdom literature in the ancient Near East was often restricted to court scribes and the elite; Proverbs opens its treasures to anyone, but especially to those most in danger of being misled. The peti is not stupid but naive—someone whose judgment is not yet developed, whose defenses against deception are not yet formed, who can still be easily enticed or led astray.

The gifts offered are shrewdness (ormah) and knowledge paired with discretion (mezimmah). Ormah is a fascinating word: it is the same term used to describe the serpent's cunning in Genesis 3:1. It is morally neutral—the capacity to perceive hidden things, to navigate deception without being deceived, to discern what others intend. For the naive, ormah is not a vice but a necessary protection. Mezimmah, often translated as 'discretion' or 'wisdom' (related to zimam, 'to plan or counsel'), suggests strategic thinking—the ability to look ahead and see consequences. Together, these equip the young to navigate a world full of temptation, exploitation, and hidden danger without becoming cynical or corrupt themselves. Proverbs does not write off the naive; it equips them.

word_study.meaning: From patah ('to open, to be open, to be enticed'). The peti is someone whose character is open, still forming, capable of being led in either good or bad directions. Not foolish or lacking intelligence, but untested and vulnerable to seduction.
word_study.significance: The term does not denigrate the simple; it describes a developmental stage. Proverbs is explicitly written for people in this stage—young people whose judgment is not yet fully formed, who need guidance on how to navigate temptation and deception. This is why Proverbs is ultimately a book of urgent love: the wise are writing to protect the vulnerable.

word_study.meaning: Craftiness, cunning, the capacity to perceive and navigate hidden intentions and deceptions. The same word used to describe the serpent in Genesis 3:1. It is morally neutral—can be used for good (to protect oneself from being exploited) or evil (to exploit others).
word_study.significance: The KJV's 'subtilty' has negative connotations in English, but in context, Proverbs is arming the naive with the ability to see through deception. The gift being offered is not corrupt cunning but protective awareness. The naive need to become streetwise without becoming cynical—to perceive danger without becoming dangerous themselves.

word_study.meaning: Daat is knowing or knowledge; mezimmah (from zimam, 'to plan, to counsel, to intend') is foresight, strategic counsel, prudence—the ability to think ahead and consider consequences.
word_study.significance: These gifts work together: knowledge of what others intend (daat) paired with the foresight to plan accordingly (mezimmah). The young person thus equipped can evaluate options, foresee consequences, and make wise decisions rather than being passively swept along by circumstance or manipulated by others' intentions.

cross_references.connection: States that 'the simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going.' This expands on verse 4—the simple must learn to exercise caution and foresight rather than naive credulity.
Declares that 'a prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished.' Directly illustrates how mezimmah (foresight) protects the young from danger.

Jesus instructs His disciples to 'be wise as serpents, and harmless as doves'—echoing the paradox of Proverbs 1:4: the young must acquire shrewdness (like serpents) without becoming corrupt or exploitative (remain harmless as doves).

The Lord teaches that sin includes not only overt transgression but also failing 'to observe and keep the commandments which I have given,' connecting knowledge with responsibility—the young who gain daat and mezimmah from Proverbs incur the responsibility to use these gifts righteously.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, the transition from childhood to adulthood (marked for boys around age 12-13) involved increasing responsibility and vulnerability to moral failure. Young men were expected to leave the household and engage in work, commerce, and social relationships where they could be exploited, seduced into sexual sin, or led into dishonest dealings. The 'young man' of verse 4 was literally at risk. Proverbs serves as a kind of protective guide for this vulnerable stage of life. The book's repeated warnings against adultery, folly, laziness, and corrupt dealings (themes prominent in chapters 2-7) are not moral haranguing but urgent counsel to those most in danger. Ancient Near Eastern wisdom literature consistently targeted this age group, recognizing that character formation in youth determines the trajectory of a life.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 37:2-10 functions similarly to Proverbs 1:4, with Alma counseling his young son Helaman, providing him with 'knowledge' of the spiritual dangers he will face and 'discretion' about how to navigate them. The Book of Mormon consistently frames wisdom as protective counsel for the young. Moroni's promise in Moroni 10:3-5 likewise gives young readers a method for testing truth and avoiding deception—equipping them with the shrewdness to discern what is of God from what is not.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 38:30 teaches that 'if ye are prepared ye shall not fear,' connecting preparation (daat and mezimmah—knowledge and foresight) with protection. D&C 68:25-28 emphasizes that parents and teachers have a sacred responsibility to instruct the young 'in all things that pertain to the gospel of Jesus Christ,' suggesting that formal wisdom instruction (like Proverbs provides) is part of the covenant responsibility toward youth.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Young members are often encouraged to approach the temple and its covenants with the kind of preparation Proverbs 1:4 describes—not naive or untested, but having acquired knowledge of God's ways and the discretion to recognize truth. The temple itself serves as a protective covenant, arming the young with understanding about the challenges they will face in mortality.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's compassion for the vulnerable and the young is evident throughout the gospels. In Matthew 19:14, He insists 'Suffer little children to come unto me,' and in Matthew 18:10-14, He teaches that causing a child to stumble is abhorrent to God and that He seeks with urgency to restore the lost. His parables often teach the kind of practical wisdom that protects the naive—recognizing false prophets (Matthew 7:15), guarding against greed (Luke 12:15), perceiving hypocrisy (Matthew 23). Christ's role as teacher is fundamentally protective: He equips His followers with the discernment to navigate a world of spiritual danger without losing faith or becoming cynical.
commentary.application: Proverbs 1:4 speaks to you differently depending on your stage of life. If you are young and relatively untested: This book is written for you, precisely because you are at the threshold of encountering temptation, deception, and exploitation. Rather than waiting until you've been burned, equip yourself now with the shrewdness to perceive hidden intentions and the foresight to see consequences before you act. If you are older: Reflect on young people in your sphere—your children, grandchildren, mentees. How are you equipping them with daat and mezimmah? Are you dismissing their questions as naive, or are you taking seriously the work of formation? Proverbs suggests that the wise have a responsibility to pass protective knowledge to the vulnerable.

text_kjv: A wise man will hear, and will increase learning; and a man of understanding shall attain unto wise counsels:

commentary.narrative:
Verse 5 introduces a critical principle that paradoxically subverts the usual understanding of wisdom: the already wise still need to hear and learn. This is the inverse of verse 4, which targeted the naive. Here, Proverbs reaches toward those who already possess chokmah and binah—the wise and the discerning. The shock of the statement lies in its negation of completion. In many cultures, the wise person is imagined as one who has arrived, who possesses answers, who teaches but does not learn. Proverbs shatters this image. The chakham (wise person) actively hears and adds to their learning (yoseph leqach); the binon (person of understanding) acquires tachbulot (steering, guidance, strategy).

Tachbulot is etymologically fascinating: it derives from chobel ('rope'), specifically the rope used to steer a ship. Thus wisdom, even for the wise, is navigational—the ongoing capacity to steer one's course through complex circumstances. The parallelism of verse 5 suggests that wisdom and understanding are not static attainments but dynamic processes. You do not 'have' wisdom; you are continually acquiring it. This explains why Proverbs, attributed to Solomon at the height of his fame and power, is presented as guidance not just for the young but for anyone willing to keep learning. The book claims that even Solomon's three thousand proverbs (1 Kings 4:32) represent not mastery but an ongoing pursuit. This principle also suggests why Proverbs expects to be reread and internalized—each reading reveals new depths, and each season of life requires renewed navigation.

word_study.meaning: Chakham is the wise person—one possessing chokmah, embodied competence and good judgment. Shama means 'to hear' but in Hebrew often implies not passive listening but active hearing with response and integration—to hear in such a way that one is changed by what one hears.
word_study.significance: The combination suggests that the marks of a truly wise person is not the refusal to listen but the active, humble receptivity to new understanding. This inverts the common stereotype of the wise sage as self-contained and complete. Biblical wisdom is fundamentally humble—it never claims to have finished learning.

word_study.meaning: Yoseph means 'to add, to increase'; leqach means 'learning, doctrine, that which is received.' The phrase literally means 'add to learning' or 'increase in receiving instruction.'
word_study.significance: This is not acquisition of new facts but the ongoing internalization and application of wisdom. The wise person is characterized by perpetual growth, not complacency. This principle undergirds the entire Proverbs project: even someone as wise as Solomon would benefit from returning to these proverbs repeatedly.

word_study.meaning: From chobel ('rope'), specifically the nautical ropes used to steer a ship. By extension: steering, guidance, strategy, the capacity to navigate complex terrain and steer one's course.
word_study.significance: The nautical metaphor suggests that wisdom is navigation—constantly assessing where you are, where you're going, how to steer amid currents and obstacles. The wise acquire tachbulot not by sitting on the shore but by engaging repeatedly with circumstances that demand navigational skill. This is why Proverbs is not theoretical but practical; it prepares you for the actual work of navigation.

cross_references.connection: Declares 'Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser.' This echoes verse 5's principle that wisdom is perpetual growth, not completion.
Notes that 'a prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself; but the simple pass on, and are punished.' The tachbulot (wise navigation) of verse 5 is illustrated in foresight that protects.

Paul instructs Timothy to entrust teachings 'to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also,' suggesting that wisdom is perpetually passed on, with each generation adding to their learning from those who came before.

The Lord teaches that 'that which is of God is light; and he that receiveth light, and continueth in God, receiveth more light,' affirming the principle that wisdom grows as one remains open to continued revelation.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, royal wisdom was understood as a kind of ongoing political and strategic navigation. Kings consulted advisors, read reports, and adjusted their governance based on circumstances. The metaphor of tachbulot—steering a ship—would have resonated with anyone involved in trade, travel, or military strategy. Moreover, the insistence that the wise continue to learn would have countered the temptation toward tyranny or rigidity that sometimes afflicted aged rulers. A king who stopped learning, who ceased to listen to counsel, was a king heading toward ruin. This principle was not unique to Israel but was widely recognized in Near Eastern wisdom traditions.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 29:3-4 exemplifies this principle: even though Alma has achieved spiritual authority as chief judge and high priest, he wishes he had 'the voice that could shout to all the ends of the earth' and could 'declare the word with thunder.' His desire to learn more, to become more effective in his ministry, illustrates how the wise continue to grow. Nephi's willingness to be taught by an angel (1 Nephi 11) despite his already-considerable spiritual understanding models the receptivity verse 5 describes.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 76:5-9 describes Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon's vision as an unveiling of truth that came through their openness to see and hear more than they had previously understood. This illustrates the operative principle: continuing revelation comes to those wise enough to remain open. D&C 93:36-39 teaches that continued growth in light and truth requires 'harkening to the voice of the Spirit'—the perpetual hearing of verse 5.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple worship, especially endowment and sealing ceremonies, involves repetition and deepening. One returns to the temple repeatedly and discovers new layers of meaning in ceremonies encountered before. This mirrors verse 5's principle: the wise acquire tachbulot—navigational wisdom—by returning to sacred patterns and allowing them to guide and redirect understanding.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's earthly development, as described in Luke 2:52 ('Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man'), exemplifies verse 5. Despite His divine nature, the incarnate Christ engaged in a process of growth and learning. His parables often teach about perpetual spiritual navigation—the need to continually assess one's course, repent, and adjust. His role as teacher is fundamentally one of helping His followers acquire tachbulot—the wisdom to navigate the narrow way amid cultural pressure and spiritual danger. In John 16:12-13, He promises that the Holy Ghost will 'guide you into all truth,' suggesting that wisdom is not a final attainment in this life but a perpetual navigation toward fuller understanding.
commentary.application: This verse is a mirror held up to your own relationship with learning. At what point in your life do you tend to stop listening, to assume you've figured things out? The wise person of Proverbs is characterized by perpetual receptivity. Practically: (1) Identify an area where you consider yourself knowledgeable or experienced. Can you identify one perspective, one insight, from someone younger, from a different culture, or from an unexpected source, that might add to your understanding? (2) What is one truth you believed ten years ago that you now understand more deeply? Commit to regular re-engagement with Proverbs, scripture, or counsel you've previously heard, expecting that your listening will reveal new layers. (3) Seek out a wise person—a mentor, an elder, a trusted counselor—and genuinely ask for tachbulot: their navigational wisdom for a specific challenge you're facing. Receive it not defensively but humbly.

text_kjv: To understand a proverb, and the interpretation; the words of the wise, and their dark sayings.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 6 brings the purpose statement to its climactic formulation: the book exists to enable readers to penetrate proverbial utterance and the enigmatic speech of the wise. This is the deepest level of the Proverbs' pedagogical agenda. The verse shifts from stating what the reader will gain (verses 2-5) to stating what the reader will learn to do (verses 4-6). Specifically, readers must learn to understand not just the obvious surface of a proverb but its underlying meaning and application. Moreover, they must become comfortable with darkness—with riddles, enigmas, and hidden sayings that do not yield meaning immediately or transparently.

The two terms here are crucial. Mashal refers, as we saw in verse 1, to a governing analogy—a compressed truth that reshapes understanding. Melitsah is a 'figure of speech' or enigmatic saying—language that obscures as much as it reveals. The wise deliberately speak in figures and riddles not to confuse but to engage the hearer in active interpretation. When the hearer must work to understand, that very work becomes formative. A maxim received passively is easily forgotten; a riddle that demands wrestling with its meaning is internalized. The final phrase—'their dark sayings' (chidotam, plural of chidah, 'riddle')—emphasizes that wisdom literature is deliberately obscure, inviting and requiring the reader to penetrate beneath the surface. This explains why Proverbs cannot be read quickly or superficially. It demands the kind of meditative, repeated engagement that slowly transforms the reader's perception.

word_study.meaning: As established in verse 1, mashal derives from m-sh-l ('to rule, to compare, to represent'). It is a compressed, governing analogy that exercises authority over the hearer's understanding. A mashal is not a simple saying but a complex utterance that must be unpacked.
word_study.significance: To 'understand a proverb' is to receive its governing authority into one's perception and allow it to reshape how one sees the world. This is not intellectual analysis but internalization. The mashal, properly understood, becomes a lens through which the reader henceforth views situations and relationships.

word_study.meaning: A word, saying, or utterance that speaks indirectly or enigmatically. Melitsah can mean satire, irony, or any speech that requires interpretation. It is language that deliberately obscures its meaning, requiring the hearer to work to understand.
word_study.significance: The Proverbs deliberately uses indirect speech—figures of speech, irony, and paradox. Understanding melitsah requires the reader to think actively, to perceive multiple layers of meaning, to move from surface to depth. This is intentional pedagogy: direct commands are easily forgotten, but utterances that puzzle and provoke are internalized.

word_study.meaning: A riddle, puzzle, or obscure saying. Chidah comes from a root meaning 'to tie in knots' or 'to bind together.' A riddle binds together apparent contradictions or hides meaning in layers.
word_study.significance: The inclusion of chidot in verse 6 signals that Proverbs is not a simple book offering easy answers. It expects the reader to be puzzled, to wrestle, to return repeatedly to a saying until its meaning emerges. This is wise pedagogy: the wisdom that comes easily is as easily lost. The wisdom acquired through struggle—through working with a riddle until it yields—becomes part of the reader's deepest understanding.

cross_references.connection: Declares 'It is the glory of God to conceal a thing: but the honour of kings is to search out a matter.' This principle justifies the intentional obscurity of wisdom literature—God Himself conceals truth, requiring seekers to search it out.

The psalmist promises to 'incline mine ear to a parable' and to 'open my dark saying upon the harp.' This merging of riddle, parable, and music illustrates that obscure speech was a characteristic feature of wisdom and prophetic utterance in Israel.

Jesus explains that He speaks in parables so that 'seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand'—the truth is deliberately veiled from those not prepared to receive it, while those who seek understanding will find it. This principle mirrors Proverbs' use of enigmatic speech.

The Lord presents the Word of Wisdom with the statement that 'all wholesome herbs God hath ordained for the constitution, nature, and use of man,' requiring readers to perceive the broader principles behind the specific commandments—similar to how Proverbs requires interpretation.

commentary.historical_context: Riddle-contests were a recognized feature of ancient Near Eastern and Israelite culture. Samson's riddle (Judges 14:12-18) and the Queen of Sheba's testing of Solomon with hard questions (1 Kings 10:1) illustrate that wisdom was often demonstrated through the ability to pose and solve enigmas. Wisdom schools in the ancient Near East employed riddles and enigmatic sayings as pedagogical tools precisely because they forced active engagement. The method is not unique to Israel; Egyptian wisdom literature (such as the Instructions of Ptahhotep) and Mesopotamian wisdom texts employ similar strategies. The underlying pedagogical principle is sound: a truth received as a direct command can be rejected or forgotten easily; a truth that emerges through one's own work of interpretation becomes integrated into the self.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 12:25-30 discusses how Christ conceals and reveals truth according to the faith of the people. Alma teaches that 'there are many mysteries which are kept from this generation' and that 'all things which have been given of God of him are the typifying of him.' The Book of Mormon itself employs this principle: it is a text that yields deeper meaning to those who read it repeatedly and prayerfully. The Book of Mormon is, in a sense, a collection of riddles—historical narratives that obscure as much as they reveal until the reader's own spiritual development allows deeper perception.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 63:23 affirms that 'that which breaketh a law, and abideth not by law, but seeketh to become a law unto itself, and willingly rebelleth against the law, is pride.' This principle is embedded in Proverbs' enigmatic approach: if the reader is too proud or lazy to work at understanding the riddle, they miss the wisdom. The text requires humility and effort. D&C 50:24 teaches that 'that which is of God is light; and he that receiveth light, and continueth in God, receiveth more light'—those who engage repeatedly with Proverbs' obscure sayings, seeking light, will find increasing illumination.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple ordinances employ obscure and symbolic language deliberately. The temple endowment does not simply state truth; it enacts it through ritual and symbol, requiring the participant to interpret and internalize. Like Proverbs, the temple expects that repeated engagement will yield ever-deeper understanding. First-time participants grasp certain truths; those who return regularly perceive layers of meaning they initially missed. Both Proverbs and temple work operate on the principle that transformative truth requires the reader/participant's active engagement.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's use of parables (Matthew 13) mirrors the method described in Proverbs 1:6. He teaches through indirect utterance, through figures of speech and riddles, requiring the hearer to work at understanding. In John 6:51, His saying 'I am the living bread which came down from heaven' is enigmatic—it requires listeners to move beyond literal interpretation to spiritual meaning. The difficulty of His teaching ('How can this man give us his flesh to eat?' — John 6:52) is not accidental but essential. It separates those ready to receive the deepest truth from those satisfied with surface understanding. His parables, like the riddles of Proverbs, are designed to be misunderstood by those not ready for the truth they convey and to deepen the understanding of those who persist in seeking.
commentary.application: Proverbs 1:6 is an invitation to slow down and to engage interpretively. Our modern world trains us to skim, to seek information quickly, to move on. But Proverbs demands something different: it asks you to sit with a saying until its meaning emerges, to return to it in different seasons of life and discover new applications. Practically: (1) Choose one short proverb from the coming week's reading. Write it down. Sit with it. Ask: What does this mean? What does it NOT mean? How does it apply to a situation I'm currently facing? (2) Notice how many proverbs seem to contradict each other (e.g., 'He who hesitates is lost' vs. 'Look before you leap'). Rather than seeing this as incoherence, recognize that Proverbs is riddling—wisdom requires wisdom to know which maxim applies in which context. (3) Choose to read Proverbs as a practice of meditation rather than of information-gathering. Read a chapter, then sit in silence and let the sayings work in your imagination. Return to the same chapter a month later and notice what new meanings have emerged.

text_kjv: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.

commentary.narrative:
This verse announces the thesis of the entire book of Proverbs. The fear of the LORD (yirat YHWH) is not paralyzing terror but reverent awe—a lived recognition that God is real, sovereign, and the definer of all values. This fear functions as an epistemological foundation: it is the starting point from which all genuine knowledge emerges. Without it, mere intelligence becomes clever foolishness, divorced from moral reality. The verse creates a fundamental binary that will structure the entire book: those who fear the LORD and pursue wisdom versus those who despise both.

The second half delivers the counter-thesis with devastating simplicity. Evilim (fools) are not intellectually limited people but morally obstinate ones—those who actively reject wisdom and discipline. The verb bazu (despise) is stronger than mere disagreement; it conveys contempt, a willful turning away. By placing the objects of rejection (wisdom and discipline) before the verb of rejection, the Hebrew syntax emphasizes what is being thrown away. The fool's tragic flaw is not inability but refusal.

word_study.meaning: Yirah encompasses a spectrum from terror to reverent worship, but in wisdom literature it crystallizes into a specific meaning: the lived acknowledgment that God is real, sovereign, and the ultimate arbiter of truth and value. It is the correct orientation toward reality itself.
word_study.significance: This is not an emotion to be cultivated through psychological effort but a reality to be recognized and acted upon. The person who fears the LORD has correctly identified who is in charge of the universe. In Latter-day Saint terms, this is akin to the recognition that God has revealed Himself through living prophets and that obedience to His word is the path to truth.

word_study.meaning: Reshit means 'beginning' or 'first principle,' but carries qualitative weight beyond mere chronological sequence. The same word opens Genesis (bereshit, 'in the beginning'). Here it functions as both temporal and qualitative: where you start, and what is most important.
word_study.significance: The fear of the LORD is not step one of a self-improvement program to be completed and transcended. It is the soil in which all knowledge grows. Every true insight, every wise decision, every accurate understanding of reality must be rooted in this foundational reverence.

word_study.meaning: Not the intellectually limited but the morally obtuse—those characterized by a refusal to acknowledge God's sovereignty and wisdom's value. The fool's defining trait is stubborn rejection, not inability.
word_study.significance: Throughout Proverbs, the fool is culpable for his folly because it stems from will, not capacity. This distinction is crucial: the Bible does not despise intellectual limitation, but it does condemn the hardened refusal of wisdom.

word_study.meaning: To hold in contempt, to treat with scorn, to actively reject as worthless. It goes beyond disagreement to express hostility toward wisdom itself.
word_study.significance: The fool does not merely fail to understand wisdom; he actively scorns it. This willful contempt is the heart of folly and sets the terms for the entire book's moral landscape.

cross_references.connection: Repeats the identical formula ('the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom'), forming an inclusio that brackets the first major section of Proverbs and reinforces the thesis.
Declares that fear of the Lord is wisdom and to depart from evil is understanding—establishing that reverence toward God and moral obedience are inseparable from true knowledge.
States 'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom'—the same formula, emphasizing that this principle spans wisdom literature and is not peculiar to Proverbs alone.

'Search these commandments, for they are true and faithful, and the prophecies and promises which are in them shall all be fulfilled'—emphasizing that seeking God's word with reverence leads to knowledge of truth.
Discusses the alignment of faith and reason, teaching that genuine knowledge begins with recognition of God's reality—the Restoration's articulation of yirat YHWH.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite pedagogy, the father's role as primary instructor was paramount, but wisdom was understood as a cosmic reality—the ordering principle by which God had structured creation and by which human life should be organized. To fear God meant to align oneself with that cosmic order. The fool, by despising wisdom and discipline, was not merely being rebellious against human authority but was foolishly placing himself at odds with the way the world actually works. Ancient Near Eastern wisdom literature (Mesopotamian, Egyptian) also emphasizes the necessity of proper orientation toward the divine as the prerequisite for acquiring useful knowledge.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma's instruction to his sons employs the same pedagogical framework: he teaches them to fear God (Alma 36:3, 37:35) as the foundation for receiving knowledge and living wisely. The Book of Mormon consistently ties fear of the Lord to practical wisdom and protection from deception.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 90:24 emphasizes that true knowledge comes through searching God's commandments with faith—reflecting the same principle that reverent attention to God's word is where genuine understanding begins. The entire structure of D&C Section 1, the Lord's preface to the Doctrine and Covenants, rests on the conviction that God's word is truth and that heeding it is essential to knowledge.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The progression of temple ordinances reflects this principle: the candidate begins by taking upon themselves reverence for God's covenants and a willingness to be instructed. This is not mere ritual but the embodiment of yirat YHWH—the lived acknowledgment of God's reality and sovereignty as the basis for receiving higher knowledge.

commentary.christological_typology: In the New Testament, the apostle Paul describes Christ as 'the wisdom of God' (1 Corinthians 1:24) and teaches that 'in him are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge' (Colossians 2:3). The fear of the LORD—the reverent acknowledgment of God's reality and authority—finds its fullness in Christ, who perfectly embodied obedience to the Father and who is himself the revelation of divine order. In Latter-day Saint doctrine, Christ is the expression of God's character and truth; to fear the Lord is ultimately to recognize His nature as revealed through His Son.
commentary.application: For a modern covenant member, this verse establishes that Gospel knowledge and spiritual discernment cannot be separated from reverence toward God. Academic learning, scriptural literacy, and even theological sophistication can become forms of clever foolishness if they are not rooted in a genuine, lived fear of the Lord—a daily acknowledgment that God is real, that His word through His prophets is true, and that obedience to His direction is the path to genuine understanding. The question posed to each reader is direct: Am I building my approach to knowledge on a foundation of reverent submission to God, or am I cultivating a kind of intelligence that, however impressive it may seem, is ultimately untethered from moral reality?

text_kjv: My son, hear the instruction of thy father, and forsake not the law of thy mother:

commentary.narrative:
The shift from the thesis statement of verse 7 to direct address marks the beginning of sustained parental instruction. The father-sage now addresses 'my son' (beni) in the second person, establishing an intimate pedagogical relationship that will characterize the first major section of Proverbs (chapters 1-9). This verse simultaneously honors both parents as authoritative sources of wisdom, which was a countercultural assertion in ancient Near Eastern societies where formal instruction was often the father's exclusive domain.

The parallelism between father's musar (discipline, instruction) and mother's torah (law, instruction) is theologically significant. By placing the mother's teaching at equivalent authority with the father's, the proverb affirms that wisdom is transmitted through both lineages and that a young person who despises either parent's instruction cuts himself off from essential knowledge. The verb 'forsake' (tazub) suggests active abandonment—not merely disagreeing but deliberately turning away from an established source of guidance. This verse establishes the book's emphasis on receptivity: wisdom is not discovered through individual reasoning alone but received through submission to established authority.

word_study.meaning: To listen, to heed, to obey. Shema is not passive auditory reception but active compliance—to hear is to accept and act upon what is heard.
word_study.significance: This is the same verb that opens the Shema prayer ('Hear, O Israel'), emphasizing that hearing God's word and accepting it as binding are inseparable. In the covenant context of Latter-day Saint theology, shema is the posture required before receiving revelation.

word_study.meaning: Discipline, correction, instruction that includes rebuke and training through consequence. It is not merely information transfer but formative correction aimed at character development.
word_study.significance: Musar appears throughout Proverbs as a precious commodity (13:24, 22:15, 23:13). The fool rejects musar; the wise embrace it. In Restoration theology, this aligns with the concept that God's prophets sometimes deliver difficult instruction (D&C 121:43)—'chastenings' that are meant for our growth.

word_study.meaning: Law, instruction, teaching. Torah can refer to the Pentateuch, but here it means authoritative instruction or guidance that shapes how one lives.
word_study.significance: By using torah for the mother's teaching, the proverb elevates her instruction to the highest level of authority. This is not casual advice but binding guidance that should shape behavior and character.

word_study.meaning: To leave, abandon, forsake deliberately. It implies a choice to walk away from something established.
word_study.significance: The negative formulation 'do not forsake' emphasizes the danger of active rejection. The temptation is not merely to ignore instruction but to deliberately cast it off as no longer binding.

cross_references.connection: Repeats the injunction to heed father and mother's instruction, establishing this as a recurring theme and setting the stage for warnings against specific temptations.
The command to honor father and mother is foundational covenant law; Proverbs 1:8 grounds this honor in the practical reality that parents transmit essential wisdom.

Moses instructs that God's words should be in the heart and taught diligently to children—establishing the cultural framework within which Proverbs operates: instruction within family covenantal structures.

Alma tells his son Helaman that he received instruction from his father 'concerning all the affairs of the church'—mirroring the Book of Mormon's affirmation that parental instruction in covenant matters is essential to spiritual growth.

The Lord commands parents to 'teach their children to understand the doctrine of repentance'—establishing in Restoration theology the principle that parents are primary instruments of transmitting spiritual wisdom.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, formal education was limited and typically available only to the elite or scribal class. For most children, the family—particularly the mother in early childhood and the father in later formation—was the primary source of instruction in wisdom, law, and practical skills. Elevating the mother's torah to equal authority with the father's musar was a remarkable affirmation in a patriarchal culture. Egyptian wisdom literature (such as the Instructions of Ptahhotep) shows a similar pedagogical model where a father instructs his son, but the inclusion of the mother as an equally authoritative source reflects Israelite values. Archaeological evidence suggests that women in ancient Israel, particularly in household contexts, held significant authority in transmitting cultural wisdom and covenant obligations.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly emphasizes parental instruction as the mechanism through which covenantal life is perpetuated. Lehi's teachings to his sons (2 Nephi 1-4), Alma's instruction to each of his sons (Alma 36-42), and Jacob's teachings to his people (Jacob 1-4) all model the figure of the father-sage imparting wisdom. Interestingly, the Book of Mormon also gives voice to mothers (such as Sariah's faithful example and the 'mothers' referenced in Alma 56:47) as bearers of covenant identity and moral formation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 68:25-28 declares that 'every parent' (not just fathers) has responsibility to teach children 'the doctrine of repentance, faith in Christ the Son of the living God, and of baptism and the remission of sins.' This expands the principle of Proverbs 1:8, affirming that spiritual instruction flows through parental relationships established by covenant.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment includes a dimension of parental instruction and covenant reception. In Latter-day Saint theology, the eternal family unit is the context in which the highest knowledge is transmitted. This verse grounds that principle in the ordinary practice of family instruction as the means by which wisdom is passed from generation to generation.

commentary.christological_typology: While this verse does not directly prefigure Christ, it establishes the principle that truth is mediated through authorized instructors. In Latter-day Saint theology, Christ is the ultimate Teacher and Guide, and the chain of instruction from God through prophets to parents to children reflects the pattern of how divine wisdom flows into human life. Hebrews 5:8 states that Christ 'learned obedience by the things which he suffered,' suggesting that even the Son received instruction and discipline—honoring the principle that receptivity to authoritative teaching is essential, not beneath dignity.
commentary.application: For a contemporary Latter-day Saint adult, this verse invites reflection on the quality of attention one gives to established sources of wisdom within the covenantal community. Just as the young person is called to 'hear' and not 'forsake' parental instruction, the adult member is called to actively receive and not deliberately reject the instruction that flows through the restored Church—from prophets, from parents and grandparents whose example witnesses to gospel truths, from leaders and teachers called within the covenant structure. The warning is against the subtle modern temptation to treat such instruction as merely one opinion among many, to be accepted or rejected according to personal preference. Verse 8 calls for genuine receptivity, not credulous passivity, but receptivity nonetheless.

text_kjv: For they shall be an ornament of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck:

commentary.narrative:
This verse answers an implicit question: Why should I listen to my parents and not forsake their instruction? The answer reveals a crucial feature of biblical wisdom: it is not a burden imposed from above but an adornment—something that enhances the person who receives it. The imagery of a livyat chen (garland of grace) and anaqim (pendants, necklaces) transforms discipline from something restrictive into something beautiful and honorific. In the ancient Near East, such ornaments were not trivial accessories; they signaled social standing, honor, and blessing. A person adorned with such jewelry was recognized as one of status and favor.

The verse operates on multiple registers simultaneously. Literally, it promises that the child who receives parental instruction will be visibly enhanced—distinguished in the community as one who has been formed by wisdom. Morally, it teaches that obedience to instruction is not a diminishment of freedom but an increase in dignity. Theologically, it suggests that wisdom's fruit is not hidden but publicly displayed; the wise person bears marks of grace visible to the community. The passage thus answers a deep human anxiety: Will accepting instruction and discipline make me less of a person? The answer is a resounding no—it will make you more recognizable as blessed, more honored, more bearing the marks of divine favor.

word_study.meaning: Livyat is a wreath or garland; chen means grace, favor, or beauty. Together they suggest adornment that is both physically beautiful and spiritually significant—marks of being favored.
word_study.significance: This is the language of blessing and honor. The Covenant Rendering's choice of 'garland' over 'ornament' better captures the sense of something woven together, integrated, the product of careful formation.

word_study.meaning: Head, but in Hebrew thought, the seat of understanding, the place from which decisions and character flow.
word_study.significance: To place wisdom as a garland on the head is to place it in the seat of judgment and character formation. This is where your understanding originates; wisdom adorns the very source of your thinking.

word_study.meaning: Necklaces, pendants, ornamental chains worn around the neck as signs of honor and wealth. In ancient texts, such adornments marked status and distinction.
word_study.significance: The shift from head to neck suggests that wisdom is integrated into the whole person—from the seat of thought to the visible markers of one's identity in community. There is nothing hidden about it; wisdom marks you publicly.

word_study.meaning: Because, for—a causal conjunction introducing the reason or purpose for the preceding command.
word_study.significance: This word establishes the motivational structure: obey your parents' instruction not from fear of punishment but from recognition of the good it will produce in you. The pedagogy is one of attraction toward the good, not mere compliance.

cross_references.connection: Declares that exalting wisdom will lead to honor: 'She shall bring thee to honour, when thou dost embrace her.' Wisdom's rewards include public recognition and honor.
Promises that wisdom and discretion will be 'life unto thy soul, and grace to thy neck'—using identical imagery of grace adorning the neck as a mark of blessing.
Contrasts outward adornment with 'the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price'—suggesting that true adornment is character formed by submission to wisdom.

Promises that those who exercise faith, virtue, knowledge, temperance, patience, brotherly kindness, and godliness will have 'thy confidence waxed strong in the presence of God'—describing how living according to divine instruction produces public recognition and honor.
Alma speaks of Alma the Elder's righteous example creating a form of social honor and influence—demonstrating that faithfulness to wisdom produces visible marks of blessing in the community.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern societies, jewelry was not merely decorative but carried social meaning. Gold necklaces and wreaths were awarded to honored officials, soldiers, and wise counselors. Egyptian and Mesopotamian texts depict kings and nobles adorned with precisely such chains and wreaths as marks of status. In Israel, such ornaments could signify priestly honor (Exodus 28), royal dignity (2 Samuel 12:30), or victory (2 Maccabees 15:30). The imagery would have resonated powerfully with young listeners: accepting parental discipline is not a humiliation but a path to honor. This verse works against the temptation to view wisdom's demands as something lesser, second-rate—as if true freedom consisted in throwing off restraint. Rather, it presents wisdom as the path to genuine distinction and public recognition.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly presents the righteous as bearing marks of blessing that are publicly visible. The people of Ammon, after accepting Alma's instruction, are described as a distinguished people known for their covenant faithfulness (Alma 17-26). Nephi speaks of his efforts to 'magnify mine office' such that his work would be known and honored (1 Nephi 11:3). The principle is consistent: faithfulness to wisdom produces not hidden virtue but publicly recognized marks of blessing.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 121:45-46 employs similar imagery: those who conduct themselves according to divine wisdom will have 'confidence waxed strong in the presence of God,' and 'the Holy Ghost shall be [their] constant companion.' This is the Restoration's equivalent of the garland and chains—visible marks of divine favor and blessing that distinguish the wise in the community.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment includes the receipt of sacred garments and insignia that mark the covenant member as one set apart. In Latter-day Saint theology, these marks are not external validation but signs to oneself and the community of one's commitment to divine order. Proverbs 1:9 prefigures this principle: wisdom's adornments mark you as belonging to a community of the favored.

commentary.christological_typology: In Revelation 4:4, the elders around the throne of God wear crowns of gold. In Matthew 25:31-46, Christ as judge honors those who have lived according to divine wisdom by seating them at His right hand—a glorification. The principle is that faithfulness to God's instruction results in honor before God and the community. In Latter-day Saint theology, endurance in the covenant leads to exaltation, the ultimate 'adornment' of honor and divine recognition. Christ Himself, having perfectly received the Father's instruction and discipline, wears 'many crowns' (Revelation 19:12) as the marked one of ultimate honor.
commentary.application: This verse addresses a fundamental human anxiety about obedience: Will living according to wisdom make me less impressive, less successful, less honored in the eyes of others? The answer Proverbs offers is counterintuitive and potentially liberating: No. Living by the counsel of those who genuinely possess wisdom—parents, prophets, experienced teachers in the faith—results in a kind of distinction and grace that cannot be achieved through selfish independence. For a modern member, this suggests that resistance to prophetic counsel often stems from a misunderstanding about what honor and success really are. The invitation is to trust that receiving correction and instruction from authorized sources places upon you marks of blessing—not obvious to every casual observer, perhaps, but visible to those with eyes to see, and real in the community of the faithful. The question for application is: Where am I resisting instruction because I fear it will diminish my standing, when in fact it would mark me as someone of grace?

text_kjv: My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not.

commentary.narrative:
The pedagogical tone shifts abruptly from promise to warning. Having established the attractiveness of wisdom—it adorns you with grace—the father now addresses the most immediate and practical threat: sinners will attempt to recruit the young person into their schemes. The verb yefattukha (entice, seduce) comes from the same root (patah) that was used to describe the peti (naive, simple) in verse 4. The naive are those susceptible to enticement; sinners deliberately target this vulnerability. This is not a theoretical warning but practical mentoring: sinners actively hunt for recruits, and they will use persuasion, appeal to acceptance, and the language of camaraderie to accomplish their ends.

The father's response is admirably direct and allows no room for negotiation: al tove (do not consent, do not go along, do not be persuaded). There is no suggestion of dialogue with the sinner's invitation, no 'hear them out' or 'consider their perspective.' This is not because wisdom is closed-minded but because the father recognizes that certain invitations carry a dynamic momentum. Once you begin to entertain them, once you 'consent' to even preliminary involvement, the logical and social pressure to proceed escalates. The command is therefore preventive: refuse at the moment of initial approach, before the machinery of rationalization can engage. This verse establishes a principle that will be developed extensively in verses 11-19: the sinner's invitation is attractive precisely because it offers the appearance of belonging, excitement, and shared purpose—but these are covers for predatory intent.

word_study.meaning: To entice, seduce, persuade toward wrongdoing. The root can mean to open (as in opening a door) but in this context means to open someone's defenses through persuasion.
word_study.significance: This verb suggests that sinners employ rhetoric and appeal—they do not simply demand but persuade. This makes them more dangerous than obvious criminals; their threat is subtle.

word_study.meaning: Sinners, those who miss the mark, who deviate from the way of wisdom and justice. In Proverbs, 'sinners' is a category of those whose fundamental orientation is away from God.
word_study.significance: The term is not judgmental in the sense of moral superiority but diagnostic: these are people whose trajectory is toward destruction, and they actively invite others to join them.

word_study.meaning: To go, to walk, to proceed. In this context, 'consent' captures the sense of 'go along with them' or 'agree to join them'—a verb of motion and agreement combined.
word_study.significance: The command is not merely 'do not agree mentally' but 'do not go along, do not proceed with them.' It is a call to complete refusal, not partial disagreement.

cross_references.connection: Repeats the warning: 'Enter not into the path of the wicked, and go not in the way of evil men...avoid it, pass not by it.' The command is not merely to refuse participation but to distance oneself completely.

Declares 'He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.' This establishes the principle that association itself shapes character—you become like those you consent to follow.

Paul warns that 'evil communications corrupt good manners'—establishing that even exposure to the rhetoric of sinners corrupts character. The New Testament affirms Proverbs' teaching that you cannot safely entertain a sinner's invitation.

Nephi cries out 'O Lord, I have trusted in thee, and I will trust in thee forever...O curse the devil, because he is the author of all sin.' He recognizes that the fundamental issue is not curiosity about evil but resistance to the Devil's recruitment.

The Lord teaches that 'Verily I say unto you, He that is ordained of me and sent forth to proclaim the truth by the Comforter, in the Spirit of truth, doth he preach it by the Spirit of truth, or some other way? And if it be by some other way it is not of God.' The principle is that you must distinguish true from false invitation, and false invitations—from 'sinners'—must be completely refused.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, as in all human societies, young men faced recruitment into criminal enterprises, gang activity, and vice. The streets of Jerusalem, the trade routes, the gathering places were contexts in which organized criminals sought to recruit the naive. Proverbs speaks to this concrete danger. The phrase 'sinners' often refers in ancient Hebrew to organized groups of wrongdoers—those who operate in bands. The warning against 'consenting' to their invitation reflects awareness that such groups are powerful precisely because of their cohesion and their ability to make membership seem attractive. The father's teaching is therefore both universal and specific: universally, beware of those who invite you toward wrongdoing; specifically, beware of their rhetoric of belonging and shared purpose.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly depicts the temptation of wicked enticement. Korihor 'went about from place to place, enticing the people with his words' (Alma 30:18). King Noah's court drew people into wickedness through enticement and appeal to pleasure (Mosiah 11). The Sons of Mosiah, initially following a path of enticement into wickedness, later recognize the danger and turn from it (Mosiah 27-28). The Book of Mormon is consistent with Proverbs: refusal must come at the point of initial enticement, because once engaged, the momentum toward destruction accelerates.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 50:23-24 and D&C 100:15 establish that the Spirit bears witness to truth, whereas deceptive invitations come from another source. The principle is that the young person must develop discernment to distinguish true from false invitation. D&C 121:4-6 addresses the danger of false authority and false invitations to power and control, teaching that such invitations are fundamentally at odds with divine order.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment includes the explicit teaching of distinguishing true from false priesthood authority and true from false covenants. Proverbs 1:10 is foundational to this: the ability to refuse false invitation is essential to covenant keeping.

commentary.christological_typology: In Matthew 4, Christ is offered three temptations by Satan—invitations to turn from His Father's will toward shortcuts to power and satisfaction. Christ's response is consistent refusal, rooted in complete orientation toward His Father. He does not debate the Devil's offers or ask for clarification; He refuses. In Hebrews 5:8, Christ 'learned obedience,' suggesting that His capacity to refuse temptation was developed through the discipline of alignment with His Father's will. For Christians, Christ models the posture Proverbs calls for: complete refusal of sinners' enticement, rooted in ultimate loyalty to God.
commentary.application: For a contemporary adult member, this verse invites honest reflection on moments of 'enticement'—not merely obvious criminal recruitment but the subtle daily invitations to compromise principles, to 'go along' with groups or decisions that subtly drift from covenant values. The father's blunt command—'consent not'—removes the middle ground. The temptation in modern contexts is to rationalize: 'I'll just listen to what they have to say,' 'I need to understand their perspective,' 'I don't want to be judgmental.'
