By positioning Wisdom in the street, Proverbs democratizes access to understanding in a way that was radical for its time.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly employs the image of prophets calling publicly to the people. Abinadi stands before King Noah and his court, proclaiming with boldness. Alma cries repentance throughout the cities of Zarahemla. Samuel the Lamanite stands on the wall, calling the people to turn from their wickedness. In each case, as with Wisdom in Proverbs, the call is public, insistent, and cannot be avoided by those within earshot. The refusal of the message is not due to its unavailability but to the hardness of hearts (Alma 10:25).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: The Doctrine and Covenants emphasizes that the call of God and truth must be proclaimed openly. In D&C 21:4-5, the Lord tells Joseph Smith that the Church must 'be called Zion...and be the strength and stability of all things.' The public proclamation of Wisdom in Proverbs parallels the mandate in D&C 1:4 that 'the voice of the Lord is unto all men' and 'that every man may hear in his own language.' Truth, in the Restoration, is not esoteric or hidden; it is proclaimed openly to all.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple presents truth and covenants openly to those who come with faith. Like Wisdom crying in the streets, the temple's ordinances are available to all who prepare themselves to enter. The accessibility of the temple covenant (though requiring worthiness) reflects the principle that Wisdom establishes: the most important truths are proclaimed openly, and those who miss them do so by choice, not by unavailability.

commentary.christological_typology: Wisdom's public proclamation in the streets and squares prefigures Christ's ministry, particularly his teaching in the temple and synagogues, and his preaching to the multitudes. In Matthew 21:12-17, Christ cleansed the temple and taught openly, much as Wisdom makes herself heard in public spaces. More profoundly, in John 1:1-3, Christ is identified with the Logos (Word/Reason), and in Proverbs 8:22-31, Wisdom is portrayed as present at creation. The New Testament application of Wisdom language to Christ suggests that his incarnation and public ministry represent the ultimate fulfillment of this call: Wisdom made flesh, crying out in the streets of Jerusalem, offering the way of life to all who have ears to hear.
commentary.application: This verse exposes a common excuse for spiritual blindness: the claim that truth was hidden or unavailable. Wisdom cries aloud in the streets where you live, work, and make decisions. The question is not whether truth is accessible but whether you are listening. For modern disciples, this verse should prompt an honest self-examination: Where is Wisdom calling in my life? What voices am I giving attention to instead—the seductions of gain, the plausibility of the world, the reassuring whispers of friends going the wrong way? Wisdom does not require isolation or withdrawal from the normal spaces of life. She stands precisely where decisions are made: in the marketplace, in the place of negotiation, in the forum of public life. The invitation is to develop the ear to hear her voice there, amid the noise and temptation. This verse also serves as a check against elitism in spirituality: if Wisdom cries in the street, then access to understanding is not restricted to the scholarly or the privileged. Every person has the opportunity to hear. Refusal cannot be blamed on unavailability.

text_kjv: She crieth in the chief place of concourse, in the openings of the gates: in the city she uttereth her words, saying,

commentary.narrative: Wisdom's proclamation becomes more specific and urgent. The verse moves from the general category of 'streets and squares' to the most consequential locations in the ancient city: the gates, where justice is administered and public decision-making occurs. The phrase 'chief place of concourse' (rosh homiyot in Hebrew, literally 'the head of the noises' or 'the chief of the crowds') refers to the busiest, most crowded junction, the exact place where influence is greatest and attention most contested. The 'openings of the gates' (pithei shearim) were not peripheral but central—the entry points to the city where merchants conducted business, strangers arrived with news, and the community's most important transactions occurred. The city gate in ancient Israel was the legal and commercial heart. Elders sat there to judge disputes (Ruth 4:1-11); transactions were made there; the community's defense was organized there. By positioning Wisdom at the gates, Proverbs claims that she is not addressing the foolish alone but calling to leaders, judges, merchants, and all who have power to make consequential decisions.
commentary.narrative_continued: The repetition of the phrase 'uttereth her words, saying' (amaareha tomer) signals that what follows is the content of Wisdom's proclamation. We are about to hear Wisdom speak directly, in her own voice. The structure of the passage is masterful: the father warned in private (verses 8-19); now Wisdom speaks in public (verses 20-33). Both address the same young man who must choose between the path of the sinners and the path of Wisdom. But Wisdom's setting is intentionally more visible, more authoritative, more official. She speaks where decisions matter, where power is exercised, where a refusal to listen has consequences not merely for the individual but for the community.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: A key insight emerges from this verse: Wisdom addresses not only the naive or the young but also the powerful and the established. The elders and judges sitting at the gate doors hear the same proclamation as the merchants and travelers. Wisdom is not offering comfort to the downtrodden or a separate gospel for the powerful; she offers the same path to everyone. This universality is radical. It suggests that the way of Wisdom is not class-specific, not reserved for the educated or the privileged, but equally available and equally demanding for all. The young man of verse 8 is not the only audience; he is part of a community called to hear and respond.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'at the head of the noises' or 'the chief of the crowds.' Homiyot is the feminine plural of hemiyah, which relates to crowds, commotion, or loud noise. Berosh means 'at the head' or 'at the chief point.'
word_study.significance: This phrase suggests not merely a location but a moment—the moment of greatest crowding, greatest noise, greatest public attention. Wisdom does not choose a quiet corner but the epicenter of urban life. The term 'noises' (homiyot) may also evoke the confusion and chaos of the market; Wisdom's voice rises above that confusion and claims the central place.

word_study.meaning: The entrances or openings of the gates. Pithach means 'to open,' and shaar means 'gate.' The plural shearim suggests the multiple gates of a walled city.
word_study.significance: Ancient cities were walled and had multiple gates serving different commercial, military, or administrative functions. Each gate opening was a liminal space—a threshold between the outside and inside, between the foreign and the domestic, between one space and another. By positioning Wisdom at these thresholds, Proverbs suggests that she stands at all the critical passages and transitions of life. She guards the entry points to decision-making and community.

word_study.term_english: uttereth her words / speaks her words
word_study.meaning: Her words/sayings she speaks/says. The phrase combines 'amarim' (words, sayings) with the verb 'amar' (to say), creating an emphatic construction that emphasizes the act of speaking and the reality of what is said.
word_study.significance: The repetition (noun and cognate verb) gives weight and authority to what Wisdom is about to declare. It is not mere opinion or suggestion but an utterance, a pronouncement. In biblical language, such constructions often precede statements of truth or law.

cross_references.connection: Boaz conducts his legal transaction 'in the gate' before the elders, showing that the gates were the site of binding legal and social transactions. Wisdom's presence at the gates positions her as an authority figure comparable to the community leaders and judges.

The psalmist speaks of 'them that are at the gate,' suggesting that control of the gates was equivalent to control of the city. Wisdom's proclamation at the gates is a claim to the heart of communal power and authority.

Jeremiah is commanded by the Lord to 'Stand in the gate of the children of the people...and speak there this word.' Like Wisdom in Proverbs, Jeremiah is positioned at the gate as the bearer of a crucial message from God to the whole community.

Christ teaches that there are two gates—one wide and one narrow—and that few find the narrow gate of life. Wisdom's proclamation at the gates in Proverbs foreshadows Christ's teaching that choosing the right path requires passing through the right gate.

The Lord describes the gates of the New Jerusalem and their guardians. Like Wisdom standing at the city gates in Proverbs, the restored Church is positioned at the gates of salvation, calling all to enter and receive the covenant.

commentary.historical_context: The city gate in ancient Israelite society was far more than a defensive structure; it was the administrative, judicial, and commercial center. Archaeology has revealed gate complexes with chambers and seating areas where elders and officials conducted business. The gates served as the public forum where news was announced, disputes were resolved, transactions were witnessed, and authority was exercised. A figure speaking at the gates would have commanded attention comparable to a speaker at a modern city hall or courthouse. The accessibility of the gates was significant: they were not restricted to the elite but were open to all who had business in the city. By placing Wisdom at the gates, Proverbs positions her as speaking to those with power and responsibility—judges, merchants, and community leaders—who had the greatest capacity to influence others toward either the path of wisdom or the path of folly.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon frequently depicts prophets and righteous leaders speaking in gatherings and assemblies—the public equivalent of the city gates. Alma's address in Alma 5 is delivered to the Church assembled, addressing not only the members but the community. Moroni's speech at the head of his armies in Alma 43 is delivered to soldiers who have power to make life-and-death decisions. In each case, like Wisdom's proclamation, the message addresses those who have agency and responsibility.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: In D&C 1, the preface to the Doctrine and Covenants, the Lord speaks 'unto all people' and declares that 'the voice of the Lord is unto all men.' The accessibility of Wisdom at the gates is paralleled by the Restoration's claim that truth is proclaimed openly to all, regardless of status or education. Doctrine and Covenants 88:81 teaches that all should hear 'in their own language,' echoing the principle that Wisdom speaks not in the private language of the learned but in the public square where all can hear.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is described in Restoration texts as a place where all are invited to come and receive ordinances and instruction. Like Wisdom at the gates, the temple stands as a calling place at the threshold of covenant life, inviting all to enter and be instructed. The gates of the temple are open to the worthy, and the message within addresses leaders and the led equally.

commentary.christological_typology: The gates are associated throughout scripture with judgment and authority. In Matthew 16:18-19, Christ speaks of building his Church on the rock of Peter and of giving him 'the keys of the kingdom of heaven.' The gates of hell will not prevail against the Church. Christ positions himself as the ultimate authority at the gates—the judge and guard of the way into eternal life. In Revelation 3:20, Christ stands at the door and knocks; in Revelation 22:14-17, the Spirit and the Bride cry, 'Come!' The proclamation of Wisdom in the gates prefigures Christ's standing at the gate of salvation, calling all who will hear.
commentary.application: This verse challenges us to recognize that Wisdom addresses us not in our isolation but in our places of responsibility and decision-making. If you are a parent, a leader, an employer, or someone with influence, Wisdom cries at your gate. The verse asks: Where are your gates? Where do you exercise judgment, make decisions, conduct business, or influence others? Wisdom is calling there. The verse also suggests that we should listen for Wisdom not only in devotional settings but at the thresholds of ordinary life—in the meetings where decisions are made, in the conversations where influence flows, in the moments where we have the power to choose between the path of integrity and the path of expediency. The ancient image of the city gates reminds us that wisdom is not abstract; it speaks to concrete situations of power, responsibility, and choice. Finally, the verse's emphasis on Wisdom's accessibility at the public gates challenges any notion that spiritual truth is esoteric or available only to the specially educated. The gates are open to all. The question is whether we will listen.

text_kjv: How long, ye simple ones, will ye love simplicity? and the scorners delight in their scorning, and fools hate knowledge?

commentary.narrative: Now Wisdom speaks directly, and her opening is a lament. The phrase 'How long?' (ad matay in Hebrew) is the classic language of lamentation found in the Psalms—the cry of those who suffer and cry out to God asking when relief will come (Psalm 13:1-2: 'How long wilt thou forget me, O Lord? For ever? How long wilt thou hide thy face from me?'). By using this language, Wisdom positions herself as lamenting over the foolish. She does not address them with anger or mockery but with the pathos of one who grieves what her audience is choosing. The intensity of this opening should not be underestimated: Wisdom is not merely instructing; she is mourning. Three categories of people appear in this verse, arranged in a spectrum of resistance to wisdom: the petayim ('simple ones,' or as The Covenant Rendering suggests, 'the naive'), the letsim ('scorners'), and the kesilim ('fools'). Each is defined not by their actions but by what they love or hate—their fundamental orientation toward wisdom and knowledge.
commentary.narrative_continued: The 'simple ones' (petayim) are not inherently wicked; they are undirected, open to influence, but defenseless against seduction. The question 'How long will ye love simplicity?' assumes that their condition is chosen, a preference. The word for 'simplicity' (petayot) is the feminine form of petiuth—naivety, openness, ingenuousness. The simple ones love their openness because it requires no effort, no reflection, no judgment. They are comfortable being swayed by persuasive voices like the sinners of verses 10-14. The scorners (letsim) are more actively resistant. They 'delight in their scorning' (latsah)—they mock and sneer at wisdom, taking pleasure in the ridicule itself. The Hebrew word latsah means not merely to laugh but to scoff, to mock with contempt, to treat seriously what deserves respect as if it were foolish. The scorners love their mockery; it gives them identity and power. The fools (kesilim) represent the third and darkest category: they 'hate knowledge' (sane'u da'at). Unlike the simple ones, who merely drift, and unlike the scorners, who actively resist, the fools are defined by an active, visceral rejection of knowledge itself. They do not merely ignore wisdom; they despise it.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The progression from petayim to letsim to kesilim represents a deepening of resistance. The simple ones might be turned if the right voice catches them; the scorners actively war against wisdom but might be shamed or corrected; the fools have moved beyond the reach of ordinary persuasion. They hate the very thing that would save them. Wisdom's lament asks how long she must call to those who are actively choosing against her. The verse suggests that this choosing is not momentary or accidental but habitual ('love,' 'delight,' 'hate'). The simple ones do not momentarily drift; they love drifting. The scorners do not casually mock; they delight in mockery. The fools do not occasionally reject knowledge; they hate it. Wisdom grieves not momentary lapses but settled dispositions.

word_study.meaning: How long, until when. This is the standard Hebrew formula for lament, the cry of one who suffers and awaits relief.
word_study.significance: The use of this lament formula identifies Wisdom's tone as one of pathos and suffering, not judgment. She grieves over her audience's choices. This frames wisdom-giving not as superior condescension but as compassionate plea.

word_study.meaning: The simple, the naive, the undirected. The word petaiuth (simplicity, naivety) does not necessarily imply moral failure but rather an openness to influence, an inability to distinguish between good and bad counsel, a lack of discernment.
word_study.significance: The simple ones are not malicious but dangerously vulnerable. They can be seduced (as in verses 10-14) or instructed. Their condition is remediable, but only if they cease to love their own simplicity and embrace the difficulty of discernment and wisdom.

word_study.meaning: Will love, will be enamored with, will delight in simplicity/naivety. The verb 'ahav (to love) suggests emotional attachment, not merely intellectual agreement.
word_study.significance: The simple ones do not accidentally remain simple; they cherish their simplicity. They love it as one loves a comfortable familiar thing. This explains why mere exposure to instruction is insufficient; they must first cease to love their own naivety and embrace the harder work of wisdom.

word_study.meaning: Scoffers, mockers, those who sneer and deride. The root latsah means to mock, to sneer, to treat with contempt and ridicule.
word_study.significance: The scorners represent a class of resistant fools—not weak but actively defiant. They have chosen rebellion and cloaked it in mockery. The scorner is dangerous because he has built an identity around resistance to wisdom and has recruited others to share in his mockery (Proverbs 29:8: 'Scornful men bring a city into a snare').

word_study.meaning: In scorning/mockery they delight, they take pleasure in it for themselves. The verb chamad (to delight, to desire, to take pleasure in) suggests that the scorners have made mockery itself into an end good, not merely a means of defense.
word_study.significance: This reveals the scorner's condition as worse than mere resistance; he has made rebellion into an identity and pleasure. He mocks wisdom not merely to defend himself but because he enjoys it. This makes him largely unreachable through ordinary argument.

word_study.meaning: Fools, those who lack sense or direction. The root kesil carries connotations of foolishness rooted in inattentiveness, lack of insight, or stubborn refusal to see.
word_study.significance: The fool (kesil) is distinguished from the simple one (peti) by his active hostility to wisdom. The fool does not merely drift; he resists. The fool is a recurring figure in Proverbs, often portrayed as someone who has hardened into folly, whose character has become set against wisdom.

word_study.meaning: Will hate, will despise knowledge. The verb sane'a (to hate) is a strong word suggesting active, visceral rejection, not mere indifference.
word_study.significance: The fools do not merely lack knowledge; they hate it. This suggests that their condition has progressed from simple ignorance to active antagonism. They have come to see knowledge itself as a threat. The phrase 'hate knowledge' appears again in Proverbs 1:29, where it describes those who deliberately reject Wisdom's call.

cross_references.connection: Wisdom declares, 'For that they hated knowledge, and did not choose the fear of the LORD.' This verse develops the category of those who hate knowledge, showing that such hatred is not accidental but a deliberate rejection rooted in refusal to fear the Lord.

The psalmist opens with the same lament formula: 'How long wilt thou forget me, O Lord? How long wilt thou hide thy face from me?' The parallel structure shows that Wisdom's lament echoes the language of divine complaint, identifying her as a voice of divine concern.

Proverbs teaches that 'Scornful men bring a city into a snare.' The scorners (letsim) introduced in this verse are shown throughout Proverbs to be corrosive to community. Their mockery spreads and hardens others in folly.

The text states, 'A scorner seeketh wisdom, and findeth it not: but knowledge is easy unto him that understandeth.' This shows that the scorner's mockery actually blinds him to the very wisdom he ridicules, making his condition self-perpetuating and tragic.

Christ laments over Jerusalem: 'O Jerusalem, Jerusalem...how often would I have gathered thy children together, and ye would not!' Like Wisdom's lament in Proverbs 1:22, Christ uses the language of grief and longing to address those who reject his call.

Amulek warns that 'if ye reject these things' (the words of Christ), 'a great and terrible day of judgment' awaits. Like Wisdom's three categories of resistance, Amulek addresses those at various stages of rebellion, from the undecided to the actively hardened.

commentary.historical_context: The three categories of fools—the simple, the scornful, and the obstinate—appear to reflect actual social types in ancient Israel and the broader ancient Near East. The 'simple ones' (petayim) may have included young people without patrons or formal education, vulnerable to seduction by criminals or false teachers. The 'scorners' (letsim) appear to have constituted a social class or faction—those who rejected traditional wisdom and mocked its authority. The 'fools' (kesilim) represented those who had so hardened in their folly that they were beyond ordinary reach. The use of the lament formula 'How long?' ties Wisdom's complaint to the language of prophetic complaint in the Psalms and the prophetic books, suggesting that the refusal of wisdom is not merely personal failure but a social and spiritual crisis. The intensity of Wisdom's opening suggests that by the time Proverbs was composed, the resistance to wisdom had become institutionalized and habitual—not a momentary temptation but a settled posture.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly describes the three categories of resistance that Proverbs identifies. In Alma 5, Alma addresses the Church and describes the 'fallen sons of the Church,' those who have become hardened in sin. In 2 Nephi 28, Nephi laments over those who say 'peace and safety' while ignoring the warnings of prophets—the equivalent of loving their simplicity while the scorners mock those who accept truth. The Book of Mormon's repeated use of the lament form ('O that I could weep') echoes Wisdom's opening in Proverbs 1:22.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: The Doctrine and Covenants contains multiple instances of the Lord's lament over those who reject truth. In D&C 29:2, the Lord expresses sorrow over the wickedness of the world. In D&C 43:17, the Lord tells Joseph Smith that the people are 'a wicked and perverse generation.' In D&C 112:1-2, the Lord laments that his servants are 'sometimes in the wrong' and need correction. The pattern of divine lament over resistance to wisdom and truth runs throughout the Restoration.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant requires the initiate to accept knowledge and covenants freely. The language of Wisdom's lament in Proverbs—addressing those who love their simplicity, delight in mockery, and hate knowledge—describes those who are spiritually unprepared for or resistant to the temple. The covenant space assumes a willingness to move from simplicity to understanding, a rejection of scoffing, and a love of truth. Those who enter with the disposition Wisdom laments cannot receive what the temple offers.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's lament over Jerusalem (Matthew 23:37) and his expression of grief over those who reject him (Luke 13:34) parallel Wisdom's opening lament. Christ addresses the three categories present in Jerusalem's leadership: those who have become simple in their understanding (the masses), those who have become scorners of his message (the Pharisees and scribes), and those who actively hate the truth (the chief priests). Christ's lamenting tone throughout the Gospels, particularly as he moves toward his crucifixion, reflects the same grief that Wisdom expresses over humanity's refusal to listen. The cross itself becomes an ultimate expression of Wisdom's cry: the ultimate love for those who hate knowledge, offered not to compel but to grieve and invite.
commentary.application: This verse demands honest self-examination. Which category do you inhabit? Are you simple, still vulnerable to seduction by half-truths or plausible lies? Are you a scorner, defending yourself through mockery of what you do not understand? Or have you hardened into active hatred of what you know would demand transformation? The verse's use of the lament form—Wisdom's grief—should itself be moving. Wisdom does not approach with condemnation or superiority but with the pathos of one who sees the tragedy unfolding. The question 'How long?' is not merely rhetorical; it invites response. How long will you love your own simplicity? How long will you take pleasure in mockery? How long will you reject the knowledge that could remake you? The verse suggests that these postures are chosen, habitual, loved. They are not accidental. Therefore, moving beyond them requires a deliberate choice to cease loving simplicity, to lay down mockery, and to choose knowledge even when it demands change. For those in leadership or teaching positions, this verse provides a model of how to address resistance: not with contempt but with genuine lament. Wisdom's opening tone—grief rather than anger—models how to call people to account while maintaining genuine love for their transformation.

text_kjv: Turn you at my reproof: behold, I will pour out my spirit unto you, I will make known my words unto you.

commentary.narrative: After the lament, Wisdom offers an astonishing turnaround. The offer is radical: if you will turn (shuvu, 'repent, return') at her reproof, she will pour out her spirit (ruach) upon you and make her words known to you. The condition is simple and clear—repentance—and the reward is nothing less than the gift of Wisdom's spirit and complete access to her counsel. The Hebrew verb shuv (to turn, to return) is the root of teshuvah, the Hebrew concept of repentance. Wisdom is offering not mere instruction but transformation. She will not simply teach the wise words she knows; she will pour out her spirit, making wisdom not an external commodity but an internalized reality. The abundance of the language—'I will pour out' (abi'ah, suggesting a gushing forth or a bubbling up) conveys that Wisdom's offering is not rationed or limited. She gives lavishly and without reserve to those who repent.
commentary.narrative_continued: This verse is the hinge point of Proverbs 1:8-33. The father warned of the path of greed and death (verses 8-19). Wisdom lamented over the resistant (verses 20-22). Now Wisdom opens the door to salvation through repentance. The verse does not promise that such repentance will be easy or that Wisdom will compromise her standards. The reproof (tokachah) must be accepted; Wisdom will not soften her critique. But if it is accepted, if the listener turns, then the relationship changes entirely from one of judgment to one of intimacy—Wisdom's spirit, Wisdom's words, become the listener's treasure. The structure here mirrors the Gospel pattern found throughout scripture: conviction of sin, call to repentance, and the offering of grace. Wisdom is not primarily a scold but an inviter, a lover of those who will turn.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The parallel structure of verse 23 is revealing: 'I will pour out my spirit unto you' matches with 'I will make known my words unto you.' Spirit and word are linked; they are not separate gifts. To receive Wisdom's spirit is to be able to understand and live by Wisdom's words. This echoes prophetic language throughout Scripture, where the Spirit of God enables the reception and living out of God's word. The promise is not that life will become easy—indeed, verse 24 will reveal what happens to those who reject this offer—but that those who repent will receive both the internal reality (spirit) and the external instruction (words) necessary for transformation. The offer is made to everyone addressed in verse 22: the simple ones, the scorners, and the fools. No one is excluded. The only requirement is turning.

word_study.meaning: Turn, turn back, return, repent. The verb shuv is the root of teshuvah (repentance), one of the central concepts in Jewish theology. It means not merely intellectual change but a turning around, a reorientation of direction and trajectory.
word_study.significance: The use of shuv instead of merely 'listen' or 'obey' emphasizes that what Wisdom requires is not compliance but conversion. The whole direction of life must change. This is repentance not as mere regret but as reorientation.

word_study.meaning: Reproof, rebuke, correction. The noun tokachah refers to the act of correcting or rebuking someone, often in the context of warning or admonition. It carries the sense of both critique and instruction.
word_study.significance: Wisdom's reproof is not arbitrary scolding but corrective guidance. To turn 'at' (or 'to') her reproof means to accept her correction as the pathway to transformation. The reproof is the medicine, not the poison.

word_study.meaning: I will pour out, I will cause to bubble forth, I will gush out. The verb naba means to bubble up or gush forth, suggesting abundance and vigor, not a measured dispensing.
word_study.significance: Wisdom does not dole out her spirit in rations. She pours it out in abundance, like water from a spring. The image conveys generosity, lavishness, and the inability to withhold—if one turns, Wisdom gives everything.

word_study.meaning: My spirit, my breath, my wind. The word ruach encompasses the animating principle of life, the breath or wind, the inner life or disposition, and in theological contexts, the Spirit of God or divine presence.
word_study.significance: Wisdom's offer to pour out her spirit is extraordinary. It claims that Wisdom herself has a spirit (ruach) that can be transmitted to those who repent. This reaches toward the personification of Wisdom as a quasi-divine figure, one whose very essence can indwell the repentant.

word_study.meaning: I will make known, I will inform, I will reveal. The verb yada (to know) in the hiphil form (odi'a, 'I will cause to know') emphasizes active revelation, not mere passive availability.
word_study.significance: Wisdom does not simply make her words available; she actively causes them to be known, to be understood, to penetrate and transform. The promise includes not only the words themselves but the capacity to understand them.

word_study.meaning: My words, my sayings, my utterances. The Hebrew devar encompasses both the word itself and its effect—a word is never merely linguistic in Hebrew thought; it carries power and consequence.
word_study.significance: Wisdom's words are not abstract principles but powerful utterances. To receive her words is to receive something that shapes reality and transforms the hearer. The gift of Wisdom's words is not merely informational but formative.

cross_references.connection: The Lord promises to 'pour out my spirit upon all flesh.' Wisdom's promise in Proverbs 1:23 echoes this pattern of divine grace—the pouring out of God's spirit is the ultimate gift, available to all who turn from their wickedness.
The Lord promises to give a new heart and a new spirit to those who return. Like Wisdom's offer in Proverbs 1:23, the transformation requires both inward renewal (spirit) and new capacity (heart).

The psalmist cries, 'Create in me a clean heart, O God...cast me not away from thy presence; take not thy holy spirit from me.' Like Wisdom's offer to pour out her spirit, the psalmist understands that the greatest gift is the presence and spirit of divine wisdom.

Christ cries out, 'If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink...out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.' The imagery of pouring out and abundance parallels Wisdom's promise in Proverbs 1:23.

The Lord tells Emma Smith that if she will keep his commandments, 'he will sustain her upon the throne of my kingdom.' Like Wisdom's promise, the Lord offers the outpouring of his spirit and the revelation of his words to those who turn and receive.

Alma teaches that if ye will 'nourish the word, yea, nourish the tree as it beginneth to grow...it will become a tree springing up unto life eternal.' Like Wisdom's promise of words made known, Alma describes how the word becomes internalized and transformative.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern context, the offer of a patron's spirit or presence was an extraordinary claim of intimacy and power. The pouring out of a deity's spirit was associated with ecstatic prophecy and divine empowerment (1 Samuel 10:6, 1 Samuel 19:20-24). By offering to pour out her spirit, Wisdom makes an offer comparable to divine favor. The historical context suggests that this verse was remarkable and even dangerous to those who understood the implications: Wisdom was claiming the capacity to transform not merely the intellect but the very inner being of those who received her. The reproof (tokachah) that Wisdom requires reflects the role of wisdom teachers in ancient Israel, who functioned as counselors and correctors, often in relationship to kings and princes.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly employs the pattern of Wisdom's offer in Proverbs 1:23. In Alma 32, Alma invites the poor who have been cast out to receive the word, promising that if they nurture it, 'it will become a tree springing up unto life eternal.' In 3 Nephi 9:13-14, Christ offers, 'Ye are the children of those prophets; and ye are of the house of Israel...come unto me, and I will heal you.' The pattern of repentance leading to the outpouring of spirit and the revelation of words runs throughout the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: The Doctrine and Covenants repeatedly employs the language of Proverbs 1:23. In D&C 21:4-5, the Lord promises that the Spirit will be given to guide the Church. In D&C 88:15-26, the Lord describes how his word is the power that governs all things and promises that 'the Spirit of the Lord is in all these things.' In D&C 76:10-12, the revelations are described as being given that 'ye may know the mysteries and peaceable things—that which bringeth joy, that which bringeth life eternal.' The Restoration affirms Wisdom's promise that turning and receiving leads to the outpouring of spirit and the knowledge of truth.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant is structured around the pattern of Wisdom's offer: the covenantee is brought through stages of instruction and covenant, leading to the receipt of the Patriarchal Blessing (the sealing). The receipt of the temple endowment parallels Wisdom's promise to 'pour out my spirit unto you; I will make known my words unto you.' The temple is the place where this transformation is enacted and promised. The turning required (repentance, worthiness) is the condition Wisdom names. The reception of the spirit and the words (the ordinances and their meaning) is the promise fulfilled.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ embodies and fulfills Wisdom's promise in Proverbs 1:23. In John 4:14, Christ promises living water that springs up unto eternal life. In John 16:12-14, Christ promises that the Spirit will come and 'guide you into all truth' and will 'take of mine, and shall shew it unto you.' Most directly, in Acts 2:38-39, Peter calls people to repent ('Turn you,' using language that echoes shuv in Hebrew), and promises that those who do will 'receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.' Christ's entire ministry is Wisdom made flesh, calling people to turn and receive the spirit and the truth. The promise in Proverbs 1:23 is fulfilled in the outpouring of the Holy Ghost at Pentecost and in the ongoing gift of the Spirit to all who repent and come unto Christ.
commentary.application: This verse is an invitation to examine whether you are in the condition Wisdom requires: willingness to turn. Repentance is not merely the regret of past sins; it is a fundamental reorientation of direction. Wisdom does not require that you have already arrived at wisdom but only that you turn toward it, that you accept her reproof, that you cease moving in the opposite direction. The verse's promise is that such turning is met with lavish generosity—Wisdom's spirit is poured out without ration or limit. For those struggling with the demands of discipleship, this verse offers hope: you do not need to manufacture the strength to change. Wisdom promises her spirit to sustain and transform you. For those who feel distant from God or from spiritual truth, this verse invites a concrete action: turn. Accept correction. Let Wisdom reprove you. And in that turning, expect the outpouring of her spirit and the revelation of her words to become real in your life. The promise is not that life becomes easy but that you are no longer alone in it, and that you receive the wisdom needed to navigate it well.

text_kjv: Because I have called, and ye refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded;

commentary.narrative: The tone shifts dramatically again. After Wisdom's offer of grace in verse 23, verse 24 introduces the alternative: the consequences of refusal. Wisdom moves to past tense—'I have called, and ye refused.' This is not a single moment but a pattern. Wisdom has been calling, and the people have been refusing, repeatedly. The phrase 'I have stretched out my hand' (natiti yadi) is a gesture of offering, even pleading—imagine a hand outstretched in appeal, in invitation, in compassion. Yet 'no man regarded' (ve'ein maqshiv)—no one paid attention. The word maqshiv (from qashav, 'to listen, to hear attentively, to heed') is precise: it is not that the call was not heard but that it was not heeded, not taken seriously, not responded to. The people heard but refused to listen, in the deepest sense. They heard the sound but refused to accept the message, to be changed by it, to respond to it.
commentary.narrative_continued: This verse reveals a tragic pattern: Wisdom has been persistent in her calling, has made herself accessible (verse 20-21), has even offered lavish grace (verse 23), yet the people have consistently refused. The refusal is not intellectual disagreement but a settled disposition of non-responsiveness. They have heard but would not heed. This context makes clear what Wisdom's next words will be (verses 25-31): she will cease to offer, and when disaster comes, she will not answer. The verses pivot on the principle of correspondence—those who refuse Wisdom's call will find that Wisdom refuses their desperate cry for help. It is not punishment imposed from outside but the natural consequence of a relationship refused. If you will not hear Wisdom when she calls, Wisdom will not hear you when you call.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The structure of verses 23-24 is theologically profound. Wisdom does not move directly from grace to judgment. Between them stands a historical reality: 'Because I have called.' The judgment in verses 25-31 is not arbitrary or unexpected; it is the natural outcome of a long pattern of refusal. Wisdom has called; people have refused. Wisdom is describing not a momentary invitation but a history of relationship—of calling and resistance. The use of the past tense ('I have called, and ye refused') suggests that we are already in a condition of accumulated refusals. The final offer in verse 23 is thus more urgent—it may be the last call, the last chance to turn before Wisdom ceases to call at all. The young man to whom the father was speaking (verse 8) is being warned: Wisdom has been calling to your generation, and many have refused. Do not join them. Do not accumulate more refusals.

word_study.meaning: I have called, I have summoned, I have cried out. The verb qara (to call, to summon, to cry out) is used throughout Scripture for divine calling—the calling of prophets, the calling of nations, the calling to repentance.
word_study.significance: Wisdom uses the same language applied to God's calling. She has been summoning the people as God summons, with urgency and authority. The refusal of Wisdom's call is thus equivalent to the refusal of God's call.

word_study.meaning: And you refused, and you rejected, and you were unwilling. The verb ma'an means to refuse, to reject, to be unwilling to do something. It carries the sense of deliberate rejection, not mere accident.
word_study.significance: The refusal is not passive or accidental. It is active and deliberate. The people did not merely fail to hear; they refused to accept Wisdom's call. This deliberate quality makes the refusal a moral choice.

word_study.meaning: I have stretched out, I have extended my hand. The phrase depicts a gesture of reaching out, offering, pleading, or beckoning.
word_study.significance: The hand stretched out is a gesture of intimacy and invitation. It suggests that Wisdom has not remained distant or neutral but has actively reached toward the people, made herself available, and beckoned them to turn. The image is one of compassion, not threat.

word_study.term_english: no man regarded / no one paid attention
word_study.meaning: And there is no one paying attention, no one listening carefully, no one heeding. The noun maqshiv (or participial form) derives from qashav, which means to listen carefully, to pay attention, to heed attentively.
word_study.significance: The distinction between hearing and heeding is crucial. The people may have heard the sound of Wisdom's call, but none paid careful, attentive, obedient attention to it. Heeding is not passive reception but active turning toward and responsive action. The refusal of maqshiv is the refusal to take seriously, to respond, to change in light of the call.

cross_references.connection: Wisdom promises, 'Then shall they call upon me, but I will not answer; they shall seek me early, but they shall not find me.' This verse (24) sets up that consequence: because they have refused Wisdom's call, Wisdom will refuse their call.

The Lord says, 'I have spread out my hands all the day unto a rebellious people...that say, Stand by thyself.' Isaiah uses the same language of stretched-out hands and refused calling, applied to God's relationship with Israel.

The Lord tells Jeremiah, 'Since ye did all these works...I spake unto you, rising up early and speaking, but ye heard not.' The pattern of calling and refusal, which Wisdom describes, is a pattern throughout the prophetic corpus.

Christ laments, 'How often would I have gathered thy children together...and ye would not!' Christ echoes both Wisdom's call and the people's refusal, using the same pattern from Proverbs and the prophets.

The Lord tells Joseph Smith that the people 'hear not thy voice' and do not heed the Lord's words spoken through his servants. The pattern of Wisdom's calling and humanity's refusal is reaffirmed in the Restoration.

Alma teaches that 'it is given unto many to know the mysteries of God...yet there are many that do not believe...therefore they must needs remain under condemnation.' Like Wisdom in Proverbs, Alma describes the tragedy of those who have access to truth but refuse to embrace it.

commentary.historical_context: The image of Wisdom stretching out her hand echoes ancient Near Eastern depictions of deities offering favor and blessing to worshippers. The refusal to heed or regard such an offer was understood as a profound rejection, one that would bring about its own consequences. In the historical context of ancient Israel, this verse likely reflects the experience of the prophetic tradition—the repeated cycle of prophetic calling and national refusal that characterizes much of Israel's history. The prophets called; the people refused. The cycles of judgment and restoration in the history of Israel can be seen as the outworking of this pattern. The verse suggests that by the time Proverbs was composed, this pattern had become recognized and tragic—Wisdom's calling had become a historical reality repeatedly ignored.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon powerfully depicts the pattern of Wisdom's calling and human refusal. In Alma 8-10, Alma travels throughout the cities preaching, facing refusal and rejection at nearly every turn. In Helaman 13-14, Samuel the Lamanite cries from the wall, calling Zarahemla to repentance while the people refuse and mock. The pattern of verse 24—repeated calling and repeated refusal—is woven throughout the Book of Mormon, culminating in the destruction of the Nephite nation. The Book of Mormon thus validates and illustrates the pattern Wisdom describes.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: The Doctrine and Covenants repeatedly affirms that the Lord has been calling to humanity and that much of humanity has refused. In D&C 39:15-16, the Lord tells Joseph Smith that he has been 'speaking these things to the inhabitants of the earth' but 'they receive them not, for they perceive not the light.' In D&C 88:33, the Lord teaches that 'he that hath ears to hear, let him hear,' implying that many have ears but will not hear. The pattern of calling and refusal is central to the Restoration's understanding of human agency and divine patience.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant requires readiness to hear and heed the voice of the Lord. Those who enter the temple do so having already turned toward Wisdom's call; they have heard and heeded. The temple ordinances can be understood as Wisdom's final gift to those who have responded to her call. Those who refuse to turn, who refuse to enter the temple, remain outside the full promise. The temple thus enacts the reality described in Proverbs 1: those who turn receive Wisdom's spirit and words; those who refuse receive nothing.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's entire incarnate ministry is captured in the pattern of Proverbs 1:24. He called the disciples; they were slow to understand. He called the Pharisees; they refused and plotted his death. He called Jerusalem; Jerusalem rejected him. His lament in Matthew 23:37 ('How often would I have gathered thy children...and ye would not') is the direct echo of Wisdom's lament. Yet Christ's response to refusal was not to withdraw his love but to pour it out on the cross itself. In that sense, Christ exceeds even Wisdom's promise: he continues to stretch out his hand even toward those who crucify him, offering forgiveness even to those who refuse. Yet the offer remains—it can still be refused, still be refused eternally. The refusal to respond to Christ's call leads to the same consequence Wisdom warns of: the voice that was offered will not hear your cry in the day of trouble.
commentary.application: This verse is a sobering reminder that Wisdom's patience, while immense, is not infinite. The call to repentance is not a single invitation but an ongoing one; yet there may come a time when the call ceases, when Wisdom withdraws her persistent calling, when the opportunity passes. The verse warns against the assumption that there will always be another chance to turn. The Hebrew phrase 'I have called, and ye refused' suggests a history of choices that creates a trajectory. Each refusal makes the next refusal more likely; each time you do not heed Wisdom's call, you become more accustomed to not heeding. For those who feel that they have heard Wisdom's call but have not yet responded, this verse suggests urgency. For those who teach or preach, this verse cautions against despair when people refuse. You are echoing the pattern of Wisdom herself—calling, stretching out your hand—and the refusal is ultimately theirs to make. But do not stop calling while there is still breath, because you do not know when the moment of final refusal has arrived. For all of us, this verse should make us ask: Am I heeding Wisdom's call today? Or am I adding to the long history of refusals? The hand is still stretched out. The call is still being made. The question is whether I will regard it, pay attention to it, turn in response to it.

text_kjv: But ye have set at nought all my counsel, and would none of my reproof:

commentary.narrative: Wisdom now turns from pleading to accusation. The Hebrew verb tifre'u ('you let loose, you neglected') carries weight beyond simple rejection—it means to release, to let slip away, to abandon restraint. The Covenant Rendering captures this: 'you ignored all my counsel.' This is not passive disinterest but active negligence, a deliberate unclenching of the hands that once held truth. The parallel phrase 'would none of my reproof' uses the Hebrew lo' avitern ('you did not accept, you refused')—reproof (tokhachat) is not punishment but correction, the loving redirection that a teacher offers to a student who has strayed. The fools in this passage have rejected both the positive guidance (counsel) and the negative correction (reproof). They have rejected the entire educational apparatus of wisdom.

word_study.meaning: you let loose, you released, you neglected, you abandoned restraint. The root is parua', used of Pharaoh 'letting go' Israel (Exodus 5:4). The sense is not of passive indifference but of active release—as if holding something precious and then, deliberately, letting it drop.
word_study.significance: This verb choice reveals that the fools did not stumble into error; they made a choice to release what they were holding. Wisdom's counsel was within their grasp, but they unclenched their fists.

word_study.meaning: correction, reproof, rebuke, argument. The root is yakach, 'to prove, to convince, to rebuke.' Tokhachat is the corrective word spoken to bring someone back to understanding.
word_study.significance: In LDS theology, reproof is covenant language—Doctrine and Covenants 121:43 teaches that reproof must be given 'by the power of the Holy Ghost' and followed by 'show forth afterwards an increase of love.' Wisdom's reproof is not meant to humiliate but to redirect.

cross_references.connection: The Lord's instruction on reproof echoes Wisdom's offer: reproof must be accompanied by love and increase of love afterward—precisely what Wisdom extends to those who listen.
Earlier in the same passage, Wisdom offers 'Turn you at my reproof'—reproof is presented as redemptive, an invitation to turn around, which the fools now refuse.
The covenant language of rejecting counsel appears in Israel's history—a people who receive counsel but refuse to follow it face exile and loss.
The Book of Mormon describes those who 'would not receive the word of God' and the spiritual consequences—a parallel to Proverbs' depiction of those who reject wisdom's counsel.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern wisdom literature, the teacher-student relationship was sacred. The refusal of reproof was not a minor offense but a fundamental breakdown of the covenant between teacher and learner. In the context of ancient Israel, wisdom teachers (often scribes and elders) functioned as transmitters of divine understanding. To refuse their counsel was to refuse, by extension, the counsel of God himself. The verb tifre'u, used of Pharaoh letting Israel go, carries an ironic resonance: just as Pharaoh 'released' Israel, these fools 'release' or 'let go' of wisdom—they become enslaved not to Pharaoh but to their own folly.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon frequently employs this pattern of rejecting prophetic counsel. Nephi's family refuses his reproof (1 Nephi 2:12-13); Laman and Lemuel consistently reject instruction. Alma describes the Zoramites' active rejection of God's word, using language similar to Proverbs 1:25—they 'despise the word of God' (Alma 31:8). The pattern is consistent: rejection is not passive but active, deliberate, and ultimately self-destructive.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:14 warns that those who 'set at naught' the counsels of God will be judged. The phrasing echoes the KJV of this verse ('set at nought'), suggesting that the counsel rejected in Proverbs 1:25 is ultimately God's counsel speaking through wisdom.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The covenant of learning and obedience is central to temple worship. Just as the endowment teaches correct principles and invites covenant members to receive and follow them, Wisdom invites—and is rejected. The pattern prefigures the temple's presentation of divine truth and the individual's free choice to accept or reject.

commentary.christological_typology: Wisdom (Chokmah) in Proverbs is closely associated with Christ—both in patristic interpretation and in Latter-day Saint understanding of Jehovah as the source of wisdom before his mortal ministry. Christ's repeated offers of truth to Jerusalem echo Wisdom's plea here; his warning that 'you would not' echoes this refusal (Matthew 23:37). The rejection of Wisdom prefigures the rejection of the Christ.
commentary.application: Modern readers face the same choice: Do we actively release the counsel we have received—from scripture, from living prophets, from the still small voice—by refusing to let it shape our lives? The verb tifre'u suggests that we can hold truth in our hands and then, deliberately, let it fall. The real question is not whether we have access to wisdom but whether we will unclinch our fists and hold it fast.

text_kjv: I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when your fear cometh;

commentary.narrative: This verse is among the most difficult in wisdom literature, and for good reason. Wisdom, who has pleaded, does not now remain silent; she speaks again, but now her words are words of judgment, not mercy. The Hebrew verb eshchaq (I will laugh) and el'ag (I will mock) describe an action that mirrors exactly what the fools have done to Wisdom. They mocked her counsel; now she mocks their calamity. This is not the cruelty of a superior being enjoying another's suffering; it is the inexorable logic of cause and effect. The fools thought they were wise in their mockery; they did not realize they were mocking the very source of life and safety. The reversal is complete: the one they dismissed will not be there to help when they need help most. The Hebrew word for 'calamity' (eidchem, 'your disaster') is not accidental suffering but the natural result of spurning wisdom. And their 'fear' (pachdem) is not yet the calamity itself but the dread that precedes it—the growing awareness that they have made a terrible mistake.

word_study.meaning: I will laugh, I will deride, I will find amusement in. The root is sachaq, which can mean laughter of joy or laughter of scorn, depending on context.
word_study.significance: The context makes clear that this is derision, not joy. Wisdom's laughter is the opposite of the 'laughter' that sin sometimes offers in the short term (Proverbs 14:13 notes that 'the end of that mirth is heaviness'). This is laughter that comes only when the reckoning arrives.

word_study.meaning: I will mock, I will jeer, I will treat with contempt. The root is la'ag, and the sense is deliberate derision.
word_study.significance: The parallelism between eshchaq (I will laugh) and el'ag (I will mock) is exact—two words for the same reality: scorn. Wisdom promises not silence but active, present derision. The fools scorned her; she will scorn them.

word_study.meaning: disaster, calamity, sudden trouble. The word implies not gradual decline but sudden, overwhelming ruin.
word_study.significance: This is not natural consequence playing out slowly; it is calamity arriving suddenly, like the storm imagery that follows in verse 27. The fools will not have time to adjust or prepare.

cross_references.connection: Wisdom promises 'I love them that love me'—the inverse of this verse. Love is met with love; rejection is met with abandonment.

Christ says 'how often would I have gathered thy children together...and ye would not.' Like Wisdom, Christ offers mercy and is refused; unlike Wisdom here, Christ does not promise to mock but to weep.
'He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision.' God's laughter at those who reject his counsel is presented as the response of divine power to human foolishness.

Alma describes the Nephites' rejection of the prophets and the resulting calamity, suggesting that the refusal to hear carries inherent consequences—the mockers will find themselves mocked by their own ruin.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern literature, the reversal of fortune was understood as a cosmic principle. The Babylonian Ludlul Bel Nemeqi describes a righteous man's suffering followed by restoration; Egyptian wisdom literature frequently depicts the fool receiving 'the wages of folly.' This verse fits within that tradition: mockery of wisdom is not a victimless act; it invokes a response from the order of the cosmos. To mock Wisdom is to mock the principle of order itself, and order will reassert itself—against you. The personification of Wisdom as a feminine figure (chokmah in Hebrew is feminine) adds another layer: she is not abstract principle but a living, responding presence.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records multiple instances of Wisdom's judgment falling on mockers. The Nephites mock Nephi and are delivered to their enemies; Korihor mocks God and loses his ability to speak; the Zoramites mock Alma and are delivered to destruction. The pattern is consistent with Proverbs 1:26—the mockers are met not with continued patience but with the consequences of their own choice.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 63:32-34 warns that those who mock God's covenants will 'surely die' in their sins. The principle is that mockery of divine truth has an inherent cost. Wisdom's laughter in this verse is the principle itself responding to contempt.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that rejection of light has consequences. The progression of Proverbs 1:25-32 (rejection followed by judgment) mirrors the temple's teaching on covenants: accept and live, reject and face judgment. Wisdom's withholding of herself is the natural consequence of being refused.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is Wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30 in NT; also D&C 93:11 associates Christ with 'light and truth'). His promise to 'gather thy children together' is refused, and the consequence—for Jerusalem, and for all humanity—is judgment. Yet Christ's judgment is ultimately redemptive, not merely punitive. Where Wisdom's mockery in this verse is final derision, Christ's judgment includes the possibility of repentance and return. The difference illuminates both passages: Wisdom speaks of the logic of rejection; Christ embodies the possibility of redemption even within judgment.
commentary.application: This verse teaches a hard truth: God's grace is not infinite in the sense of being infinitely patient without response. Rejection has consequences. Mockery of truth does not go unnoticed by the universe itself. For modern readers, the question is whether we truly understand the weight of our choices when we dismiss or mock the counsel we have received—whether from scripture, from the Spirit, from parents, or from prophets. The laughter of Wisdom is not the end of the story if we repent, but it is the end of the line for those who refuse to turn.

text_kjv: When your fear cometh as desolation, and your destruction cometh as a whirlwind; when distress and anguish cometh upon you.

commentary.narrative: The verse shifts from Wisdom's response to a description of what the fools will face. The imagery is violent and overwhelming: fear arrives as desolation (sho'ah), a word that can mean both spiritual waste and physical devastation; destruction arrives as a whirlwind (sufah), sudden and irresistible. The pairing is intentional—desolation and whirlwind suggest both that the calamity is total (covering all ground, all space) and that it is sudden (there is no time to prepare or escape). The phrase 'distress and anguish' (tsarah ve-tsuqah) is a Hebrew rhyming pair that underscores the completeness of the suffering. This is not merely one problem but a comprehensive assault of troubles. The Hebrew conveys that the fools will be caught in a kind of storm—not a localized affliction but an overwhelming system of consequences. What makes this verse particularly penetrating is the progression: first, fear itself comes (their dread arrives); then, that fear is followed by the very thing they feared. The anticipation of calamity is itself part of the calamity.

word_study.meaning: desolation, devastation, storm, destruction. The word appears in descriptions of divine judgment and overwhelming loss.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering uses 'storm' to capture the sense that desolation is not static but active, moving, overwhelming. It is not the quiet absence of something but the violent presence of destruction.

word_study.meaning: whirlwind, tempest, storm. The word evokes sudden, irresistible force that sweeps away everything in its path.
word_study.significance: In biblical imagery, the whirlwind is often the vehicle of divine judgment (Nahum 1:3; Zechariah 9:14). Wisdom's judgment is not delivered slowly but arrives with the force of nature itself—sudden, overwhelming, impossible to resist.

word_study.meaning: distress, trouble, straits, narrowness. The root conveys the sense of being hemmed in, with no way out.
word_study.significance: Tsarah is external pressure that constrains and confines. Combined with tsuqah (anguish, which involves inner pressure and constriction), the two together suggest being crushed from without and within simultaneously.

word_study.meaning: anguish, constraint, distress. The root is related to tsuq, meaning 'to press, to narrow.' The sense is of being squeezed, confined, unable to breathe.
word_study.significance: Where tsarah is external, tsuqah is internal—the sense of suffocation, of being pressed in. Together, tsarah ve-tsuqah describes total affliction: no room to escape outside, no room to breathe inside.

cross_references.connection: The whirlwind appears again: 'When the whirlwind passeth, the wicked is no more: but the righteous is an everlasting foundation.' This verse clarifies that the whirlwind of judgment destroys the wicked while the righteous endure.

The whirlwind is described as God's instrument of judgment and power: 'Out of the south cometh the whirlwind...by the breath of God frost is given.' The storm imagery in Proverbs 1:27 draws on this tradition of divine power acting through nature.

The Lord describes the coming of his judgment: 'the wicked...shall be as stubble...in the day that I shall come in my glory.' The idea that judgment arrives suddenly and completely, like a storm or whirlwind, is consistent with Restoration teaching.
Ammon describes how the Spirit 'swelleth my soul' and compares it to being filled with power; the opposite—being overwhelmed by calamity—involves a similar totality of experience, as in this verse.
The psalmist asks God to pursue the wicked 'with thy whirlwind, and terrify them with thy storm.' The whirlwind as an instrument of divine judgment is a recurrent biblical image.

commentary.historical_context: Storm imagery in ancient Near Eastern literature frequently represents divine judgment. The Ugaritic texts depict Baal as a storm god; Egyptian texts describe pharaonic judgment using water and storm metaphors. In biblical literature, the whirlwind is associated with theophanies—direct appearances of divine power. Job 38-41 presents the whirlwind as the context of God's speaking to Job about divine power and wisdom. Against this background, Proverbs 1:27 presents the judgment on the fools as a natural and cosmic event: they will be caught in forces beyond their control or comprehension, much like the fools in the book of Job who fail to understand the whirlwind's significance.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon frequently describes calamity arriving suddenly and completely. The destruction of the Jaredites comes with overwhelming swiftness (Ether 15:32-34); Nephi describes the Nephites' destruction as following the pattern of one calamity after another (2 Nephi 26:6). The pattern in Proverbs—rejection followed by mounting, overwhelming consequences—is reflected throughout the Book of Mormon's narrative.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 109:29 speaks of the Lord gathering his people away from calamity. The inverse is Proverbs 1:27—those who reject Wisdom are not gathered away but caught in the flood. D&C 45:26-27 describes the coming of the Son of Man and the upheaval of nature; the imagery is similar to the whirlwind in Proverbs.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony includes warnings and conditions. Those who reject the covenants offered are said to have brought consequences upon themselves. The swift, overwhelming nature of those consequences is reflected in the storm imagery of this verse.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the source of Wisdom (Colossians 2:3 in NT; D&C 93:11). His warnings about judgment are similarly structured: rejection of truth has consequences that arrive like a storm. In Matthew 24:37-39, Christ describes the sudden arrival of judgment in the days of Noah, when the flood came 'and took them all away.' The suddenness of the whirlwind in Proverbs 1:27 prefigures the sudden judgments Christ warns about.
commentary.application: Modern readers often assume they have unlimited time to change course. This verse teaches otherwise. The storm of consequences may seem distant until it arrives suddenly and completely. The practical question is not 'When will calamity come?' but 'Why am I waiting to turn? What am I waiting for?' The verse's urgency is meant to prompt not fear but action—to accept Wisdom's counsel now, while there is still time to listen.

text_kjv: Then shall they call upon me, but I will not answer; they shall seek me early, but they shall not find me:

commentary.narrative: This verse presents the most devastating consequence of all: when the fools finally turn to Wisdom in desperation, Wisdom will not answer. The Hebrew verbs yiqra'uneni (they will call upon me) and yeshacharuneni (they will seek me urgently, diligently) employ language typically reserved for prayer and the seeking of God. The verb shachar is particularly loaded—it means to seek early, at dawn, with urgency and devotion. In other contexts, it describes how a person in distress seeks God (Psalm 63:1: 'My soul thirsteth for thee...my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is'). Yet despite this urgent seeking—even at the cost of desperation and sleeplessness—Wisdom will not be found. This is not because Wisdom has moved or hidden; it is because the fools have already made their choice. Wisdom's silence is not cruelty but the inevitable consequence of rejection. The fools tried to live without Wisdom's guidance; now they will attempt to live without Wisdom's assistance. The verse teaches a sobering truth: there is a point beyond which rejection becomes irrevocable. Not because Wisdom arbitrarily withdraws, but because the spiritual and moral reality of the universe has been established by their own choices.

word_study.meaning: they will call upon, they will invoke, they will cry out to. The root is qara', and the sense is direct address, invocation, calling by name.
word_study.significance: Qara' is the word used throughout Scripture for calling upon God in prayer (e.g., Psalm 4:1; Genesis 12:8). The fools use the language of prayer to address Wisdom, but prayer requires a prior relationship of trust. Having spurned that relationship, their calling goes unanswered.

word_study.meaning: they will seek me urgently, diligently, at dawn. The root shachar means to seek early, to seek with devotion, to seek at the first light of day.
word_study.significance: In biblical language, seeking Wisdom or God at dawn (at the earliest hour) represents total devotion and desperation. Psalm 63:1 uses this verb to describe the psalmist's urgent seeking of God. The fact that even this devoted seeking will be fruitless makes the tragedy complete: desperation and urgency will not reverse a decision already made.

cross_references.connection: The cycle is complete: Wisdom called (verse 24), the fools refused (verse 25), now they call but Wisdom refuses. The rejection is symmetrical and absolute.

God says to Israel, 'when ye spread forth your hands, I will hide mine eyes from you: yea, when ye make many prayers, I will not hear.' The principle is the same: persistent rejection of God's ways leads to God's refusal to hear.
The Lord tells Jeremiah that He will not listen to the prayers of Judah because they have forsaken Him. 'Though they cry unto me, I will not hearken unto them.'

By contrast, the righteous seeks the Lord and is heard: 'Hear, O LORD, when I cry with my voice...Thou hast said, Seek ye my face; my heart said unto thee, Thy face, LORD, will I seek.' The faithful seeker is promised that seeking will be rewarded.

Mormon describes how the Nephites called upon the Lord but found no answer, because their wickedness had separated them from Him. The principle of rejection followed by divine silence is consistent across Restoration scriptures.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient wisdom pedagogy, the teacher-student relationship involved a specific progression: the teacher calls, the student responds, and understanding follows. To refuse the teacher's call was to break that covenant of learning. The reversal in this verse—the student now calls but the teacher does not answer—represents the dissolution of that covenant. In the ancient Near Eastern legal and social context, covenants were not infinitely patient; there was a limit to how many times an oath could be broken before consequences became irreversible. Proverbs 1:28 reflects this understanding: rejection has a point of no return.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 40:13-14 describes the separation of the spirits after death, suggesting that choices made in life determine the state of the soul. The fools who rejected Wisdom in life will find that their seeking in extremity comes too late. The Book of Mormon's depiction of Nephite destruction—the point at which prayers go unanswered—parallels this verse exactly.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 112:24-26 warns against taking the Holy Ghost for granted: 'It is not meet for me to command in all things; for he that is compelled in all things, the same is a slothful and not a wise servant.' The principle is that those who continually reject guidance will eventually find that guidance withdrawn. D&C 63:32 similarly warns that those who mock covenants will find themselves 'denied' access to the blessings they scorned.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony presents conditions: those who enter into covenants are promised divine help, but those who break covenants may find themselves separated from that help. The silence that Wisdom imposes on the fools in this verse mirrors the consequence of broken covenants.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ presents this principle in Matthew 25:1-13 (the parable of the ten virgins) and Matthew 7:22-23 ('Depart from me, I never knew you'). In the latter passage, those who cry 'Lord, Lord' find their pleas rejected because they never truly accepted the conditions of discipleship. Wisdom's refusal to answer in Proverbs 1:28 prefigures Christ's final refusal to hear those who reject Him until it is too late. Yet Christ's mercy offers a final invitation; Wisdom's silence in this verse is presented as final.
commentary.application: The verse presents a deeply uncomfortable question: Is it possible to wait too long? Is there a point at which turning back becomes impossible not because God is cruel but because we have shaped ourselves into a form that cannot turn back? Modern readers facing this verse should take it as urgent counsel: Do not assume that desperation will create an opening for repentance. The time to listen is now. The fools discovered too late that calling upon Wisdom without having accepted Wisdom's counsel is a prayer that goes unanswered. The application is immediate: accept counsel now, while it is being offered.

text_kjv: For that they hated knowledge, and did not choose the fear of the LORD:

commentary.narrative: This verse provides the explanation for everything that precedes it: Why does Wisdom laugh? Why do the fools face the whirlwind? Why does Wisdom not answer when they call? Because they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the Lord. The verse contains two parallel assertions that explain the root of all spiritual failure. First, 'they hated knowledge'—not merely that they were ignorant or foolish, but that they actively hated what they encountered. The Hebrew verb sanu ('hated') suggests not neutral disinterest but active hostility toward truth. Second, 'they did not choose the fear of the LORD.' The verb bachar ('to choose, to select') is critical. The fear of the Lord is not an emotion that happens to you; it is a decision you make. It is a choice. The fools did not choose it. This diagnosis reveals the heart of the matter: the fools' problem was not intellectual but volitional. They had the capacity to understand; they simply would not. They had the opportunity to reverence God; they simply chose against it. The verse thus moves from consequences (verses 26-28) to cause (verse 29). Understanding this order is crucial: the fools are not the victims of circumstances but the architects of their own ruin.

word_study.meaning: they hated, they despised, they actively rejected with enmity. The root sane' conveys not mere dislike but active hostility.
word_study.significance: Hatred is a choice, a stance, a decision to regard something as an enemy. By using sanu rather than a word for mere ignorance or indifference, the text establishes that the fools' problem was not lack of access to knowledge but active opposition to it. They saw Wisdom coming and they hated it.

word_study.meaning: knowledge, understanding, discernment. In the Hebrew wisdom tradition, da'at is not merely intellectual knowledge but intimate, experiential understanding—knowing something or someone deeply.
word_study.significance: The fools did not hate information; they hated intimate understanding of God and reality. They hated the kind of knowledge that changes you, that demands something of you, that orients your entire life toward truth.

word_study.meaning: they chose, they selected, they preferred. The root bachar means to actively select, to prefer one thing over another.
word_study.significance: This verb makes clear that 'the fear of the Lord' is not a matter of circumstance or accident; it is a choice. The fools had the capacity to choose reverence but actively chose against it. They preferred their own way.

word_study.meaning: the fear of the Lord, reverence before God, the deep respect and awe that comes from understanding God's nature and power. It is both emotional and volitional—something felt and something chosen.
word_study.significance: In the wisdom literature, yirat Yahweh is 'the beginning of wisdom' (Proverbs 1:7; 9:10). It is the foundational posture toward reality: recognizing that there is someone—God—who is greater than yourself, whose judgment matters, whose character defines righteousness. To not choose it is to refuse the very foundation upon which all wisdom rests.

cross_references.connection: The earlier verse states, 'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.' To hate knowledge and refuse the fear of the Lord is to refuse the very foundation on which Proverbs itself is built.

Wisdom says, 'For whoso findeth me findeth life...But he that sinneth against me wrongeth his own soul: all they that hate me love death.' The fools' hatred of knowledge is presented as equivalent to hating Wisdom itself, which is equivalent to loving death.

In the New Testament, Christ describes those who 'hate the light'—who refuse to come to it because their deeds are evil. The pattern is identical: active rejection of truth, rooted in the will's resistance to what truth demands.
The Lord states that Zion is that place where 'the pure in heart' dwell—those who have chosen to reverence God and align their wills with His. The inverse of Proverbs 1:29 is the covenant principle.

The converted Lamanites describe their previous state: they 'hated the light' and 'rejected every word of God.' This is the condition Proverbs 1:29 diagnoses—not ignorance but active hatred of what is true.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern wisdom tradition, the fear of the god (or gods) was the foundational posture. Egyptian wisdom texts consistently emphasize that the proper approach to the gods begins with fear and reverence. To refuse this was to position oneself outside the moral and cosmic order. In ancient Israel, yirat Yahweh ('the fear of the Lord') was not a minority position or one option among many; it was the assumed framework within which all life was understood. To refuse it was to refuse the entire covenantal reality that structured Israelite society and religion.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly describes those who 'hated the word of God' or 'rejected the word of God.' Alma 24:8 describes the Anti-Nephi-Lehies' previous state: 'we were taught to hate them, and to murder them, and to rob and to plunder them.' The parallel structure (hatred as the root of all wickedness) is consistent. Similarly, Alma 31:8 describes the Zoramites who 'despise the word of God'—active rejection rooted in a volitional choice.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 93:39 teaches that 'the glory of God is intelligence, or, in other words, light and truth.' To hate knowledge is to refuse the very means by which God manifests glory. D&C 10:5 warns against those who 'will not hear my voice'—the refusal to choose the fear of the Lord is the refusal to hear God.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony requires covenant-makers to accept certain truths and commit to certain principles. To refuse (as Proverbs 1:29 describes) is to refuse to enter into covenant with God. The choice is always available; the consequences of refusal are also always present.
