Do you take genuine delight in righteousness and truth, or have you begun to find entertainment and satisfaction in compromise, gossip, cynicism, or criticism? The wicked of Proverbs are warned not because they commit occasional sins but because they have reorganized their emotional and spiritual lives around perversion. The safeguard is to deliberately cultivate joy in wisdom, in God's word, in covenantal living — to make rightness feel like home, not like obligation.

text_kjv: Whose ways are crooked, and they froward in their paths:

commentary.narrative: Verse 15 returns to the navigational metaphor to describe the external consequences of the wicked person's inverted values. The contrast with verse 13 is now complete: where verse 13 described the abandonment of 'paths of uprightness' (yosher), verse 15 describes paths that are 'crooked' (iqqeshim) and ways where they 'are devious' (nelozim). The image is of someone who has not simply taken a wrong turn but who actively bends and twists as they go, unable to walk straight, perpetually turning aside. This is not a geographical description alone but a portrait of moral chaos — the wicked have so thoroughly rejected truth that they cannot maintain any consistent path. They live in permanent crookedness. The double description (crooked paths + devious ways) emphasizes that there is no straight way left in their lives; the entire trajectory has been bent.

word_study.meaning: Crooked, twisted, perverse. The opposite of yosher (straight). Can refer literally to a crooked path or metaphorically to a crooked person or crooked morality.
word_study.significance: Iqqesh is the visual opposite of uprightness — it evokes something bent out of shape, something that cannot fulfill its intended function. A crooked path cannot lead to its destination.

word_study.meaning: They are devious, they turn aside, they wander from. From a root suggesting perpetual deflection. Implies habitual deviation, not a one-time wrong turn.
word_study.significance: Nelozim captures the active, ongoing nature of the wicked's crookedness. They are not merely on a crooked path; they are actively twisting, constantly turning aside from any straight course.

cross_references.connection: Keep sound wisdom and discretion; so shall they be life unto thy soul. The righteous maintain a straight course because they hold to wisdom; the wicked abandon it and become crooked.
As for those that turn aside unto their crooked ways, the Lord shall lead them forth with the workers of iniquity. The Psalms confirm that crookedness and iniquity walk together.
The wicked walk in crooked ways and fall short of the glory of God. The New Testament applies the same metaphor of crooked versus straight to the Christian path.

Describing the straight and narrow path in the marriage covenant, contrasting it with those who turn aside to crooked ways. The Restoration reinforces that covenantal paths are straight, while apostasy involves twisting and deviation.

commentary.historical_context: The concept of the straight path versus the crooked way was ubiquitous in ancient wisdom tradition. In Egyptian wisdom, ma'at (truth, order, righteousness) is represented by straightness and balance, while isfet (chaos, disorder, transgression) is represented by crookedness and imbalance. The physical act of walking a crooked path was understood as an apt metaphor for moral disorder because it was universally comprehensible — everyone knew what it meant to lose your way. In ancient Israel, the metaphor had specific legal and covenantal resonance: to 'walk in the way' of the Lord meant to align yourself with His commandments and character.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 12:37 describes the effect of rejecting God's word: the wicked become 'carnal, sensual, and devilish' — unable to maintain moral coherence. Their crookedness follows from their fundamental rejection of light.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:30 affirms that the Lord's Church is 'the only true and living church' because it maintains the straight way; outside it, paths become crooked. Section 27:12-13 speaks of holding to the iron rod (the word of God) to stay upon the straight and narrow path.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Navajo word for the temple means 'the place where we go up to the straight way.' Temple worship is fundamentally about realigning oneself with the Lord's straight path after the world has made us crooked.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the Way (John 14:6) — not merely one option among many but the true and only way that leads to life. The crooked ways of verse 15 are crooked precisely because they deviate from Him. In the Book of Mormon, the iron rod (which represents the word of God, which is Christ) is the instrument that keeps travelers from falling into the paths of darkness on either side.
commentary.application: Notice how crookedness is habitual and progressive, not static. The wicked are not merely on a wrong path; they are actively, continuously twisting away from truth. For modern members, this suggests that compromise, if indulged, does not stabilize — it progressively distorts your entire life. The person who rationalizes one dishonesty finds themselves rationalizing others. The person who turns a blind eye to one injustice finds their conscience increasingly dulled. The antidote is not trying harder to walk straight but regularly returning to the iron rod — the revealed word of God through living prophets — which realigns you even when you've drifted.

text_kjv: To deliver thee from the strange woman, even from the stranger which flattereth with her words;

commentary.narrative: Verse 16 introduces the second great threat wisdom protects against: the forbidden woman (ishah zarah). The father's teaching (and the reader's wisdom) serves to deliver the young man from her seductive power. The Covenant Rendering identifies her as 'the forbidden woman,' capturing the Hebrew nuance that she is not merely unfamiliar but prohibited — her strangeness marks her as off-limits, her outsider status a sign of danger. She will dominate chapters 5 through 7, but here receives her first appearance as the counterpart to the evil man of verse 12. Together they represent the twin seductions: violence (the man) and illicit pleasure (the woman). Her primary weapon is language: 'her words are smooth' (amareiha hecheliqah). The verb chalaq ('to smooth, to slick, to make smooth') describes language designed to reduce resistance, to make the dangerous seem effortless. Her speech flatters, cajoles, promises — it is the verbal opposite of the father's hard-truth teaching and Wisdom Woman's reproof (tokachat). Where the father says 'this will harm you,' the forbidden woman says 'you deserve this pleasure.' Her smoothness makes the slippery path feel like solid ground.

word_study.meaning: A woman who is zarah (strange, foreign, estranged). The root zur means 'to be a stranger, to be estranged, to be outside the covenant.' She stands outside the boundaries of legitimate relationship — whether ethnically, morally, or both.
word_study.significance: The term carries both sexual and covenantal overtones. She represents any relationship or pleasure that stands outside the boundaries of the covenant. The Covenant Rendering's rendering as 'forbidden woman' captures the implicit prohibition better than 'strange woman.'

word_study.meaning: A foreign woman, outsider, one from outside the community. While sometimes referring to literal foreigners, in wisdom literature it often emphasizes those outside the moral and covenantal community.
word_study.significance: The pairing of zarah ('forbidden') with nokhriyyah ('outsider') emphasizes that she is doubly outside — strange by nature and strange by status. Her outsider position is itself a warning.

word_study.meaning: To smooth, to slick, to make slippery. The root appears in 'slippery' (chalakah) and describes language designed to reduce friction, to make danger feel safe. Her words flow smoothly, removing obstacles to compliance.
word_study.significance: Chalak reveals the forbidden woman's method: she does not coerce but seduces. She makes wickedness feel frictionless. This is why she is dangerous — she does not announce herself as a threat but as an opportunity.

cross_references.connection: For the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil. The forbidden woman's smooth speech is her defining characteristic, described at length in chapter 5.
The most extended warning about the forbidden woman; she uses precisely the 'smooth words' of verse 16 to lead the simple young man to his destruction.
But shun profane and vain babblings; for they will increase unto more ungodliness. Smooth words leading away from truth are a consistent theme in Scripture.
He that is of God hearkeneth unto the voice of God. The Lord's voice is true and straight, never smooth with flattery or deception.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern literature, the forbidden woman (often depicted as an adulteress or foreigner) is a recurring figure. Egyptian wisdom texts warn against 'loose women.' Mesopotamian literature includes warnings against foreign women who might introduce alien religious practices or undermine family stability. In the Israelite context, the ishah zarah carries added weight because of concerns about intermarriage with foreign women who might lead covenant members away from the worship of Yahweh (as occurred historically with Solomon and in the days of Ezra). However, in Proverbs the woman functions primarily as a symbolic figure representing seductive danger generally — whether literal adultery, idolatry, or the personification of Folly herself. Her smooth words are her power because in an oral culture, words are the primary instrument of persuasion and social bonding.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains extensive warnings about those outside the covenant path who seek to lead the faithful astray through flattery and smooth words. Nephi's warnings about the devil's methods (2 Nephi 28:21-22) include: 'And others will he pacify, and lull them away into carnal security, that they will say: All is well in Zion.' The devil uses smooth language precisely as the ishah zarah does.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 50:8 establishes the fundamental principle: 'All truth is independent in that sphere in which God has placed it, to act for itself, as all intelligence also; otherwise there is no existence.' Truth stands on its own merits and does not need smooth words or flattery. The use of flattery signals departure from truth.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes explicit renunciation of worldly enticements and promises of pleasure outside the covenant. The forbidden woman represents all seductive alternatives to covenantal fidelity. The temple teaches that the Lord's path, though narrow, is the only one that leads to exaltation.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ teaches truth plainly; he does not use smooth words to seduce. In contrast, the adversary's method is always deceptive flattery. The forbidden woman of Proverbs parallels the seductive voice of the tempter in the wilderness who offered Jesus shortcuts to glory that would circumvent sacrifice and obedience (Matthew 4). Christ's resistance to her modern versions reveals the pattern: truth requires no smoothing.
commentary.application: Be alert to the seductive power of smooth words. This applies not only to literal sexual temptation but to any alternative seduction: the flattering promises of wealth without righteousness, of influence without integrity, of pleasure without covenant. In a world of unprecedented information and persuasion technology, the forbidden woman's smooth words are everywhere — in advertising, entertainment, political rhetoric, and social media. Test every voice against the straight clarity of revealed truth. The father's teaching and Woman Wisdom's reproof may be harder to hear than the forbidden woman's flattery, but they lead to life. She leads to Sheol.

text_kjv: Which forsaketh the guide of her youth, and forgetteth the covenant of her God;

commentary.narrative: Verse 17 provides the forbidden woman's backstory, revealing that her seductiveness operates against a foundation of broken faith. She is not simply a victim of circumstance or a woman pursuing an alternative lifestyle — she is an apostate who has abandoned her covenants. The 'companion of her youth' (alluf ne'ureiha) refers to her husband, the intimate friend of her early years. By abandoning him, she simultaneously abandons her covenant with God. The verb azav ('abandons') reappears from verse 13, creating a structural parallel: just as the wicked man abandons the paths of uprightness, the forbidden woman abandons her husband and her God. Her transgression is simultaneously personal (marital infidelity), relational (betrayal of her most intimate bond), and covenantal (rupture with Yahweh). The verb shakhach ('has forgotten') implies not memory failure but willful disregard — she has chosen to put out of mind what she knows to be binding. This verse reveals the hidden nature of her danger: she was once a covenant keeper. Now she knows exactly which boundaries she is transgressing and does so anyway. Her smooth words carry the persuasiveness of someone who once kept the path and knows its attractions — and its demands.

word_study.meaning: To abandon, forsake, leave behind. As established in verse 13, this verb implies prior acquaintance and deliberate breaking of relationship.
word_study.significance: The reappearance of azav links the forbidden woman's betrayal to the wicked man's apostasy — both have abandoned what they knew. This creates moral symmetry: the wicked man abandons uprightness; the forbidden woman abandons covenant.

word_study.meaning: The alluf (companion, intimate friend, chief) of her youth (ne'urim). Most scholars understand this as her husband, the one who should be closest to her. Alluf suggests intimacy and priority — he is her chief companion.
word_study.significance: The term 'companion of her youth' emphasizes the depth of the bond she is breaking. This is not a casual relationship but the primary human relationship, formed in youth when bonds are deepest.

word_study.meaning: To forget, to be forgetful of, to disregard. In Hebrew, shakhach often implies willful disregard rather than simple memory failure — a deliberate putting out of mind.
word_study.significance: She does not forget the covenant as one forgets a name; she forgets it as one forgets an obligation one chooses to ignore. This is deliberate apostasy.

word_study.meaning: The covenant of her God. Berit (covenant) is the binding agreement between God and His people, sealed with oath and often involving sacrifice. Here, her covenant with God is likely mediated through her marital covenant.
word_study.significance: Her faithlessness to her husband is simultaneously faithlessness to her God — the marriage covenant and the covenantal relationship with Yahweh are inseparable. To break one is to break the other.

cross_references.connection: The Lord testifies against those who deal treacherously with the wife of their youth, for they have dealt treacherously with one another. The same covenantal language appears in Malachi's indictment of marital infidelity.
Rejoice with the wife of thy youth. The companion-of-youth language in Proverbs 2:17 is echoed positively in the exhortation to cherish one's youthful wife.
The Lord's law of conjugal relations: adultery is condemned as covenant-breaking. The marriage covenant is held as sacred and binding.
Alma rebukes Corianton for sexual transgression as a breaking of the covenants made with God. The Book of Mormon applies Proverbs' connection between marital and covenantal faithfulness.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, marriage was a covenantal bond sealed before witnesses and God. To violate it was not merely personal betrayal but religious transgression. The connection between marital fidelity and covenantal faithfulness ran deep in Israelite theology — breaking the marriage covenant was understood as breaking faith with God Himself. This makes the forbidden woman's transgression particularly grave: she is not making a private choice but committing public apostasy visible to everyone who knows her history. The Israelite legal codes (such as those found in Exodus and Deuteronomy) treated adultery as a serious crime, often capital, precisely because it was understood as covenant violation. Her position as a woman who once kept the covenant and now breaks it gives her particular power — she can speak to the attractions of sin from personal knowledge of righteousness.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Gideon describes the tragic fall of those who know truth and abandon it: 'They have fallen because of the wickedness of the church' (D&C 121:11 speaks in similar terms). Alma's warning to his son Corianton (Alma 39) emphasizes that sexual transgression is graver when one has been raised in the faith — one knows what one is abandoning.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 132:41-44 teaches that those who violate marriage covenants lose the blessings of their covenants. The Lord makes clear that covenantal promise is conditioned upon faithfulness — to forget or abandon the covenant is to forfeit its promised blessings.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The marriage covenant, when performed in the temple, is specifically 'the new and everlasting covenant of marriage.' To break this covenant is to break a covenant made before God, angels, and witnesses. Verse 17 describes the tragedy of such violation.

commentary.christological_typology: The forbidden woman's abandonment of her covenant parallels Lucifer's rebellion — a deliberate turning away from what was known and sacred. Her smooth words echo the serpent's rationalization of transgression in Eden. Christ, by contrast, never abandoned His covenant with the Father, and His blood ratifies the new covenant that restores what was broken. The woman of verse 17 represents those who 'turn away from the living God' (Hebrews 3:12) after having known Him.
commentary.application: If you have made covenants before God — particularly the marriage covenant in the temple — understand that faithfulness is not optional or contextual. The forbidden woman's history reveals a chilling truth: it is possible to know the path, to walk it, to be blessed by it, and then deliberately abandon it. The safeguard is not presumption that you would 'never' break covenant but rather active, regular renewal of your covenants. For members who struggle with adultery, pornography, or any violation of marital faithfulness, this verse should pierce the rationalization that 'everyone does this' or 'it's not that serious.' God calls it what it is: abandonment of covenant. Yet the remedy is repentance and renewed commitment — the Lord who breaks covenant with no one receives all who return with sincere hearts.

text_kjv: For her house inclineth unto death, and her paths unto the dead.

commentary.narrative: Verse 18 concludes the portrait of the forbidden woman by describing the geography of her existence: it is a vertical descent toward death. Her house 'sinks down' (shachah) toward death, and her paths 'lead to the shades' (refa'im) — the diminished dead of Sheol who have lost vitality and dwell in darkness. The Covenant Rendering's 'her house sinks down to death' captures the gravitational pull implied by the Hebrew shachah (which means to bow down, to incline, to lower oneself). Being in her presence, accepting her smooth words, following her paths — all of this is movement downward. There is no horizontal alternative with the forbidden woman; there is only descent. The refa'im (the shades, the dead, those without strength) are the ultimate destination. Sheol in Hebrew thought is not primarily a place of active punishment (that is later Jewish and Christian development) but the realm of the dead where vitality ceases, where the dead are mere shadows of their former selves. To enter into the forbidden woman's world is to begin the process of becoming a shade — diminished, lifeless, cut off from God's light. This is not metaphorical threat but the actual trajectory of moral life as Proverbs understands it: transgression leads to death, not eventually in some abstract future sense, but progressively, now, as one's life loses vitality and meaning.

word_study.meaning: To sink down, to incline downward, to bow down, to lower. Suggests gravitational movement, the natural descent of weight. Often used for bowing in worship or submission.
word_study.significance: The vertical imagery is crucial — following the forbidden woman is not walking a path horizontally but descending into depths. The house itself (implying the woman's entire sphere of influence) has an inherent gravitational pull downward.

word_study.meaning: Death, the state of being dead. In Hebrew wisdom, death is both literal cessation and metaphorical loss of vitality, meaning, and blessing.
word_study.significance: The forbidden woman's house leads to death not as metaphor alone but as actual destination — separation from God, loss of blessing, transition to Sheol. Her enticements promise life but deliver death.

word_study.meaning: The shades, the dead, the inhabitants of Sheol. From a root meaning 'weak, powerless.' The refa'im are the ghosts or shades of the dead — diminished, weak, lacking vitality or power.
word_study.significance: The refa'im are not actors but sufferers of diminishment. They are not in active torment but in passive weakness. To follow the forbidden woman is to join them in this state of powerlessness and separation.

word_study.meaning: Paths, ways, tracks. A specific term for the footprint or trail one leaves, suggesting the trajectory of one's life journey.
word_study.significance: The forbidden woman's paths (maglot) are marked routes of descent. Every step on her path is a step deeper into Sheol. This reiterates the navigational metaphor of the entire passage: the direction matters, and her direction is downward.

cross_references.connection: Her house is the way to hell, going down to the chambers of death. This verse concludes the extended warning about the forbidden woman in chapter 7 with the same imagery of descent to death.
Her feet go down to death; her steps take hold on hell. The Book of Proverbs hammers home repeatedly that the forbidden woman's path is one of fatal descent.
The wages of sin is death. Paul's doctrine echoes the Proverbs teaching that transgression carries within it the seed of destruction.

That which is of God is light, and he that receiveth light and continueth in God receiveth more light until that light groweth brighter and brighter until the perfect day. The opposite path — rejecting light for the forbidden woman's darkness — leads to spiritual death.
The devil is the father of all lies and the author of all confusion. The forbidden woman, as a tool of deception, is aligned with the devil's method of leading souls toward spiritual death.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel and throughout the Ancient Near East, Sheol was understood not as hell (active punishment) but as the underworld realm of the dead — a place of weakness, isolation, and separation from God and the living community. Death was considered the ultimate evil precisely because it severed all connection to the living God and His covenant community. To say that someone's path leads to death and to the refa'im (the shades) was to pronounce the most severe judgment possible: not merely that they would die physically but that they would lose all meaning, vitality, and connection to the sacred. The forbidden woman's house is described as leading downward because Sheol was conceived as literally beneath the earth. Archaeological evidence from Israelite tombs and burial practices reveals a genuine belief in some form of afterlife existence (the refa'im state), however diminished and disconnected from God.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 40 contains the most extensive Book of Mormon teaching on death and the spirit world. Alma teaches that the wicked 'shall be brought into a state of view of their own guilt and awful state' (Alma 40:26). The Book of Mormon conception of spiritual death — separation from God's presence — aligns with the Proverbs teaching that the forbidden woman's path leads to a state of diminishment and spiritual weakness.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:106 describes the sons of perdition (the worst state of the wicked): 'Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched — they are consigned to endless torment.' While Proverbs uses the imagery of Sheol (diminishment) rather than outer darkness (active torment), both describe states of spiritual death — separation from God.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that the path of covenants leads upward — celestial exaltation, living in the presence of God. The forbidden woman's path represents the opposite direction: downward toward Sheol, toward separation from God. The temple reinforces the vertical cosmology where God's kingdom is 'up' and rebellion leads 'down.'

commentary.christological_typology: Christ descended into the depths (Matthew 12:40 — 'three days and three nights in the heart of the earth') and rose again, opening the way for all to ascend. The forbidden woman's path goes down and stays down; Christ's path descends in order to bring us up. He harrowed hell (D&C 138) and broke the chains of death, offering escape from the refa'im state. In contrast to the woman who leads to death, Christ is 'the resurrection and the life' (John 11:25) — the path that ascends to eternal life.
commentary.application: Take the vertical geography of verse 18 seriously: some paths lead up; others lead down. The forbidden woman (representing any seductive alternative to covenant fidelity) promises pleasure and exhilaration but delivers progressive spiritual diminishment. You do not have to commit catastrophic sin to experience this — the slope is gradual. Small compromises, small lies, small betrayals of your deepest values create a gravitational pull downward. Conversely, covenant fidelity, integrity, and alignment with revealed truth create an upward trajectory. You are not merely making momentary choices; you are marking your path. The question Proverbs poses is: which direction is your path taking you? Are you ascending toward God's presence and celestial light, or descending toward the dimness and separation of Sheol? The good news: it is never too late to change direction. Repentance is the pivot point where downward-moving paths are redirected upward toward God.

text_kjv: My son, forget not my law; but let thine heart keep my commandments:

commentary.narrative: The opening of this instruction establishes the fundamental posture of the wisdom seeker: active retention of paternal teaching. The father addresses his son directly, moving from the general exhortation of Proverbs 1–2 to specific commands that demand obedience. The verb 'forget' (tishkach) in Hebrew carries deeper weight than mere memory failure; it means to disregard, to treat as irrelevant or obsolete. The father's concern is not that the son will innocently misplace the teaching, but that he will consciously choose to abandon it when circumstances pressure him differently. This is why the second clause emphasizes the heart's active role: the heart must 'guard' (yittsor) the commands—not merely store them, but actively preserve and protect them, treating them as precious and non-negotiable.
commentary.narrative_continued: The opening verse establishes a covenant relationship within the family structure. The father's 'instruction' (torah, but here the father's personal torah, not the Mosaic Law) is presented as the binding authority for the son's life. Notice the parallelism: forgetting is countered by guarding; law is paralleled by commandments. Both sides of the instruction demand the same energy—vigilant resistance to forgetting and vigilant commitment to keeping. This is the educational core of wisdom literature: not knowledge as intellectual possession, but wisdom as embodied practice, written into the heart's operating system.

word_study.meaning: to forget, disregard, treat as irrelevant; in Hebrew cognition, forgetting is a matter of will, not merely of memory. To forget is to cease regarding something as binding.
word_study.significance: The Hebrew understanding of 'forgetting' is volitional—it involves choosing to treat something as no longer authoritative. The father is warning against the willful abandonment of teaching, not innocent memory loss.

word_study.meaning: my instruction, my teaching; torah here refers not to the Mosaic Law but to the father's authoritative didactic teaching—the accumulated wisdom passed from mentor to disciple.
word_study.significance: Torati (my torah) grounds parental instruction in the same covenantal authority structure as the Mosaic revelation. The father speaks with the weight of transmitted wisdom.

word_study.meaning: your heart; in Hebrew, the heart is the center of intellection, emotion, will, and decision-making—the whole inner person. The heart is where values are formed and from which life choices flow.
word_study.significance: The instruction to let the heart 'guard' the commands means the son must internalize them, making them part of his core value system, not merely external rules to follow.

word_study.meaning: to keep, guard, preserve, watch over; the verb conveys active protective custody, not passive obedience.
word_study.significance: The heart's role is not servile compliance but protective vigilance—treating the commands as treasure that must be defended against all erosion and corruption.

cross_references.connection: Moses commands Israel to keep God's words in their heart, establishing the pattern of internalized covenant obedience that Proverbs now applies to paternal instruction.
The psalmist stores God's word in his heart to avoid sinning against Him, showing the same link between internal retention and external faithfulness.
Nephi charges his children to keep the commandments in their hearts, echoing the father's instruction in Proverbs and applying it within the Restoration covenant.
The Lord teaches that seeking and keeping His word in the heart is the pathway to understanding divine things and growing in knowledge.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern pedagogy, the father-son relationship was the primary vehicle for transmission of practical wisdom, moral values, and professional knowledge. Wisdom literature emerged from scribal schools and royal courts where such mentorship was formalized. The emphasis on 'not forgetting' reflects the oral culture's dependence on memory and recitation; students were expected to internalize teaching through repetition and meditation. The heart as the seat of moral memory underscores that wisdom was not abstract philosophy but lived practice embedded in daily decision-making.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:26 echoes this instruction when Alma teaches his son Helaman to remember the captivity of his fathers and to remember the mercies of the Lord—memory here, as in Proverbs, is active retention of covenant truth.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5 presents the Lord's words to the Church as something that must be kept in the heart, extending Proverbs' father-son dynamic to the covenant relationship between God and His people.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The charge to write and guard commandments in the heart anticipates the endowment's emphasis on covenant keepers 'proving themselves faithful.' The heart-guarding motif echoes the temple's call to preserve sacred covenants in mind and heart.

commentary.christological_typology: The father's role as transmitter of life-giving instruction prefigures Christ as the Father's spokesman. In the Gospel of John, Jesus insists that His words are not His own but the Father's (John 14:24), and He commands His disciples to keep His words in their hearts (John 14:23). The internalization of wisdom instruction becomes, in the Restoration, the internalization of Christ's voice.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse calls us to distinguish between intellectual awareness of gospel principles and active, protective custody of them in our hearts. We may 'know' the commandments in our minds yet treat them as negotiable in our decisions. The verse demands that we treat the gospel not as a collection of ideas we can examine and set aside, but as the authoritative instruction that must guard our choices, our relationships, and our priorities. This requires regular renewal—meditation, discussion, repentance when we drift—to ensure the commandments remain alive and operative in our decision-making, not merely stored in memory.

text_kjv: For length of days, and long life, and peace, shall they add to thee.

commentary.narrative: Verse 2 provides the motivation for the obedience commanded in verse 1. The father promises that adherence to his instruction yields three interconnected benefits: length of days, years of life, and peace. At first glance, this appears to be a simple bargain—keep the commands, and you will live longer and experience tranquility. But the Hebrew structure reveals something subtler. The parallel 'length of days' and 'years of life' is not redundancy; it is emphasis. The father is stressing that the promised life is not merely extended but fulfilled. 'Peace' (shalom) functions as the capstone: it is not merely the absence of conflict but the presence of completeness, wholeness, right relationship with oneself, others, and God.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verb 'add' (yossipu) is crucial: the benefits are additions, accumulations, growth. This is not a gift given once but an ongoing accrual, day upon day, relationship upon relationship, peace deepening within peace. The father promises that the obedient life is not a grim, constrained existence but one characterized by flourishing. This sets up a fundamental claim of Proverbs: the wise path is not only right but also rewarding—not in the corrupting sense of immediate gratification, but in the sense that alignment with wisdom's structure produces genuine wellbeing. The wicked may appear to prosper briefly, but the wise accumulate real goods: longevity, vitality, and shalom.

word_study.meaning: length of days; orekh means extension, prolongation; yamim means days. Together they denote extended duration of life, quantity of years.
word_study.significance: In the ancient Near Eastern worldview, long life was understood as a sign of divine blessing and the fruit of right living. The promise of orekh yamim is not merely quantity but the approval of the heavens.

word_study.meaning: peace, wholeness, well-being, harmony, completeness. Shalom is not the absence of conflict but the presence of right relationship and flourishing in all dimensions.
word_study.significance: Shalom in Hebrew encompasses physical health, relational harmony, economic security, and spiritual alignment. It is the comprehensive human flourishing that wisdom promises. The KJV 'peace' captures only the surface; the Covenant Rendering's 'well-being' better conveys the fullness.

word_study.meaning: they will add, accumulate, increase; a verb of continuous addition and growth.
word_study.significance: The plural subject (implied: the instruction and commandments) 'add' benefits, suggesting that wisdom is an active force, not a passive state. It keeps giving as long as the son remains aligned with it.

cross_references.connection: The father repeats this promise of long life to his son, indicating it is a core assurance of the wisdom tradition.
The fifth commandment promises 'that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee'—establishing that obedience to covenant brings longevity.
Moses presents the choice: obedience brings life and good, while disobedience brings death and evil—the covenantal structure underlying Proverbs' promise.
Alma teaches his son that wickedness brings misery while righteousness brings happiness, mirroring Proverbs' promise that wisdom yields genuine wellbeing.
The Lord promises that keeping the commandments brings peace in this life and eternal life in the world to come, expanding the Proverbs promise into the full covenant framework.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern wisdom literature (Egyptian Instructions, Sumerian proverbs), longevity is frequently presented as the reward for righteous living. The connection between virtue and long life reflects both the observable reality that recklessness shortens life and a deeper theological claim: that the cosmos is ordered such that right living produces thriving. Shalom in the ancient Near East was a marker of a king's successful reign—when he ruled justly, his land experienced abundant harvests, security from enemies, and social stability. Extended to the individual, shalom becomes the internal and relational consequence of wise governance of one's own life.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:3 presents a similar promise: those who keep God's commandments receive life, while those who break them receive death. The Book of Mormon emphasizes that the consequences of wisdom and foolishness are not arbitrary but built into reality itself.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 19:31-32 promises that those who hearken to the Lord's voice shall have peace and that His blessing rests upon the faithful. The Doctrine and Covenants frequently ties obedience to temporal and spiritual prosperity.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The endowment's promise of eternal increase and exaltation extends Proverbs' promise of life and peace into the fullness of covenant blessing. The temple presents obedience to covenant as the pathway to becoming like God and inheriting all that the Father has.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the source of eternal life (John 1:4) and the peace that passes understanding (John 14:27). The father's promise of shalom through obedience finds its ultimate fulfillment in Christ, who offers peace not as worldly truce but as union with the Father. His commandment is similarly life-giving: those who abide in His word receive life eternal.
commentary.application: Modern readers often approach this verse with suspicion—does it really promise that the righteous live longer? The deeper promise is not about actuarial tables but about the quality of the life you have. Obedience to wisdom brings an integrity of life, a coherence between your values and your actions, that produces genuine peace and enables you to extract meaning and flourishing from your years, however many. The promise is not that wisdom prevents death (it does not), but that it prevents the dissolution and despair that come from living against reality. For Latter-day Saints, this connects to the promise that keeping covenants brings not only spiritual blessing but temporal stability, health of mind and heart, and the accumulation of genuine goods—reputation, relationships, self-respect—that constitute real wealth.

text_kjv: Let not mercy and truth forsake thee: bind them about thy neck; write them upon the table of thine heart.

commentary.narrative: Verse 3 pivots from external reward (long life and peace) to the internal virtues that generate that reward. 'Faithful love and truthfulness' (chesed ve-emet) is the operative pair—not mercy and truth as separate virtues, but as a unified concept in Hebrew: covenant faithfulness, the combination of reliable love and steadfast truthfulness. The father's instruction is to treat these not as nice qualities to aspire to, but as non-negotiable possessions that must be guarded against loss. The verb 'forsake' (ya'azvu) means to abandon or let go; the father warns that these virtues can slip away if not actively retained. This is where the protective imagery becomes vivid: the son must 'bind them about your neck'—make them visible, publicly owned, always in view—and 'write them on the tablet of your heart'—internalize them so deeply that they become the core script governing his choices.
commentary.narrative_continued: The dual imagery—external binding and internal writing—suggests that chesed and emet are not merely private dispositions but public commitments. In the ancient world, binding something around the neck made it your emblem, your signature virtue. Writing on the heart's tablet echoes the covenant language of Deuteronomy 6:8-9, where God's words are bound as a sign and written as a reminder. Here, the father uses that same language to describe how the son must relate to love and truth: they are covenant-like commitments, visible to the world, operative in the deepest center of identity. The son cannot compartmentalize—hiding truth in business while showing love at home, or vice versa. Chesed and emet must saturate the entire self.

word_study.meaning: steadfast love, faithful love, covenant love, loyalty, kindness. Chesed is love that acts, love that commits, love that persists. It is not sentiment but reliable, protective care.
word_study.significance: Chesed appears over 240 times in the Hebrew Bible and is foundational to covenant theology. In Proverbs 3:3, it describes the father-son relationship as itself a covenant bond requiring mutual faithfulness. The Covenant Rendering's 'faithful love' captures better than 'mercy' the active, committed sense of chesed.

word_study.meaning: truth, faithfulness, reliability, consistency. Emet shares a root with emunah (faithfulness) and amen (so be it, truly). Truth in Hebrew is relational—it describes a person whose word matches reality, who is reliable.
word_study.significance: Emet is not abstract philosophical truth but relational reliability. A person of emet is someone whose yes is yes and whose no is no. Paired with chesed, it describes faithful love grounded in actual reliability, not mere sentiment.

word_study.meaning: bind them around your neck; qashar means to bind, tie, knot; gargerot means neck, throat. The image is of binding a sign or emblem around the neck, making it visible and inseparable from the person.
word_study.significance: The neck-binding imagery appears also in Deuteronomy 6:8 regarding the binding of God's words. Here it suggests that chesed and emet must be your visible identity marker, the thing people recognize about you.

word_study.term_english: write them on the tablet of your heart
word_study.meaning: write them on the tablet of your heart; katab means to write, inscribe; luach means a tablet, a writing surface; lev means heart, the center of mind and will. This is deep internalization—truth and love as the core operating system.
word_study.significance: The language of writing on the heart's tablet appears in Jeremiah 31:33, where God promises to write the new covenant on Israel's heart. In Proverbs, the father calls his son to inscribe these virtues into his innermost being so that they guide his thoughts and decisions automatically.

cross_references.connection: Moses commands Israel to bind God's words as a sign upon their hand and as frontlets between their eyes, and to write them on their houses' doorposts—the same imagery of making covenant visible and inscribed.
The prophet promises that God will write His law on Israel's heart, anticipating Proverbs' vision of internalized covenant where the law operates from within, not imposed from without.
John echoes Proverbs' insistence that love must be demonstrated in deed and truth, not merely in word.
King Benjamin teaches his people that retaining a remission of sins depends on keeping the commandments and retaining them in their hearts, mirroring Proverbs' image of internalized covenant.
The Lord commands the Church to keep His words in their hearts, extending Proverbs' personal instruction to the corporate covenant people.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern culture, neck ornaments were status symbols and identity markers. Binding something around the neck meant making it your personal emblem, the sign by which you were known. Writing on tablets was the primary method of recording important information—laws, contracts, sacred texts. In the scribal schools where wisdom literature emerged, the phrase 'write on the heart' conveyed the transformation of external instruction into internalized principle. The student did not merely memorize texts; he inscribed them into his character. The dual imagery of binding and writing together emphasizes both public embodiment and private transformation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 37:9 urges Helaman to remember the sacred records and to 'keep these sayings also in thy heart,' echoing Proverbs' image of covenant truths inscribed in the heart. 2 Nephi 32:3 similarly teaches that the words of Christ will tell you all things you should do.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 20:77-79 describes how the sacrament renews the covenant and causes the Saints to always remember Him. The renewal of covenant weekly reinforces the 'writing on the heart' that Proverbs envisions. D&C 88:63 teaches that whatever is written in the heart determines what you will become.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony repeatedly emphasizes the binding of covenants—in the oath and covenant, the endowee assumes obligations that must become part of their identity. The language of writing on the heart echoes the temple's call to internalize sacred commitments so that they govern all choices and relationships.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ embodies the perfect union of chesed and emet. His love is covenant love—faithful, atoning, redemptive—and His truth is absolute reliability; His word will never pass away. In John 1:14, Christ is described as 'full of grace and truth' (charis kai aletheia in Greek, echoing chesed ve-emet). The binding of these virtues around the neck and writing on the heart finds its fulfillment in making Christ's nature—His love and His truth—the operating system of the redeemed heart.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse challenges the compartmentalization that modern life enables. We might be honest in business but deceptive in relationships, or loving at home but selfish in our service. Proverbs demands integration: faithful love and truthfulness must be one inseparable pair, visible to all and operative in everything. This requires examining where we have separated these virtues, where we show one face to one group and another to another. The 'writing on the heart' aspect means these are not rules we follow reluctantly but values so central to our identity that we cannot imagine acting against them. For members of the Church, this connects to the temple covenant to 'live virtuous and pure lives,' where the virtues of love and truth are not cosmetic but constitutive of who we are becoming through covenant.

text_kjv: So shalt thou find favour and good understanding in the sight of God and man.

commentary.narrative: Verse 4 is the payoff clause: if you bind chesed and emet around your neck and write them on your heart, the result is favor and good repute in both the divine and human spheres. 'Favor' (chen) carries a double sense: it is the approval and blessing of authority figures (God and human leaders), and it is also grace in the sense of unmerited kindness. The son who embodies faithful love and truth will find himself the recipient of grace—people will want to help him, support him, speak well of him. 'Good understanding' or 'good repute' (sekhel tov) is not merely intelligence but prudent judgment, practical wisdom, a good name. The verse establishes that covenant faithfulness is not a burden that isolates you but a pathway that opens doors, creates alliances, and generates goodwill.
commentary.narrative_continued: The dual audience—'in the eyes of God and of people'—is significant. The son's obedience is not performed for human approval, nor is it only about vertical relationship with God. Rather, the two spheres of approval reinforce each other. The one who lives with integrity before God naturally earns the respect of discerning people. Conversely, those who lack genuine inner virtue cannot hide it forever from human perception; their duplicity eventually surfaces. The promise is that alignment with wisdom produces benefits in both directions: God sees and blesses, and humans recognize and honor.

word_study.meaning: favor, grace, charm, attractiveness. Chen describes both the attractiveness of a person and the benevolent regard of a superior. It is the quality that makes others want to help and support you.
word_study.significance: Chen is not something earned through flattery or manipulation but flows naturally from genuine virtue. The father promises that authentic covenant faithfulness will make the son attractive to others—not in a superficial sense, but in the sense that people will recognize his trustworthiness and want to associate with him.

word_study.meaning: good understanding, good judgment, good sense, good repute. Sekhel means understanding, perception, practical wisdom. Tov means good, well, favorable. Together: the reputation for good judgment and sound decision-making.
word_study.significance: Sekhel tov is not mere intelligence but practical wisdom applied to life—the kind of judgment that others recognize and respect. It is the reputation of one who makes sound choices and whose advice is worth taking.

word_study.meaning: in the eyes of, from the perspective of, in the judgment of. The idiom 'in the eyes of' parallels 'in the mind of' or 'in the assessment of.'
word_study.significance: The phrase emphasizes that favor and reputation are not self-conferred but recognized and granted by observers—by God whose vision is complete, and by humans whose discernment recognizes genuine worth.

cross_references.connection: Joseph finds favor (chen) in the sight of the keeper of the prison, reflecting how his integrity and trustworthiness generate goodwill even in adverse circumstances.
Samuel grows 'in favour both with the LORD, and also with men,' showing that favor in both spheres is the natural result of a covenant keeper's integrity.
Jesus increased 'in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man,' embodying the Proverbs promise of approval in both divine and human dimensions.
Moroni is described as one 'who did obtain favor in the sight of God' because of his righteousness, showing how covenant faithfulness generates divine approval.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern court culture, favor (chen) was the essential currency of advancement. Those who won the favor of kings and nobles advanced in position and wealth. Wisdom literature promises that genuine virtue—not flattery, manipulation, or cunning—is the most reliable path to such favor. Archaeologically, we see this reflected in royal inscriptions where successful officials are praised for their integrity and trustworthiness. The connection between personal character and social advancement was understood as built into reality itself, not as arbitrary reward.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 17:11 notes that when the sons of Mosiah taught with exactness and with power, they 'obtained favor in the sight of all people,' reflecting Proverbs' promise that covenant faithfulness wins recognition from all sides.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:45-46 promises that 'the doctrines of the priesthood distill upon thy soul as the dews from heaven' and that 'thy dominions shall be an everlasting dominion.' Right use of authority, grounded in love and truth, produces approval from both heaven and earth.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that keeping covenants results in exaltation and the increase of dominion. The promise of favor and good reputation extends into eternity as the covenant keeper becomes more like God and is recognized and honored accordingly.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ perfectly embodied this principle: He grew in favor with God and humanity (Luke 2:52) because His entire being was devoted to love (chesed) and truth (emet). His favor with God flowed from His perfect submission to the Father's will, and His favor with humanity flowed from His healing, teaching, and redemptive work. All who come to Him through repentance likewise 'find favor' in both the divine and human spheres as His grace transforms them.
commentary.application: This verse offers a corrective to a common misreading of wisdom literature: it does not promise that the righteous will prosper materially or that everyone will like them. Rather, it promises that genuine covenant faithfulness will be recognized by those of discernment and will generate appropriate goodwill. For modern members, this might mean that your integrity in a business transaction will create a reputation for reliability that brings clients back. It might mean that your truthfulness in difficult conversations will eventually be recognized and respected, even if it costs you in the short term. It means that God sees what others might miss and will vindicate your faithfulness. The promise is not popularity but the deeper satisfaction of genuine approval from sources that matter: from God, and from people whose judgment is sound.

text_kjv: Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.

commentary.narrative: Verse 5 is the epistemological hinge of the chapter: it directly addresses the question of where ultimate authority lies. The command 'Trust in the LORD' (betach el-YHWH) demands total transfer of dependence from self to God. The verb betach means to feel secure in, to rely on, to make oneself vulnerable to. It is not mere intellectual assent but existential commitment. The phrase 'with all your heart' (be-khol libbeka) emphasizes totality: not trusting God in spiritual matters while relying on yourself in practical affairs, but a unified commitment of your entire being. The second clause—'do not lean on your own understanding'—might seem to contradict the entire premise of the book, which has been urging the son to seek wisdom and understanding. But the father makes a crucial distinction: pursuing and possessing understanding is good; leaning on it—making it your load-bearing foundation—is the error.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verb 'lean on' (tisha'en) suggests putting your weight on something, using it as a structural support. The father's point is that your understanding is a tool and a possession, but it is not a foundation. You can never know all the factors affecting your decisions. Your perspective is limited by your experience, your biases, your finite knowledge. What you understand seems true, but you may be mistaken about things that matter enormously. The Lord, by contrast, sees the full picture and understands the future. Therefore, the wise posture is this: develop understanding passionately (as the rest of Proverbs urges), but hold it humbly, always submitting it to God's wisdom. Use your understanding in service to trusting God, not as an alternative to trusting Him. This is the deepest wisdom: to be deeply knowledgeable and deeply humble about what you know.

word_study.meaning: to trust, rely on, feel secure in, make oneself vulnerable to. Betach implies a transfer of dependence and a willingness to be vulnerable to the one trusted.
word_study.significance: Betach in the imperative form is a demand for a complete reorientation of your dependence. You must move your center of gravity from your own perception to YHWH's reliability. It is not blind faith—it is informed reliance on the one whose understanding is actually complete and whose love is devoted to your wellbeing.

word_study.meaning: your understanding, your insight, your discernment. Binah is the faculty of comprehension, the ability to perceive connections and meanings. It is a good thing to pursue (2:2-3) but a bad thing on which to lean.
word_study.significance: The deliberate choice of binah is telling. The book has urged the son to seek binah repeatedly. Now it warns against making binah your ground of trust. The point is not that understanding is bad, but that it is insufficient. You need both—understanding developed through wisdom-seeking, and trust that subordinates that understanding to God's wisdom.

word_study.meaning: to lean on, to support yourself on, to rest your weight on, to depend on for structural support. The verb conveys putting your full weight on something.
word_study.significance: The distinction between possessing understanding and leaning on it is vital. You can have a tool without depending on it. You can have knowledge without making it your foundation. The father warns against the latter: do not make your limited understanding the thing that holds you up in life. That role belongs to God alone.

word_study.meaning: with all your heart, with your entire being, with undivided devotion. The heart in Hebrew is the center of intellection, emotion, will, and decision-making.
word_study.significance: The requirement of totality means you cannot compartmentalize. You cannot trust God in prayer while relying on yourself in business decisions. The whole of your life, in all its dimensions, must be oriented toward God.

cross_references.connection: The Shema commands Israel to love the LORD with all their heart, soul, and might—establishing the pattern of total devotion that Proverbs here applies to trust.

Jeremiah teaches that the wise should not glory in wisdom, strength, or riches, but only in understanding and knowing the LORD—paralleling Proverbs' warning against leaning on one's own understanding.
Isaiah emphasizes that God's thoughts are not our thoughts and His ways are not our ways, establishing the theological foundation for why human understanding cannot be trusted as ultimate.
Alma teaches his son Helaman to place trust in God and not to rely on the wisdom of the world, echoing Proverbs' warning against dependence on human understanding.
The Lord rebukes those who trust in the arm of flesh and fail to trust in Him, establishing the Restoration principle that ultimate dependence must be on God, not on human capability.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern thought, the gods were understood as the true source of knowledge and fate. Humans possessed partial knowledge; the gods possessed complete knowledge. Wisdom literature operates within this framework: the father teaching his son is transmitting wisdom, but even the wisest father cannot see the future or comprehend all things. Therefore, even perfect understanding is limited. The father teaches his son to distinguish between developing practical wisdom (which is good and necessary) and making that wisdom autonomous (which is prideful and dangerous). This reflects a mature understanding of human limitations in a world ordered by powers greater than oneself.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Jacob 4:10 teaches that the Jews who stumble do so 'because they will not believe in my God with all their hearts,' emphasizing the Restoration principle that total trust in God is the safeguard against error. Alma 57:21 describes how trusting in the Lord rather than in the arm of flesh enables the Lamanite stripling warriors to achieve victory.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 9:8-9 teaches Oliver Cowdery that feeling the promptings of the Spirit requires trust and confidence in God, not reliance on one's own understanding. D&C 88:119-120 promises that those who keep the commandments with trust in God 'shall grow up in me.' The principle throughout the Doctrine and Covenants is that spiritual progression requires subordinating human understanding to divine guidance.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The endowment teaches the principle of sacred knowledge shared with those who prove themselves trustworthy and willing to submit to the Lord's direction. The temple oath reflects this verse: trusting in and obeying God's will above one's own understanding becomes the defining feature of the covenant keeper.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ embodies perfect trust in God the Father. In Gethsemane, He demonstrates the distinction Proverbs teaches: His understanding is perfect, yet He submits it entirely to the Father's will, saying 'not my will, but thine be done' (Luke 22:42). He teaches His disciples that unless they become as little children—dependent and trusting—they cannot enter the kingdom. The redeemed life consists of developing understanding while maintaining the trust of a child toward their Father in Heaven.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse challenges a subtle form of pride that affects educated, capable people: the assumption that if you understand a problem, you can solve it yourself. The verse calls for a different posture: develop your understanding through study and experience, but hold it humbly, always asking 'What does the Lord want me to do?' This is especially relevant in family decisions, professional choices, and ethical dilemmas where your understanding is genuine but incomplete. The verse does not ask you to abandon your mind but to subordinate it to divine guidance. In practice, this might mean seeking counsel from priesthood leaders, studying the scriptures and conference talks, praying for confirmation, and being willing to change direction if the Spirit prompts differently than your natural reasoning. It means trusting that the Lord sees what you cannot see and that submission to His will, even when you don't fully understand, is the wisest course.

text_kjv: In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.

commentary.narrative: Verse 6 completes the instruction of verse 5 and applies it comprehensively: 'In all your ways acknowledge Him.' The verb 'acknowledge' (da'ehu) is not mere intellectual recognition but the deep, relational knowing that characterizes covenant relationship throughout Scripture. To 'know' someone in Hebrew is to be in intimate relationship, to understand them deeply, to act on that knowledge. The phrase 'in all your ways' (be-khol derakhekha) extends this acknowledgment beyond the spiritual or religious—it means in every sphere of life, every decision, every path you take. The daily commute is a way. The business decision is a way. The interaction with your children is a way. The relationship with your spouse is a way. Every moment offers an opportunity to acknowledge God and to seek His guidance. The father promises that such comprehensive acknowledgment yields comprehensive direction: 'He will make straight your paths.'
commentary.narrative_continued: The verb 'make straight' (yeyyasher) deserves close attention. God does not merely point out the correct direction; He straightens the road itself. In Proverbs, the straight path is the path of wisdom, and the crooked paths are the paths of the wicked (2:15). The promise is not just that you will understand where to go (though that is included), but that your entire trajectory will be straightened. The crooked places will be made level. The obstacles will be removed. The Lord becomes an active agent in your life, not just a consultant to whom you occasionally turn. The comprehensiveness of verse 6 stands in perfect tension with verse 5: you cannot lean on your own understanding in isolation from God, but you also cannot sit passively waiting for God to make all decisions for you. Rather, you acknowledge Him in all your ways—bringing every decision, every path, every situation to Him—and He, seeing your heart's genuine desire to align with His will, orchestrates your way forward.

word_study.meaning: know Him, acknowledge Him, understand Him. The verb yada in Hebrew means to know through relationship and experience, not merely through intellectual comprehension.
word_study.significance: The KJV 'acknowledge' captures part of the meaning, but da'ehu carries the fuller sense of intimate, relational knowing. To know God in this sense is to be in covenant with Him, to understand His character through experience, and to live as though His reality shapes your behavior.

word_study.meaning: in all your ways, in every path you take, throughout the entire sphere of your journey. Derekh means way, path, journey, direction. The plural ways suggests not just one spiritual path but the multitude of daily decisions and directions.
word_study.significance: The comprehensiveness is crucial: the son is not told to acknowledge God in prayer or at the temple, but in all ways. This universalizes the acknowledgment to every arena of life. There is no sphere in which the Lord is irrelevant.

word_study.meaning: make straight, level, make level, make direct. The verb yashar means to be straight or to make straight, implying both the removal of obstacles and the establishment of a clear path.
word_study.significance: The imagery of straightening paths evokes both the removal of obstacles (verse 5 warned that your own understanding might lead you astray—God removes that confusion) and the establishment of a clear direction (you will not wander aimlessly, but will move with purpose toward your destiny).

word_study.meaning: your paths, your journeys, your ways, your routes. Orach is similar to derekh (way) but often has the sense of a habitual path, a well-worn trajectory, one's life-pattern.
word_study.significance: The plural and the use of orchot (often referring to habitual patterns) suggests that what is straightened is not just isolated decisions but the entire trajectory of one's life—the pattern formed by many choices adding up to a direction.

cross_references.connection: A man plans his way but the LORD establishes his steps, showing that direction comes through the coordination of human intention and divine ordering.
David asks the LORD to teach him His way because his enemies surround him, reflecting the conviction that God's guidance in our paths protects us from misdirection.

The prophet promises that if you turn to the right or to the left, your ears will hear a voice behind you saying 'This is the way, walk in it,' picturing God's active guidance of those who acknowledge Him.
The Lord promises that 'he that keepeth the law of God hath no need to break the laws of the land,' showing that alignment with God's will produces straightened paths in multiple dimensions.
Alma teaches Helaman that the Liahona (which works according to faith and diligence in keeping commandments) is a type of the word of Christ that will guide you in all your ways if you look to it.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern thought, the path of the righteous and the path of the wicked were understood as cosmic realities, not merely moral categories. The gods were thought to establish and maintain the paths of the righteous while the wicked wandered in confusion. The imagery of straightening paths likely derives from ancient construction and road-building: a straight road is an achievement, created by removing obstacles and establishing a clear route. In wisdom literature, it becomes a metaphor for the divine ordering of the cosmos such that those aligned with wisdom prosper while the foolish encounter obstacles.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 56:47 describes how the Lamanite stripling warriors, having placed their trust in God and acknowledged Him in all their ways, experienced protection and success. 1 Nephi 4:6 shows Nephi 'being led by the Spirit,' which is the practical application of verse 6—knowing God (da'ehu) in the actual moment and having one's way made straight by divine guidance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 112:10 teaches that 'if thou art faithful and walk in the paths of virtue before me, I will make thy way prosperous,' directly applying Proverbs 3:6 to the Latter-day context. The entire Doctrine and Covenants assumes that acknowledging God and seeking His will results in a divinely straightened path through life.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that those who keep their covenants receive the guidance of the Holy Ghost and are led toward exaltation. The covenant itself becomes a path, and faithfulness in keeping it results in the Lord straightening that path. The role of temple covenants is precisely to align one's entire trajectory (one's ways) with the Lord's purposes.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the way (John 14:6), and He walked perfectly straight paths because He acknowledged the Father in everything. His entire life was oriented toward the Father's will. In the garden, He submitted His understanding to the Father's; on the cross, He walked the path the Father had established. All who follow Him commit to knowing Him and having their paths straightened by His guidance. The Resurrection and ascension represent the ultimate straightening of the path that appeared crooked through the cross.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 6 calls for a practical integration of decision-making and faith. This is not about seeking God's will only in major life decisions, but in all ways—which job to apply for, which words to use in a difficult conversation, whether to speak up or stay silent, how to spend your evening, what to do with a windfall. The principle is that everything matters to God because everything shapes who you become. This requires developing patterns of acknowledgment: scripture study, prayer, listening for the Spirit's promptings, discussing decisions with trusted mentors, and maintaining sensitivity to the Spirit. Over time, as you acknowledge God in all your ways, you develop confidence that your path is being straightened. You encounter fewer dead ends. You discover opportunities you could not have created on your own. You find yourself in relationships and situations that seem providentially arranged. This is not magical thinking; it is the natural result of aligning your entire being with the Lord's wisdom and letting Him order your steps.

text_kjv: Be not wise in thine own eyes: fear the LORD, and depart from evil.

commentary.narrative:
This verse stands as a direct challenge to the most seductive form of foolishness: self-confidence in one's own judgment. The warning is not against being intelligent—Solomon himself was legendary for wisdom—but against the conviction that your own understanding is sufficient. The Covenant Rendering captures the precision here: 'Do not be wise in your own eyes' identifies the precise danger as internal assessment rather than external reality. A person can believe they are wise while being catastrophically wrong. This verse echoes verse 5, creating a paired instruction: accept instruction from God's word, and refuse to trust your unaided perception.

The antidote is neither blind obedience nor intellectual surrender. Instead, it is a reorientation of authority: fear the LORD replaces self-confidence as the foundation of judgment, and 'turn away from evil' becomes the practical test of wisdom. The Hebrew sur mera ('turn from evil') is not abstract moral sentiment but concrete redirection—you change direction, you walk away from the trap. Note the sequence: fear comes first (reorientation of the will toward God), then turning from evil follows (practical obedience). This is not hesitation followed by action; it is worship that naturally produces separation from what God opposes.

In the context of Proverbs 1–3, this verse addresses a critical vulnerability: the moment you believe your judgment is sound, you stop listening. You become unreachable. The book's entire project—summoning the young to seek wisdom, instruction, understanding—collapses if the reader concludes he already possesses what he needs. Verse 7 is a surgical strike against that self-deception.

word_study.meaning: Wise in your own eyes—your own assessment, your own judgment. The phrase 'in your eyes' (be-eynekha) emphasizes subjective perception, not objective reality. You think you are wise; that is the problem.
word_study.significance: This formulation appears only here in Proverbs, though the concept recurs (26:12, 28:11). The danger is not ignorance but false confidence. A fool knows nothing; the self-wise fool thinks he knows everything. The Covenant Rendering preserves the internal, self-referential nature of the Hebrew.

word_study.meaning: Fear, reverence, awe directed toward the LORD (Yahweh). This is not terror but a posture of submission and respect toward God's character and authority. The object of fear is explicitly the God of covenant, not an abstract principle.
word_study.significance: This phrase anchors the entire book of Proverbs (1:7, 9:10, 14:26, 19:23). Fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. It is the reorientation that makes all other instruction possible—you fear God more than you fear man, more than you fear loss, more than you trust your own judgment.

word_study.meaning: Turn away, depart, withdraw from evil. The verb sur carries the sense of active redirection—not merely avoiding evil but moving away from it, maintaining distance.
word_study.significance: This is not passive restraint but active separation. The pairing of 'fear the LORD' with 'turn from evil' suggests that proper fear produces behavioral change. Fear is not mere sentiment; it is the root of obedience.

cross_references.connection: Seest thou a man wise in his own conceit? there is more hope of a fool than of him. This verse makes explicit what Proverbs 3:7 implies: self-assessed wisdom is more incurable than admitted foolishness.

Woe unto them that are wise in their own eyes, and prudent in their own sight! Isaiah applies Proverbs' warning to a national level—Israel's self-confidence in political and military judgment will lead to destruction.
Be not wise in your own conceits. Paul quotes Proverbs 3:7's principle directly into his exhortation to the Roman church, making humility essential to Christian community.
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge. Verse 7 restates the foundational principle: fear is the prerequisite to all sound judgment.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern context, the wise man (chakham) held significant social authority—he was counselor, administrator, and teacher. The warning against self-assessed wisdom is therefore a direct challenge to social status and privilege. A young person might inherit position but must still cultivate the humility to receive instruction. The phrase 'in your own eyes' also reflects the Hebrew understanding of the eye as the seat of desire and judgment (as in 'covetousness' coming from the eye). Self-assessment was considered particularly unreliable because the eye is deceived by what it desires.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 39:11 warns Corianton against trusting his own judgment regarding moral boundaries. Similarly, Jacob 4:10 exhorts the Nephites not to suppose they know more than to hearken to the words of the prophets. The Book of Mormon repeatedly insists on the insufficiency of unaided reason when it comes to matters of God.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 6:36 contains a promise to Oliver Cowdery: 'Look unto me in every thought; doubt not, fear not.' This reverses reliance on self-assessment to reliance on divine guidance. The principle of Proverbs 3:7—fear the LORD rather than trust yourself—becomes the foundation for receiving revelation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The fear of the LORD central to this verse is cultivated and renewed in the temple. The covenants made there explicitly reject the sufficiency of personal judgment and commit the member to obey the voice of the Lord through His prophets. The turning from evil is simultaneously a turning toward the Light.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ embodies the reversal of Proverbs 3:7. He alone could have been 'wise in His own eyes' with perfect justification—His judgment was infallible. Instead, He consistently deferred to the Father: 'I can of mine own self do nothing' (John 5:30). He modeled the fear (reverence) toward God and separation from evil that the verse commands. His willingness to humble Himself became the pattern for all who follow Him.
commentary.application: The force of this verse strikes directly at the modern conviction that expertise in one field transfers to all others, or that education substitutes for spiritual discernment. A skilled professional, a successful entrepreneur, a person of talent and achievement must still ask: Am I wise in my own eyes regarding my marriage, my children, my relationship with God? The verse calls for periodic auditing of your own judgments—especially the ones you most trust. What would change if you feared the LORD more than you trusted your track record? What evil might you be walking toward while confident in your direction?

text_kjv: It shall be health to thy navel, and marrow to thy bones.

commentary.narrative:
The transition from verse 7 to verse 8 is crucial: the moment you reorient from self-confidence to fear of the LORD, accepting His discipline and turning from evil, you experience healing. This is not magical thinking but the reality of wholeness. The Covenant Rendering renders this more precisely than the KJV: 'It will be healing for your body and refreshment for your bones.' The healing is not merely spiritual sentiment but total—it restores the physical person.

Hebrew thought did not compartmentalize body and spirit as Western dualism has. The body carries the effects of the soul's condition. A person living in rebellion against God—characterized by self-reliance and evil—is literally unwell. The ancient observer would see the ravages: the tense shoulders, the sleepless nights, the digestive turmoil that comes from chronic anxiety and moral compromise. Verse 8 promises reversal. When you submit to God's order, when you accept His instruction (verses 1-2) and His discipline (verse 7), the physical person heals. Your bones—the deepest structural part of you—are refreshed. This is not sentimental; it is observable.

The promise connects directly to the firstfruits instruction of verse 9. The person who gives to God first experiences abundance returning to them. But the abundance is not only material (verse 10's overflowing barns); it is biological, cellular—healing penetrates to the bone. The body is the ultimate test of integrated wisdom. A person who intellectually assents to faith while living in chronic anxiety, resentment, or self-reliance is contradicted by their own flesh.

word_study.meaning: Healing, health, restoration. The root raphah means to heal, to make whole. Rifu't is the noun form—the state of being healed.
word_study.significance: This word appears only here in Proverbs, though the verb form recurs in wisdom literature and the Psalms. The promise is active healing, not merely the absence of disease. Wisdom produces health.

word_study.meaning: Navel, belly, body. The shor is the center of the body, sometimes metaphorically the seat of appetite or desire. It is the most vulnerable interior part.
word_study.significance: The KJV 'navel' is anatomically precise but sounds odd to modern ears. The Covenant Rendering's 'your body' captures the Hebrew intent: this is speaking to the core of your physical self. Wisdom heals you at your center.
