word_study.meaning: Moisture, drink, refreshment. The root shaqah means to give drink, to drench. Shiqquy is the moisture that sustains.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'refreshment' captures the sense better than KJV's 'marrow.' Bones need moisture to remain supple and strong. This is not mere poetic language—a body without moisture becomes brittle. Wisdom provides the refreshment that keeps you flexible and resilient.

word_study.meaning: Bones, skeletal structure, the framework of the body. In Hebrew thought, bones represent strength, durability, and the deep structure of a person.
word_study.significance: The Bible often speaks of bones as the seat of being: 'bone of my bones' (Genesis 2:23), or breaking of bones as utter destruction. When wisdom refreshes your bones, it restores your deepest structural integrity.

cross_references.connection: A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones. Contrasts peaceful wisdom with the physical decay envy produces—again, the body reflects the soul's condition.
A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones. The joy produced by accepting God's order provides healing, while despair literally desiccates you.

There is no soundness in my flesh because of thine anger; neither is there any rest in my bones because of my sin. David describes the physical ravages of guilt and separation from God—the inverse of Proverbs 3:8's promise.

I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth. John's benediction directly connects the state of the soul to the health of the body, echoing Proverbs' integrated anthropology.

commentary.historical_context: Ancient Near Eastern wisdom assumed a direct relationship between moral order and physical wellbeing. This was not naïve superstition but accurate observation: chronic anxiety, unresolved guilt, internal conflict, and rebellion against community and cosmos produce measurable physiological effects. The promise of healing in verse 8 would have been understood literally—the person who orders their life according to wisdom becomes visibly healthier. Modern psychosomatic medicine has vindicated this observation through measurable stress hormones, immune function, and inflammation markers.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:3 records Alma's transformation: his soul was racked with torment, his frame drenched in sweat, wracked with inexpressible anguish—until his repentance brought relief. The Book of Mormon validates the principle that spiritual reorientation produces physical healing and peace.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 89:18-21 promises health to those who obey the Word of Wisdom: 'And all saints who remember to keep and do these sayings, walking in obedience to the commandments, shall receive health in their navel and marrow to their bones; and shall find wisdom and great treasures of knowledge, even hidden treasures.' This is a direct quotation and application of Proverbs 3:8 in Restoration context, making explicit that obedience to revealed wisdom produces observable physical benefits.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The washing and anointing of the body in temple ordinances symbolize the healing and restoration promised in verse 8. The covenants made at the temple commit the participant to the order of wisdom that produces healing. The endowment's teaching of the Fall and Redemption locates the believer within God's order, promising restoration of the whole person.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's healing miracles—the woman with the issue of blood, the leper, the man with the withered hand—are not mere signs of divine power but illustrations of this principle: submission to God's order produces wholeness. Christ is the source of all healing because He embodies perfect alignment with the Father's will. His resurrection is the ultimate vindication of the promise that obedience to God produces life in the body.
commentary.application: This verse invites you to notice the state of your own body as a barometer of your spiritual alignment. Do you sleep well? Are you prone to injury and illness? Do your shoulders carry tension? Do you have energy for your relationships? These are not moralistic questions but diagnostic ones. The promise is that as you reorder your life around God's wisdom—accepting instruction, fearing the LORD, turning from evil, giving generously—your physical self will heal. Not magically, but as a natural consequence of integrated, obedient living. What change in your daily rhythm, your submission to God's order, would produce visible healing in your body?

text_kjv: Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase:

commentary.narrative:
The verb kabbed—'honor,' 'give weight to'—contains a revolutionary economic principle. To honor the LORD with your substance means to treat Him as the heaviest reality in your financial life. Not one of many concerns, but the one that carries the most weight. This is not generosity as philanthropy; it is recognition of priority. The question every financial decision answers is: Who do I treat as most important in how I allocate resources?

The instruction specifies not an arbitrary portion but the firstfruits—reshit kol tebu'atekha—'the first and best of all your produce.' This is the Deuteronomic principle that appears throughout the law (Deuteronomy 26:1-11): the first portion of the harvest, before you know how the rest will turn out, before you see if there is scarcity coming, before you calculate how much you need. You give this portion to God as an act of covenant trust. You are saying by your action: I acknowledge that everything I have comes from God; I trust Him to provide; I refuse to live by calculation and scarcity.

This appears before verse 10's promise of overflowing abundance, not after. The promise follows the practice. The person who gives firstfruits does not give because they are already secure; they give as the basis of security. This inverts the natural human impulse, which is to give from surplus only after accumulating enough to feel safe. Proverbs insists on the opposite order: honor the LORD first (with the firstfruits), and abundance follows. This is the practical test of whether you actually believe verse 7's command to fear God instead of trusting your own calculation.

word_study.meaning: To honor, to give weight to, to make heavy. The root can mean to load with weight or importance. To honor is to treat something as weighty, significant, deserving of respect.
word_study.significance: This is not mere politeness or sentiment. To kabbed the LORD in the context of economics means to make Him the weight-bearing reality of your financial decisions. What you honor, you order your life around.

word_study.meaning: Wealth, substance, possessions, capital. This refers to accumulated resources and property.
word_study.significance: The term is neutral—neither inherently good nor evil—but its use reveals character. Will you honor God with your hon, or treat it as your own private kingdom?

word_study.meaning: Beginning, first, firstfruits. Reshit literally means 'the beginning.' Giving the reshit means giving from the beginning, the first portion that comes in.
word_study.significance: This is not giving leftovers or surplus. It is giving before you know the full outcome, before you have calculated security. This is the principle of trust.

word_study.meaning: Harvest, produce, increase, yield. This refers to the fruit of labor, the abundance that results from work.
word_study.significance: By giving the firstfruits of your tebu'ah, you acknowledge that all increase—all that comes to you through work—is ultimately from God. You are recognizing His lordship over your productivity.

cross_references.connection: The firstfruits law prescribes the exact practice Proverbs 3:9 references. The Israelite is to bring the first of the produce to the priest and make a formal declaration of God's covenant provision. This is the legal and liturgical background for the wisdom instruction.

Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse and test me now in this, says the LORD. Malachi applies the firstfruits principle to the tithe, challenging Israel to give fully and watch God open the windows of heaven. The principle of proving God through generosity runs consistently through Scripture.

The immediate next verse promises the consequence: full barns and overflowing wine vats. Verse 9 is the condition; verse 10 is the promise. This inseparable pairing shows that giving firstfruits is not loss but the path to abundance.

Upon the first day of the week let every one of you lay by him in store. Paul applies the firstfruits principle to the church collection, establishing giving as a regular, covenantal practice for Christians.
The Lord's law of tithing in Latter-day Saint practice directly applies Proverbs' principle: give the Lord's portion first, acknowledging His ownership and your stewardship of what remains.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, firstfruits giving was both a legal requirement and a lived reality tied to agricultural cycles. A farmer's entire economic security depended on the harvest. To give the first portion before knowing the outcome of the rest required genuine faith. The practice also had social dimensions: the firstfruits supported the priesthood and the Temple, the institutions that maintained covenant community. Giving firstfruits was not private piety but public participation in God's kingdom order. In agrarian societies where harvest was everything, this was not a suggestion; it was the foundation of survival.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 4:26 teaches that those who refrain from giving to the poor are refusing the atonement of Christ and retaining their sins. The Book of Mormon frames generosity as connected to the Atonement itself. When you give firstfruits, you are not just following a rule; you are acting out the principle that Christ taught: all you have is a gift, and you are called to stewardship.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 119:1 reveals the law of tithing: 'Verily, thus saith the Lord, I require the residue of the church property to be consecrated to me.' And later: 'Now, as to the poor and the needy...' Tithing, consecration, and care for the poor are interwoven. The Restoration clarifies that the principle of firstfruits giving continues as a core covenant practice.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The covenants made at the temple commit the participant to God as Lord over all they possess. The law of tithing accompanies temple participation. To enter the temple is to declare publicly that you honor God above your substance—a lived application of Proverbs 3:9.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus embodied the principle of verse 9: He gave the firstfruits of His life to God. He did not preserve Himself, calculate His safety, or keep something back. He offered Himself completely, trusting the Father's promise of resurrection. His cross is the ultimate firstfruits offering—the first and best of all life—given before the promise of abundant life beyond was publicly visible. In the Incarnation, God honored humanity by giving His own substance first.
commentary.application: The hard question is: Where is God actually honored in your financial life? If you calculate your comfort first and give to God from surplus, you are honoring your security, not the LORD. The test is not the amount but the timing and priority. Do you give firstfruits—the first, before calculating the rest—or do you give remainder fruits—only what you can spare? Most of us operate on remainder principles, then wonder why anxiety about money persists. Proverbs invites you to reverse this: identify a concrete 'firstfruits'—your first paycheck, the first day of your week, the first fruits of a new project—and honor the LORD with it. Watch what happens to your sense of security and abundance.

text_kjv: So shall thy barns be filled with plenty, and thy presses shall burst out with new wine.

commentary.narrative:
The consequence of honoring the LORD with firstfruits (verse 9) is abundance—the full asamim (barns, granaries) and overflowing yeqavim (wine vats). The verb yifrotsu—'will burst, will break through'—conveys excess beyond containment. This is not adequacy; this is surplus. The barns are filled to the point of bursting; the presses overflow with new wine. The Covenant Rendering's 'burst with new wine' captures the Hebrew sense of superabundance.

This promise sits at the very heart of Proverbs' retributive theology, and it requires careful reading. Proverbs operates within a framework of moral-material causation: right living produces prosperity; wrong living produces loss. This is demonstrably true in many cases and across many contexts. A person who manages money wisely, maintains relationships of trust, works diligently, and lives within community norms will generally prosper materially. A person who steals, squanders, breaks promises, and isolates himself will generally decline. Proverbs is not wrong about this.

But the Rest of Scripture—especially Job, Ecclesiastes, and Jesus's teachings—will dramatically nuance this. Not all suffering is caused by personal sin; not all prosperity is evidence of righteousness. Verse 10's promise is real and often observed, but it is not absolute. This is why Proverbs must be read within the full canonical context. For the covenant person who fears God and honors Him with firstfruits, abundance often flows—but the flow is not automatic, and its absence does not indicate failure. Verse 10 is a true promise, not a guarantee of individual outcome.

word_study.meaning: Barn, granary, storehouse. A place where grain is stored and preserved. In singular asam; plural asamim.
word_study.significance: Barns represent storage, preservation, security—the accumulated reserves that ensure survival through seasons of scarcity. To have your barns filled is to have security established.

word_study.meaning: Filled to satisfaction, filled with abundance. Sava means fullness, satiety, plenty.
word_study.significance: This is not partial filling but complete, satisfying abundance. Nothing is lacking.

word_study.meaning: Wine vat, wine press. The vessel or pit into which wine is pressed and stored. Plural yeqavim.
word_study.significance: Wine vats represent liquid wealth, the preserved product of the vineyard. Wine was valuable currency in ancient economies. Full wine vats meant wealth in the most portable, tradeable form.

word_study.meaning: To break through, to burst, to break out, to make a breach. The image is of containment exceeded—the boundaries can't hold the abundance.
word_study.significance: This verb is forceful, active, almost violent in its suggestion of overflow. It is not gentle increase but exuberant excess. The Covenant Rendering's 'burst' captures this dynamism well.

word_study.meaning: New wine, fresh wine, must. The term typically refers to the freshly pressed juice before full fermentation.
word_study.significance: New wine represents the most valuable, most desirable portion of the harvest—the pristine product of the year's labor. To have vats bursting with tirosh is to have the best at hand.

cross_references.connection: The LORD shall command the blessing upon thee in thy storehouses, and in all that thou settest thine hand unto. Moses's blessing of the faithful reiterates this promise: obedience leads to overflowing storehouses.

Job challenges the retributive theology that verse 10 represents: the wicked often prosper and their houses are safe. This complicates Proverbs' promise, showing that material abundance is not always the result of righteousness.

Jesus tells the parable of the rich fool whose barns are full to bursting but whose soul is not rich toward God. Abundance without attention to God's purposes is emptiness. This relativizes verse 10's promise.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient world, full barns and wine vats represented not luxury but life itself. A harvest failure meant famine, displacement, or servitude. The abundance promised in verse 10 would have been understood as literally existential—the difference between thriving and survival. The imagery also connects to Egypt in the Joseph narrative: Pharaoh's dreams of full ears of grain represent both blessing and the possibility of famine. For an agricultural society, the promise of overflowing storehouses touches the deepest form of security.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 2:19-26 records King Benjamin's teaching that God sustains all beings, and everything we possess is from Him. The Book of Mormon does not reject material blessing but frames it as God's gift for the purpose of caring for His people. Abundance is for stewardship, not selfish security.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 104:1-3 reveals that 'the Lord's scourge shall pass over by night and hide itself that it may not slay.' The faithful are protected and provided for even in times of general scarcity. The principle of verse 10 is affirmed: those who honor God with firstfruits are preserved in abundance.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The promise of verse 10 echoes in the temple's teaching of celestial order: those who make and keep covenants are promised peace and prosperity in this life and exaltation in the world to come. The barns and wine vats represent the confidence of the covenant people.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the source of the abundance promised in verse 10. In the feeding of the five thousand, His multiplication of loaves and fishes demonstrates that those who follow Him experience provision beyond natural calculation. His teaching that 'man shall not live by bread alone' (Matthew 4:4) does not negate verse 10's promise but subordinates it to the deeper abundance of living by God's word. The Resurrection is the ultimate 'bursting forth' of abundance—life beyond death, inexhaustible provision.
commentary.application: The challenge of verse 10 is not to be greedy for abundance but to trust the promise enough to honor God with firstfruits. Most people withhold firstfruits because they don't yet see the full barns. Verse 10 reverses this: the barns fill when you give firstfruits, not before. The practical question is: Where do you see God's abundance in your life, and are you positioned as a grateful steward or a anxious accumulator? If you were convinced that verse 9 and 10 are actually true—that honoring God produces abundance—how would your financial decisions change? Begin with a small act of firstfruits giving and watch what happens to your sense of security over the next season.

text_kjv: My son, despise not the chastening of the LORD; neither be weary of his correction:

commentary.narrative:
The tone shifts abruptly. Verses 1-10 have promised blessing, abundance, healing, and provision. Now verse 11 introduces the reality of discipline. The phrase 'my son' signals direct, intimate address—this is a father speaking to his child. The warning addresses two possible responses to suffering: tim'as ('despise, reject, refuse') and taqots ('loathe, grow weary, feel disgust'). These are the two ways people resist divine correction: outright rejection and slow-burning resentment.

This verse is crucial to understanding Proverbs' theology. The book does not promise that the righteous escape suffering; it promises that those who accept God's discipline flourish. The promise of abundance (verses 1-10) is not a guarantee that nothing difficult will happen. It is a declaration of who will prosper ultimately and how they will get there. The path includes discipline. The LORD's musar (discipline, instruction, formation) and tokhachto (His correction, His reproof) are not punishment meted out by an angry God; they are the loving formation of a Father. This is the interpretive key to Proverbs: all wisdom literature is framed by covenant relationship. Even the hard parts are offered from love.

The TCR's translation 'do not reject the LORD's discipline, and do not loathe His correction' captures precisely what is at stake. To reject divine discipline is to cut yourself off from the very means by which God shapes you into wisdom. To loathe it is to poison your heart against your own good. Neither response is acceptable. The implied exhortation is to welcome discipline, to receive it as evidence of God's care rather than evidence of His indifference.

word_study.meaning: To reject, despise, refuse, to treat as worthless. To regard something with contempt and cast it aside.
word_study.significance: This is active rejection—not merely suffering through discipline but consciously scorning it. The person who ma'as God's discipline is not just experiencing hardship; they are refusing to learn from it.

word_study.meaning: Discipline, instruction, formation, correction. Musar is the entire process by which someone is shaped toward wisdom. It includes both teaching and the experience of consequences.
word_study.significance: This is the same musar mentioned in Proverbs 1:2 as one of the book's central purposes. Musar is not punishment but formation. It is God's pedagogical work in your life.

word_study.meaning: To loathe, to feel disgust, to abhor, to be weary of. The root suggests revulsion, the kind of disgust you feel at something foul.
word_study.significance: This captures the insidious second response to discipline: not violent rejection but slow-burning revulsion. The person becomes sick of God's correction, resentful, worn down by it. This is perhaps more dangerous than outright rejection because it disguises itself as resignation.

word_study.meaning: Reproof, rebuke, correction, argument. From the verb yakach, to prove, to argue, to reason with. Tokhachat is correction that reasons with you, that makes an argument for your own good.
word_study.significance: This is not arbitrary punishment but reasoned correction. God's tokhachat is Him making a case for why you need to change, why this is necessary, why it is good for you.

cross_references.connection: Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish. Loving God's instruction and accepting His reproof are marks of wisdom; refusing them is brutish.
He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes. Parents who genuinely love their children correct them; those who refuse to discipline them are failing in love.

My son, despise not thou the chastening of the Lord... For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth. Hebrews quotes Proverbs 3:11-12 directly, making it the foundation of Christian understanding of suffering as fatherly discipline rather than divine punishment.
Behold, happy is the man whom God correcteth: therefore despise not thou the chastening of the Almighty. Job affirms the principle despite his wrestling with the experience of undeserved suffering.

Verily, thus saith the Lord unto you who have assembled yourselves together to receive my word... I am not pleased with the inhabitants of Zion. The Lord disciplines His own people, and this discipline is a sign of covenant relationship, not rejection.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern wisdom tradition, the discipline of youth by both parents and teachers was normative. Proverbs reflects a society where instruction was expected to be firm, sometimes painful, but always for the young person's benefit. The cultural assumption that verse 11 addresses is that suffering could be interpreted as evidence of divine rejection or indifference. The verse refutes this: discipline is evidence of God's attention and investment in your formation. In this context, the person who receives correction is honored, not shamed.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:3-20 records Alma's description of his torment at his sin and his eventual repentance. He frames his suffering not as punishment but as the necessary consequence through which God brought him to humility and faith. The Book of Mormon validates the principle that accepting divine correction leads to joy.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:27-28 reveals: 'Wherefore, I the Lord, knowing the calamity which should come upon the inhabitants of the earth, called upon my servant Joseph Smith, Jun., and spake unto him from heaven, and gave him commandments... Therefore, I the Lord, knowing the calamity which should come upon the inhabitants of the earth, called upon my servant Joseph Smith.' The Lord calls prophets into difficult circumstances precisely because He loves them and His people. Discipline flows from God's covenantal commitment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The covenants of the temple include a submission to God's will and a willingness to be refined through experience. The temple teaches that God's correction is part of the path to exaltation, not a sign that you are failing.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ accepted the ultimate discipline: suffering and crucifixion. He did not despise or loathe His Father's correction but submitted to it as the necessary path to redemption. Hebrews 5:8 states: 'Though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered.' Christ models complete acceptance of divine discipline as the expression of perfect love.
commentary.application: The force of verse 11 strikes at how you actually respond when life brings difficulty. Do you interpret hardship as evidence that God doesn't care, or as evidence that He does? Do you become weary and resentful of correction, or do you receive it as formation? The verse invites you to audit your inner response to difficulty. When you face consequences of your choices, when circumstances force change, when people offer hard feedback—do you reject it, resent it, or receive it as God's discipline forming you? The person who can welcome correction, who can hear the father-voice in the difficulty, is positioned to become wise. Those who refuse or resent correction cut themselves off from their own transformation.

text_kjv: For whom the LORD loveth he correcteth; even as a father the son in whom he delighteth.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 12 provides the theological foundation for verse 11's command: Why should you accept God's correction? Because correction is the expression of His love. The connection 'for' (ki) establishes causation: the reason you should receive discipline without despising or loathing it is that YHWH yokhiach (the LORD corrects, rebukes, reasons with) the one He loves. The verb yakach—translated here as 'correcteth'—carries the sense of arguing a case, of proving, of reasoning with someone because their understanding or behavior is incomplete or wrong. It is legal and relational, not merely punitive.

The comparison illuminates everything: 'as a father the son in whom he delights.' The original Hebrew ke-av et ben yirtseh uses yirtseh from the verb ratsah, which means 'to be pleased with, to delight in, to accept.' This is remarkable: the son whom God disciplines is the son God has accepted, the one in whom God delights. Discipline and delight are not opposites but expressions of the same relationship. A father who did not care about his son would not correct him; he would simply ignore him, letting him destroy himself. The father who loves and is pleased with his son will correct him precisely because the son's wellbeing matters.

This verse, quoted directly in Hebrews 12:5-6 and applied to Christian suffering, reframes all adversity within covenant theology. The question shifts from 'Why is this happening to me?' to 'What is God trying to shape in me?' The person experiencing correction is not a failure outside God's love but a son or daughter inside God's affection and intention. This reinterpretation of suffering as love is central to all Scripture's approach to hardship. It does not make suffering pleasant, but it relocates it within relationship. You are being corrected by Someone who delights in you, not by an impersonal universe or a punitive judge.

word_study.meaning: To love, to have affection for, to choose, to delight in. This is emotional and relational attachment.
word_study.significance: The verse states as a foundational reality that God loves those He corrects. This love is not conditional on their perfection; it precedes and motivates the correction.

word_study.meaning: To correct, to rebuke, to argue with, to prove, to reason with. The verb yakach means to make a case, to argue in court, to convince someone of error.
word_study.significance: This is not arbitrary punishment but reasoned correction. God is making a case to you, proving your error, reasoning with you toward change. It is legal and relational.

word_study.meaning: To be pleased with, to delight in, to accept, to be satisfied with. The same verb is used for God's acceptance of sacrifices.
word_study.significance: This is not grudging tolerance but genuine pleasure. The one God corrects is one He is pleased with, one He has accepted. The correlation to sacrifice (Leviticus 1:4) suggests that the corrected one is being refined in offering, moving toward greater value and acceptability.

word_study.meaning: Father/son—the primary human relationship of guidance, care, and formation. This is not distant but intimate.
word_study.significance: By using family language, the verse locates divine discipline within the warmth of familial relationship. You are not a subject of the King; you are a child of the Father. Discipline flows from this relationship.

cross_references.connection: My son, despise not the chastening of the LORD. Verse 12 provides the reason for verse 11's command: the chastening comes from love.

Hebrews quotes Proverbs 3:11-12 directly and expands on it: 'Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.' The New Testament grounds Christian suffering theology in Proverbs.

And he shall put his hand upon the head of the burnt offering; and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him. The verb 'accepted' (yirtseh) links acceptance of sacrifice to the acceptance of the corrected child, suggesting that discipline refines us into acceptable offering.

Thou shalt also consider in thine heart, that, as a man chasteneth his son, so the LORD thy God chasteneth thee. Moses applies the father-child metaphor to God's discipline of the nation, grounding national suffering in God's parental love.

For thus saith the Lord—I, the Lord, am merciful and gracious unto those who fear me, and delight to honor those who serve me in righteousness and in truth unto the end. The Restoration affirms that God delights in those whom He serves, echoing the ratsah ('delight') of verse 12.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern family structures, the father's role included both provision and correction. The responsible father was expected to correct his sons; failure to do so was seen as negligence and a sign of indifference. The verse draws on this widely recognized cultural reality: discipline is a marker of relationship and care, not abandonment. This would have resonated with a family-oriented society where the father-son relationship was the primary model for authority and love.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 26:29-31 reveals: 'Therefore I say unto you, Go, and whosoever transgresseth against me, him shall ye judge; but if he confess his sins before thee and me, and repenteth in the sincerity of his heart, him shall ye forgive, and I will forgive him also... And ye shall also forgive one another your sins.' The Book of Mormon teaches that correction flows from the desire for return and restoration, not punishment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:43 reveals the nature of the priesthood: 'No power or influence can or ought to be maintained by virtue of the priesthood, only by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned.' This describes how God exercises authority—through love, not force. Discipline is always persuasion, not domination.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches of a covenant Father who takes pleasure in His children and guides them through instruction and experience. The endowment's narrative of humanity's journey through the world and the Veil includes both comfort and instruction, both promise and test. These are all expressions of a loving Father's desire to bring His children to exaltation.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate expression of verse 12. He is the Son in whom the Father delights (Matthew 3:17: 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased'). Yet He also experienced the ultimate correction and suffering—the cross—through which His perfect obedience was tested and refined. Hebrews 5:8-9 teaches: 'Though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered; and being made perfect, he became the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him.' Christ models the principle perfectly: the beloved Son received correction and suffering, and through it was perfected and exalted.
commentary.application: The deepest application of verse 12 is reinterpretation of your own suffering. When you face difficulty, loss, disappointment, or correction, the verse offers a radical reframing: This is happening to you by Someone who loves you and is pleased with you. Not because you are being punished for failure, but because you are being formed for something greater. The difficulty is evidence of God's delight in you, not His indifference toward you. This does not make the difficulty pleasant or easy, but it places you within a relationship of love rather than abandonment. Practically, this means: In your next experience of difficulty, pause and ask, 'What is the Father trying to teach me? What am I being formed to become?' This simple reorientation from victimhood to sonship/daughterhood can transform how you move through hardship.

text_kjv: Happy is the man that findeth wisdom, and the man that getteth understanding.

commentary.narrative: This verse opens a sustained hymn to wisdom that runs through verse 20, mirroring the structure of Psalm 1:1, which also begins with 'Ashre' ('how fortunate'). The use of this term signals that we are entering into a beatitude — a declaration of blessedness for those who attain a particular condition. But this is not passive happiness. The verb 'matsa' (to find) appears throughout Proverbs as an active seeking: wisdom is discovered by those who search earnestly. The parallel structure of the verse reinforces that finding wisdom and obtaining understanding are simultaneous acts — wisdom and understanding are not separate acquisitions but facets of the same pursuit. The Hebrew suggests that this discovery is available to 'adam' — any person, any human being — not merely the elite or the educated. This democratizes wisdom: it is not the possession of the wealthy or the powerful, but something found by the seeker.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verb 'yafiq' (to bring forth, to extract, to obtain) that accompanies understanding carries connotations of effort and deliberate action. As The Covenant Rendering notes, the image is like drawing water from a well — understanding must be drawn out, extracted through disciplined seeking. This is crucial for the modern reader accustomed to thinking of wisdom as inspiration or intuition. Here, wisdom is work. The repetition of 'adam' (the person, the man, the human being) emphasizes that this beatitude applies universally to whoever undertakes the quest. The verse establishes the opening claim that will sustain the entire section: the pursuit of wisdom is not an optional luxury or an elite philosophical exercise, but the fundamental path to blessing.

word_study.meaning: A declaration of blessedness, fortune, or well-being. The term opens Psalm 1:1 and is the standard Hebrew beatitude formula, appearing 45 times in the Psalter. It denotes not merely emotional happiness but the condition of flourishing that comes from right relationship with God and alignment with His order.
word_study.significance: By opening with 'ashre,' the text claims that wisdom-seeking is not a burdensome duty but the path to genuine flourishing. The person who finds wisdom experiences the deepest form of human blessing — not circumstantial happiness, but structural well-being.

word_study.meaning: To find, to discover, to obtain. The verb is frequent in Proverbs (8:17, 17:20, 24:3) and denotes active discovery rather than mere chance encounter. In some contexts it means to reach or attain a goal.
word_study.significance: Wisdom is not stumbled upon passively; it is found by the seeker. The verb implies both availability and the necessity of seeking. There is a real discovery to be made, and it requires intentional search.

word_study.meaning: Understanding, discernment, intelligence. Derived from the root 'byn' (to distinguish, to separate, to understand). Tevunah is the faculty of discernment — the ability to discriminate between true and false, wise and foolish. It is understanding that penetrates beneath surface appearances to perceive the actual nature of things.
word_study.significance: Tevunah is paired with chokmah (wisdom) throughout Proverbs, often as a complementary gift. If wisdom is the capacity to see the right goal, tevunah is the capacity to discern the right means. Together they constitute mature judgment.

cross_references.connection: Opens with the identical 'ashre' formula, declaring blessedness for those who meditate on God's law — establishing a parallel between meditating on Torah and seeking wisdom.
Wisdom speaks: 'I love them that love me; and those that seek me early shall find me' — emphasizing that finding wisdom requires active seeking and mutual love.
Lays out the prerequisites for finding wisdom: receiving words, treasuring commandments, applying heart to understanding, seeking it as hidden treasure — wisdom requires disciplined pursuit.
The Lord teaches that those who seek by diligent heed to the words of eternal life shall find — aligning with the Proverbs 3:13 principle that seeking precedes finding.

commentary.historical_context: The 'ashre' formula was standard in ancient Near Eastern wisdom literature and appears prominently in Egyptian wisdom texts as well. The Instruction of Ptahhotep and other Egyptian instructional literature open with similar declarations of blessedness for those who follow wisdom. The Psalter's use of 'ashre' at its opening (Psalm 1:1) suggests that by the time Proverbs was compiled, this formula had become the classical marker of wisdom teaching across Hebrew literature. The idea that wisdom must be actively sought reflects the didactic context: a teacher is addressing students and encouraging them to undertake the disciplined study necessary to acquire understanding.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Jacob in Jacob 4:13 declares that those who 'believe in Christ and endure to the end' are made 'white and pure before Him' — a Restoration parallel to the beatitude structure, offering blessing to those who actively engage in faith. The Book of Mormon emphasizes active seeking throughout: 'Ask, and ye shall receive; knock, and it shall be opened unto you' (3 Nephi 27:29), paralleling the active verbs in Proverbs 3:13.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 11:7-8 directly applies the principle: 'Seek the Lord early, and in the morning, and again in the evening, and let thy diligent heed be unto the words of eternal life.' The Doctrine and Covenants adapts Proverbs' language of seeking and finding to the context of seeking divine truth in the Restoration. Section 88:63 teaches 'Seek the Lord early,' echoing the urgency of the seeker.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The beatitude structure anticipates covenant blessing. Just as the temple-endowed find access to sacred knowledge through covenant engagement, so the wisdom-seeker finds understanding through active pursuit. The promise in verse 13 — blessing for those who find — parallels the temple promise of blessings to those who worthily enter and engage with covenant knowledge.

commentary.christological_typology: In LDS theology, wisdom literature points toward Jesus Christ as Wisdom incarnate (as developed in Jacob 4:13 and expanded in Doctrine and Covenants teachings). To 'find wisdom' is ultimately to find Christ, the source of all understanding. The beatitude formula applied to wisdom-seeking here finds its ultimate fulfillment in the blessedness promised to those who believe in and hold fast to Christ.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 13 invites honest self-examination: Are you actively seeking wisdom, or are you passively hoping wisdom will find you? The verse promises blessedness not to the wise but to the seeker — to those who understand that acquiring understanding requires disciplined effort. In the context of discipleship, this means engaging scripture study, seeking counsel, following prophetic guidance, and reflecting prayerfully on life's experiences. The beatitude is not for the comfortably satisfied but for those who recognize their need and actively pursue greater understanding. This is particularly relevant during FHE, personal scripture study, and in teaching situations: blessing belongs to those who earnestly seek.

text_kjv: For the merchandise of it is better than the merchandise of silver, and the gain thereof than fine gold.

commentary.narrative: The economic metaphor deepens the value proposition established in verse 13. If verse 13 declares blessing for the wisdom-seeker, verse 14 explains why: wisdom's return on investment exceeds all precious metals. The Hebrew 'sachrah' refers specifically to commercial profit or merchant trade, suggesting that wisdom functions like a high-yielding investment portfolio. In ancient Near Eastern commerce, silver and gold were the ultimate standards of wealth — the currency against which all other goods were measured. To claim that wisdom's 'sachrah' (trade-profit) surpasses silver, and her 'tebu'atah' (yield, harvest, income) surpasses even 'charutz' (fine gold, pure gold), is to establish wisdom as the supreme commodity. This is not hyperbole but a systematic revaluation of values. The text inverts the standard hierarchy: what people normally pursue (wealth) is less valuable than what they should pursue (wisdom).
commentary.narrative_continued: The language of merchant trade runs throughout Proverbs, reflecting a society where commercial activity was understood and valued. Proverbs 31 describes the woman of strength engaging in commerce (31:14, 31:18, 31:24), and Proverbs 11:15 and 20:14 invoke the marketplace as a metaphor for moral exchange. But here, wisdom itself becomes the supreme investment. The metaphor is not merely poetic; it is practical. The teacher is addressing people who understand profit and loss, investment and yield. In their own language and conceptual world, he is arguing that wisdom outperforms every competitor. The repetition of comparative language ('better than,' 'surpasses') creates a sense of decisive superiority. This is not a marginal advantage; wisdom leaves silver and gold behind.

word_study.meaning: Trade, commerce, merchandise, profit from trading. Derived from the root 'schr' (to trade, to merchandise). The term specifically denotes the activity of buying and selling and the profit generated thereby.
word_study.significance: By invoking merchant terminology, the text speaks to the audience in its own idiom. Wisdom is presented not as an abstract philosophical good but as a concrete economic asset with measurable returns. The term legitimizes the pursuit of wisdom by framing it in the commercial language the listener understands.

word_study.meaning: Yield, harvest, income, produce. Derived from the root 'yb' (to bring forth, to produce). Originally refers to agricultural harvest but extends metaphorically to any productive output or income.
word_study.significance: The shift from 'sachrah' (merchant profit) to 'tebu'ah' (harvest/yield) adds a second metaphor: wisdom is also like a productive field that yields abundant harvest. The combination of commercial and agricultural imagery suggests that wisdom generates returns through multiple channels — not merely immediate profit but sustainable, growing yield.

word_study.meaning: Fine gold, pure gold, gold that has been refined and separated from base metals. The root suggests cutting, division, or refinement — charutz is gold that has been cut away from impurity.
word_study.significance: Charutz represents gold in its highest form — the ultimate luxury material of the ancient world. To claim wisdom surpasses even this superlative category is to place wisdom above any conceivable earthly treasure. The word choice also suggests refinement: wisdom, like refined gold, is precious because impurity has been removed.

cross_references.connection: Wisdom speaks: 'Receive my instruction, and not silver; and knowledge rather than choice gold. For wisdom is better than rubies; and all the things that may be desired are not to be compared to it.' — a direct parallel where wisdom herself repudiates material wealth as inferior.

Job's discourse on wisdom describes an extensive search for wisdom as more valuable than gold, silver, precious stones, and jewels — establishing wisdom's supremacy across the wisdom literature tradition.

The woman of strength ('eshet chayil') is valued 'far above rubies' — using the same evaluative framework applied to wisdom, suggesting that wisdom and virtuous strength are interconnected commodities.

The Lord teaches that 'all things have their price in the sight of God' — establishing a divine economics that revalues earthly goods according to their true spiritual worth, paralleling Proverbs' inversion of material values.

Jesus' parable of the merchant seeking goodly pearls describes one who 'when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it' — replicating Proverbs' logic that wisdom justifies the surrender of all material goods.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Levantine economy, silver and gold were the ultimate standards of wealth and the basis of long-distance commerce. The Amarna Letters reveal that kings and rulers calculated tribute and trade in precise weights of precious metals. Proverbs' audience would have understood the absolute supremacy of gold and silver in their economic system. By claiming wisdom surpasses these, the text is making a shocking revaluation. Ancient Egyptian wisdom literature (such as the Instruction of Ptahhotep) similarly emphasizes the value of wisdom above material goods, suggesting a shared ancient Near Eastern conviction that the truly wealthy person is wise, not merely monetarily rich. The commercial language also reflects the cosmopolitan context of Proverbs: this is wisdom literature from a trading society that understood commerce and profit in sophisticated ways.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 37:43-45 presents a Restoration parallel: Alma treasures the brass plates and stone records, recognizing that the knowledge they contain is worth more than all material possession. The Book of Mormon consistently revalues worldly goods according to spiritual value: 'Wherefore, do not spend money for that which is of no worth, nor your labor for that which cannot satisfy' (2 Nephi 9:51).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:32 teaches that in the last days, the righteous 'shall cast all their treasures into the treasury of the Lord.' This revaluation of material goods in light of spiritual priorities directly applies Proverbs' principle. D&C 6:7 declares that no one 'can serve two masters' — implying the fundamental choice between material and spiritual investment that Proverbs 3:14 invokes.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant involves the voluntary surrender of all earthly possessions (symbolically) in exchange for exaltation and eternal life — a lived enactment of the principle in verse 14 that wisdom justifies the relinquishment of material wealth. The endowment path explicitly revalues earthly goods in light of heavenly knowledge.

commentary.christological_typology: In Latter-day Saint theology, Christ is identified as Wisdom (see Jacob 4:13). To value wisdom above all material goods is ultimately to value Christ above all earthly possessions — fulfilling the principle that 'no man can serve two masters' (Matthew 6:24) and that disciples must be willing to 'take up his cross and follow me' (Matthew 16:24), surrendering all else.
commentary.application: Verse 14 confronts modern members with a radical challenge: What am I actually investing in? The verse suggests that time, energy, and resources devoted to acquiring material wealth are time diverted from wisdom. This is not an ascetic rejection of earning a living, but a call to right prioritization. If wisdom's yield is superior to gold, then reading scripture should be valued above the extra work hours that buy luxury goods. Seeking counsel should take priority over hoarding resources. Studying doctrine should claim time that might otherwise go to entertainment or status-seeking. The verse invites a practical audit: Am I arranging my life so that wisdom-seeking yields the greatest return?

text_kjv: She is more precious than rubies: and all the things thou canst desire are not to be compared unto her.

commentary.narrative: This verse intensifies the valuation of wisdom by moving from comparative economic analysis (verse 14) to an absolute assertion: nothing you desire can compare with her. The image shifts from commercial profit and harvest to precious gems — specifically 'peninim,' which scholars identify variously as pearls, corals, or rubies, but which in any case represents the highest category of gemstone. The use of feminine language ('she,' 'her') personalizes wisdom as a woman of surpassing beauty and value, a literary device developed fully in Proverbs 8. What is striking about this verse is its logical absoluteness: not merely that wisdom is more valuable than specific goods (silver, gold, rubies), but that 'all the things thou canst desire are not to be compared unto her.' This eliminates every rival entirely. In Hebrew, 'kol chafatzekha' (all your desires, all your delights) encompasses everything a person might want or wish for — not merely material goods but any conceivable object of human longing. The verse claims universal superiority for wisdom.
commentary.narrative_continued: The rhetorical force of this verse lies in its absoluteness and its appeal to the listener's own experience of desire. Rather than telling you what you should want, the text acknowledges what you actually do want — 'all the things thou canst desire' — and then asserts that wisdom exceeds all of it. This is not renunciation but reorientation. You do not need to suppress desire; you need to redirect it toward the true object of desire. The feminine personification of wisdom creates a subtle shift: wisdom is not merely an abstract quality but a woman who can be loved, embraced, held (as verse 18 will develop). The comparison to 'peninim' (the highest precious materials) implies that wisdom itself is beautiful, lustrous, and worthy of aesthetic appreciation. Ancient listeners would have associated precious gems with royalty, prestige, and power — all things humans naturally desire. To claim wisdom surpasses all of this is to offer wisdom as the ultimate status symbol, the ultimate beauty, the ultimate treasure.

word_study.meaning: Precious, valuable, honored, weighty. Derived from the root 'qr' (to be heavy, valuable, honored). The term denotes not merely material value but weight, significance, and dignity.
word_study.significance: Yekarah encompasses both market value and intrinsic worth. Wisdom is not merely expensive; it is objectively weighty and dignified. The root resonates with 'kavod' (honor, glory, weight), suggesting that wisdom carries absolute significance in the order of creation.

word_study.meaning: Generally understood as precious gems or stones, possibly pearls, corals, or ruby-like materials. The exact identification is debated by scholars, but the term consistently denotes items of the highest material value. The word appears in Job 28:18 in an identical comparison, and in Proverbs 31:10 in reference to the woman of strength.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering helpfully notes the identification uncertainty, reflecting scholarly consensus. Regardless of the precise material, 'peninim' represents the pinnacle of precious items — the most rare and valuable gemstones available in the ancient world. By claiming wisdom surpasses peninim, the text places wisdom at the apex of value.

word_study.meaning: Desires, delights, things desired, things one takes pleasure in. From the root 'chfz' (to delight in, to desire). The term encompasses both conscious wishes and deep longings.
word_study.significance: The plural form 'chafatzekha' (your delights, your desires) suggests the totality of human yearning — not merely one specific wish but the full range of human want. The verse's claim is that wisdom surpasses every possible object of desire, eliminating all alternatives.

cross_references.connection: Job's parallel passage describes an extensive search for wisdom as more valuable than topaz, gold, coral, crystal, and rubies — establishing wisdom's universal supremacy across the wisdom tradition.
Wisdom speaks: 'For wisdom is better than rubies; and all the things that may be desired are not to be compared to it' — nearly identical wording, with wisdom herself making the declaration.
The woman of strength is described as 'far above rubies' — using the same framework, suggesting that wisdom and virtue are interconnected supreme values.
Jesus teaches: 'Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth...But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven' — replicating Proverbs' principle that spiritual goods surpass material treasures.
The Lord teaches the seeker that those who 'shall give diligent heed to the words of eternal life' shall find — establishing that eternal knowledge surpasses all earthly acquisition.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern culture, precious gems were not merely luxury items but symbols of power, divine favor, and immortality. They adorned temples, crowned rulers, and were buried with the deceased to accompany them into the afterlife. The accumulation of gemstones was a marker of wealth and status that transcended mere money. Egyptian tomb inscriptions frequently celebrate the placement of precious stones in sacred contexts. By claiming wisdom surpasses peninim, Proverbs elevates wisdom into the category of items that were understood to carry spiritual and cosmic significance. The parallel in Job 28:18, which also compares wisdom to peninim, suggests that this comparison was a standard formula in Israelite wisdom tradition. The feminine personification of wisdom reflects a broader pattern in ancient Near Eastern literature where abstract qualities (Egyptian Ma'at, Mesopotamian Me) were personified as female figures of supreme value.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Jacob 4:14, Jacob teaches that 'none of these iniquities come unto our descendants' if they hearken unto the words of the prophets — the core principle being that words of divine wisdom redeem and perfect what material might never purchase. The Book of Mormon repeatedly invokes the 'precious' language: the 'more precious than silver' plates (Alma 37:3), the 'precious promises' of salvation (Moroni 10:34) — systematically revaluing goods according to spiritual worth.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:34-36 teaches that the 'rights of the priesthood' cannot be exercised 'in any degree of unrighteousness' — implying that spiritual authority is a treasure for which no compromise is acceptable. D&C 82:3 states that 'in consequence of covenants broken,' people lose their inheritance — reinforcing that covenant knowledge and obedience are the supreme goods, surpassing all earthly acquisition.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment promises access to divine knowledge and eternal life — the supreme precious goods in LDS theology. The covenant to live by sacred principles is offered in exchange for the relinquishment of earthly focus. The temple clothing symbolizes the taking on of heavenly raiment, representing the aesthetic and material superiority of spiritual realities to worldly glamour.

commentary.christological_typology: In LDS teaching, Jesus Christ is Wisdom incarnate (Jacob 4:13). The comparison of wisdom to the most precious materials points typologically to the declaration that Christ is 'more precious than all else' — that the knowledge of His atonement, the reality of His Resurrection, and the covenant He offers surpass any earthly good. The feminine personification of wisdom in Proverbs also prefigures the Bride of the Lamb metaphor in Revelation, where Christ's people are united with Him as their supreme treasure.
commentary.application: For modern disciples, verse 15 poses a searching question: If someone were to catalog everything you actually pursue — in terms of time, energy, money, and focus — would wisdom appear as your supreme value? The verse suggests a radical reorientation of desire itself. Rather than overcoming desire, the listener is invited to redirect desire toward the true object. This is not about guilt-driven renunciation of normal wants, but about recognizing that wisdom itself is beautiful, honorable, and worthy of devotion. In practical terms: Are you treating scripture study as a chore or as a precious thing to be desired? Are you treating prophetic counsel as instruction or as a treasure? Are you pursuing the acquisition of eternal knowledge with the same intensity you pursue material security or social status? The verse invites a recalibration of what you actually count as precious.

text_kjv: Length of days is in her right hand; and in her left hand riches and honour.

commentary.narrative: The personification of wisdom reaches its visual apex in this verse: she is depicted as a woman extending both hands, offering complete and comprehensive blessing. The image is vivid and memorable — wisdom is not an abstract principle but a living figure who actively bestows good. The right hand holds 'orekh yamim' (length of days, long life, extended years), and the left hand holds 'osher ve-khavod' (riches and honor, wealth and dignity). This creates a bipartite promise: wisdom offers both longevity and prosperity, both duration and dignity. In ancient thought, long life was understood not merely as extended years but as a sign of God's favor, a reward for righteousness, and the context in which all other goods could be enjoyed. Without long life, wealth and honor were hollow prizes. But wisdom offers both. The image of extending hands is rich with resonance: it evokes the giving of blessing (as in priestly blessing), the offering of gifts (as in hospitality), and the gesture of welcome. Wisdom actively extends both goods to those who hold her.
commentary.narrative_continued: The comparison to Egyptian iconography (as noted in the translator's notes) is instructive. The goddess Ma'at, representing divine order and truth, was similarly depicted with life in one hand and prosperity in the other — suggesting that this image of dual blessing reflected broader ancient Near Eastern concepts of how divine order manifested in human flourishing. The specificity of 'right hand' and 'left hand' may carry further significance: in ancient Hebrew thought, the right hand was the position of honor and strength (as in the concept of God's right hand), while the left hand was subsidiary. Yet both hands offer genuine goods. The pairing of 'riches and honor' (osher ve-khavod) itself deserves attention: wealth without honor is viewed as corrupting (seen throughout Proverbs in descriptions of fools who acquire riches), while honor without wealth is socially precarious. But wisdom offers them together, in proper proportion. The verse does not promise unlimited wealth or absolute immortality, but appropriate long life and fitting prosperity to those who wisely order their affairs.

word_study.meaning: Length of days, long life, extended years. 'Orekh' (length, duration, extent) combined with 'yamim' (days). In Hebrew thought, length of days was a primary measure of blessing and divine favor.
word_study.significance: Long life was understood as both a practical good (more years to enjoy fruits of labor) and a theological sign of covenant blessing. Throughout Proverbs, obedience and wisdom are connected to longevity, while foolishness and wickedness are connected to premature death. The promise here is not immortality but the natural lifespan enjoyed as a gift from God.

word_study.meaning: Right hand, the position of honor and strength. In Hebrew usage, the right side carries connotations of strength, blessing, and supremacy (as in 'My right hand shall uphold thee,' Isaiah 41:10).
word_study.significance: That long life is specifically in the right hand (rather than the left) emphasizes its primacy. Life itself is the supreme good, the necessary condition for all other blessings. The right hand position suggests that wisdom grants life not by chance but by design — as the primary and supreme offering.

word_study.meaning: Left hand, the subsidiary side. In contrast to the right hand, the left hand represents secondary but genuine blessing.
word_study.significance: The placement of riches and honor in the left hand, while life is in the right, creates a proper hierarchy of values. Material goods are genuine blessings from wisdom, but they are secondary to life itself. A wise person values longevity and health before wealth and status.

word_study.meaning: Wealth and honor/glory. 'Osher' (wealth, riches) refers to material abundance, while 'kavod' (honor, glory, dignity, weight) refers to social standing, respect, and dignity.
word_study.significance: The pairing of osher and kavod appears throughout Proverbs as the comprehensive material-social good that wisdom enables. But importantly, they are paired: wisdom does not promise wealth at the cost of honor, nor honor at the cost of integrity. Proverbs contrasts sharply with the fool who gains wealth through dishonest means, sacrificing honor. Wisdom offers both in proper alignment.

cross_references.connection: The Lord promises: 'With long life will I satisfy him, and shew him my salvation' — linking long life directly to divine blessing and salvation, paralleling Proverbs' connection between wisdom and longevity.
The command to honor parents comes 'that thy days may be long upon the land' — establishing in Torah itself that righteousness and wisdom lead to extended life.
A parallel principle: 'The fear of the Lord prolongeth days: but the years of the wicked shall be shortened' — confirming that wisdom-seeking (manifested in the fear of the Lord) leads to longevity.

'By humility and the fear of the Lord are riches, and honour, and life' — offering the same tripartite blessing (riches, honor, life) as verse 16, emphasizing that all three flow from wisdom-based living.

The Word of Wisdom promises that those who obey 'shall receive health in their navel and marrow to their bones; And shall find wisdom and great treasures of knowledge, even hidden treasures' — directly applying Proverbs' principle of wisdom leading to both physical well-being and prosperity.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern societies, long life was a primary marker of blessing and divine favor. Egyptian wisdom literature similarly promises that following ma'at (order/truth) leads to long life and prosperity. The Mesopotamian concept of 'ume aruka' (long days) was similarly viewed as a sign of the gods' blessing. In Israelite covenant theology, obedience to the covenant brought blessing including health and longevity, while transgression brought curse including plague and shortened life (Deuteronomy 28). The image of the goddess (or in this case, personified wisdom) extending both hands reflects artistic conventions from the ancient Near East where divine or royal figures are depicted offering gifts or blessing. The Proverbs text makes wisdom female, which was an effective pedagogical choice: just as a young man might be drawn to a beautiful woman, so he is drawn to beautiful wisdom, creating an emotionally compelling motivation for seeking wisdom.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 7:14-16 teaches that those who believe in the Son of God 'shall obtain his salvation' and shall be 'brought to stand before him to be judged of him according to the deeds they have done.' The promise includes both eternal life (the ultimate 'length of days') and eternal status ('honor' in standing before God). The promise of 'long life' is transformed in Restoration theology to eternal life.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 59:3 declares that 'the earth is full of the goodness of the Lord,' promising that those who receive wisdom shall also inherit the earth's abundance. D&C 89 (the Word of Wisdom) explicitly promises that obedience brings 'wisdom and great treasures of knowledge, even hidden treasures' — directly connecting wisdom to both spiritual knowledge and material well-being. D&C 42:61 teaches that 'Inasmuch as ye do these things with your might, ye shall receive,' establishing the principle that wise action brings both spiritual and material blessing.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment presents the hands of the Lord extending blessings and knowledge to His people. The covenant of the priesthood (D&C 84:40) promises that those who magnify their callings 'shall receive a fulness of the Holy Ghost,' which in turn brings both spiritual knowledge and earthly blessing. The symbolism of hands extending blessing is central to temple theology, directly paralleling Proverbs 3:16.

commentary.christological_typology: In Latter-day Saint theology, Christ is Wisdom incarnate (Jacob 4:13), and He is depicted as offering 'life' in its fullest sense — eternal life through His atonement (John 5:24, 10:28). The image of wisdom extending both life and honor prefigures Christ extending redemption and exaltation to those who accept His covenant. The 'extending of hands' resonates with the crucifixion narrative (the extended arms on the cross) and with the inclusive gesture of Christ welcoming all to come unto Him.
commentary.application: Verse 16 invites members to trust that wisdom-seeking produces comprehensive blessing — not merely spiritual knowledge that ignores material well-being, but true flourishing that encompasses health, longevity, honest prosperity, and earned honor. This counters a false dichotomy many feel: that becoming spiritual means becoming materially destitute, or that pursuing material security means losing spiritual integrity. The verse promises that wisdom integrates both. In practical terms: Are you making life and health (physical and spiritual) your primary pursuit, trusting that other goods follow? Are you seeking honor through service and integrity rather than through compromise? The verse invites a trust that if we prioritize wisdom and righteousness, we will be blessed with both the duration to enjoy the fruits of our labor and the standing to be respected in our communities. This is less about wealth-accumulation and more about the confidence that a wise and moral life produces sustainable well-being.

text_kjv: Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace.

commentary.narrative: This verse completes the personification of wisdom by describing not merely what she gives, but what she is — her character and the experience of following her. The focus shifts from the rewards of wisdom (long life, riches, honor) to the journey itself. The use of 'ways' (darkhim) and 'paths' (netivot) invokes the fundamental metaphor of life as a journey, where the choices one makes determine the road traveled. Wisdom's roads are characterized by two qualities: 'no'am' (pleasantness, sweetness, beauty, delight) and 'shalom' (peace, wholeness, harmony, well-being). This is a striking claim because it presents wisdom not as a difficult, joyless duty that happens to produce results, but as intrinsically delightful and peaceful. The modern reader influenced by the Protestant work ethic might expect that gaining wisdom requires suffering, discipline, and grim determination. But the Hebrew text insists otherwise: the way of wisdom is pleasant. This does not mean easy — Proverbs throughout acknowledges that fools choose easy paths — but rather that wisdom's path, though demanding, is fundamentally satisfying and beautiful. Every path wisdom offers leads to flourishing.
commentary.narrative_continued: The universality of the claim ('all her paths') is significant. Not merely the major decisions of life, but every moment-by-moment choice within the wisdom path is characterized by peace. This suggests a coherence and integration: a person following wisdom experiences consonance between intention and action, belief and behavior. There is no internal conflict between what one claims to value and how one actually lives. The term 'no'am' (pleasantness) is particularly evocative in Hebrew. It denotes not merely the absence of pain, but the presence of beauty, sweetness, and delight. In Psalm 27:4, the psalmist seeks 'to behold the beauty [no'am] of the Lord.' The application of this term to wisdom's paths elevates them beyond mere functionality to genuine loveliness. And 'shalom' extends beyond mere absence of conflict; it denotes completeness, wholeness, the full integration of all things in their proper place. A person walking wisdom's paths experiences not merely avoiding evil but actively experiencing harmony — with God, with self, and with others.

word_study.meaning: Ways, paths, roads. Both terms employ the fundamental life-journey metaphor. 'Darkhim' (ways) is the more common term, while 'netivot' (paths) adds a sense of specific, worn paths — trails that are established and known.
word_study.significance: The repetition of journey metaphors emphasizes that wisdom is not a destination but a way of living. The choice of 'netivot' (worn paths) suggests that these are not newly invented roads but ancient, established ways proven by generations of the wise.

word_study.meaning: Pleasantness, sweetness, beauty, delight, grace. A noun form suggesting something that is innately beautiful and satisfying. The word appears in Psalm 27:4 ('to behold the beauty of the Lord') and Psalm 90:17 (the beauty of the Lord), suggesting associations with divine loveliness.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's choice of 'delight' captures the active, positive quality of the experience. This is not the absence of unpleasantness, but the presence of genuine joy and beauty. The application of this term to wisdom's ways elevates them beyond mere efficiency to loveliness.

word_study.meaning: Peace, wholeness, completeness, harmony, well-being. A comprehensive term denoting the full integration of all things in their right place — peace with God, peace with others, peace within oneself.
word_study.significance: Shalom is not merely the absence of conflict, but the presence of flourishing — when all things are in right relationship. The promise here is that wisdom's path produces shalom: internal coherence, relational harmony, and spiritual well-being. This is the opposite of the fragmentation and discord that result from folly.

cross_references.connection: David declares: 'In thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore' — using 'no'am' (pleasantness) similarly to describe the experience of righteous living in God's presence.
'In the way of righteousness is life; and in the pathway thereof there is no death' — parallel assertion that the way of wisdom is characterized by life and wholeness, not fragmentation and death.
'Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee' — the same promise of shalom resulting from alignment with God's way, matching Proverbs' claim that wisdom's paths are peace.
'When wisdom entereth into thine heart, and knowledge is pleasant unto thy soul' — linking the pleasantness ('no'am') of wisdom's knowledge directly to the interior experience of the wise person.

The Lord teaches: 'Did I not speak peace to your mind concerning the matter?' establishing that divine guidance produces peace in the recipient, paralleling Proverbs' claim that wisdom's paths are peace.

commentary.historical_context: The journey metaphor for life appears throughout ancient Near Eastern literature and is particularly prominent in Proverbs. Egyptian wisdom literature similarly uses the metaphor of walking 'the straight way' or 'the way of Ma'at' (divine order) to describe righteous living. The pairing of pleasantness with moral living reflects a conviction that virtue is not merely obligatory but genuinely satisfying. This counters a common modern misconception that morality is a burden one endures for external reward. The ancient teacher understood that living rightly produces internal satisfaction — that the conscience is quieted, the mind is at rest, and the inner being experiences harmony. The term 'shalom' became central to Israelite theology, eventually denoting not merely peace but the fullness of God's blessing in every dimension of life.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 41:10 teaches that 'wickedness never was happiness' and that 'all that is good cometh of God,' establishing that the path of righteousness is inherently more pleasant than the path of folly. The Book of Mormon repeatedly describes the peace that follows righteous living: 'And it came to pass that the people of Nephi began to prosper again in the land, and began to build up waste places' (Helaman 6:4), linking obedience to flourishing. Jacob 3:1 promises that the righteous shall 'know of a surety that ye have eternal life' through the Spirit, describing the peace that passes understanding.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 19:23 offers a remarkable promise: 'Learn of me, and listen to my words; walk in the meekness of my Spirit, and you shall have peace in me' — directly offering the peace of wisdom's paths. D&C 88:121 teaches that 'cease to be idle; cease to be unclean; cease to find fault one with another; cease to sleep longer than is needful' — offering practical wisdom that, when followed, produces peace.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple experience is designed to produce the 'peace' described in verse 17. The quiet, beautiful setting; the clear instruction; the covenants made with God — all are structured to create shalom: alignment between inner conviction and outer commitment, between self and God. The temple recommend itself is a form of 'walking the ways of wisdom,' and those who engage faithfully report the peace that Proverbs 3:17 describes.

commentary.christological_typology: In New Testament theology, Christ offers the peace described in verse 17: 'My peace I give unto you' (John 14:27). Christ is Wisdom incarnate (1 Corinthians 1:24 in Christian tradition), and to follow Christ is to walk in peace. The 'ways of pleasantness' become the gospel path that produces both internal satisfaction and eternal wholeness.
commentary.application: For modern members, verse 17 offers a profound invitation: Test the claim. If you are currently following a path of wisdom — being honest, serving others, repenting of sins, seeking divine guidance — you should experience internal peace and genuine satisfaction, not merely duty-driven grimness. If your pursuit of righteousness feels joyless and burdensome, the verse suggests you may be missing the 'pleasantness' (no'am) that wisdom genuinely offers. This might mean: (1) Repent of areas where you're still following folly, creating internal discord; (2) Cultivate gratitude for the beauty and goodness in the righteous path you're walking; (3) Recognize that if you're experiencing fragmentation and internal conflict, it may be a sign you've wandered from wisdom's path. The verse is not merely promising future reward but present flourishing. As you make wise choices today — in honesty, kindness, integrity, obedience — those choices should produce a sense of peace and rightness, a consonance between your values and your actions. This is verifiable, not speculative: the person walking wisdom's paths experiences shalom today.

text_kjv: She is a tree of life to them that lay hold upon her: and happy is every one that retaineth her.

commentary.narrative: This verse delivers the climactic image of the hymn to wisdom (verses 13-20). Wisdom is not merely valuable, not merely beautiful, not merely pleasant — she is a 'tree of life.' This phrase resonates across all of scripture with extraordinary theological weight. It appears only in Genesis 2:9 and 3:24 (the tree in Eden from which Adam and Eve were separated by the Fall), here in Proverbs (3:18, 11:30, 13:12, 15:4), and then again in Revelation 22:2 (the tree in the New Jerusalem). By calling wisdom a tree of life, the text makes an audacious claim: what was lost in Eden — access to unending life — is available again through wisdom. The tree of life in Eden was not forbidden to Adam and Eve as punishment but was lost to them when they were driven from the garden following their transgression. The promise here is that through wisdom, that access is restored. The verbs 'machazikim' (those who take hold, those who grasp firmly) and 'tomkheiha' (those who hold her, support her) are visceral and physical: wisdom is not admired from a distance but grasped and held. There is an intentional physicality to this action — you must seize wisdom, grip her, and continue to hold her. And those who do are 'me'ushar' (considered fortunate, blessed) — using the same root as 'ashre' from verse 13, creating a literary frame: the hymn opens with 'ashre' (blessed is the seeker) and closes with 'me'ushar' (blessed are the holders).
commentary.narrative_continued: The theological implications are staggering. The translator's notes rightly point out that 'the way back to Eden runs through wisdom — that the knowledge Adam and Eve seized in violation of God's command is now offered freely to those who fear the LORD.' This reframes the entire narrative: what was lost through transgression is regained through wisdom. Adam and Eve wanted to 'be as God, knowing good and evil' (Genesis 3:5) — they grasped after forbidden knowledge. But here, true knowledge (wisdom) is offered as a tree, freely available to any who will hold it. The image of the tree itself is crucial: a tree is alive, organic, rooted, productive, growing. It is not an abstract principle but something living, something that sustains life. To 'lay hold upon' a tree of life is to grasp something that actually gives life. In the context of Genesis, Adam and Eve's eating from the tree would have given them immortality ('lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever' — Genesis 3:22). So the promise here is that wisdom leads to life — not merely temporal flourishing but the overcoming of death itself.
