word_study.significance: The verse places heart-level joy as the response to the light of another's eyes. This is not superficial happiness but something that touches the person's deepest being.

word_study.meaning: good news, a good report, positive word/message. A communication that brings encouragement or positive information.
word_study.significance: The 'report' might be news about oneself (receiving praise or good standing) or about external circumstances (good news in general). Information affects well-being.

word_study.meaning: makes fat, fattens, enriches, strengthens. From the root dashen, meaning to be fat or to nourish richly.
word_study.significance: In ancient thought, 'fatness' was not negative but positive—a sign of health, strength, prosperity, and vigor. To make the bones fat is to make a person robust and strong.

word_study.meaning: bones, skeletal frame, the fundamental structure of the body. In Hebrew idiom, the bones represent the deepest physical being.
word_study.significance: To affect 'the bones' means to affect one's fundamental physical being and vitality. The verse suggests that good news produces real physiological effects, not merely emotional ones.

cross_references.connection: A merry heart doeth good like a medicine. Proverbs repeatedly affirms the health-giving power of joy and the devastating effects of despair.
Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life. Good news and realized hope produce life and health; the lack produces sickness.
Wherefore comfort yourselves together, and edify one another. The New Testament applies this principle: encouraging words and uplifting presence strengthen others.

And wine that maketh glad the heart of man...that he may make his face to shine. The psalmist uses similar language about what brings joy and vitality, and about the brightening effect of joy on appearance.
Jesus wept, expressing his deep emotional response to human need and faith. The Book of Mormon affirms that genuine human emotion and warmth are divine attributes.

commentary.historical_context: The verse reflects ancient wisdom about the integrated nature of human beings—body, emotion, and spirit are not separate domains but a unified whole. In an agricultural society without modern medicine, the correlation between emotional state and health was more visible and more understood than in modern times. A person living under chronic stress (like the wicked person in verse 29, alienated from God) would visibly deteriorate: loss of appetite, weight loss, weakened resistance to disease. Conversely, someone experiencing joy and peace would flourish physically. The proverb likely draws on careful observation of how people in the community responded to good or bad news. A farmer receiving news that his crops would prosper would experience visible relaxation and vigor. The verse also reflects the social importance of facial expression and greeting in ancient Near Eastern culture. A warm welcome—indicated by the brightness of the eyes and openness of the face—was a form of honor and blessing. To be greeted with 'the light of the eyes' was to be treated as valued, as someone worth the gift of genuine warmth.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Helaman 5:12-13 teaches that Nephi and Lehi were filled with joy and received the Holy Ghost, and their joy was so evident that 'they did shine exceedingly' and had power to imprison those who came against them. The brightness and joy of the righteous have visible, even miraculous power. Mosiah 4:11-12 teaches that receiving God's mercy produces internal joy that must flow outward in service and kindness to others.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 59:23-24 promises that those who keep the Lord's commandments shall receive an abundance of peace, and the Lord shall give them power to overcome all things. The fullness of the gospel produces both spiritual and physical well-being. D&C 122:7-8 teaches that trials are for the righteous person's good and will eventually work for their benefit—suggesting that faith produces an interior peace that affects countenance and health.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that living covenant produces gladness and peace. Temple worshippers report experiencing joy and a sense of well-being during and after temple attendance. The principle that relational alignment with God (through the temple) produces visible brightness and vitality is embedded in temple culture.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate embodiment of 'the light of the eyes'—his gaze was filled with compassion, and his presence brought healing and joy. The Gospel accounts repeatedly record that people experienced transformation and gladness in Christ's presence. His Resurrection is the ultimate 'good report'—the proclamation that death is overcome and life eternal is secured. His continual intercession for us (as the righteous prayed to God in verse 29) is the ultimate source of the good news that produces strength and vitality in the souls of believers.
commentary.application: This verse is a gentle but powerful call to recognize the power of your presence and expression toward others. The 'light of your eyes'—your smile, your warmth, your genuine interest in others—is not a small thing but something that literally affects others' well-being and joy. For people working in care, leadership, or service: your facial expression and demeanor matter profoundly. A nurse, teacher, or leader whose eyes shine with care and genuine concern heals in ways that go beyond the task itself. For individuals: pay attention to the power of good news and positive reports. Seek out encouraging information and relationships; avoid those that constantly drain and discourage. Recognize the connection between joy and physical vitality—joy is not luxury but a form of medicine. For families: creating a home where people experience the 'light of the eyes' in each other's faces is creating an environment of health and strength. A critical, cold, dismissive family environment produces literal deterioration; a warm, affirming family environment produces flourishing. The verse invites us to take seriously the power of our emotional presence with others and to use that power as a form of blessing and healing.

text_kjv: The ear that heareth the reproof of life abideth among the wise.

commentary.narrative:
This verse establishes a fundamental principle: receptivity to correction is the gateway to wisdom. The Hebrew phrase "ear that listens to life-giving correction" (ozen shoma'at tokhachat chayyim) portrays reproof not as punishment but as medicine — painful perhaps, but vital and life-sustaining. The person who can hear such correction and integrate it into their life naturally gravitates toward and dwells among the wise. The verb talin ("will dwell, will lodge") suggests both a present state and an ongoing residence; the wise community becomes the natural habitat of the one who accepts rebuke.

Ancient wisdom literature recognized that the human capacity to receive criticism separates the fool from the wise. This is countercultural in any age: most people defend their ego rather than defend their future. But Proverbs insists that the "ear that hears" — the person with genuine intellectual humility — becomes part of a community of wisdom. This is not about mere intellectual knowledge but about practical wisdom that shapes how one lives. The reproof discussed here is not malicious critique but correction aimed at life (chayyim) — at enabling the person to flourish.

word_study.meaning: The ear as the organ of hearing, but metonymically representing receptivity, obedience, and attentiveness. In Hebrew thought, the ear is the gateway to understanding because hearing precedes comprehension.
word_study.significance: The focus on the ear emphasizes that wisdom begins with listening. In covenant language, "hearing" often means covenantal obedience (shema Israel). The ear that listens is the ear aligned with truth.

word_study.meaning: Rebuke, correction, reproval. The term carries the sense of conviction or confrontation aimed at correction. It is verbal correction that exposes error with the goal of amendment.
word_study.significance: Tokhachat is not gentle feedback but sharp correction. That Proverbs frames this as 'life-giving' (chayyim) shows that true wisdom embraces uncomfortable truth. In Latter-day Saint terms, this aligns with how prophetic correction is framed as necessary for spiritual survival.

word_study.meaning: Life in its fullest sense — vitality, flourishing, duration, and well-being. Not mere existence but abundant living.
word_study.significance: The reproof is 'life-giving' because it preserves and enhances life. Refusing correction leads to slow death; accepting it leads to flourishing. This echoes the choice in Deuteronomy between blessing and curse, life and death.

word_study.meaning: To lodge, to dwell, to abide. Conveys a sense of taking up residence, finding one's home.
word_study.significance: The wise community becomes the dwelling place of the person who accepts correction. It is not a temporary visit but a residence — an identity shift toward wisdom.

cross_references.connection: A wise son heareth his father's instruction; connects the receptivity to correction across the family and wisdom community contexts.
Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser; shows that the wise continuously grow through correction.
Smite a scorner, and the simple will beware; establishes the contrast between those who accept and those who reject correction.
If ye reject the words of the prophets, ye shall be visited with blindness; parallels the Book of Mormon's teaching that refusing correction leads to spiritual blindness.

Whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same; shows that in Restoration doctrine, receptivity to correction—whether from God directly or through servants—opens pathways to truth.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern wisdom traditions, the ability to receive correction was a hallmark of the educated and the elite. Ancient Egyptian wisdom texts (such as the Teaching of Ptahhotep) similarly exalt the man who listens to instruction. In Israelite culture, the household and court contexts required young men to develop the ability to hear reproof from fathers, elders, and kings. The person who could not accept correction was seen as undisciplined and dangerous—a threat to the family and the state. The 'wise' (chakhamim) were not merely intelligent but were trained, humble practitioners of traditional knowledge who understood that their own perception was limited and required constant refinement through the wisdom of the community.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon frequently contrasts those who 'harden their hearts against the word' (Alma 15:3) with those who are 'willing to receive the word of God' (Alma 32:6). Alma's teachings on faith and receptivity echo Proverbs 15:31's principle that openness to correction leads to spiritual dwelling among the righteous. The trajectory of Nephite and Lamanite history pivots on whether people will hear and accept prophetic correction.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 21:4-6 emphasizes the importance of hearkening to the president of the Church for guidance and correction. The principle that the 'ear that listens' finds itself among the wise is embedded in the Latter-day Saint practice of sustained leadership and the covenant to follow living prophets. The structure of the Church itself is built on the assumption that members will listen to correction from those called to lead.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes the principle of receiving instruction and correction in righteousness. The temple endowment portrays the journey of learning through listening, and the covenants themselves are a form of 'life-giving correction'—they redirect human will toward God's purposes.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ exemplified perfect receptivity to the Father's will. His willingness to listen, learn, and submit to correction (even though He was sinless and needed no correction) modeled the humility described in Proverbs 15:31. His exhortation to 'take up thy cross and follow me' is an invitation to embrace correction and discipline as the path to eternal life. The wise community that Christ builds is composed of those who hear His voice and follow Him.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse invites examination of how we respond to correction—from spouses, parents, Church leaders, prophets, and even the Spirit's quiet promptings. Do we listen with the intent to improve, or do we defend ourselves? The verse suggests that willingness to hear reproof is not weakness but the entrance fee to wisdom and to community with the wise. In a culture obsessed with validation and affirmation, Proverbs 15:31 calls us to cultivate what might be called 'correctability'—the spiritual maturity to receive feedback and change course.

text_kjv: He that refuseth instruction despiseth his own soul: but he that heareth reproof getteth understanding.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 32 sharpens the contrast introduced in verse 31. To refuse discipline is not a neutral choice—it is an act of self-contempt. The Hebrew phrase pore'a musar mo'es nafsho ('one who rejects discipline despises his own soul/life') frames the rejection of correction as a form of self-sabotage so profound it constitutes self-hatred. This is theologically striking: to refuse guidance that could improve one's life is, in the logic of Proverbs, to actively despise oneself. The person who will not hear reproof is literally choosing destruction over flourishing, which amounts to choosing death over life.

The second half of the verse presents the alternative: whoever listens to correction (shome'a tokhachat) qoneh lev—'acquires heart,' or as the KJV renders it, 'getteth understanding.' The Covenant Rendering notes that 'the heart can be purchased through the currency of humility.' This captures something profound: understanding is not bestowed on the passive observer but is actively acquired by those willing to pay the price of accepting hard truths about themselves. The parallelism between the two halves makes it clear that there is no middle ground. One either despises one's own soul through refusal, or acquires a functioning heart through receptivity.

word_study.meaning: To reject, to let go, to dismiss. The root suggests actively pushing away or disregarding something that has been offered.
word_study.significance: This is not passive ignorance but active rejection. The person who refuses discipline makes a choice to push away what could save them.

word_study.meaning: Discipline, instruction, correction, training. The term connotes the painful but necessary shaping of character through discipline. It is not mere information but formative discipline.
word_study.significance: Musar is the instrument by which the soul is shaped and trained. To reject musar is to reject the very process by which one becomes wise and whole. In rabbinic Judaism, musar (ethical discipline) became a major focus of spiritual practice.

word_study.meaning: To despise, to treat with contempt, to reject with disgust. Strong language indicating revulsion and disdain.
word_study.significance: The person who refuses correction expresses contempt for their own soul. This is not a mild disagreement but a profound act of self-rejection. In the logic of Proverbs, to refuse correction is to express self-hatred.

word_study.meaning: The soul, the self, the seat of desires and the life-force. In Hebrew psychology, the nephesh is the integrated whole of the person—not a disembodied spirit but the living person in their totality.
word_study.significance: To despise one's nafsho is to despise oneself completely. The rejection of correction is framed as self-contempt at the deepest level of being.

word_study.meaning: To hear, to listen, to obey. In Hebrew thought, hearing implies more than passive audition; it includes comprehension and responsive action.
word_study.significance: The shome'a (hearer) is the one who both listens and responds. This is covenantal language—the shema of 'Hear O Israel' is not mere listening but committed obedience.

word_study.meaning: Rebuke, correction, reproval; verbal confrontation aimed at amendment.
word_study.significance: As in verse 31, tokhachat is the sharp word of truth spoken to correct course. Hearing it leads to the acquisition of understanding.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'acquires heart' or 'purchases heart.' Qoneh means to acquire, buy, or obtain; lev (heart) in Hebrew psychology is the seat of understanding, wisdom, and will.
word_study.significance: Understanding is not passive knowledge but something actively acquired through the discipline of accepting correction. The Covenant Rendering's note that the heart is 'purchased through the currency of humility' captures the transactional nature: one pays the price of swallowing one's pride and receives understanding in return. This aligns with the principle that wisdom has a cost.

cross_references.connection: He is in the way of life that keepeth instruction: but he that refuseth reproof erreth; directly parallels the choice between life and error.
Apply thine heart unto instruction, and thine ears to the words of knowledge; emphasizes the active acquisition of understanding through receptivity.
To obey is better than sacrifice; Saul's refusal to hear Samuel's correction led to his rejection as king, illustrating the consequences of despising reproof.

And now Alma began to expound these things unto him, saying: It is given unto many to know the mysteries of God; nevertheless they are laid under a strict command that they shall not impart only according as they are directed... those who harden their hearts; illustrates the Book of Mormon's teaching that understanding is conditional on receptivity to correction.

Therefore, fear not, little flock; do good; let earth and hell combine against you, for if ye are built upon my rock, they cannot prevail; affirms that those who listen to God's word and correction are built on a foundation that endures.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern societies, the refusal of instruction was seen as profoundly dangerous—not merely to the individual but to the social order. An undisciplined person was a liability to family, tribe, and state. The concept of 'despising one's own soul' would have resonated with the understanding that to refuse wisdom is to actively choose a path toward destruction. In the royal courts of the ancient Levant, advisors who refused the king's correction could be executed; the principle that one's own refusal to hear amounts to self-contempt gave philosophical weight to such practical consequences. The language of 'acquiring the heart' reflects the ancient understanding that understanding was not a matter of mere intellectual capacity but of character development—the heart had to be trained and formed through discipline.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma's teachings on the 'natural man' (Mosiah 3:19) include the observation that the natural man opposes correction and rebels against the word of God. The Book of Mormon portrays refusal to hear correction as the beginning of spiritual death. Conversely, those who humble themselves and accept correction (like the people of King Benjamin) experience spiritual life and understanding.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:24-28 describes the consequences of refusing the Lord's word—the strong will perish and the meek will inherit. The principle that refusal of correction leads to self-destruction is central to D&C theology. Conversely, those who receive the word and reproof gain understanding and guidance.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple represents the acquisition of understanding (lev) through receptivity to sacred instruction and covenants. One cannot progress through the temple while resisting its teachings; progression requires the humility to hear and respond to instruction.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the embodiment of the one who 'hears reproof' in the highest sense. In Gethsemane, His prayer 'Not my will, but thine be done' shows perfect receptivity to the Father's correction and redirection of His own desires. His willingness to accept the cross—the ultimate reproof of human sin and the ultimate correction of human course—enabled the acquisition of divine understanding and the salvation of all who hear and follow Him.
commentary.application: This verse invites honest self-assessment: When I receive criticism, do I listen defensively or receptively? Do I dismiss feedback too quickly, or do I pause to consider whether there is truth in it? The verse suggests that every moment of resisting reproof is a moment of despising my own soul—of choosing a path toward spiritual diminishment. Conversely, every moment I accept correction and integrate it is a moment of acquiring understanding and moving toward wisdom. In marriage, parenting, and Church community, this principle transforms how we engage with feedback. It reframes correction not as an attack but as an opportunity to acquire the understanding that leads to flourishing.

text_kjv: The fear of the LORD is the instruction of wisdom; and before honour is humility.

commentary.narrative:
This verse serves as the climactic summary of Proverbs 15 and unites the chapter's dominant themes: the fear of the Lord, discipline, wisdom, and the proper ordering of human ambition. The opening assertion—'The fear of the LORD is the instruction of wisdom' (yir'at Yahweh musar chokhmah)—establishes that reverence for God is not separate from the pursuit of wisdom but is identical to it. The fear of the Lord is not craven terror but the foundational posture of receiving God's instruction. God Himself is the Supreme Teacher, and the fear of Him is the discipline that shapes wisdom in the human soul.

The second half of the verse—'before honour is humility' (lifne khavod anavah)—reveals the paradoxical pathway to genuine honor. Those who grasp for honor directly miss it; honor comes to those who have already surrendered the quest for it through humility. This is not a counsel of passivity but of right ordering: the person who first establishes themselves in humility before God becomes capable of receiving honor that is genuine and lasting. The verse closes the chapter with a profound reordering of human values. In a world that pursues honor, wealth, and power directly, Proverbs insists that the pathway to these goods runs through the fear of God and humility. This theme echoes throughout the Restoration—the meek shall inherit the earth, the last shall be first, the servant is the greatest.

word_study.meaning: Fear in the sense of reverence, awe, respect, and the fear of God. Not mere terror but the trembling awe that comes from encountering the divine. It connotes a mixture of fear, respect, obedience, and love.
word_study.significance: Yirat Adonai (fear of the Lord) is the cornerstone of wisdom in Hebrew Scripture. It is the posture of the creature before the Creator—acknowledging both God's power and His authority over one's life. In Latter-day Saint terms, it approaches the reverent submission implied in 'thy will be done.'

word_study.meaning: The covenant name of God in Israel; the God who made and sustains the covenants with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and the God who redeemed Israel from Egypt.
word_study.significance: The use of the divine name (rather than Elohim, God in general) emphasizes the covenantal relationship. The fear of the Lord is fear of the covenant God, the God who has bound Himself to Israel.

word_study.meaning: Discipline, instruction, training, correction. The formative discipline by which character is shaped.
word_study.significance: As in verses 31-32, musar is the instrument of transformation. The fear of the Lord IS the discipline by which wisdom is formed in the human heart. To fear God is to submit to His shaping, molding discipline.

word_study.meaning: Wisdom, insight, understanding, practical skill. Not mere knowledge but the integrated understanding of how to live well in alignment with reality and God's order.
word_study.significance: Chokmah is the supreme good of Proverbs. This verse insists that true wisdom begins not with intellectual attainment but with the fear of God—with proper alignment to the divine reality.

word_study.meaning: Before, in front of, in the presence of. Indicates priority and sequence.
word_study.significance: The word suggests both spatial and temporal priority: humility comes before honor, both in sequence and in value. One must pass through humility to reach honor.

word_study.meaning: Honor, glory, dignity, weight, importance. Kavod literally means 'weight' or 'heaviness,' metaphorically indicating the gravity and substance of a person's influence and respect.
word_study.significance: Kavod is the honor and recognition that comes from living well and being recognized for it. Proverbs insists that this honor cannot be directly grasped but comes to those who have first embraced humility.

word_study.meaning: Humility, meekness, lowliness. The posture of the one who has renounced pride and positioned themselves rightly before God and others.
word_study.significance: Anavah is not weakness or self-denigration but right relationship—acknowledging one's actual status before God and not claiming more than is one's due. It is the opposite of arrogance and the foundation of wisdom.

cross_references.connection: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge; establishes at the book's outset the foundational principle that knowledge and wisdom begin with reverencing God.
By humility and the fear of the LORD are riches, and honour, and life; explicitly states that riches, honor, and life follow from humility and the fear of the Lord.

Likewise, ye younger, submit yourselves unto the elder... God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble; parallels the principle that humility precedes honor and that God's grace flows to the humble.

And again I say unto you as I have said before, that as ye have come to the knowledge of the glory of God, or if ye have known of his goodness and have tasted of his love... ye should remember and always retain in remembrance, the greatness of God... and his mercy and his long-suffering patience towards you; echoes the Book of Mormon's emphasis that awe of God's greatness should produce humility in the recipient of His mercies.

And now, after the many testimonies which have been given of him, this is the testimony, last of all, which we give of him: That he lives!... And that he is the Only Begotten of the Father—that by him, and through him, and of him, the worlds are and were created, and the inhabitants thereof are begotten sons and daughters unto God; frames the context in which awe of God (the fear of the Lord) is the appropriate response, leading to humility before His majesty.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern wisdom literature, the fear of God/gods was universally recognized as the foundation of wisdom. Egyptian wisdom texts, Mesopotamian proverbs, and Hittite instructions all emphasize this principle. However, the Israelite emphasis on the fear of the covenant God (YHWH) takes this further—it is not merely philosophical reverence but covenantal submission. The cultural context of honor and shame in the ancient Mediterranean and Near East provides the backdrop for understanding the paradox of verse 33: in these societies, honor was the supreme social good, yet Proverbs insists that direct grasping for honor leads to shame and loss, while humility paradoxically leads to genuine honor. This would have seemed counterintuitive to those acculturated to honor-seeking societies, making the wisdom teaching even more striking.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma's teachings in Alma 32 emphasize that faith—a form of humble receptivity—is the beginning of understanding. King Benjamin's address (Mosiah 2-4) teaches that recognition of God's greatness should produce humility and meekness in God's people. The Book of Mormon consistently frames the pathway to honor and exaltation as beginning with humility before God.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 112:10 states: 'Be thou humble; and the Lord thy God shall lead thee by the hand, and give thee answer to thy prayers.' D&C 64:34 teaches: 'Wherefore, be not deceived, but continue in steadfastness, looking unto the end. Learn that he who endureth to the end the same shall be saved.' The principle that fear of the Lord and humility are the conditions for divine guidance and salvation permeates D&C. D&C 1:28 adds: 'What I the Lord have spoken, I have spoken, and I excuse not myself; and though the heavens and the earth pass away, my word shall not pass away, but shall all be fulfilled, whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the supreme expression of the fear of the Lord and humility. One enters the temple only by covenanting to place oneself under God's authority and to live in submission to His will. The progression through the temple is a progression in humility—shedding the garments of pride and worldly status to stand as a humble petitioner before God. The temple itself teaches the paradox of verse 33: those who humble themselves in the temple receive covenants and blessings of eternal honor.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the perfect embodiment of verse 33. His entire earthly ministry manifested both the fear of the Lord (His absolute submission to the Father's will) and profound humility (His self-emptying, his willingness to serve, his refusal of worldly honor). Yet He received the ultimate honor—at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, both in heaven and on earth (Philippians 2:10). His path to exaltation ran through humiliation and the cross, exemplifying the principle that honor comes through humility. The Incarnation itself—God emptying Himself to take human form—is the supreme expression of the paradox: the highest honor (being God) coexists with the deepest humility (becoming human and dying).
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 33 invites radical reordering of priorities. In a culture obsessed with status, recognition, and advancement, this verse asks: Am I seeking honor directly, or am I placing myself in alignment with God and allowing honor to come as a byproduct of that alignment? The verse suggests that humility before God (acknowledging His majesty and my dependence on Him) is not a loss but a gain—it positions me to receive His instruction and guidance, which lead to genuine flourishing. Practically, this means cultivating the discipline to receive feedback without defensive pride, to acknowledge my limitations, to serve others without calculating return, and to fear God more than I fear human judgment. In families, workplaces, and Church callings, those who practice this principle—establishing themselves in the fear of God and humility—paradoxically become trusted leaders and sources of influence. They have already surrendered the pursuit of honor and thus are free to be honored authentically.

text_kjv: The preparations of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, is from the LORD.

commentary.narrative: Proverbs 16 opens with a fundamental paradox about human agency and divine sovereignty. A person may arrange his thoughts, organize his words before speaking, and carefully prepare what he will say—all of which are legitimate human responsibilities. Yet when the critical moment arrives, when the tongue actually answers, the outcome belongs to God. This is not a license for carelessness; rather, it subordinates human planning to divine governance. The tension captures a distinctly biblical perspective: we are responsible for our preparation, but God controls the performance. The military metaphor in the Hebrew (ma'arkhe, 'battle formations') suggests the heart lines up its thoughts like troops marshaled for battle, yet the actual engagement—what emerges in real time—belongs to the Commander.
commentary.narrative_continued: The verse launches a sustained meditation on divine sovereignty that dominates Proverbs 16:1–9. In a wisdom text, this is crucial framing. Proverbs teaches practical human skill—how to speak, work, plan, and prosper—but it grounds all such instruction in the recognition that ultimate outcomes rest with God. This prevents wisdom from becoming mere technique or self-help. The gap between what we prepare and what we actually accomplish is where faith lives. A young man may rehearse his words before meeting a king, but whether his speech persuades belongs to heaven. A business owner may craft a plan, but whether the market cooperates is God's domain. The verse invites readers to plan diligently while holding outcomes loosely.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: For Latter-day Saints, this verse resonates with the doctrine of moral agency within divine omniscience. We are commanded to work, plan, study, and prepare (D&C 88:119), yet we acknowledge that God knows all things and governs all things. Proverbs does not resolve this tension philosophically; it simply asserts both truths together and invites trust. The 'answer of the tongue' may also carry covenantal weight—the tongue that answers before God, the words we speak in sacred spaces, the testimony we bear. All such utterance, while prepared by human effort, ultimately comes through divine enablement.

word_study.meaning: Arrangements, orderings, battle formations. From the root arakh, 'to arrange in order.' In military usage, ma'arakhah denotes a line of troops arranged for combat. The metaphor suggests the heart carefully lines up its thoughts like soldiers in formation.
word_study.significance: The word choice elevates human planning from mere thinking to strategic ordering. We are not passive beings; we actively arrange our thoughts. Yet the military connotation also suggests limitation—a well-formed battle line can be defeated by a superior force. Our 'arrangements' are honorable but finite.

word_study.meaning: Answer, response, reply. From the root anah, 'to answer, respond, testify.' Can mean both the direct reply to a question and a more general response or outcome.
word_study.significance: The 'answer of the tongue' is not just a reply but the actual performative utterance that emerges in the moment. What the tongue says in answer—when it is called upon—comes from the LORD. This suggests that in moments of decision, challenge, or witness, God's hand shapes what we are enabled to speak.

word_study.meaning: The orderings, arrangements, or formulations of the inner self. The heart (lev) is the seat of thought, intention, and will in Hebrew anthropology.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering highlights the human capacity to organize thought and prepare intention. 'A person may arrange his thoughts'—this is within human capacity and is not forbidden or unnecessary. But the gap between arrangement and utterance is where God works.

cross_references.connection: Continues the same theme: 'A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps.' Human planning is real, but divine direction determines the actual path.
Commands members to seek knowledge and engage in preparation and study, yet within the framework of divine governance and eternal purpose.
The word 'faith' is tied to the gap between what we can control and what we must trust to God—planting a seed and watching what God causes to grow.

When Moses protests that he is 'slow of speech,' God replies, 'Who hath made man's mouth?' and promises to be with his mouth and teach him what to say—expressing the same principle of divine governance over speech.

Jesus tells disciples not to premeditate what they will say when brought before authorities, for 'it shall be given you in that same hour what ye shall speak.' The tension between preparation and trust is here resolved in radical reliance on the Spirit.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern wisdom literature, the relationship between human effort and divine will was a persistent theme. Egyptian wisdom texts (Ptahhotep, Amenemope) similarly acknowledge human planning while attributing ultimate success to the gods. The Mesopotamian King of Kings inscriptions boast of human achievements while crediting divine favor. Hebrew wisdom, however, places greater emphasis on the limits of human knowledge and the inscrutability of divine purpose. Proverbs reflects a cultural context in which planning and risk-taking were essential to survival—ancient trade, agriculture, governance all required foresight—yet the speaker also inhabited a world of genuine uncertainty: crop failure, political upheaval, disease, and divine judgment. The verse thus speaks to an existential awareness: we must plan, but we cannot control outcomes. The metaphor of battle formations may also reflect Israel's military experience, where even the best-trained army could be routed by superior numbers or by God's intervention (as in Joshua's conquest narratives or the deliverance at the Red Sea).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:12 expresses a similar trust: Ammon boasts not in his own strength but acknowledges that 'by the power of God we have been supported.' The Nephite prophets consistently teach that human effort and divine enablement work together. Nephi's declaration, 'I will go and do the things which the Lord hath commanded' (1 Nephi 3:7), combines decisive human commitment with dependence on divine support.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 58:26–28 instructs that 'the Lord loveth the cheerful giver' and that those who 'do not go forth, the same is not my will, saith the Lord.' The principle is that God expects human initiative and planning, but always within the framework of His direction. Similarly, D&C 9:8–9 teaches Oliver Cowdery that he must 'study it out in [his] mind' before asking God for confirmation—human thinking precedes divine answer.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple covenants, the endowment presents the human journey as one of preparation and obedience within a cosmos ordered by divine intelligence. The candidate prepares and acts, but progression depends on celestial law and divine approval. The principle in Proverbs 16:1 resonates with the pattern: we make covenants and keep them, but exaltation is God's to grant.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ embodies the perfect unity of human preparation and divine utterance. In the Garden, he prepares himself in prayer (Luke 22:39–44), yet his words and works proceed from the Father: 'The words that I speak unto you I speak not of myself: but the Father that dwelleth in me, he doeth the works' (John 14:10). The Incarnation itself is the supreme instance of human limitation and divine full expression inhabiting one person. Christ is the answer of the tongue—the Father's ultimate utterance, the Word made flesh (John 1:1, 14).
commentary.application: This verse invites modern covenant members to distinguish between legitimate preparation and idolatrous reliance on self-sufficiency. In education, career, family, and discipleship, we are called to prepare thoroughly—to study, to practice, to think ahead, to make plans. But we are also called to hold those preparations with open hands, acknowledging that God may have a different answer than we scripted. A student may prepare extensively for an exam, but the test itself—and what he is actually able to articulate under pressure—belongs to God. A missionary may rehearse lessons and scripture, but the Spirit determines what words will pierce a heart. A parent may plan carefully for a child's upbringing, but that child's actual choices and character development unfold under God's governance. The verse calls for diligent effort without anxiety, for careful thought without the burden of believing our preparation determines everything. It is an invitation to trust.

text_kjv: All the ways of a man are clean in his own eyes; but the LORD weigheth the spirits.

commentary.narrative: This verse cuts to the heart of human self-deception. A person's ways—his behavior, choices, and conduct—seem entirely clean and justified to himself. Self-interest is a powerful lens that distorts perception. We are expert justifiers, capable of rational-sounding accounts for our worst actions. A man cheats on a contract and tells himself he was merely 'negotiating harder.' A woman spreads rumors and believes she was 'just sharing concerns.' An employer underpays and calls it 'market conditions.' A student cuts corners on research and insists the outcome is still excellent. The human eye is fixed on surfaces and surfaces are easy to make presentable. We see our intentions (which feel good to us), our circumstances (which seem to justify us), and our outcomes (which we interpret favorably). The verse does not deny that we are capable of seeing anything at all; it asserts that our self-perception is unreliable.
commentary.narrative_continued: But the LORD weighs the spirits. The verb 'weighs' (tokhen) carries connotations of careful measurement, testing, and valuation. It appears elsewhere in Proverbs as the image of a scale that calculates worth. God does not merely glance at surfaces; He measures the ruach—the inner drive, motive, intention, and animating spirit behind visible behavior. An act of charity motivated by pride and a desire for recognition weighs differently from the same act flowing from pure compassion. Two business decisions that look identical in outcome may be weighed very differently if one came from honest effort and the other from corner-cutting. God's measurement is precise, comprehensive, and uncorrupted by self-interest. What the LORD weighs is not behavior alone but the spirit from which behavior flows—the heart's actual orientation, not its self-assessment.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: For a Latter-day Saint, this verse connects directly to the doctrine of divine omniscience and the judgment. Nothing is hidden from God. In the premortal council, the Father could see who each of us really was, beneath any facade. At the judgment bar, Christ will judge not by our reputations or our self-justifications, but by the spirit of our choices. This verse also guards against a particular danger in covenant religion: the temptation to believe that external obedience (keeping rules, showing up to meetings, performing service) automatically validates our spiritual state. Obedience is necessary, but God weighs whether it flows from love of Him or love of approval, from genuine faith or fear, from charity or performance anxiety. The verse invites radical honesty before God.

word_study.meaning: Ways, paths, journeys, methods of conduct. From the root derek, fundamental to biblical anthropology—one's 'way' is how one walks through life, one's pattern of behavior and choices.
word_study.significance: The term encompasses not just isolated acts but the habitual direction of a life. 'All a person's ways'—everything about how he conducts himself—seems clean from the inside. This suggests the pervasiveness of self-justification.

word_study.meaning: Clean, pure, innocent, transparent. Can mean physically clean (as in water) or morally pure. Implies clarity, lack of contamination, blamelessness.
word_study.significance: The word carries both physical and moral senses. To the self-deceived person, his ways do not merely appear acceptable—they appear pure, innocent, without stain. This heightens the irony: we not only justify ourselves; we convince ourselves of our essential innocence.

word_study.meaning: Weighs, measures, determines, tests, counts. From the root kun/tokhen, suggesting precise measurement on a scale or careful examination.
word_study.significance: God does not approximate or overlook. He measures carefully. The verb suggests the kind of exact accounting a merchant would do with his scales—nothing escapes the divine measurement. It also suggests testing or assaying, like metal tested for purity.

word_study.meaning: Spirits, winds, breaths, inner vital forces, intentions, inclinations. The plural of ruach, which in Hebrew anthropology refers to the animating principle of a person, the inner self, the will and intention.
word_study.significance: God weighs the ruchot—the actual motives, the true inclinations, the real spiritual orientation of a person. The plural may suggest the multiplicity of a person's inner drives and desires; God measures all of them. This goes deeper than behavior; it reaches the source.

cross_references.connection: Nearly identical formulation: 'Every way of a man is right in his own eyes: but the LORD pondereth the hearts.' Emphasizes that self-assessment and divine assessment are radically misaligned.
The Lord tells Samuel, 'Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.' God's evaluation penetrates to what humans cannot see.

In Joseph Smith's vision of the celestial kingdom, the Lord declares that all who have not heard the gospel and 'would have received it with all their hearts shall be judged according to the desires of their hearts.' God measures the inner orientation, not merely external circumstances.

Alma warns that at the judgment, you will be judged by your works and the desires of your hearts, for God knows all things. 'The Lord doth grant unto all nations, of their own nation and tongue, to teach his word, yea, in wisdom, all that he seeth fit that they should have' according to their hearts' desire.
Jesus teaches that what defiles a person comes from within—from the heart and mouth. The Lord looks to the inner source of action, not merely the external deed.

commentary.historical_context: The verse assumes an ancient Near Eastern context in which honor, reputation, and public perception were paramount. In honor-shame cultures, what people think of you matters immensely for social standing, livelihood, and family welfare. A person's 'way' (how others perceive you to walk) determined much of your actual position and opportunity. Yet Proverbs insists on a hidden auditor—God—whose evaluation operates on entirely different criteria than public opinion. This was countercultural and liberating: if what truly matters is divine judgment, then reliance on human approval becomes less tyrannical. At the same time, it was challenging: one could not hide behind reputation. The verse also assumes a cosmology in which the divine is intimately attentive to human interiority, not distant or indifferent. This reflects a distinctly Israelite understanding in contrast to some ancient Near Eastern conceptions of gods as primarily concerned with temples, rituals, and public order.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mormon 8:17 warns against those who 'do seek to excuse themselves in the things which they have done.' Jacob 2:22–23 indicts those whose hearts are set upon riches and fine clothing while they claim to be righteous—the divide between self-assessment and reality. Moroni's appearance to Joseph Smith emphasized the precise knowledge God has of actual human hearts and intentions, not merely outward conformity.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:27 declares that the Lord knows the thoughts and intents of the heart. D&C 6:16 promises that the Comforter will reveal to the faithful 'the things that are to come.' God's knowledge is not of behavior alone but of the spiritual substance from which behavior flows. D&C 42:27 commands honesty and sincerity in all things, not mere external compliance.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony assumes that God's eye penetrates all layers of pretense. Covenants made before God in the temple are binding not because others witness them but because God witnesses them and knows the true state of each person's heart. The promise of blessing or curse depends not on whether one can fool the temple president but on what one is really committing to before the Almighty.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the one whose ways are entirely clean, whose spirit is perfectly aligned with the Father's. Yet he submitted himself to be 'weighed'—to be tested, judged, and found perfect by God. He also becomes the true Judge who will weigh all spirits on the last day. In his earthly ministry, he consistently saw through human self-justification: he perceived the scribes' pride beneath their piety, the Pharisees' self-righteousness beneath their law-keeping, and the rich young ruler's attachment beneath his claims of perfect observance. Christ is the manifestation of divine accuracy in measurement of the human heart.
commentary.application: This verse calls members to ruthless honesty before God about their own motives. It is not enough to keep rules or perform service if the spirit from which we act is pride, self-promotion, fear, or manipulation. A teenager who obeys his parents out of fear of punishment may avoid external rebellion, but God weighs whether his spirit is moving toward genuine respect and love. A member who gives generously but with an eye toward recognition gives something very different from what the modest giver offers. A missionary who serves with ambition to be seen and praised offers a different spirit than one laboring in obscurity. The verse invites each person to ask: If no one but God would ever know, what is my true motive? What spirit am I offering? What would God's scale reveal? This is uncomfortable, but it is also liberating—because it shifts the court of judgment from human opinion (which we cannot fully control) to the one account that truly matters (and to which we can be radically honest).

text_kjv: Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established.

commentary.narrative: The Hebrew verb gol ('to roll') carries the vivid image of rolling a burden off one's own shoulders onto someone else's. To 'commit thy works unto the LORD' is not a passive or mystical act; it is concrete: take the weight of what you are undertaking—your labor, your projects, your initiatives—and roll that weight onto God's shoulders. The image suggests trust enacted, confidence embodied. You are not abandoning your work; you are ceasing to carry it alone. In ancient contexts, rolling a stone onto someone would be an act of trust (the other person accepts the burden), confidence (you believe they are strong enough), and surrender (you acknowledge you cannot carry it yourself). The verse follows naturally from the first two: you prepare your thoughts (verse 1), you acknowledge that God weighs your motives (verse 2), and now you roll the actual work—the implementation, the outcomes, the results—onto the LORD.
commentary.narrative_continued: The result promised is that 'thy thoughts shall be established'—Hebrew yikkonu machshevotekha, meaning your plans will be made firm, stable, secure. Interestingly, the promise is not that you will achieve everything you planned, but that your plans themselves will be established. This suggests that plans placed in God's hands acquire a different kind of security: not the false confidence of thinking 'I control all outcomes,' but the genuine stability of being aligned with divine purpose. A plan that aims at success through dishonesty will not be established by rolling it to God; it will collapse. A plan that aims at righteousness, growth, or service—rolled into God's governance—acquires the backing of an infinite intelligence. The TCR rendering clarifies: 'Commit your actions to the LORD, and your plans will be established.' This is neither fatalism nor passivity. You still make plans. But you make them in the presence of God, acknowledging His superior knowledge, and you entrust their execution to His wisdom.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The movement from verses 1–3 is instructive: prepare (verse 1), acknowledge God's judgment (verse 2), surrender and trust (verse 3). This is not three separate doctrines but a sequential spiritual discipline. First, do your work—prepare, think, plan. Do not be passive. Second, recognize that your self-assessment is limited and God's judgment is accurate; confess that your way is not automatically the right way. Third, having done your part and acknowledged His sovereignty, release the outcome to Him. This combines Latter-day Saint theology perfectly: we have agency and responsibility, yet ultimate governance belongs to God. We act as if everything depends on us, and pray as if everything depends on God.

word_study.meaning: To roll, to roll away, to roll upon someone. In this context, to roll a burden onto someone else—to transfer weight and responsibility.
word_study.significance: The verb is concrete and kinetic—not a passive wish but an active, physical-metaphor act. You roll your works onto the LORD as you would roll a heavy stone onto another person. It is an image of decisive surrender and transfer of burden. The verb appears in Joshua 5:9 ('I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt') and Psalm 37:5 ('Commit thy way unto the LORD') using the same root.

word_study.meaning: Works, deeds, actions, labor, undertakings. From the root asah, 'to do, to make, to work.' Encompasses both the labor itself and its outcomes.
word_study.significance: The term is concrete—not your abstract hopes but your actual works, what you are actually doing. You roll your labor, your projects, your implementations onto God.

word_study.meaning: Will be established, made firm, prepared, secured, set up. From the root kun, 'to be firm, to stand, to be established.'
word_study.significance: The verb suggests stability, permanence, and being set upon a solid foundation. A plan yikkun is not a plan that succeeds inevitably, but one that is made firm, secure, and aligned with reality. It will not crumble; it will not be built on illusion.

word_study.meaning: Thoughts, plans, schemes, intentions, designs. From the root chashav, 'to think, to plan, to reckon.'
word_study.significance: Machshevot are not mere idle thoughts but purposeful plans, strategic designs. When you roll your works onto God, your intentional designs—your strategic thinking—become established.

cross_references.connection: Identical language and idea: 'Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass.' Rolling one's way onto the LORD results in divine action and establishment.
Extends the idea: 'A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps.' We devise; God directs. The sequence parallels verse 3.
The Lord prizes those who 'do go forth, and not in idleness; neither in fulness, neither in shame.' Initiative is expected, but it must be offered to the Lord and synchronized with His direction.

Alma counsels Helaman: 'Let all thy doings be unto the Lord, and whithersoever thou goest, go with the Lord; and with all thy might, and pray always that thou mayest not be led into temptation.' Works and dependence on God are combined.
Paul teaches that through prayer and petition, believers make requests known to God, and God's peace will guard their hearts and minds. Rolling one's cares onto God in prayer leads to stability.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, the relationship between human initiative and divine favor was understood through concepts of divine blessing and human effort working in concert. Egyptian wisdom (Amenemope) similarly encourages the wise man to make plans while acknowledging that the gods control outcomes. Mesopotamian wisdom acknowledges the unpredictability of life—harvests could fail, rulers could turn hostile, fortune could shift—despite careful planning. In Israel's story, this theological conviction had been tested repeatedly: Abraham's plan to have a child through Hagar was rolled into God's purpose, which established a different outcome (Isaac). Moses' leadership plans depended entirely on God's miraculous provision. The kings of Israel and Judah learned that political strategy, however brilliant, could not establish a kingdom without God's covenant backing. The verb gol may carry overtones of Israelite covenant practice: the rolling away of stones, the rolling away of Egypt's reproach, the rolling of debts in jubilee years. To 'roll' one's works onto the LORD is thus to place them within the covenantal structure, where God guarantees establishment and blessing.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 7:12 presents Nephi committing his actions to the Lord and relying on divine strength. Helaman 10:4–5 promises Nephi that 'whatsoever ye shall ask me to give unto you, ye shall have power to do it.' The pattern: do your part, offer it to God, and God establishes the result.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:33 declares, 'I give unto you a commandment that ye shall covenant with each other, and bind yourselves by a covenant to support the one the other.' But all such covenants are within a larger framework: 'all things must be done in order, and by common consent in the church' (D&C 28:13), which itself must align with God's direction. D&C 9:8–9 teaches that to 'ask in faith' requires having 'studied it out in [your] mind'—human preparation followed by divine confirmation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant process itself enacts the principle of Proverbs 16:3. A person commits (or 'rolls') his or her life to the Lord through covenants, and those covenants establish that person's path. The endowment presents the human journey as genuine striving within a cosmos ordered by God's law. Your covenantal works, offered to God, become established as part of the eternal order.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ perfectly demonstrates this principle in Gethsemane. He prepares and plans his redemptive work ('My soul is exceeding sorrowful,' Matthew 26:38), he acknowledges the finality of God's judgment ('Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done,' Luke 22:42), and he rolls his works—the entire weight of redemption—onto his Father. The result is that his purpose is established: 'It is finished' (John 19:30). His works become the foundation of all that is, because they were entirely committed to the Father's will. Christ is the model of one whose plans are established because they are rolled entirely onto God.
commentary.application: For a modern member navigating career, education, family, and discipleship, this verse cuts through two opposite errors. First, it rejects the prosperity-gospel temptation to believe that if you work hard enough, plan cleverly enough, and manage risk, you will inevitably succeed. Life is not that simple. Business plans fail despite brilliance. Health fails despite preparation. Children disappoint despite wise parenting. The verse invites release from the illusion of control. Second, it rejects passivity or victim-mentality—the belief that rolling your works onto God means you don't have to plan, study, work, or take initiative. The verse clearly assumes you are doing all that. The question is what you do with the weight once you have worked at it. The practice invited is: work hard and carefully at whatever lies within your power. Prepare, think, plan. Then, having done what you can, acknowledge that outcomes are not in your hands. Roll the burden—the results, the success, the establishment—onto God. Pray about your plans not to substitute for work but to synchronize your work with divine wisdom. This creates a spiritual posture that is both engaged and at peace, both responsible and trusting.

text_kjv: The LORD hath made all things for himself: yea, even the wicked for the day of evil.

commentary.narrative: This verse asserts a comprehensive divine sovereignty that extends to the most troubling corners of existence: even the wicked have a place in God's design, and their destined end—'the day of evil'—is part of that design. The statement 'The LORD hath made all things for himself' could mean 'for His own purpose' or 'as responses to His wisdom.' Everything created serves God's purposes. The verse does not claim to resolve the problem of evil philosophically; rather, it asserts that God's governance encompasses even evil actors and outcomes. The extension to 'the wicked for the day of evil' is meant to be striking and even troubling. It forces the reader to wrestle with divine justice: God has made the wicked, and part of that creation includes their appointment to judgment. This is not the same as saying God made people to be wicked (a Calvinist predestination that contradicts agency), but rather that within God's knowledge and sovereignty, even wicked people serve a purpose—they will receive the judgment they have earned.
commentary.narrative_continued: The Hebrew la-ma'anehu (for its purpose/answer/response) is deliberately ambiguous. It can mean 'for its own purpose' (each thing has a function) or 'for His purpose' (God is the ultimate end). This ambiguity is likely intentional—it allows readers to hold both truths: things have intrinsic purposes, and God ultimately governs. The statement challenges the reader's comfort. If even the wicked—whom we despise—are part of God's design, what does that say about divine justice? The verse does not smooth over this tension with false comfort. Instead, it insists on both truths: God is sovereign; judgment is real. The wicked will meet their day. This is not tyranny, but the establishment of moral order within an infinite governance.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: For Latter-day Saints, this verse raises fundamental questions about God's knowledge and the nature of agency. The Doctrine and Covenants makes clear that God knows all things 'from the beginning' (D&C 130:7), yet mortals have genuine agency to choose good or evil (D&C 29:39). Proverbs 16:4 does not resolve this paradox but asserts both sides emphatically. God knows that some will choose wickedness; He has a purpose even in their wickedness (that they will be judged, that through their existence justice will be manifest). But this does not remove their responsibility or their agency. The verse invites readers into an acceptance of mystery—a willingness to say 'I trust God's justice even though I cannot fully understand how omniscience and agency coexist.'

word_study.meaning: Made, worked, wrought, fashioned, created. From the root paal, 'to work, to make, to create, to accomplish.'
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes creative action and bringing into being. The LORD actively made all things. This is not accidental or marginal but a fundamental assertion of divine creative power.

word_study.meaning: All, every, the whole, the totality. The most comprehensive word for universality.
word_study.significance: Not 'many things' or 'good things,' but 'all things.' Nothing falls outside God's creative governance. The wicked, the evil, the tragic—all are included in 'all things.'

word_study.meaning: For its answer, for its purpose, for its response, for Himself. The term ma'aneh can mean 'answer,' 'response,' 'purpose,' 'function.' The suffix hu (him/his) can refer either to each thing (neuter) or to God (masculine).
word_study.significance: The ambiguity is rich: each thing answers to (has a purpose within) God's design. Or: all things exist to answer God's purposes. Both readings are true. The Covenant Rendering captures this: things have their own ma'aneh (purpose/response to God's design).

word_study.meaning: Wicked, ungodly, guilty, criminal. One who transgresses divine law and refuses moral instruction.
word_study.significance: In Proverbs, the rasha is not a peripheral figure but a central contrast to the righteous (tzaddiq). The verse's assertion that even the rasha is made by God is theologically momentous.

word_study.meaning: Day of evil, day of trouble, day of calamity, the day of reckoning. Ra'ah encompasses evil, harm, trouble, misfortune, and judgment.
word_study.significance: This is not just 'a bad day' but the appointed day of judgment and reckoning. The wicked are made 'for' this day—they are created, and their eventual judgment is part of the divine order.

cross_references.connection: Paul addresses this very tension: God makes vessels of wrath 'fitted to destruction' and vessels of mercy 'afore prepared unto glory.' The question of how divine sovereignty and human agency coexist is explicitly addressed.
God declares that mortals are 'free according to the flesh' to choose good or evil, and the consequences follow. God's omniscience does not override agency; both are true.
God 'knoweth all things, and there is not anything save he knows it.' His knowledge is comprehensive, yet it does not negate the genuine responsibility of those who choose wickedness.
'I form the light, and create darkness: I make peace, and create evil: I the LORD do all these things.' God's sovereignty encompasses all outcomes, including evil and judgment.
The great white throne judgment, where the wicked meet their appointed day. The judgment of the wicked is part of God's eternal design from the beginning.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern royal ideology, kings presented themselves as creating order by establishing a cosmos in which every element served a function. The Babylonian Enuma Elish describes Marduk creating the world and assigning each god and element its role. Israel's theological assertion goes further: not just order, but justice is built into the fabric of creation. Even evil serves God's purposes because evil will be judged. The verse reflects Israel's struggle with suffering and injustice during periods of exile and oppression. In such times, the assertion that 'the wicked for the day of evil' becomes a theodicy—an affirmation that God has not lost control, that judgment is coming, and that the cosmic order is ultimately just. This was not abstract theology but existential hope: when Babylonia rules over Israel, this verse whispers that the oppressor is also made by God, and the day appointed for their reckoning will come. The verse assumes a linear history with a final judgment, a frame profoundly different from cyclical pagan cosmologies where time merely repeats.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 41:3–5 teaches that God has appointed 'that all things shall be restored to their proper order.' Even wickedness will be met with its proper consequence. Moroni 7:16–17 asserts that God is 'able to make all things known unto all men' and that judgment is part of God's design. The Book of Mormon prophets consistently affirm both human agency and divine omniscience without resolving the paradox philosophically.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:40 declares that all things are 'governed by law' and have 'bounds and conditions.' Within this order, even the wicked are governed. D&C 76:28–32 describes the sons of perdition—those who sinned against the Holy Ghost—and affirms that even they are part of a divinely ordered cosmos where judgment and place are appointed. D&C 101:78 teaches that 'when the Lord shall come' all things will be revealed and all injustice will be made right.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony teaches that God has set 'bounds' and created order, and that each person chooses where they will stand within that order. The kingdoms of glory (D&C 76) represent a cosmos where even those who reject God's full offer are placed according to their choices and capacities. Nothing falls outside God's knowledge or governance.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the one through whom and for whom all things were made (Colossians 1:16–17). Yet He also comes to judge, to separate the righteous from the wicked, to appoint each 'for the day of evil' according to their deeds (Matthew 25:31–46). In His earthly ministry, He moved among sinners with compassion, yet He also spoke with uncompromising clarity about judgment. He is the manifestation of both God's creative power and God's justice. In the Atonement, Christ takes upon Himself the consequences of wickedness, offering a way out of judgment for all who repent—but those who refuse that mercy face the appointed day of reckoning.
commentary.application: This verse invites members into a mature faith that can hold paradox without requiring complete philosophical resolution. It is okay to acknowledge that you cannot fully understand how God's omniscience and human agency coexist, and yet to trust both as true. It is okay to believe that evil is real, that judgment is real, yet that God is ultimately just and in control. In personal life, the verse suggests that even troubling people—those who have hurt us, opposed us, or chosen wickedness—are ultimately within God's governance and will face appropriate judgment. This can be liberating: you do not have to achieve vengeance; you can forgive, because you trust that 'the day of evil' is appointed and that God's justice will be done. In broader contexts—social injustice, tyranny, oppression—the verse offers the comfort of an assurance that tyrants, for all their power, are not outside God's design. Their day will come. This is not an excuse for passivity in addressing injustice now, but it is a ground for patience and trust that ultimate justice rests with God. The verse also cautions against spiritual pride: if even the wicked are part of God's design, then my own moral achievements are also encompassed within a divine order. This should cultivate humility and dependence on God's mercy rather than confidence in my own righteousness.

text_kjv: Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD: though hand join in hand, he shall not be unpunished.

commentary.narrative: This verse delivers one of Proverbs' most emphatic statements about the sin God hates most: pride. The Hebrew phrase gevah lev ('lifted up of heart, arrogant heart') appears throughout Proverbs as the root of nearly every other evil. The proud person rearranges reality in his mind to put himself at the center. He judges others from a position of supposed superiority. He dismisses correction. He will not listen to wisdom because he already believes himself wise. He is, in Proverbs' terms, a fool (for fools despise wisdom). And such a person is to'avat Yahweh—an abomination to the LORD. The Hebrew to'evah denotes something detestable, revolting, an object of disgust in God's sight. The word is strong. God's emotional response to pride is one of revulsion. This is not a small failing; it is an offense against the divine dignity itself.
commentary.narrative_continued: The second clause deepens the threat: 'though hand join in hand, he shall not be unpunished.' The idiom yad le-yad ('hand to hand') means something like 'rest assured,' 'without a doubt,' 'I guarantee you.' It is a colloquial way of saying 'you can count on it.' The TCR rendering captures this: 'be assured, he will not go unpunished.' The proud person cannot escape judgment through alliances, through wealth, through status, through having friends or supporters. No matter how much power he accumulates or how many allies stand with him (hand to hand), judgment will find him. This is a radical assertion: in a world of patronage networks and power structures (as the ancient Near East certainly was), the verse declares that status and connections will not protect the proud from God's judgment. This would have been countercultural and hopeful for the powerless: if you are oppressed by the proud, take comfort—their hand-in-hand alliances will not save them.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The verse also continues the meditation on divine judgment that opened the chapter. Verse 1: God controls the actual utterance. Verse 2: God weighs the motives. Verse 3: God establishes plans when offered to Him. Verse 4: God governs all outcomes including the wicked's destined judgment. And now verse 5: specific judgment falls on pride. The chapter is building a theological vision in which God's sovereignty is exercised through precise moral judgment, and the first target of that judgment is the arrogance by which humans resist God's rule. For a Latter-day Saint, the verse connects to the doctrine that pride is the fundamental sin—not because it is the most dramatic, but because it is the root of all others. Pride is the refusal to be dependent on God, the insistence that I am sufficient, that I can manage without divine help. A proud person cannot genuinely pray, because prayer assumes dependence. A proud person cannot repent, because repentance assumes being wrong and needing to change. A proud person cannot serve, because service assumes that others matter and that you are not central. Pride thus blocks access to all the divine channels of grace.

word_study.meaning: Lifted up of heart, arrogance, haughtiness, pride. Gevah denotes elevation, liftedness; when the heart is lifted up, it means the person has an inflated sense of importance.
word_study.significance: The phrase is Hebrew's primary term for the kind of pride that God opposes. It is not confidence or self-respect but an inflation of self-importance, a haughtiness that places oneself above others and above God.

word_study.meaning: Abomination, detestable thing, something that provokes revulsion or disgust. From the root ava, 'to detest, to be disgusted.'
word_study.significance: This word conveys not just disapproval but visceral revulsion. God looks at pride with something like disgust. The term is the same applied to idolatry and sexual perversion—it indicates the highest level of moral offense against God.

word_study.meaning: Every person with an arrogant heart; all arrogant people; the universal statement that whoever has pride falls under this judgment.
word_study.significance: There are no exceptions. The verse is absolute: not 'many proud people' or 'the proudest people,' but 'every one.' Universality is key. This cuts across social status—even the proud rich man is subject to this judgment.

word_study.meaning: Hand to hand, hand in hand. An idiom meaning 'rest assured, without fail, I guarantee, certainly.'
word_study.significance: The phrase originally may have referred to a solemn vow made with hand-clasping (as in Lamentations 5:6: 'We have given the hand to the Egyptians'). Over time it becomes an idiom for certainty and assurance. The point: even if the proud person has alliances and supporters joining hands with him, he will still be punished.

word_study.meaning: Will be held innocent, will go unpunished, will be acquitted, will escape. From the root naqah, 'to be clean, to be innocent, to be acquitted.'
word_study.significance: The proud person will not niqah—will not be acquitted or let off. Judgment will find him. There is no escape clause.

cross_references.connection: Lists the 'six things the LORD hateth; yea, seven are an abomination unto him,' and pride heads the list: 'A proud look, a lying tongue.' Pride is foundational to all other sins.
'I will punish the world for their evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; and I will cause the arrogancy of the proud to cease.' God's judgment specifically targets pride.
Describes the sons of perdition as having 'denied the Holy Ghost after having received it,' a fundamental act of pride—insisting on one's own judgment against God's revelation.

'God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble. Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you.' Pride draws God's active resistance; humility draws His grace.

The Lord declares that He comes to 'break down the mountains and level the valleys' and that 'every man shall hear the gospel preached by the angels, as well as by the written word'—a leveling of human pretension before God's inevitable judgment.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern royal inscriptions, pride and claims of supremacy were standard. Assyrian kings boasted of their conquests, Egyptian pharaohs proclaimed their divine status, and Babylonian kings described themselves as chosen of the gods. Israel's wisdom literature challenges this: precisely such self-exaltation invites God's judgment. In Israel's own history, pride repeatedly preceded downfall. The kings who trusted in their own military might rather than in God were defeated (Isaiah's critique of reliance on Egypt). The Israelites who believed themselves secure through ritual observance while practicing injustice were carried into exile. The verse thus reflects Israel's hard-won experience: claiming superiority, relying on power and alliance, and resisting correction all led to catastrophe. The assertion that 'hand to hand shall not be unpunished' reflects a time in which Israel was often the weaker power, surrounded by greater empires. The verse would be a source of hope: no matter how mighty the proud nations that align against us, God will judge their arrogance.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 15:6 describes the humbling of Zeezrom, whose pride caused him to fall into iniquity, but whose eventual humility became the foundation of his redemption. Mormon 8:34–36 warns sternly against pride among latter-day members: 'Beware of pride, for ye are not yet in the condition that ye ought to be.' Pride is identified as the sin most likely to lead to the fall of the Church in the latter days.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:34–37 teaches that 'Behold, there are many called, but few are chosen. And why are they not chosen? Because their hearts are set so much upon the things of this world, and aspire to the honors of men.' Pride (aspiration to honors) prevents people from being chosen. D&C 1:30 describes the Church as 'the only true and living church,' yet immediately cautions members against becoming prideful or hypocritical.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant invites members to 'hearken to the voice of the Lord,' which requires humility and willingness to follow. Pride—insisting that one's own judgment is superior to God's—is fundamentally at odds with covenant living. The patterns of the endowment present progression as dependent on obedience and willingness to be instructed, not on pride in one's achievements.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the antithesis of pride. In the Incarnation, the divine humbles itself to become human, to be subject to parents, to wash disciples' feet, to be mocked and crucified. Christ's teaching consistently exalts the humble (the widow's mite, the publican's prayer, the child as model of the kingdom) and warns the proud (the Pharisees, the rich young ruler). His own journey is one of radical self-emptying: 'he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross' (Philippians 2:8). Yet in that humiliation, He is exalted. The proud are brought low; the humble are exalted. Christ embodies this inversion of worldly values.
commentary.application: This verse demands each member to examine his own heart for the subtle forms of pride that may lurk there. Pride is not always loud boasting; it often appears as a quiet belief that 'I know better,' that 'I don't really need to ask for help,' that 'my perspective is the important one,' or that 'I can manage without God's direct guidance.'
