For women in particular, this verse models entrepreneurship and economic agency as consistent with (not opposed to) household management. She manages her household excellently and also builds a commercial enterprise. The two are not competing; the household excellence is the foundation for the commercial work. For all members, the verse suggests that faithful stewardship of talents and resources can manifest as commercial enterprise, that business relationships should be maintained with integrity, and that professional merchants and traders can be legitimate partners in a righteous economic order. The verse also invites reflection on quality and reputation: this woman's goods are valuable enough that professional merchants want to supply them. Does our work—whatever it is—command that kind of trust and value? Are we producing goods (literal or figurative) worthy of merchants' partnership?

text_kjv: Strength and honour are her clothing; and she shall rejoice in time to come.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 25 marks a transition in the poem from external accomplishments to internal character. After describing the woman's economic enterprise, textiles production, and charitable works, the poem now reveals what truly clothes her: not the fine linen and purple she produces (v22), but oz (strength) and hadar (dignity, majesty). This is a profound theological statement about the nature of real adornment. In the ancient world, as in ours, people assume that visible garments and physical appearance constitute one's real presentation to the world. The poem directly challenges this assumption—her actual clothing is her character, her capability, her moral authority.

The second clause deepens this insight by moving into the temporal dimension. She laughs at the days to come—not with mocking contempt, but with the confidence of one fully prepared. The Hebrew verb tischaq (she laughs) is the opposite of fear. While the unprepared person faces the future with anxiety, the woman whose life is built on wisdom, diligence, and righteousness faces it with something approaching joy. This is not optimism born of denial; it is earned confidence. She has done her work thoroughly, has built her household wisely, has prepared for contingency (v21: 'she is not afraid of the snow'). Therefore she can face what is coming without dread. The laughter signals freedom from fear.

word_study.meaning: Strength, power, might, force. In Hebrew thought, oz often refers to physical or moral strength, the capacity to endure and overcome. It can describe military might, resilience, or the fortitude of character.
word_study.significance: As The Covenant Rendering notes, oz is here a garment—her real clothing. This inverts the visual hierarchy of the ancient world. While others judge by linen and purple, those with wisdom see her true adornment: the inner capacity to sustain herself and others. Oz appears in Psalms 27:1 ('The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?') and Proverbs 8:14 (Lady Wisdom speaking: 'Counsel is mine, and sound wisdom: I am understanding; I have strength'). The woman embodies this principle.

word_study.meaning: Splendor, dignity, majesty, glory. Hadar describes the visible manifestation of honor—not mere reputation, but the tangible aura of authority and respect that surrounds a person of genuine worth.
word_study.significance: The pairing of oz and hadar in a single clause means her strength and dignity are inseparable—they are one garment. Hadar appears elsewhere in Proverbs 20:29 ('The glory of young men is their strength: and the beauty of old men is the gray head'). In biblical thought, hadar is something that emanates from a person of proven character. Here, the eshet chayil wears it naturally because she has earned it.

word_study.meaning: To laugh, to mock, to play, to jest. The root can express both delight and derision, but context determines which. Here, it expresses delight and confidence in the face of what is to come.
word_study.significance: The verb choice is deliberate. She does not grimly prepare or stoically endure; she laughs. This suggests a kind of spiritual freedom—the opposite of the anxious preparation that comes from fear. The same root appears in Genesis 21:6 (Sarah laughing at the promise of Isaac) and Job 5:22 (laughing at desolation and famine because one is secure in God's provision). Her laughter signals trust in the fruit of her righteousness.

word_study.term_english: Days to come / Time to come
word_study.meaning: Literally 'the day after' or 'the latter day.' Acharon means 'last, later, future.' While acharon sometimes carries eschatological weight elsewhere in Scripture, here it simply means the future—what lies ahead.
word_study.significance: The phrase captures the existential reality: no one knows what the future holds. Economic collapse, illness, loss—these are real possibilities. The woman's laughter is not denial of these risks but confidence that she will face them with the resources she has built: prudent management, physical health, a community that honors her, and most importantly, a life aligned with wisdom and the fear of the LORD. She laughs because she has done what is in her power, and she trusts in God for what is not.

cross_references.connection: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge. This entire poem of the woman of valor is built on this foundation—her strength and dignity flow from reverence for God, which will be made explicit in v30.
Lady Wisdom declares: 'Counsel is mine, and sound wisdom: I am understanding; I have strength.' The eshet chayil embodies the character that Wisdom herself possesses.
The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? Like the psalmist, the woman fears neither the future nor the uncertainty of time because her trust is in the LORD.
Rejoice in the Lord always...and the peace of God shall keep your hearts. The New Testament connection to joy in the face of uncertainty echoes the confidence expressed in this verse.

Fear and trembling shall seize the children of men; but my disciples shall stand in holy places. The covenant principle of standing firm through preparation and faith parallels the woman's readiness for what comes.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, a woman's social standing was typically determined by her husband's status and wealth. The irony of verse 25 would have struck ancient readers forcefully: this woman's true adornment has nothing to do with the external markers of status (fine textiles, jewelry) and everything to do with her own character and capability. Her oz (strength) is something she possesses in her own right—not borrowed from her husband, not granted by society, but earned through diligent, wise living. The cultural context also illuminates the phrase 'she shall rejoice in time to come.' In an agrarian economy with no safety nets, uncertainty about the future was existential. Crop failure, drought, disease, or loss of a family member could mean destitution. A woman who could face this uncertainty with laughter was truly remarkable—and that laughter would have been audible evidence to her community of her genuine security, grounded not in wealth alone but in prudent preparation and trust in divine providence.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 32:21 speaks of faith as the capacity to hope for things not seen: the woman's laughter at the future is a form of faith, a confident expectation grounded in preparation and righteousness. Moroni 8:25-26 teaches that perfect love casteth out fear; the woman's fearless laughter reflects this principle.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 90:24 teaches: 'Search these commandments, for they are true and faithful, and the prophecies and promises which are in them shall all be fulfilled.' The woman's confidence in facing the future is grounded in the same principle—that covenant keeping yields promised blessings. D&C 45:26-27 also teaches that the disciples of Jesus shall stand in holy places when fear and trembling seize others; her preparation is the spiritual equivalent.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The concept of clothing oneself with 'strength and dignity' resonates with temple theology—the garments of the priesthood represent a taking upon oneself of divine power and responsibility. The eshet chayil is clothed, metaphorically, in attributes that reflect God's own character: oz (divine strength) and hadar (divine glory and majesty). Her garments, like temple garments, represent a covenant relationship.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the ultimate embodiment of oz and hadar clothed invisibly beneath the form of a servant. In the Incarnation, He came in poverty and apparent weakness, yet His true adornment—divine strength and majesty—was always present, seen only by those with eyes to see (John 1:14: 'We beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father'). Like the eshet chayil, He faced the future—including the cross—with unswerving confidence rooted in complete obedience to the Father's will. His laughter would have been strange to His disciples at times, yet His words 'in the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world' (John 16:33) express the same principle: victory and joy rooted in righteousness.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members: This verse invites a radical reorientation of what we consider our 'real clothing'—our true self-presentation. In a culture obsessed with visible markers of status (physical appearance, brand names, social media presentation), this verse asks: What do I actually wear? What is my real adornment? The answer is: your character, your capability, your moral authority, your faithfulness. These are developed through consistent choices over time—the same kind of diligent, thoughtful work the eshet chayil performs. The verse also teaches us to face the future differently. Instead of anxiety about what might happen, we can ask: Have I prepared wisely? Have I built a foundation of righteousness? Have I aligned my life with covenants? If the answer is yes, then we can move forward with confidence. This is not complacency; it is earned peace. Finally, the verse models a kind of joy that is not dependent on circumstances but flows from the integrity of a well-lived life.

text_kjv: She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 26 shifts from external presentation to the interior quality of her speech. The poem has already shown the woman in action—buying, selling, planting, serving the poor. Now we learn what comes out of her mouth when she speaks. This verse is essential to understanding that the eshet chayil is not merely a productive machine but a teacher and moral guide. The opening phrase emphasizes the characteristic nature of her speech: when she opens her mouth, wisdom emerges. This is not occasional or situational; it is her default mode. She does not need to consult a manual or search for the right words; wisdom flows naturally from her because her life is structured by wisdom.

The second clause, 'the instruction of faithful love is on her tongue,' adds a critical dimension. The Hebrew torat chesed combines torah (instruction, teaching, law, the form and content of what is said) with chesed (faithful love, loyal kindness, covenant devotion). As The Covenant Rendering translator notes observe, torah sets the form—she teaches truth—while chesed sets the tone—she teaches with kindness. This is not sentimental; it is the most sophisticated form of communication. She combines unflinching truth with relational warmth. She does not soften truth to avoid offense, nor does she deliver truth as a weapon. Her instruction is shaped throughout by loving loyalty to those she teaches.

This verse represents the culmination of the teaching figure introduced in Proverbs 1-9, where Wisdom herself speaks and invites the simple to learn. Here we see that teaching character embodied in a real woman, living in a household, with people who depend on her words. She is not an abstract principle but a person whose speech has the power to shape those around her.

word_study.meaning: Her mouth she opens. The infinitive construct form piha ('her mouth') with the verb patechah ('opens, opens wide') emphasizes the act of speaking, the willingness to make words public.
word_study.significance: The phrase is straightforward but carries weight through what follows. The act of opening one's mouth is a commitment—words cannot be taken back. The fact that wisdom emerges when she does this is remarkable. In the ancient world, as now, opening one's mouth could lead to harm, folly, or regret. Proverbs 10:14 warns that 'a fool's mouth is his destruction.' By contrast, this woman's mouth is a reliable source of wisdom.

word_study.meaning: Wisdom, skill, prudence, understanding. Chokhmah is practical intelligence applied to living well—not mere intellectual knowledge but the capacity to discern right action in specific situations.
word_study.significance: This is the central virtue of the entire book of Proverbs. Chokhmah is what the eshet chayil embodies throughout the chapter, and now we learn it is also what she teaches. Her wisdom is both lived and transmitted; she is both a model and a mentor.

word_study.meaning: Instruction, teaching, law, guidance, direction. Torah originally meant 'instruction' or 'teaching' (as in a parent's torah to a child, Proverbs 1:8) before it came to mean specifically the written Torah, the Law of Moses. Here it retains its primary meaning: the content of what she teaches.
word_study.significance: The use of torah to describe her speech elevates it beyond mere conversation or advice-giving. She is a teacher; her words have the weight and authority of instruction. This reflects the Proverbs tradition itself: the book is framed as torah from a father and mother to a son. She participates in that chain of faithful transmission. The pairing of torah with chesed creates 'torat chesed'—instruction shaped by faithful love, not law in the sense of impersonal rules, but teaching that carries the warmth of covenant relationship.

word_study.meaning: Loyal love, faithful kindness, covenant love, merciful devotion. Chesed is love bound by commitment—not sentimental affection but love expressed through faithful action. It is God's characteristic quality toward His covenant people.
word_study.significance: This is perhaps the most theologically laden word in the verse. By describing her instruction as characterized by chesed, the poem claims that her teaching reflects God's own way of relating to His people. God teaches with truth (Torah, from Sinai) and with faithful love (chesed, the covenant bond). She does the same. This makes her speech not merely clever or effective but godly. The use of chesed here is what separates her from a stern taskmaster who teaches truth but without compassion, or from a kind person who avoids hard truths to keep peace. She is both/and: truthful and loving.

word_study.meaning: Tongue, language, speech. The tongue is the instrument of speech and stands metonymically for language, words, and discourse itself.
word_study.significance: Proverbs contains numerous warnings about the tongue: 'Death and life are in the power of the tongue' (18:21), 'A soft answer turneth away wrath' (15:1), 'Whoso keepeth his mouth and his tongue keepeth his soul from troubles' (21:23). Against these cautionary verses stands this portrait of a woman whose tongue is habitually an instrument of good—instruction wrapped in faithful love.

cross_references.connection: Hear, my son, the instruction of thy father, and forsake not the law of thy mother. This verse establishes the framework—parents (and specifically mothers) are teachers. The eshet chayil embodies this teaching role.
Lady Wisdom speaks: 'Hear; for I will speak of excellent things...For my mouth shall speak truth.' The eshet chayil embodies the teaching character of Wisdom herself.
A fool's mouth is his destruction. By sharp contrast, this woman's mouth is a source of life and instruction, not destruction.
A soft answer turneth away wrath...the mouth of the wise useth knowledge well. Her instruction combines gentleness (chesed) with wisdom (chokhmah).
The wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be entreated. Her speech embodies this New Testament description of heavenly wisdom—truth combined with gentleness.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite society, formal teaching and public instruction were typically male domains. The woman's sphere was the household. Yet this verse suggests that teaching and moral formation within the household is a vital form of instruction that shapes the next generation and sustains the community. The Hebrew term 'instruction of faithful love' (torat chesed) would have resonated with the covenant language of the Torah itself. The LORD's teaching of Israel is repeatedly described as an expression of chesed—covenant love. By describing the eshet chayil's speech in the same terms, the poem elevates domestic teaching to a status parallel with divine instruction. In the context of an oral culture, where wisdom was transmitted through speech and memorization rather than texts, the woman who spoke wisdom faithfully was a crucial link in the chain of transmission. Her role as a transmitter of values and understanding was far more significant than the constraints of her gender might suggest.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 17:2-3 describes missionaries 'resting from their labors...having waxed strong in the knowledge of the truth,' with 'the spirit of prophecy and of revelation.' This same combination of deep knowledge and the Spirit's influence on speech mirrors the eshet chayil's characteristic. Moroni 7:46-48 teaches that charity—which is the greatest commandment—should 'dwell' in our hearts; her chesed-shaped teaching reflects this principle.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:41-43 gives instruction on how to teach effectively: 'No power or influence can or ought to be maintained by virtue of the priesthood, only by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned.' The eshet chayil embodies this principle perfectly—her instruction combines truth (what needs to be said) with chesed (long-suffering, gentleness, love unfeigned).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes instruction—the sacred ordinances are a form of divine teaching. The woman who instructs with wisdom and faithful love participates in this sacred pattern, bringing to her household the same combination of clarity and covenant love that characterizes temple teaching.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus is the ultimate embodiment of wisdom and faithful love combined in speech. His teaching in the Sermon on the Mount and throughout the Gospels combines unflinching truth with profound compassion. He taught the hardest truths—about judgment, sacrifice, the cost of discipleship—yet always within the context of love for His listeners. When He rebuked the Pharisees (Matthew 23), His harsh words were prompted by His love for the people they were misleading. Like the eshet chayil, His 'tongue' (His speech, His teaching) was the instrument through which both truth and covenant love were conveyed. The combination of sophia (wisdom) and agape (love) in His teaching is the divine pattern this verse reflects.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints: This verse invites us to examine the quality of our speech, especially in teaching contexts—whether formal (Sunday School, seminary) or informal (parenting, mentoring, conversations with friends). The challenge is to hold together two things that can feel in tension: speaking truth clearly and speaking with genuine, covenantal love for the person hearing it. We can speak truth harshly or tactlessly, wounding those we hope to help. We can also soften truth so much that it loses its power. The eshet chayil shows us a third way: truthful instruction that flows from and is wrapped in faithful love. This requires humility, genuine care for the person we're teaching, and a willingness to consider how our words will land. It also requires spiritual maturity—the kind that comes from living by the wisdom we teach. We cannot speak 'the instruction of faithful love' to our children while our lives contradict it. The verse challenges us to integrate our teaching and our living, so that when we open our mouths, wisdom and covenant love flow naturally from lives that embody them.

text_kjv: She looketh well to the ways of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 27 returns to observable action after verse 26's focus on speech. The verse emphasizes two complementary commitments: watchfulness and industriousness. The first clause uses watchman/sentinel vocabulary—tsofiyyah (she watches, she observes, she keeps lookout)—suggesting that managing a household requires constant vigilance. The affairs of her household (halikhot beitah, literally 'the goings/comings' of her house) are not static; they are constantly in motion. A manager must observe, assess, and respond. This is not micromanagement born of distrust but the engaged oversight of someone responsible for the wellbeing of dependents. She knows what is happening in her household because she is paying attention.

The second clause intensifies the portrait of her industriousness. She does not eat the bread of idleness. The Hebrew construct is direct: lechem atslut lo tokhel ('bread of laziness she does not eat'). This is a statement about economic integrity—she consumes no bread she has not earned through her own labor or that of those under her care. Idleness (atslut, from atsil, 'to be lazy or idle') is presented not as a moral temptation she struggles with but as something she fundamentally rejects. The phrase 'bread of idleness' is particularly striking: it suggests that even to eat requires work, and that idle consumption is a form of theft—taking sustenance without contribution. In an agrarian economy where bread literally was the staple of life, this was a serious principle.

Together, these clauses present a vision of household management built on two virtues: attentiveness and diligence. She watches so that nothing is wasted or overlooked; she works so that she never becomes a burden on others. This is not joyless drudgery but the focused engagement of someone who understands that a household, like a farm or a business, requires constant tending.

word_study.meaning: She watches, she observes, she keeps lookout, she is vigilant. The root tzafah refers to watching or keeping watch, often with the connotation of a sentinel or watchman maintaining vigilance.
word_study.significance: The vocabulary choice is significant. She is not casually aware of her household's condition; she is actively, intentionally watching—the way a watchman watches the walls of a city. This suggests that good management requires active attention, not passive hope that things will go well. The verb form (third person feminine singular) emphasizes that this is her characteristic activity. Managing a household is her watch.

word_study.meaning: Goings, comings, journeys, activities, affairs, paths. Derived from halak ('to go, to walk'), the plural form halikhot encompasses all the movement and activity within a space.
word_study.significance: The word is not 'laws' (chokim) or 'duties' (mitzvot) but 'goings'—the lived reality of daily life in the household. She oversees the actual, dynamic activities that make up family life: the comings and goings, the work being done, the needs being met. This implies a management style that is engaged with reality rather than focused on rules alone.

word_study.meaning: Her house, her household, her home. Bayit is one of the most fundamental words in Hebrew, referring both to the physical structure and to the family unit that inhabits it.
word_study.significance: The possession form ('her' household) is important. She is not a servant managing someone else's property but has authority and responsibility for her own household. Bayit in biblical thought encompasses economic production as well as family life. Her household is both her family and her economic unit—as the previous verses have shown, she is buying and selling, producing goods, all as part of her household's activity.

word_study.meaning: She does not eat, she does not consume. Tokhel is the simple present/habitual form, indicating her characteristic practice.
word_study.significance: The negative prohibition is key to the meaning. She has established a practice of never consuming what she has not earned. This is a principle she lives by consistently, not something she struggles with. The grammar suggests habitual reality, not aspiration.

word_study.meaning: Bread of laziness, bread of idleness, bread resulting from or earned through inactivity. The construct chain lechem-atslut ('idleness-bread') treats the two as inseparably linked.
word_study.significance: The phrase is a Hebraism for idle consumption, for eating without earning. The image of bread is particularly resonant in an agricultural culture where bread represents basic sustenance, the fruit of labor. To eat bread of idleness would be to consume the fruit of others' labor without reciprocal contribution. The phrase carries a note of moral seriousness: it is not merely inefficient to be idle, it is a betrayal of covenant community—taking without giving.

cross_references.connection: Go to the ant, thou sluggard...yet a little sleep, a little slumber...and poverty shall come upon thee as one that travelleth.' The sluggard is the negative contrast to the eshet chayil's diligence.
In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury.' Her diligence and careful oversight ensure profit; idleness produces only poverty.
That ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands...that ye may have lack of nothing.' The apostolic counsel reflects the same principle: faithful work sustains.
If any would not work, neither should he eat.' The principle that sustenance is connected to labor appears in New Testament teaching as well.
Thou shalt not be idle; for he that is idle shall not eat the bread nor wear the garments of the laborer.' A direct parallel in modern revelation to the principle of this verse.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, a household was an economic unit of production as well as a family. Management of this unit—ensuring that resources were allocated efficiently, that production continued, that nothing was wasted—was a serious responsibility that could make the difference between survival and poverty, between stability and crisis. Archaeological evidence from Iron Age Palestine suggests that women's work (textile production, food preparation and storage, child-rearing) was essential to household economic security. A woman who was inattentive to these matters or who refused to contribute to the household's labor could threaten the entire family's welfare. The phrase 'bread of idleness' would have resonated as a serious moral failing in this context, not mere laziness but a betrayal of one's role in the survival and flourishing of dependents. The watchman imagery is also significant: a watchman who fell asleep at his post endangered the entire city. Similarly, a woman who did not carefully oversee her household's affairs risked catastrophe. The verse thus reflects real economic and social structures of the time while elevating the woman's role to one of genuine importance and moral weight.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Jacob 2:13-19 teaches against idleness and slothfulness, connecting them to the loss of the Lord's blessings. Alma 24:18 describes the Anti-Nephi-Lehies working diligently after their conversion. The Book of Mormon consistently teaches that diligence and careful stewardship are marks of discipleship.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 42:42 states: 'Thou shalt not be idle; for he that is idle shall not eat the bread nor wear the garments of the laborer.' This is a direct revelation that echoes the principle of verse 27. D&C 9:13 also emphasizes the importance of active mental and spiritual effort: 'It is not requisite that a man should run faster than he has strength.' The principle is balance—neither idleness nor exhaustion—but definitely not idleness.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The covenant path requires active participation and careful stewardship. Just as the eshet chayil watches over her household, covenant members are called to watch over their spiritual households—their families, their responsibilities. The temple teaches the importance of vigilance and faithful work as essential to exaltation.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ perfectly embodied this virtue. He rose early and withdrew to pray, worked diligently in His Father's business, and modeled complete dedication to His mission. He never consumed the bread of idleness, never took rest except as necessary for health. His famous statement 'My meat is to do the will of him that sent me, and to finish his work' (John 4:34) expresses the principle that sustenance—spiritual and physical—comes through faithful labor in behalf of God's purposes. He also called His followers to this same vigilance: 'Watch therefore, for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come' (Matthew 24:42). The apostles are to be watchmen, as was the eshet chayil in her household.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, especially those responsible for households: This verse challenges us to think seriously about stewardship and diligence. In a culture that tempts us toward passivity (media consumption, mindless scrolling, delegation of all responsibility), this verse calls us back to active, engaged care for those dependent on us. This doesn't mean exhaustion or perfectionism; it means paying attention. Know what is happening in your children's lives. Notice when family members are struggling. Be intentional about the work that sustains your household—not just the paid work but the maintenance, the meal planning, the emotional labor that holds a family together. The phrase about bread of idleness also speaks to financial integrity: earn your way, contribute your share, and never become a burden if you have the capacity to sustain yourself. For those in positions of organizational or spiritual leadership, the principle applies: watch carefully over those in your stewardship, know what is happening, and be engaged rather than distant. The verse's emphasis on characteristic practice ('she looketh,' 'she eateth not') reminds us that these virtues are built through consistent choice over time, not through sporadic effort.

text_kjv: Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her.
text_kjv_alt: Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband also praises her.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 28 presents the public recognition and blessing that flow from the woman's character and labor. The verse moves from her internal qualities and private actions to the external validation of her household and community. The children 'arise up' (qamu)—a phrase suggesting both literally standing and metaphorically taking initiative—to call her 'blessed' (ye'ashruha, from ashre, 'blessed, happy, fortunate'). This is not private, whispered appreciation but public declaration. They speak about her, call her by the name of blessedness. In the context of an honor-shame culture, this public recognition is extraordinarily significant. The children are publicly honoring their mother, acknowledging her worth not as a duty but as a genuine expression of their assessment of who she is.

The second clause intensifies and personalizes this recognition: 'her husband also, and he praiseth her.' The construction 'and he' (ba'alah va-yehallelah) emphasizes the person—the husband specifically, her life partner. He praises her with the verb hallal, which means to celebrate, to laud, to make a show of praise. This is not quiet appreciation but vocal, public affirmation. The whole household—children and spouse—is united in honoring her. This is the poem's emotional climax. After twenty-seven verses of describing what she does, now we see the fruit of those actions: she is loved and honored by those closest to her. The verse demonstrates a crucial principle: genuine worth, lived faithfully over time, produces authentic love and respect from those who know us best. No external flattery can substitute for the real honor that comes from family members who have lived with you and know your character.

It is important to note what this verse does NOT say. It does not say she calls attention to herself or demands recognition. It does not say she has become famous or wealthy or powerful in the public sphere. It says the people closest to her—those who know her most intimately—spontaneously acknowledge her blessedness. This is a profoundly different kind of honor than fame or status.

word_study.meaning: They rose up, they stood up, they took action. Qum is a foundational Hebrew verb meaning to stand, to rise, to take action, to establish.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests both literal standing (perhaps the children rising from their seats to speak) and the metaphorical sense of taking active initiative to honor their mother. The verb also appears in the context of building and establishing: the children are 'standing up' for their mother, establishing her worth in the community. There is an element of agency here—they are choosing to do this, not compelled or obliged.

word_study.meaning: They call her blessed, they declare her fortunate/happy. The verb ashar (from ashre, 'blessed, happy, fortunate') means to pronounce someone blessed or to consider someone fortunate.
word_study.significance: Ashre is the word used throughout the Psalms: 'Blessed are they whose ways are perfect' (Psalm 119:1). It describes a state of blessedness or flourishing. The children are not merely saying 'Mother is nice' but are publicly declaring that she is blessed—that her life is characterized by flourishing, by favor, by blessedness that is evident and measurable. This is the highest compliment: they recognize her life as blessed because they have lived its fruits.

word_study.meaning: Her husband, her master, her owner. Ba'al in older biblical usage carried the sense of authority and ownership; in later usage, it came to mean simply 'husband, man.'
word_study.significance: By this point in verse 31, the term has lost any sense of dominance. The husband is one voice in the chorus of praise, not an authority pronouncing judgment. The parallelism with the children—both children and husband praise her—emphasizes that she is honored by all those to whom she is most closely bound. In the relationship dynamics shown in this poem, the husband is a partner who recognizes and celebrates her worth.

word_study.meaning: He praises her, he sings her praises, he celebrates her. Hallal means to celebrate, to praise, to make a show of one's praise. It is the root of Hallelu-Yah ('praise the Lord').
word_study.significance: The verb suggests enthusiastic, public, vocal praise—not grudging acknowledgment but celebration. The same word is used in Psalm 113:1 ('Praise ye the LORD')—suggesting that the husband's praise of his wife echoes, in its intensity and form, the language of worship. This is not accidental; one of the ways we worship God is to properly honor those whom God has blessed. The verb also emphasizes that this praise is active and expressed, not merely felt silently.

cross_references.connection: A wise son maketh a glad father. Proverbs establishes the principle that children's respect for parents is a natural fruit of parental wisdom and virtue. This verse shows the reverse: a wise mother makes her children rejoice and causes them to bless her.

The glory of young men is their strength: and the beauty of old men is the gray head.' Like the aged, the woman who has lived wisely wears her glory naturally—it shows in the respect she receives from younger generations.

Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.' The children's spontaneous blessing of their mother is evidence that she trained them well; her training bore fruit.

The father of the righteous shall greatly rejoice: and he that begetteth a wise child shall have joy of him. The joy of parents in their children's virtue is paralleled here with the joy and honor children feel toward a virtuous parent.

Hannah's words about Samuel ('the LORD hath given me my petition which I asked of him') show a mother who recognizes her children as blessings from God, as do the children of verse 28 when they recognize their mother as blessed.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite society, public recognition was of paramount importance. Honor and shame were communal realities, not internal feelings. A person's worth was determined not by their own assessment but by the community's—and especially by the assessment of those closest to them. The testimony of one's children was particularly significant: children could not be hired or coerced to praise a parent they actually despised. If the children rose up and publicly called their mother blessed, it was a genuine assessment, making it public testimony to her virtue. Similarly, a husband's public praise of his wife was significant in a patriarchal culture. He had the power to honor or shame her; his choice to praise her publicly was meaningful. The verse reflects social realities of the time: among the most powerful forms of validation available was the spontaneous honor given by those who lived with you daily and knew your character most intimately. This verse celebrates a kind of honor that could not be faked or performed—it was the natural outflowing of respect earned through years of consistent, faithful character.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 63:16 mentions that the people 'did multiply and wax strong in the land.' Later, Alma 48:17 describes leaders whom the people 'did love...and they also did mourn exceedingly for his loss.' The principle is that genuine character produces genuine love from those around you. Also, Jacob 1:8 states that Jacob and his brethren 'were not desirous to vain glory.'—yet the people honored them because of their virtue, not despite their humility. The eshet chayil is not seeking praise; it flows naturally from her character.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:5-9 teaches about exaltation and describes those who 'overcome by faith' as receiving glory and honor. The honor the eshet chayil receives is a type of the exaltation of the faithful—recognition by God and the righteous of one's faithfulness. D&C 121:41-45 also teaches that 'persuasion, gentleness...without hypocrisy, and without guile' produces 'influence in the hearts of men and women.'—the very influence we see here as the children and husband speak.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes the promise that 'all that my Father hath shall be given unto you' (D&C 84:38). One fruit of covenant faithfulness is honor and recognition from those in our covenants—our family, our community. The eshet chayil is shown receiving the recognition that is the natural fruit of faithfully living covenant principles.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ received honor from those closest to Him—the apostles who saw His works daily rose up to testify: 'Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God' (Matthew 16:16). Peter, James, and John witnessed the Transfiguration and heard the Father's voice (Matthew 17:5). Like the eshet chayil's children and husband, these close disciples spontaneously proclaimed His worth. More broadly, Christ is praised by those who know Him most intimately. In a inverse sense, the verse also foreshadows that Christ would receive honor: 'All glory, honor, and power are thine' (D&C 109:78). The children's recognition of their mother's blessedness reflects the recognition that will be given to the Savior—a blessedness earned through perfect service and faithfulness.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, especially parents: This verse promises that genuine character and faithful devotion to family bear real fruit—the authentic respect and love of those we raise. This is not guaranteed to manifest as gushy sentiment, nor does it promise that children will never disappoint us or struggle. But there is a principle: if we live the virtues the eshet chayil embodies—diligence, wisdom, kindness, faithful love, integrity—those closest to us will recognize it and honor it. This becomes a powerful motivator to live faithfully not for external recognition but because we want to be genuinely respected by our children and spouse. The verse also invites us to ask: Would my children arise and call me blessed? If not, what would need to change? Do they see integrity, diligence, wisdom, kindness in me? Do they experience my faithful love? The verse also suggests that publicly honoring those who deserve honor (as the husband does) is important—it is one way we affirm what we value and want to cultivate. For men specifically: the verse models a husband who celebrates his wife's virtue publicly and enthusiastically. This is the opposite of taking her for granted. Finally, for those who experience honor from family members: receive it as validation that your character is producing real fruit, and let it motivate you to continue in faithfulness.

text_kjv: Many daughters have done virtuously, but thou excellest them all.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 29 is the husband's own words—his proclamation of his wife's supreme excellence. The verse begins by acknowledging that her virtue is not unique: 'Many daughters have done chayil' (many women have acted with strength, valor, and excellence). The word chayil appears here for the third time in the chapter (verses 3, 10, and 29), creating a structural frame that binds the entire poem together. In verses 3 and 10, chayil was used to describe a quality to seek or question about; now it appears as a reality that many possess. The husband's acknowledgment is magnanimous—he does not diminish other women to elevate his wife. Rather, he places her in a context: yes, many women are strong and virtuous, but you surpass them all.

The final clause, 've-att alit al-kullanah' ('but you have risen above them all'), uses the verb alah, 'to rise up, to go up, to ascend.' The implication is motion upward, surpassing, excelling. This is not comparison based on a single quality but on totality—the integration of all the virtues portrayed in the previous verses. The fact that this declaration comes from the husband is significant. He has witnessed her strength, her wisdom, her diligence, her integrity. He is not an external judge but a participant in her life, one who benefits from her excellence daily. His declaration, therefore, carries weight: this is the assessment of someone who knows her best.

Crucially, this verse does not suggest that other women are worthless or merely adequate. Rather, it celebrates a hierarchy of excellence. Many women are strong and virtuous; this particular woman embodies these qualities in a particularly compelling and complete way. The implication is that excellence is possible, that it exists in degrees, and that there can be a superlative—a woman who, through consistent faithfulness and integrated virtue, stands out even among the virtuous. This is the emotional climax of the poem: the public recognition of her blessedness reached its peak in verse 28, and now the husband's intimate and personal declaration of her supremacy adds the final layer.

word_study.meaning: Daughters, women. Banot is the feminine plural of ben/bat (son/daughter). In context, it can refer to women generally, not just biological daughters.
word_study.significance: The term places the eshet chayil within a community of women. She is not alone or unique in her gender; she is one of many. The word choice reminds us that chayil—strength, valor, excellence—is not a male prerogative. Many banot possess it. The poem celebrates not only this particular woman but also the principle that women can and do embody excellence.

word_study.meaning: They have done, they have acted, they have made. Asah is one of the most common Hebrew verbs, referring to action, work, and accomplishment.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes that chayil is not innate or passive but is achieved through doing, through action, through deliberate choices. These women have 'done' chayil; they have made it happen through their work and character. This reinforces the theme throughout the chapter: excellence is built through action and habit, not received passively.

word_study.meaning: Strength, might, valor, excellence, capability, wealth, virtue. Chayil can describe military might (a mighty warrior is gibbor chayil), economic wealth (a person of chayil has resources), or personal virtue (a person of chayil has proven capability and character).
word_study.significance: This is the third occurrence of chayil in the chapter (vv3, 10, 29), each in a different context. In v3, the king was warned about the woman who would 'devour thy chayil' (consume his strength/resources). In v10, the poem opens with the question 'Who can find a woman of chayil?' In v29, the husband declares that she has 'done chayil'—she has embodied strength and excellence. The word, as The Covenant Rendering notes, is used for mighty warriors and is thus inherently connected to power, capability, and tested strength. This woman's domestic and economic achievement is spoken of in the same language as military valor. Her domain is the household, not the battlefield, but her strength is equally real and tested.

word_study.meaning: And you, but you. The emphatic pronoun att stands alone, drawing attention to the person being addressed.
word_study.significance: The pronoun is emphatic, with the 've' ('and') providing a strong contrast: 'And YOU—you in particular—you surpass them all.' The husband is speaking directly to his wife, making the declaration personal and immediate. This is not abstract praise of women in general but concrete, personal affirmation of this specific person.

word_study.meaning: You have risen above all of them, you have ascended above them, you surpass them all. Alah means to go up, to ascend, to rise. The directional sense is upward movement.
word_study.significance: The verb alah carries connotations of exaltation, elevation, prominence. It is used in contexts of rising to power (e.g., 'Saul was king over Israel,' literally 'Saul ascended as king'). The husband's word choice suggests that his wife is elevated, exalted, supreme. The phrase 'al-kullanah' ('above all of them/all of us') makes the comparison comprehensive—not just above some, but above all others in her category.

cross_references.connection: Lady Wisdom is described as more precious than rubies, and 'all the things thou canst desire are not to be compared unto her.' The husband's declaration that his wife surpasses all others echoes this language of ultimate value.

A wise son maketh a glad father. The principle that virtue produces joy and honor in those closest to us is applied here inversely: the virtuous woman makes her husband glad and causes him to honor her publicly.

There are threescore queens, and fourscore concubines...but my dove, my undefiled is but one...the daughters saw her, and blessed her.' A parallel celebration of a beloved woman's uniqueness even among many women.

Let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit; which is in the sight of God of great price.' The eshet chayil's inner character—her strength, wisdom, and virtue—makes her supremely valuable, echoing this New Testament principle.

And then shall thy confidence wax strong in the presence of God...and thy dominions shall be an everlasting dominion.' The principle of excellence and exaltation based on character is embedded in Latter-day Saint covenant theology.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, marriages were often arranged for economic or political reasons, particularly among the upper classes. The husband's spontaneous, enthusiastic praise of his wife in verse 29 suggests a marriage based not merely on transaction but on genuine mutual respect and appreciation. The declaration 'you surpass them all' in the context of an honor-shame culture was significant—the husband is publicly conferring honor on his wife and cementing her status in the community. The reference to 'many daughters' suggests a context where the narrator is aware of women beyond his own household—perhaps in his extended family, his clan, or his community. The comparison is not made in a vacuum but in awareness of other women whose virtue is recognized. Yet the husband's declaration stands: among all the strong, capable women he knows, his wife is supreme. This would have been a powerful affirmation in a culture where women's status was often determined by their husbands' assessment. The fact that this praise emerges naturally from the circumstances of their life together (as shown in verses 1-28) means it is grounded in observed reality, not mere flattery.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 2:26 records that among many righteous people, some 'became exceeding great unto the people.' The principle of relative excellence among the virtuous appears in Book of Mormon accounts. Jacob 1:8 notes that Jacob 'took no thought for himself of the things of this world' yet 'the Lord did prosper him exceedingly.' The pattern is consistent: genuine virtue, without seeking external recognition, produces recognition from those who witness it.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 131:1-4 teaches about exaltation and the principle of increasing glory: 'there is a law, irrevocably decreed before the foundations of this world, upon which all blessings are predicated...for intelligence cleaveth unto intelligence.' The principle is that those who embody greater virtue and truth receive greater reward and recognition. The husband's declaration reflects this theological principle.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes the promise of exaltation and eternal progression. The eshet chayil is shown receiving honor and recognition in this life as a shadow of the greater honor that awaits the faithful in the next. Her supremacy among women who are virtuous mirrors the exaltation of those who keep their covenants—surpassing others in glory because they have remained faithful in all things.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is supremely excellent, surpassing all others in virtue, power, and wisdom. The Father's declaration at the Transfiguration ('This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased,' Matthew 17:5) parallels the husband's declaration that his wife surpasses all others. Jesus Christ is the supreme expression of divine virtue embodied in human form. Yet interestingly, Christ did not seek this recognition; it came as the fruit of His perfect faithfulness. Similarly, the eshet chayil does not pursue recognition but receives it naturally as the fruit of her character. The verse thus illustrates a principle of the Incarnation: genuine excellence, lived faithfully, produces its own recognition.
commentary.application: For married couples, especially husbands: This verse models a form of public affirmation from a husband toward his wife. The husband does not merely think his wife is wonderful; he declares it. In doing so, he affirms both her value and the virtues he wants to see honored in their community. For wives: receiving this kind of affirmation from your spouse is deeply meaningful, but as the poem shows, it flows from lived character over time, not from performance or from demanding recognition. For singles and all people: the verse invites us to ask what it means to 'do chayil'—to embody genuine strength, excellence, and virtue in our particular domain of responsibility. Not every person will be recognized as superlative, nor should we pursue recognition as our goal. But the verse demonstrates that faithful, consistent excellence does produce its own fruit: genuine respect from those who know us best. The broader principle is that excellence is possible, it exists in degrees, and it is worth pursuing—not for the praise it brings, but for the integrity and flourishing it produces in ourselves and those around us.

text_kjv: Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 30 is the theological capstone of the entire 31-verse poem. After twenty-nine verses depicting the eshet chayil's achievements, virtues, and the recognition she receives, this verse provides the ultimate perspective on what actually matters. It stands in sharp contrast to the preceding verse by introducing an explicit negation: all the other qualities that might seem to make a woman valuable—charm, attractiveness, beauty—are explicitly devalued. The Hebrew is direct: sheqer ha-chen, 'deception is charm, charm is a lie,' and hevel ha-yofi, 'vapor is beauty, beauty is a breath.' These are the signature words of transience: sheqer (falsehood, deception) and hevel (vapor, the distinctive Ecclesiastes word for the ephemerality of all earthly things).

Yet the poem does not condemn beauty or charm as such. They are not evil; they are simply unreliable. Charm fades, beauty withers, attractiveness is deceiving because it promises permanence and worth but delivers only fleeting advantage. In a culture as visually oriented as ours (or as theirs), this would have been a radical statement: the most obviously attractive qualities are the most unreliable indicators of genuine worth. Against this, the poem sets its ultimate standard: 'a woman who fears the LORD—she will be praised' (ishah yir'at-YHWH, hi tithallal). The emphatic pronoun hi ('she, this one') singles her out. This woman, the one whose defining characteristic is reverence for God, is the one who deserves lasting praise. The entire poem has been building toward this moment: all the eshet chayil's extraordinary achievements—her economic enterprise, her wisdom, her strength, her charitable work—flow from and are rooted in the fear of the LORD.

This verse explains why the poem began with the question 'Who can find a woman of chayil?' and then answered by showing a comprehensive, extraordinary life. The answer is implicit: you find such a woman not by seeking charm or beauty or status, but by finding one whose foundation is the fear of the LORD. That fear produces the wisdom to manage a household, the courage to engage in enterprise, the integrity to honor her commitments, the kindness to teach with love, and the diligence to never be idle. The fear of the LORD is not one virtue among many; it is the root from which all the others grow.

word_study.meaning: Chen: charm, grace, attractiveness, favor. Sheqer: deception, falsehood, lie, that which deceives.
word_study.significance: The construct phrase sheqer ha-chen ('deception is charm') inverts the typical relationship: charm is not presented as a neutral quality but as inherently deceptive. Chen appears elsewhere in Proverbs (1:9, 'an ornament of grace unto thy head'; 3:34, 'surely he scorneth the scorners: but he giveth grace unto the lowly'). Beauty and charm are not condemned, but their deceptive nature is exposed: they promise worth but deliver only surface. The pairing with sheqer (a word fraught with moral weight—it means active deception, not mere error) elevates the critique beyond mere fashion commentary.

word_study.meaning: Yofi: beauty, loveliness, physical attractiveness. Hevel: vapor, breath, that which is ephemeral and insubstantial; the signature word of Ecclesiastes for the transience of worldly things.
word_study.significance: Yofi is not inherently negative; it is used positively elsewhere in Scripture (e.g., Esther 1:11, the queen's yofi, her beauty). Here it is paired with hevel—vapor, breath. The image is powerful: beauty is as insubstantial as a breath, dissipates as quickly as vapor. This is the voice of Ecclesiastes (Vanity of vanities, all is vanity, hevel hevelim) entering Proverbs. Physical beauty is real in the moment but unreliable as a basis for lasting worth or permanent value. The pairing is not moralizing but realistic: beauty fades; charm becomes irrelevant with age; physical attractiveness is subject to change, disease, and time. Only something interior—the fear of the LORD—provides a foundation that endures.

word_study.meaning: For, because, but, yet. Ki is a conjunction that introduces contrast, explanation, or emphasis.
word_study.significance: The ki here is contrastive: 'charm is deceptive...but a woman who fears the LORD.' The word signals a complete reorientation of values. Up until this point, the world says 'charm matters,' 'beauty matters.' The verse says: 'Yes, they exist, but they're false grounds for judgment.' The true grounds for valuing a woman (or any person) are entirely different.

word_study.meaning: Woman, wife, female person. Ishah is the most common term for a female adult in Hebrew.
word_study.significance: The term reappears here, tying back to verse 10's opening question ('Who can find a woman [ishah] of chayil?'). The poem is now answering: you find such a woman when she fears the LORD. The parallelism between verse 10 and verse 30 creates a frame: the poem opens asking about a woman of valor, and it closes revealing the foundation of that valor—the fear of the LORD.

word_study.meaning: The fear of the LORD, reverence for God, awe before the divine. Yir'ah encompasses both fear (in the sense of terror or awe before the transcendent) and reverence (in the sense of profound respect and obedience).
word_study.significance: This phrase opens the entire book of Proverbs (1:7: 'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge'). It closes the book in this verse. Yir'at-YHWH is the unifying principle of wisdom literature. It is not timidity but clarity of perspective—understanding that God is real, sovereign, and worthy of devotion; understanding that violating the order He has established leads to destruction; understanding that aligning oneself with divine wisdom leads to flourishing. The eshet chayil embodies this fear: she submits to God's order, trusts His providence, and therefore lives with freedom from anxiety. Her fear of the LORD produces her strength, her diligence, her wisdom, her kindness. Everything follows from this root.

word_study.term_english: Shall be praised / Will be praised
word_study.meaning: She will be praised, she will be celebrated, she will receive honor. Hallal means to celebrate, to praise, to glory in, to make much of.
word_study.significance: This is the promise of the verse: if you fear the LORD, you will be praised. Not 'you might be,' but 'you will be.' The certainty flows from a principle: those whose lives are built on reverence for God bear fruit that others recognize as genuine worth. As verse 28 showed, she is indeed praised—her children and husband honor her. Verse 29 showed the husband declaring her supreme. Verse 30 explains why: not because she is beautiful or charming, but because she fears the LORD. Her praise is durable; it flows from those who know her character, not from those momentarily attracted by charm or beauty.

cross_references.connection: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge. This verse opens the book; verse 31:30 closes it, creating an inclusio that frames the entire book's message. All wisdom flows from the fear of the LORD.

Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.' This verse, concluding Ecclesiastes, expresses the same principle as Proverbs 31:30—that reverence for God is the foundation of a rightly-lived life.

Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; but let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit; which is in the sight of God of great price.' A New Testament echo of this verse's contrast between external beauty and internal character.

In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel...not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array; but (which becometh women professing godliness) with good works.' The apostolic counsel reflects the same principle: character matters more than appearance.

Let thy bowels also be full of charity towards all men...Then shall thy confidence wax strong in the presence of God.' The principle of lasting worth built on inner character rather than external markers is embedded in modern revelation.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, as in all times, women were often valued primarily for their physical attractiveness and their capacity to bear children. Literary depictions of beautiful women abound in ancient literature—Egyptian love poetry, Ugaritic texts, and biblical narrative all celebrate physical beauty. Against this cultural background, verse 30's assertion that 'beauty is vain' would have been counter-cultural. The poem is not denying that beauty exists or that it has social power. Rather, it is asserting that beauty is an unreliable basis for true valuation of a person. In an agricultural society where a person's actual survival and flourishing depended on character qualities—diligence, wisdom, faithfulness, good judgment—the disconnect between society's fascination with beauty and the actual requirements for flourishing would have been obvious to any thinking person. A beautiful woman who was lazy, foolish, or unfaithful would bring disaster to her household. A plain woman who was diligent, wise, and faithful would be the foundation of stability and prosperity. The poem's perspective is thus both idealistic (affirming the highest values) and ruthlessly practical (grounded in the reality of what actually sustains life).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 32:21-22 teaches that faith is the effect of understanding and of a true knowledge of the goodness and truth of God. The fear of the LORD, as understood in Latter-day Saint thought, is akin to this faith—a clear-eyed recognition of God's reality and a willing alignment with His will. Jacob 3:7 also critiques the Nephites for focusing on external adornment while neglecting inner virtue.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:78-79 teaches: 'Teach ye diligently and my grace shall attend you...And I give unto you a commandment that you shall teach one another the doctrine of the kingdom. Teach ye diligently and my grace shall attend you, that you may be instructed more perfectly.' The principle is that living in harmony with divine truth—the fear of the LORD—leads to grace attending us and to flourishing. D&C 109:8-9 also emphasizes the permanence of those principles that flow from the fear of God versus the impermanence of worldly attractions.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant emphasizes the importance of taking upon oneself the character of Christ. The fear of the LORD, as understood in Latter-day Saint theology, is the foundation of covenant keeping. Women and men who approach the temple with genuine reverence and who commit to living according to eternal principles are building their lives on the same foundation as the eshet chayil. The temple teaches that external beauty is secondary to inner transformation and alignment with divine will.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ perfectly embodies the principle of verse 30. He came not with outward beauty in the sense that attracted worldly attention. Isaiah 53:2 states: 'He hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him.' Yet His true adornment—His perfect submission to the Father's will, His complete embodiment of divine attributes, His sacrificial love—made Him supremely worthy of praise and honor. The verse is prophetic of Christ in that it asserts that lasting worth comes from alignment with God's will, not from external markers. As the eshet chayil is praised because she fears the LORD and therefore embodies His attributes, so Christ was honored (despite His apparent lack of worldly beauty) because He perfectly embodied the Father's character and will. The principle is reversed-worldly logic: the externals that seem to matter (charm, beauty, status) matter far less than the internals (character, alignment with God, integrity).
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, both men and women: This verse is countercultural in every era, including ours. We live in a time when external appearance is commodified and marketed with unprecedented power. Social media rewards physical attractiveness, youth, and curated image-making. This verse calls us to a different evaluation of worth—both in others and in ourselves. For women specifically, it asks: Are you building your identity and your sense of worth on your appearance, or on your character and your relationship with God? The verse doesn't condemn taking care of one's health or appearance; it condemns making that the foundation of self-worth or the basis on which you evaluate others. For men: this verse calls us to look past surface attraction when evaluating partnership, and to genuinely honor and value women (and people generally) for their character. The verse is also a profound invitation to recognize that the fear of the LORD—reverence for God, submission to His will, alignment with His character—is the most foundational thing any of us can build our lives upon. Everything else—our achievements, our recognition, our abilities, our appearance—flows from this root. If this is in place, we will be genuinely respected by those who know us. If it is missing, no amount of external polish will produce lasting worth. Finally, the verse is a comfort to all who have found that external markers have failed them—who have aged, lost beauty, faced illness, or simply never possessed physical attractiveness. Your ultimate worth is not dependent on these fleeting things. Your worth flows from your relationship with God and the character you build in covenant with Him. That worth is enduring.

text_kjv: Give her of the fruit of her hands; and let her own works praise her in the gates.

commentary.narrative:
Proverbs 31 concludes with the final verse of the acrostic poem celebrating the woman of valor (eshet chayil). This closing verse operates on two levels: it is simultaneously a command to honor and reward the virtuous woman, and a declaration that her works themselves become her greatest advocate. The phrase 'give her of the fruit of her hands' is not merely a practical instruction about compensation—it affirms the principle that righteous labor produces its own reward and that such reward is fitting and deserved. The woman who has managed her household, invested wisely, clothed the poor, and spoken with wisdom throughout the poem has earned recognition that goes beyond domestic acknowledgment.

The second half of the verse elevates this reward into the public sphere. 'The gates' in ancient Israelite culture were not merely entrances to the city—they were the civic and legal centers where important decisions were made, disputes were settled, and community leaders delibered (see 22:22; Amos 5:15). This is significant: the same gates where 'her husband is known in the gates, when he sitteth with the elders of the land' (v. 23) now become the place where her works are proclaimed. She does not receive honor through her husband's status alone, but through the public recognition of her own accomplishments. Her 'works' (ma'aseha) are personified as speakers—they bear witness to her character without need for self-promotion.
commentary.narrative_continued: The Covenant Rendering captures a nuance often missed: the works 'praise her'—not her husband praises her, not her children alone, but the works themselves testify. This is theologically profound. In Proverbs, wisdom produces observable, commendable results. The virtuous woman is not praised for intentions or hidden virtue, but for the concrete, visible evidence of her faithfulness. She bakes, she plants, she weaves, she serves the poor, she speaks—and these actions speak louder than any eulogy. The acrostic structure (aleph to tav, verses 10-31) means this book of Proverbs literally ends with the Hebrew letter tav and with the word ma'aseha ('her works, her deeds'). Proverbs does not end with a theory of wisdom or a maxim about virtue; it ends with a life—a woman whose fear of the LORD (v. 30) has produced works that earn public honor.

word_study.meaning: The harvest or reward produced by one's labor. Peri (fruit) conveys both literal produce and metaphorical reward; yadeiha (her hands) emphasizes personal agency and effort. In biblical idiom, the 'fruit of one's hands' is what one has earned through work, not through inheritance, luck, or external favor.
word_study.significance: This phrase appears in Psalm 128:2 ('thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands') and embodies the Proverbs teaching that diligent labor produces reward (cf. 12:14, 'A man shall be satisfied with good by the fruit of his mouth'). The virtual parallelism between 'mouth' and 'hands' shows that both speech and work produce consequences. For the woman of valor, her hands have produced actual goods—she has woven, planted, fed her household, clothed the poor. She deserves to enjoy what she has made.

word_study.term_english: let her own works praise her
word_study.meaning: Yehalleluha is the third-person masculine plural imperfect of halal (praise, celebrate, make known). Ma'aseha is the construct feminine plural of ma'aseh (work, deed, accomplishment). Literally: 'and let her works praise her.' The subject (works) praises the object (her), inverting normal power dynamics: the inanimate products of her labor become active speakers on her behalf.
word_study.significance: The verb halal appears throughout Proverbs and the Psalms to mean public recognition and celebration. What makes this verb choice remarkable is that ma'aseha (works) are the grammatical subject doing the praising. Her works are not merely observed—they are personified as testimonies. This reflects the Proverbs philosophy that integrity and faithfulness produce observable fruit that testifies independently (cf. 27:12, where 'the prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself; but the simple pass on, and are punished'—virtue produces visible results).

word_study.meaning: The gates of a city served as the public assembly, marketplace, and courthouse of ancient Israel. This is where legal disputes were adjudicated (Ruth 4:1-11), where elders held council (5:7-9), where business was transacted, and where community reputation was established or destroyed.
word_study.significance: The poem began with the woman's internal virtue—her worth is 'far above rubies' (v. 10). It progressed through her household management, her business enterprises, her care for the poor. Now it reaches its culmination in public honor. But this is not honor based on beauty or charm; it is honor earned by works. The 'gates' are the arena of public judgment, where the community assesses character and contribution. By placing her works' praise in the gates, Proverbs makes her recognition official, communal, and undeniable.

word_study.meaning: Works, deeds, accomplishments. The term encompasses both concrete products (cloth, food, land improvements) and abstract character-displays (faithfulness, diligence, generosity). This is the final word of the book of Proverbs—intentional and symbolically weighted.
word_study.significance: Ma'aseh appears 37 times in Proverbs alone, always referring to tangible fruit of action. Proverbs is fundamentally concerned with consequences—with the visible, real-world results of choices. The book does not end with advice or theory; it ends with ma'aseha, 'her works.' This emphasizes that Proverbs is not about abstract wisdom but about embodied, lived wisdom. A woman who fears the LORD (v. 30) produces works that honor her. The book closes by showing us what that looks like.

cross_references.connection: Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings'—like the woman of valor, diligent workers receive public recognition and honor. Their visible accomplishments testify for them.

Blessed is every one that feareth the LORD... For thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands: happy shalt thou be, and it shall be well with thee.' The same principle: fear of the LORD produces labor that yields reward and public happiness.

All the city of my people doth know that thou art a woman of virtue.' Like the woman of Proverbs 31, Ruth's worth is known publicly 'in the gates' because of her character and works, not her appearance.

Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.' Verse 30 explains the source of verse 31's public honor—it flows from fear of the LORD, which produces the works that praise her.
The desire of the righteous shall be granted... but the substance of the wicked shall perish.' The wicked's works produce nothing lasting; the righteous woman's works endure and speak for her.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite society, the city gates were the seat of authority and community judgment. Archaeological evidence from sites like Tel Beersheba shows gate complexes with benches where elders would sit. Legal transactions, property disputes, and public announcements all occurred here (see the book of Ruth, chapter 4, for a detailed account of gate proceedings). A woman receiving public recognition 'in the gates' was exceptionally rare and notable in patriarchal ancient Near Eastern culture. Typically, women's honor was mediated through male relatives. That Proverbs 31 envisions a woman whose own works bring her public acclaim represents a sophisticated and countercultural view of female worth. The acrostic structure (22 verses, one for each Hebrew letter) indicates this poem was pedagogically significant—young men were meant to memorize it letter by letter, learning what kind of woman embodies wisdom. The poem thus served not only to honor women but to educate men about what to value and seek.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon celebrates faithful women whose works speak for them. Abish 'smote upon her breast with exceeding joy' (Alma 19:28-29) when she witnessed the manifest power of God through Lamoni and his queen, and 'she went forth among the people, declaring glad tidings' — her works (testimony and faith) brought public recognition. Sariah, though less developed in the text, is praised for her steadfastness during the wilderness journey (1 Nephi 5:8). The Restoration emphasizes that women's contributions—spiritual and practical—are essential to the covenant community.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 25 is revealed to Emma Smith and acknowledges her role as a revelation-keeper and support to the Prophet. Like the woman of Proverbs 31, she is recognized for her specific works and faithfulness. The revelation states she should 'murmur not because of the things which thou hast not seen, for they have been withheld from thee and hidden up unto me' (D&C 25:4), encouraging her to trust in the eternal significance of her faithful service—her works will ultimately be recognized.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The woman of valor represents the covenant woman who acts with wisdom, charity, and faithful stewardship. In temple covenants, both men and women make promises related to their stewardship and contribution to the Lord's work. Verse 31 affirms that a woman's faithful 'works'—whether in her household, her community, or her covenant responsibilities—are observed and honored. The temple celebrates the eternal significance of righteous labor by both men and women.

commentary.christological_typology: The woman of valor foreshadows the wisdom and works of Christ through his earthly ministry. Just as her works praise her 'in the gates'—the center of judgment and law—Christ's works (miracles, healing, teaching) testified to his divine authority in the public sphere. Matthew 11:2-5 recounts John the Baptist's disciples coming to Jesus with a question about his identity, and Jesus responds, 'Go and shew John again those things which ye do hear and see: The blind receive their sight, and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have the gospel preached to them.' Christ's works were his witness. Moreover, Christ embodied the fear of the LORD and produced fruit that endures eternally. Like the woman's works praising her without need for external promotion, Christ's works—his resurrection, atonement, and redemption—speak eternally on his behalf.
commentary.application: This verse concludes the entire book of Proverbs with a clarion call: live so that your works testify for you. In a world obsessed with personal branding, self-promotion, and curated image, Proverbs 31:31 proposes something radical—be so faithful in your labor, so diligent in your stewardship, so wise in your choices, that your life speaks for itself. You need not announce your virtues; your actions will do it for you. For modern members of the Church, this has practical force: your commitment to your family, your integrity in business, your service to the poor, your faithfulness in keeping covenants—these are not performed for applause. But they will be observed. They will bear fruit. They will testify. The verse also reminds us to recognize and honor the faithful works of others—especially those whose contributions happen in less visible spaces. The woman of Proverbs 31 did not serve for public acclaim, but Proverbs insists that her works deserve to be seen and praised. How do we ensure that the quiet, faithful labor of others—perhaps in our families, wards, and communities—is recognized and valued?

text_kjv: The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem.

commentary.narrative: Ecclesiastes opens with a formal attribution to a royal sage—explicitly identified as the son of David and king in Jerusalem, which the ancient reader would immediately recognize as Solomon. However, the text does not name Solomon directly; instead, it introduces us to Qohelet, a title that demands attention. The book's authority rests not on who speaks but on what role the speaker occupies. This literary framing is crucial: we are not reading private journals or personal memoirs, but the collected observations of someone whose position—as a convener, assembler, and instructor—gave him unique access to human experience across multiple domains of life. The phrase 'king in Jerusalem' anchors the work geographically and politically, signaling that what follows emerges from observation of life at the center of power and culture in ancient Israel.
commentary.narrative_continued: The Solomonic attribution is not incidental; it establishes credibility and raises expectations.
