commentary.application: Verse 10 is among the most psychologically honest verses in scripture about human experience. It challenges the false piety that pretends sensory pleasure is evil or that authentic joy cannot be found in earthly accomplishment and comfort. Qohelet is saying: I found real happiness. The problem is not that happiness is fake or illusory. The problem is that happiness is not enough. For modern members, this verse invites an honest audit: What pleasures am I pursuing? Are they bringing me real joy? And is that joy sustainable and sufficient? Many people chase pleasure thinking it will finally satisfy them—the next achievement, the next experience, the next acquisition, the next adventure. Qohelet's testimony is that these deliver what they promise in the moment but leave the fundamental question unanswered. The Restoration offers a different answer: true fulfillment comes from consecrating our joys—our achievements, our relationships, our sensory experiences—to covenant purposes. A person can enjoy food, rest, music, and companionship much as Qohelet did, but when these are bound to family sealed in eternity, to service in God's kingdom, to witness of His love, they become not merely a portion (limited and temporary) but a portion of something eternal. The difference is not in denying pleasure but in recontextualizing it.

text_kjv: Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that I had laboured to do: and, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun.

commentary.narrative:
The verdict comes as a rupture. Everything Qohelet experienced in verse 10—the real joy, the genuine rejoicing, the authentic satisfaction—is suddenly reframed as "all was vanity and vexation of spirit." The shift happens not because his pleasure was false but because it was limited to the present moment. "Then I looked" (Hebrew: paniti, 'I turned around, I examined'): he pauses and evaluates the entire experiment retrospectively. This is not a moment of new experience but a moment of reflection. From the vantage point of complete knowledge—having gathered everything, enjoyed everything, retained his wisdom throughout—he looks back and sees emptiness.

The verdict uses the identical language from Ecclesiastes 1:14: "all was vanity and vexation of spirit" (hevel u-re'ut ruach). Vanity (hevel) is vapor or breath—something visible but not substantial, present but not permanent. Vexation of spirit (re'ut ruach) is pursuit or striving after wind—the futile attempt to grasp what cannot be held. The Covenant Rendering notes the precise distinction: the pleasure was real (cheleq) but the profit is nonexistent (ein yitron). Yitron means lasting gain, surplus, or profit—something that remains after the moment of enjoyment passes. This is the devastating realization: Qohelet got what he pursued. The experience was real. But there is nothing left. No accumulation, no transcendence, no meaning that persists beyond the moment. "There was no profit under the sun"—this phrase locates the futility within the temporal realm alone. The experiment was conducted under the sun (meaning in the realm of mortal, earthly life) and found no lasting value within those constraints.

word_study.meaning: And I turned, I looked around, I examined. From the root panah, meaning to turn, face, or look. The reflexive form suggests a deliberate turning of attention or change in perspective.
word_study.significance: The verb paniti marks a moment of reflection or reconsideration. This is not a new experience happening but a reevaluation of previous experience. The 'I' (ani) is emphatic—the subject of the action is deliberate and self-aware. Qohelet is not passively discovering emptiness; he is actively examining and judging his own experiment.

word_study.term_english: all the works that my hands had wrought
word_study.meaning: All my deeds/works that my hands had done. Ma'asim (works, deeds) refers to concrete accomplishments and projects. The hands are mentioned as the instrument of human action.
word_study.significance: The enumeration of 'all the works that my hands had wrought' suggests a comprehensive review—not isolated achievements but the totality of his creative and acquisitive efforts. The mention of hands emphasizes tangible, visible, producible work. Nothing is abstract or theoretical. These are things he made, built, gathered.

word_study.term_english: the labour that I had laboured
word_study.meaning: And in the toil/labor that I had toiled. Amal means labor, effort, work, struggle. The repetition (labour... laboured) emphasizes the expenditure of effort itself.
word_study.significance: The doubled usage of amal stresses the effort expended, not just the result. Qohelet is including in his review both what he accomplished and the effort it cost him. The labor was real, costly, and concentrated.

word_study.meaning: And behold, all was vapor/vanity. Havel (often translated as vanity, but more precisely vapor or breath) refers to something insubstantial and temporary.
word_study.significance: Hevel appears first in Ecclesiastes 1:2 ('vanity of vanities, all is vanity') and recurs throughout. It is the foundational metaphor: like a breath of air, human achievement is visible, real in the moment, but insubstantial and impossible to grasp or hold. The KJV translation 'vanity' carries moral overtones of pride or conceit; the more precise meaning is 'insubstantial'—not morally corrupt but lacking permanence or substance.

word_study.meaning: And striving/chasing after wind. Re'ut (from raah, to feed, shepherd, or pursue) refers to grazing or pursuit. Ruach is spirit or wind.
word_study.significance: The image is of a shepherd chasing wind—the futile pursuit of something invisible and uncatchable. Re'ut ruach captures the weariness of the pursuit itself, the exhaustion that comes from striving after what cannot be held. This is not sadness but futility—the recognition that the entire pursuit is structurally incapable of delivering what is sought.

word_study.meaning: And there was no surplus/profit/lasting gain. Yitron (from the root ytar, to be left over, remain) refers to what remains, what exceeds, surplus, profit.
word_study.significance: Yitron is distinguished in Qohelet's vocabulary from cheleq (portion). Cheleq is what you consume and enjoy in the present; yitron is what remains, accumulates, or carries forward. The Covenant Rendering makes this precise: there is a real cheleq (the joy of verse 10) but no yitron (no lasting surplus). Everything is consumed in the present moment and leaves no remainder. This is the devastating realization: Qohelet got his portion, but there is no profit.

word_study.meaning: Under the sun, in the realm of the sun. This phrase locates the judgment within the temporal, earthly realm, as opposed to what might exist beyond it.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'under the sun' becomes Qohelet's marker for the realm of mortal, earthly life alone. It appears 29 times in Ecclesiastes. By saying there is 'no profit under the sun,' Qohelet is implicitly opening a question: Is there profit elsewhere? The phrase does not deny transcendent meaning but confines his judgment to what is observable and experiential in the earthly realm.

cross_references.connection: Qohelet uses the identical phrase 'all was vanity and vexation of spirit' after investigating wisdom, making explicit that all human pursuits—whether wisdom or pleasure—yield the same verdict.

Qohelet extends this verdict: 'Therefore I hated life; because the work that is wrought under the sun is grievous unto me: for all is vanity and vexation of spirit.' The emptiness of verse 11 becomes existential burden.

'Surely every man at his best state is altogether vanity... he heapeth up riches, and knoweth not who shall gather them.' The Psalmist parallels Qohelet's recognition that accumulation cannot persist.

'For all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass... but the word of the Lord endureth for ever.' Peter contrasts the temporality Qohelet describes with the permanence of God's word.

'For all flesh is corruptible, and all things visible, these should pass away, and all things hideous and abominable should be consumed as by fire.' The Restoration confirms that the earthly realm alone is insufficient; eternal perspective is required.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern wisdom literature, the confrontation with human limitation and mortality was a recognizable theme. The Mesopotamian Epic of Gilgamesh, likely known to educated Israelites through cultural transmission, similarly deals with a king who possesses every advantage yet must face the ultimate inadequacy of human power and achievement. The Egyptian wisdom text 'Dispute Between a Man and His Ba' presents similar philosophical questioning about the value of earthly achievement in light of mortality. Qohelet's language and structure fit within this broader ancient wisdom tradition of grappling with what endures versus what passes away. The specificity of his verdict—that the pleasure was real but the profit is nonexistent—reflects philosophical sophistication. He is not saying pleasure is evil or achievement is worthless; he is making a precise logical claim: in a system where all things end and nothing can be carried beyond death, there is no yitron (lasting profit). This would have been recognized as a serious philosophical position, not merely a cautionary tale.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 9:42 teaches that the flesh is subject to the spirit, which is subject to Christ. Without this hierarchy and this transcendent relationship, the flesh's pursuits (which Qohelet has pursued exhaustively) yield no lasting profit. The Book of Mormon contextualizes Qohelet's emptiness: it results from the absence of a covenant relationship that binds the temporal to the eternal.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:36 teaches, 'We have learned by sad experience that it is the nature and disposition of almost all men, as soon as they get a little authority, as they suppose, they will immediately begin to exercise unrighteous dominion.' The Restoration recognizes that unchecked pursuit of earthly power and pleasure (Qohelet's experiment) inevitably leads to emptiness without the covenant structure that reorients all pursuit toward God's kingdom.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that all things—time, talents, possessions—are consecrated to God's purposes. Without this consecration, Qohelet's experience demonstrates, everything remains isolated in the present moment and yields no lasting profit. The temple ordinances are the means by which temporal experience is bound to eternal significance. What seems like vapor becomes substantial when connected to covenant and eternity.

commentary.christological_typology: Qohelet's judgment that 'all is vanity and vexation of spirit' might seem to be a refutation of Christ's claim in Matthew 11:28 ('Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest'), but Christ answers precisely the problem Qohelet identifies. Where Qohelet finds no profit and vexation of spirit, Christ offers burden-bearing shared with Him ('my yoke is easy, and my burden is light'—Matthew 11:30). Christ is the answer to Qohelet's problem: He is the yitron (lasting profit, remaining gain) that Qohelet could not find under the sun alone. Christ transcends the temporal realm (though He entered it) and offers union with the eternal.
commentary.application: Verse 11 is perhaps the most devastating moment in the book, and it requires honest engagement. Qohelet is describing a experience many high-achievers know: the moment after reaching a major goal when you realize the achievement did not satisfy what you hoped. The promotion happens, and the emptiness remains. The project completes, and the sense of meaninglessness returns. The accumulation occurs, and the question 'But what is this for?' will not go away. For Latter-day Saints, verse 11 invites a crucial examination: What permanent meaning am I building? The Restoration teaches that our efforts in family (sealed in eternity), in covenant relationships, and in service to build God's kingdom do yield yitron—lasting profit, genuine accumulation that persists beyond this life. But if we are building only for the present moment, only for earthly security or status or experience, Qohelet's verdict awaits us. The difference is not in working harder or accumulating more but in binding our work to eternal covenant. A mother's sacrifice for her children's education, when bound to the sealing covenant, becomes eternal building. A person's professional contribution, when connected to service and integrity in God's sight, becomes building toward the kingdom. The same actions, differently contextualized, yield either Qohelet's emptiness or the Restoration's meaning. The verse thus functions as both warning and invitation: warning against orphaning your effort from transcendent purpose, invitation to consecrate your labor to what will endure.

text_kjv: And I turned myself to behold wisdom, and madness, and folly: for what can the man do that cometh after the king? even that which hath been already done.

commentary.narrative:
With verse 12, Qohelet shifts focus from the pleasure experiment (verses 1-11) to the wisdom experiment that will occupy verses 12-16. Yet he begins by acknowledging a structural constraint: he is a king with resources no successor can match. The rhetorical question "what can the man do that cometh after the king? even that which hath been already done" is devastating in its implications. It suggests that if the king—with unlimited resources and unmatched power—cannot find lasting value in either pleasure or wisdom, then no one else will be able to either by exceeding him. The verdict will be universal. He turns now to investigate wisdom itself alongside madness and folly. The Covenant Rendering notes indicate that Qohelet is about to expand his inquiry: he will consider not just wisdom (the pursuit of understanding) but madness (the absence of judgment) and folly (the pursuit of foolish courses), to see whether wisdom has any advantage over its opposites.

The phrase "I turned myself to behold" (Hebrew: paniti ani lir'ot) mirrors the turning in verse 11, but this time it is turning toward a new line of investigation. Qohelet has tested one direction (pleasure) and found it yielding no lasting profit. Now he tests another (wisdom) to see if it fares better. The acknowledgment that his conditions cannot be exceeded—that he is the pinnacle of what any human experiment could be—makes his findings universally applicable. If he cannot find lasting meaning, no one can do so by exceeding him. Therefore, his investigation is not merely personal but paradigmatic.

word_study.meaning: And I turned, I myself, to see/behold. Paniti means I turned or faced; ani is the emphatic first person; lir'ot means to see or observe.
word_study.significance: This phrase appears in verse 11 as well, marking Qohelet's deliberate turning toward investigation or new perspective. The repetition establishes a pattern: he investigates, finds vanity, then turns to investigate something else. The emphasis on 'I' (ani) stresses that this is a self-directed and intentional inquiry.

word_study.meaning: Wisdom (understanding, knowledge), madness (senselessness, recklessness), and folly (foolishness, lack of sense). Chokmah is the opposite of both madness and folly; madness and folly are related but distinct conditions.
word_study.significance: The trio sets up a spectrum from wisdom (the pursuit of understanding and good judgment) to madness (the absence of judgment) to folly (the pursuit of foolish courses). By including all three, Qohelet is setting up a comparison that will become significant: Does wisdom have any advantage over madness and folly if all lead to the same ultimate vanity?

word_study.meaning: What can the man/person who comes (do)? The question is rhetorical, asking what a successor could accomplish.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'what can the man' (mah ha-adam) is existential rather than merely practical. It is not simply asking 'what resources would a successor have' but 'what is it within human capacity to do' in light of the king's exhaustive experiment. The question opens onto ontological territory: What can a human being do in the face of the king's findings?

word_study.meaning: That comes after the king, who follows in succession to the king. This refers literally to the successor, but also implies temporal and hierarchical succession.
word_study.significance: The phrase positions the successor as subordinate and subsequent—having less power, fewer resources, and coming after the king has already exhausted the experiments. This positioning is crucial: if even the king cannot find yitron, the successor has no possibility of exceeding him.

word_study.term_english: even that which hath been already done
word_study.meaning: That which has already been done. The phrase emphasizes that the king has already executed the complete investigation, and the successor can only repeat, not exceed.
word_study.significance: The word kvar ('already') is crucial—it marks temporal finality. The king's experiment is complete and conclusive. The successor can only do what has already been done, repeating rather than discovering. There is no new frontier, no new possibility, no new avenue to explore that the king has not already exhausted.

cross_references.connection: Qohelet states there 'there is no new thing under the sun.' Verse 12's claim that the successor can only repeat what has been done reflects this foundational principle.

Qohelet will immediately follow this verse by exploring the relationship between wisdom and folly, asking whether wisdom has any advantage—a question foreshadowed here by the juxtaposition of the three.
Solomon prays for wisdom, and God grants it; Qohelet now turns to investigate whether this wisdom, which he possesses, actually provides lasting advantage or meaning.
Proverbs exalts wisdom as supreme and eternal; Ecclesiastes will test whether this exaltation is borne out in actual experience when wisdom is possessed and exercised.

'And as all have not faith, seek ye diligently and teach one another words of wisdom; yea, seek ye out of the best books words of wisdom.' The Restoration honors the pursuit of wisdom within a covenant framework, which Qohelet's wisdom lacked.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient world, the ideal of the philosopher-king or the wise ruler was well established. Plato's 'Republic' (written later than Ecclesiastes but reflecting broader assumptions) imagines a state ruled by those with wisdom. Egyptian wisdom literature similarly idealized the wise ruler who possesses both insight and power. Qohelet's position—as a king investigating wisdom, madness, and folly—would have been understood by ancient readers as the ideal position to conduct such inquiry. He has the resources to pursue wisdom without distraction, the power to explore its implications, and the security to be honest about its limitations. The rhetorical question about the successor also reflects the historical reality of succession—each king inherits from his predecessor and must establish his own legitimacy. Qohelet's claim that the successor can only 'do that which hath been already done' reflects both the limitations of human knowledge (nothing truly new under the sun) and the exhaustion of human possibility when faced with the finite and temporal.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Jacob 4:7-8 teaches that the Nephites understood 'all things have been done in the wisdom of him who knoweth all things. Wherefore, we search the prophets,' indicating that Restoration epistemology places human wisdom in relation to divine wisdom. Qohelet's wisdom, achieved without relation to revelation or covenant, is inherently limited. The Book of Mormon suggests that wisdom itself must be grounded in revelation to become eternal.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:37 teaches that 'all things unto me are spiritual; and not at any time have I given unto you a law which was temporal.' This principle reframes the question Qohelet is asking: if all things are spiritual (i.e., oriented toward eternity and covenant), then wisdom attained apart from this framework is not truly wisdom but only cleverness.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that true wisdom comes through covenant relationship with God, not through independent investigation alone. The endowment presents wisdom as revealed truth, not achieved knowledge. Qohelet's investigation of wisdom as an independent human pursuit represents a category error—wisdom, in Restoration thought, must be received, not merely pursued.

commentary.christological_typology: Qohelet's investigation of wisdom, madness, and folly foreshadows Christ's teaching in Matthew 23, where Christ critiques the wisdom of the Pharisees and scribes, calling them 'blind guides' who have inherited but not truly understood wisdom. Christ offers Himself as the source and embodiment of true wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:24, 'Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God'). Where Qohelet investigates wisdom as a human achievement, Christ is wisdom incarnate—not attained through human investigation but given through relationship. Furthermore, Christ's voluntary emptying of power (Philippians 2:6-7) stands in contrast to Qohelet's use of unlimited power to investigate. Christ's wisdom is demonstrated not through accumulation but through sacrifice.
commentary.application: Verse 12's rhetorical question—'what can the man do that cometh after the king?'—carries a surprising modern relevance. In an age of information abundance and technological acceleration, we often believe the next innovation, the next discovery, the next advancement will finally deliver what previous efforts could not. Qohelet's principle suggests otherwise: if the wisest and most powerful predecessor has exhausted the available avenues and found them all yielding no lasting profit, then incremental advancement will not solve the underlying problem. This does not suggest resignation or stagnation but rather a reorientation of inquiry. The question 'What can we do that hasn't already been done?' is partly Qohelet's question. But the Restoration reframes it: What can we do that connects the temporal to the eternal? What can we build that will endure? For Latter-day Saints, the answer is covenant-based work: family sealed in eternity, communities of saints, service to build God's kingdom. These are not innovations in the worldly sense but applications of eternal principles. Verse 12 invites a shift in how we measure achievement: not 'Have we done something new?' but 'Have we bound our work to what endures?' The verse thus functions as both humility and hope—humility about the ultimate limitations of human innovation within a purely temporal frame, hope that covenant provides the frame within which effort becomes meaningful.

text_kjv: Then I saw that wisdom excelleth folly, as far as light excelleth darkness.

commentary.narrative:
Qohelet makes his first explicit concession: wisdom is genuinely superior to folly. This is not a grudging admission but a clear-eyed endorsement. The comparison to light versus darkness is the strongest possible metaphor in ancient Hebrew thought — light represents knowledge, order, life, and divine presence, while darkness represents ignorance, chaos, death, and separation from God. By using this comparison, Qohelet affirms that wisdom provides real advantage in navigating the world. He is not anti-wisdom; he has not concluded that all knowledge is futile or that fools and sages are equivalent in their daily functioning.

Yet the translator notes point to the crucial tension: the question is not whether wisdom is better, but whether it is enough. This opening observation sets a trap for the reader. We expect Qohelet to build an argument that wisdom is therefore worth pursuing above all things. But in the verses that follow, he will systematically undermine that expectation. The light-darkness comparison will become ironic — wisdom may illuminate the path, but it cannot illuminate a way around death.

word_study.meaning: Advantage, surplus, profit, gain. From the root yatar ('to remain, to exceed'). In Ecclesiastes, yitron refers to what is left over after accounting for losses — a net gain. The word carries both economic and existential weight: a surplus that justifies effort.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'has an advantage' captures the economic nuance better than 'excelleth.' Qohelet is asking: Does wisdom yield a profit? A remainder? This mercantile language hints that he is assessing wisdom as an investment, not merely as a state of being. The same word will recur in 2:15 and 3:9, each time sharpening the question: What is the return on wisdom?

word_study.meaning: Foolishness, stupidity, lack of discernment. From sekhel ('sense, reasoning, understanding'). Folly is not mere ignorance but active misdirection of mind — a failure to perceive what is plain to see.
word_study.significance: The contrast between wisdom (chokhma) and folly (sikhlut) is not between knowledge and ignorance but between two active orientations to reality. A fool does not lack information; he lacks the discernment to use it rightly. This matters because it means foolishness is partly a choice — a turning away from what can be known.

word_study.meaning: Light: illumination, clarity, life, divine presence. Darkness: concealment, confusion, death, divine absence. These are the most fundamental binary metaphors in biblical thought — not merely physical but cosmological and theological.
word_study.significance: This metaphor appears throughout Scripture to signify the difference between covenant knowledge and spiritual blindness (John 8:12; D&C 93:36–37). Qohelet's use here is conventional and affirming, but its power will be drained as the argument progresses. If wisdom is light, why does it not illuminate a path around death?

cross_references.connection: Solomon's explicit teaching that wisdom is supreme and worth acquiring 'more than all things.' Ecclesiastes 2:13 echoes this hierarchy while later questioning its sufficiency.
The New Testament develops the light-darkness metaphor as a marker of spiritual knowledge and fellowship with God, affirming the biblical precedent Qohelet invokes here.

Qohelet's earlier experiment with wisdom and knowledge, which led him to conclude that 'in much wisdom is much grief.' This verse shows he still affirms wisdom's objective superiority even as he wrestles with its existential limits.
The Doctrine and Covenants affirms that 'the light shineth in darkness, and the darkness comprehendeth it not.' Wisdom as light operates against the backdrop of human ignorance and mortality.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern wisdom literature, the superiority of wisdom over folly was axiomatic. Egyptian Instruction texts, Mesopotamian proverbs, and Israelite wisdom all taught that the wise person prospers while the fool suffers. Qohelet's audience would have expected him to build a case for wisdom cultivation based on this acknowledged superiority. The light-darkness metaphor was standard — Egyptian texts describe the wise as those who 'see' (in Amarna wisdom) while fools 'stumble in darkness.' The cultural context makes Qohelet's later reversal even more jarring. He is not introducing a novel claim; he is accepting the conventional wisdom and then systematically dismantling its practical implications.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:35–36 contains Alma's acknowledgment of the Lord's hand despite human limitations: 'Now when our hearts are truly repentant, and we truly believe in Christ, then is his grace sufficient for us.' The Book of Mormon repeatedly affirms wisdom's reality while insisting that Christ's grace, not human wisdom alone, is the answer to mortality and sin.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 11:11–12 teaches Joseph Smith that 'a great and marvelous work is about to come forth among the children of men. Therefore, O ye that embark in the service of God, see that ye serve him with all your heart, might, mind and strength.' Wisdom is valued, but it must be directed toward the Lord's purposes, not toward self-sufficiency.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment presents light and darkness as the fundamental contrast between the terrestrial and celestial orders. The progression from darkness to light in temple ordinances symbolizes the movement from ignorance to knowledge — yet even that knowledge is preparatory, not ultimate. Qohelet's question 'is light enough?' has resonance in the LDS understanding that mortal knowledge is incomplete until reunited with divine knowledge.

commentary.christological_typology: The light-darkness motif foreshadows Christ as the Light of the World (John 8:12). Qohelet's question about whether wisdom-light can overcome darkness points toward the need for divine illumination beyond human knowledge. Only Christ can provide the light that penetrates the deepest darkness — the shadow of death itself. Wisdom can enlighten the mind; only Christ can redeem the mortal condition that makes all earthly wisdom ultimately insufficient.
commentary.application: Modern Latter-day Saints often face the same tension Qohelet identifies. We affirm the value of education, critical thinking, and rational understanding — the wisdom-light comparison matches our commitment to learning. Yet we also wrestle with the limits of human knowledge when confronted with mortality, suffering, or moral complexity. This verse invites us to hold two truths simultaneously: wisdom is genuinely superior to folly in navigating daily life, yet wisdom alone cannot answer the deepest questions of meaning and mortality. The practical application is intellectual humility — pursue wisdom vigorously, but remember that it answers 'how' questions better than 'why' questions, and it cannot overcome death.

text_kjv: The wise man's eyes are in his head; but the fool walketh in darkness: and I myself perceived also that one event happeneth to them all.

commentary.narrative:
The first half of this verse elaborates the light-darkness metaphor with almost comic vividness. The wise person's eyes are in his head — this is an obvious statement that becomes profound precisely because of its obviousness. It is a compact way of saying: the wise person can see; he has foresight, awareness, and the ability to perceive danger. The fool walks in darkness and cannot see. This makes immediate, practical sense. In daily life, wisdom genuinely does provide advantage. The wise merchant calculates; the fool squanders. The wise king foresees threats; the fool stumbles into ruin.

But then comes the turning point marked by 'and I myself perceived also' — Qohelet introduces personal witness. The phrase 'one event happeneth to them all' introduces the word miqreh (fate, what happens) for the first time in Ecclesiastes. The reader is not told explicitly what this 'one event' is, but the context makes it unmistakable: death. Both wise and fool face the same miqreh. This is the crack in wisdom's armor. Wisdom gives you eyes in your head so you can see where you are going — but it cannot help you escape the destination that awaits all travelers. The observation is not yet an argument, but it plants the seed of Qohelet's central complaint: the structural injustice of death erasing all human distinctions.

word_study.meaning: Literally: 'his eyes [are] in his head.' A compressed metaphor for foresight, awareness, and the ability to perceive what is coming. The head is the seat of wisdom and discernment in Hebrew thought.
word_study.significance: This phrase is unique to Ecclesiastes 2:14 and illustrates how vivid concrete language can express abstract ideas. The Hebrew wisdom tradition often uses body-part metaphors: the heart is the seat of understanding, the ears are for receiving instruction, the eyes are for perceiving truth. Qohelet's formulation is almost humorous — it is so self-evident that it borders on tautology — yet that obviousness is the point. It emphasizes the basic, incontrovertible fact that wisdom enables perception.

word_study.meaning: The fool walks in darkness — stumbling, unable to perceive, moving without awareness or foresight.
word_study.significance: The word order in Hebrew (fool, in-darkness, walks) places emphasis on the fool's active movement despite blindness. He is not stationary; he is actively stumbling. This captures the dynamic danger of foolishness — it is not passive ignorance but active misdirection.

word_study.meaning: One fate, one occurrence, one thing that happens. Miqreh derives from qarah ('to encounter, to befall') and refers to what happens to a person — especially death — through no choice or effort of their own. Echad emphasizes singularity and inevitability.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'one fate' captures the sense better than 'one event.' This is not a random happening but a destined occurrence. Miqreh appears again in 2:15 and 3:19, always referring to death or the universal human condition. The term introduces the theme of what lies beyond human agency and wisdom.

word_study.meaning: Befalls all of them. The verb qarah in the imperfect tense emphasizes what regularly, inevitably happens. The direct object marker et- makes explicit that this fate 'seizes' or 'overtakes' all of them without exception.
word_study.significance: The use of et-kulam ('all of them') is crucial — not just some, not even most, but all without exception. This universality is what makes Qohelet's complaint pressing. It is not that death is unfair to particular individuals; it is that death obliterates the meaning of all human distinction.

cross_references.connection: Paul writes, 'the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life.' The New Testament affirms the universality of death that Qohelet observes, while offering a resolution through Christ's resurrection.
Paul's proclamation that death is swallowed up in victory through Christ directly addresses the problem Qohelet identifies: that wisdom cannot overcome the one fate that befalls all humanity.

Job sarcastically acknowledges the conventional wisdom that the wise possess understanding, echoing the same tension between acknowledged superiority and its insufficiency against suffering and death.

The Doctrine and Covenants teaches that all must pass through death: 'And it shall come to pass that those that die in me shall not taste of the second death,' affirming both the universality of death and the possibility of resurrection.
Qohelet will expand on this same observation: 'all have one breath, so that a man hath no preeminence above a beast,' and 'all go unto one place; all are of the dust.'

commentary.historical_context: The observation that death is universal and that it erases social distinctions was a recurring theme in ancient Near Eastern literature. The Mesopotamian Poem of Gilgamesh (composed perhaps 2000 years before Qohelet) explores Gilgamesh's quest for immortality and ultimately his recognition that death is inevitable for all humans regardless of status or achievement. Egyptian wisdom texts, while often focused on prosperity and legacy, sometimes acknowledged that death comes for king and commoner alike. However, Qohelet's tone is distinctive — rather than accepting this as part of the natural order (as Egyptian texts often did), he treats it as an outrage that undermines the meaning of wisdom itself. The cultural context shows that this was not a novel observation but that Qohelet's emotional response to it was unusually stark.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma's teachings on the resurrection in Alma 11:43–45 directly address Qohelet's problem: 'Now this is the state of the souls of the wicked... it is given unto them to know good from evil; therefore they choose evil works rather than good; but behold, if they have rejected the word of God and have rejected all the prophets and Alma himself... [they are] consigned to a state of misery and endless torment.' The Book of Mormon affirms Qohelet's observation that wisdom alone cannot save, while asserting that Christ's atonement and resurrection provide the answer.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 128:15 teaches that in the resurrection, 'those who have died in my gospel are exalted to greater glory and honor than all others.' This directly responds to Qohelet's complaint that death makes all distinctions meaningless — in the Restoration, death is reframed as a transition through which divine distinctions become operative.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ordinance of baptism for the dead (D&C 124:29–33) represents the LDS response to Qohelet's dilemma. If death erases all earthly advantages, the temple covenant extends the reach of saving ordinances beyond the grave. The sealing power ensures that death does not separate or nullify covenant relationships.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's incarnation directly confronts the problem Qohelet identifies. Jesus was the only human being who possessed both perfect wisdom and perfect foresight ('eyes in his head') yet still faced death. His crucifixion shows that even the wisest and most righteous cannot escape 'the one event' through human power alone. Yet Christ's resurrection provides the answer Qohelet cannot find within the mortal frame of reference: death is not the final fate that renders all wisdom meaningless. Through Christ's victory, the 'one event' is transformed from erasure into transition.
commentary.application: This verse speaks directly to the experience of grief and the apparent meaninglessness that can follow the death of a wise, virtuous, or beloved person. It addresses the person who asks: 'Why did this person have to die when they lived so wisely and well?' The verse validates the emotional force of that question while pointing beyond it. The practical application is twofold: (1) recognize that wisdom, while genuinely valuable for living well, does not and cannot extend life; and (2) this recognition should push us beyond the scope of mortal wisdom toward faith in resurrection and eternal perspective. For Latter-day Saints specifically, this verse can motivate engagement with temple work for the dead — a concrete way of affirming that the one fate does not have the final say.

text_kjv: Then said I in my heart, As it happeneth to the fool, so it happeneth even to me; and why was I then more wise? Then I said in my heart, that this also is vanity.

commentary.narrative:
The verse moves from observation to anguished reasoning. Qohelet speaks internally ('in my heart'), processing the implications of what he has just perceived. If the same miqreh (fate) befalls both wise and fool — if both die — then what advantage does wisdom confer? The question 'why was I then more wise?' is not a rejection of wisdom but an existential crisis. Qohelet has invested enormous energy in becoming wise (as detailed in 1:12–18). He has pursued knowledge, experience, pleasure, and achievement. Now he faces the realization that all this striving ends in the same place as the fool's ignorant wandering.

The translator notes observe that this is 'an anguished recognition of its limits,' not a wholesale dismissal of wisdom. Qohelet is not saying wisdom is worthless in the moment. He is saying that when confronted with the fact of death, the net gain (yitron) of all that wisdom becomes questionable. The conclusion — 'this also is vanity' — applies not to wisdom itself but to the assumption that wisdom can conquer mortality. The Hebrew word hebel (vapor, breath, vanity) captures both the insubstantiality of human endeavor and its transience. Wisdom, like all human effort, is hebel — it disappears like breath.

word_study.meaning: I said to myself; I spoke internally. The heart (lev) in Hebrew is the seat of thought, reasoning, and decision — not primarily emotion as in English. To speak 'in the heart' is to reason through something inwardly.
word_study.significance: This phrase recurs throughout Ecclesiastes (also 1:16, 2:1, 3:17) and marks Qohelet as an internal, reflective voice. He is not making public pronouncements but working through questions in solitude. This intimacy invites the reader into Qohelet's thought process rather than merely presenting conclusions.

word_study.term_english: As it happeneth to the fool, so it happeneth even to me
word_study.term_original: כְּמִקְרֵה הַכְּסִיל גַּם־אֲנִי יִקְרֵנִי (ke-miqreh ha-kesil gam-ani yiqreni)
word_study.meaning: The same fate that overtakes the fool will overtake me as well. The comparative ke- ('as, like') and the emphatic particle gam ('also, even') stress the absolute equivalence of outcome.
word_study.significance: The equation is stark and non-negotiable. Miqreh makes the fate inevitable, not a possibility. Qohelet is not expressing doubt about whether he will die; he is stating it as a fixed fact and questioning what it means for his life project.

word_study.term_english: why was I then more wise?
word_study.term_original: וְלָמָּה חָכַמְתִּי אֲנִי אָז יוֹתֵר (ve-lamma chakhamti ani az yoter)
word_study.meaning: Why was I more wise then? The adverb yoter ('more, excessively') modifies the perfective verb 'I was wise,' suggesting that the extra effort, the additional pursuit of wisdom, now appears pointless.
word_study.significance: The question is not rhetorical but genuinely anguished. Qohelet is not denying that he was wise; he is asking whether the extra exertion ('more wise') yields anything in the face of death. This formulation distinguishes between basic wisdom (which keeps you functional) and ambitious wisdom-seeking (which pursues mastery and understanding). The latter is what feels threatened.

word_study.meaning: Vapor, breath, mist, transience, insubstantiality. From an onomatopoetic root suggesting the sound of breath. Hebel describes things that appear solid but dissipate, that exist momentarily but leave nothing lasting. The Covenant Rendering renders it 'vapor' throughout.
word_study.significance: Hebel is the key interpretive term in Ecclesiastes, appearing 38 times. It is not quite 'meaningless' (a modern philosophical term) but rather 'ephemeral, insubstantial, transitory.' Qohelet is not claiming that wisdom has no meaning in the moment; he is claiming that it is ultimately vapor — it does not endure. The term is phenomenological: it describes what wisdom appears to be when confronted with mortality.

cross_references.connection: Qohelet's first pursuit of wisdom, which resulted in the conclusion 'in much wisdom is much grief.' This verse shows him circling back to the same problem from a different angle — the insufficiency of wisdom to address death.
Job similarly observes that both the righteous and the wicked come to death, and 'his bones are full of the sins of his youth,' raising the question of whether virtue provides lasting advantage.

The psalmist reflects on death as the common fate: 'for he seeth that wise men die, likewise the fool and the brutish person perish,' yet with an affirmation of resurrection that Qohelet has not yet reached.
Peter acknowledges his own approaching death while affirming that wisdom transmitted before death has lasting value — a counterpoint to Qohelet's despair.

commentary.historical_context: The question of whether virtue and wisdom yield tangible benefit was a central concern in ancient Near Eastern wisdom literature. Egyptian wisdom texts often promised that the wise person would prosper in this life and achieve a good death and favorable afterlife judgment. Mesopotamian texts were more pessimistic about human prospects but still affirmed that wisdom led to better outcomes in the present. Qohelet's question is not whether wisdom is theoretically better — all traditions affirmed that — but whether the actual payoff justifies the investment when death erases all earthly distinctions. This was a transgressive question in the context of conventional wisdom teaching. Qohelet's audience may have expected him to resolve the tension by appealing to reward in the afterlife (as Egyptian and later Israelite texts do), but he does not make that move here. He leaves the question open and pressing.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 40:11–14 addresses the separation of spirit from body at death and the waiting period before resurrection: 'Now, concerning the state of the soul between death and the resurrection— Behold, it has been made known unto me by an angel, that the spirits of all men... are taken home to that God who gave them life.' The Book of Mormon affirms Qohelet's observation that death is universal while providing a framework (spirit continuation and eventual resurrection) that allows wisdom and righteousness to have lasting significance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:5–10 describes the vision of degrees of glory, in which different individuals who lived with different levels of understanding and obedience achieve different postmortal states. This suggests that wisdom and righteousness do have differential outcomes — not in mortality (where both die), but in the resurrection. This directly addresses Qohelet's despair.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple's emphasis on covenant-making across time suggests that wisdom invested in covenants with God has significance that transcends death. The sealing of families and the work for the dead affirm that the distinctions created by wisdom and righteousness are not erased at death but are preserved and elevated in the eternal order.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ embodies the resolution to Qohelet's dilemma. Christ was supremely wise — his teachings, his foresight, his understanding of all things were perfect. Yet Christ died. His death seemed to render his wisdom irrelevant, at least from a mortal perspective. But Christ's resurrection proved that wisdom directed toward eternal purposes is not vanity — it accomplishes something that survives death. Moreover, Christ's wisdom is the wisdom that can answer Qohelet's question: only by losing life can one find it (Matthew 16:25). This reorients the very meaning of wisdom itself.
commentary.application: This verse speaks to the despair that can follow the realization that education, achievement, and intellectual mastery do not prevent suffering or death. A successful career, a Ph.D., years of study — all prove ephemeral when confronted with mortality or loss. For young people just beginning to invest in wisdom and knowledge, this verse can induce a kind of philosophical despair: 'Why study hard if I'm going to die anyway?' The application is not to abandon wisdom but to re-ground it. For Latter-day Saints, the answer is to invest in wisdom directed toward eternal purposes: learning about God, developing Christlike attributes, understanding covenants. This redirects wisdom from self-aggrandizement or worldly achievement toward ends that do not vanish at death. The verse thus becomes an invitation not to abandon learning but to transform its orientation.

text_kjv: For there is no remembrance of the wise more than of the fool for ever; seeing that which now is in the days to come shall all be forgotten. And how dieth the wise man? as the fool.

commentary.narrative:
Qohelet deepens his argument by moving from the fact of death to the fact of oblivion. Death itself is the universal miqreh, but death is compounded by forgetting. The wise person and the fool both die, and both are forgotten with equal finality. The phrase 'no remembrance... for ever' echoes Ecclesiastes 1:11 and introduces the theme of memory-failure as a structural feature of human existence. Nothing that is done under the sun leaves a lasting trace in human memory.

The assertion that 'all shall be forgotten' is not pessimistic in tone alone; it is a claim about the fundamental structure of time. Future generations will not remember Qohelet's achievements, wisdom, or person any more than they remember the fool he references. The parallelism 'how dieth the wise man? as the fool' is a question framed as if in protest — the verb translated 'dieth' uses the present tense to create immediacy, as if Qohelet is witnessing it. The expressive power of the verse comes from the contrast between the permanence humans desire (lasting remembrance, legacy) and the transience that actually characterizes all human endeavor. The wise are forgotten no less than the foolish. If wisdom's advantage is supposed to show itself in lasting accomplishment or legacy, then wisdom has no advantage at all.

word_study.meaning: No memory, no trace, no record. Zichron refers to remembrance in both the active sense (the act of remembering) and the passive sense (what is remembered, the record or trace left behind).
word_study.significance: In Hebrew thought, zichron is crucial to meaning and identity. God's name is invoked as 'a memorial' (l'zichron), and the Passover is commanded to be remembered as a 'memorial' to preserve its significance. For Qohelet to claim that there is no zichron is to claim that wisdom leaves no meaningful mark on the world. This is especially pointed because legacy and remembrance are often presented as ways that human achievement transcends death — at least one's name or works live on.

word_study.term_english: seeing that which now is in the days to come shall all be forgotten
word_study.term_original: בְּשֶׁכְּבָר הַיָּמִים הַבָּאִים הַכֹּל נִשְׁכָּח (be-shechevar ha-yamim ha-baim ha-kol nishkach)
word_study.meaning: For already/since the days to come, everything is forgotten. The word shekhvar ('already, since') suggests that forgetting is not a future possibility but a present reality — things are already being forgotten as new days come.
word_study.significance: This formulation is striking because it presents forgetting not as a temporal event in the distant future but as an ongoing process. Each new day brings new concerns that obscure what was previously known. The wave of time washes over all remembrance. The Covenant Rendering's 'in the days to come everything will already be forgotten' captures this sense of inevitable, progressive erasure.

word_study.term_english: And how dieth the wise man?
word_study.meaning: And how does the wise person die? The interrogative eikh ('how?') paired with the verb 'to die' creates both a question and an exclamation — 'how can it be that the wise person dies...?'
word_study.significance: The verb yamut in the present/imperfect tense suggests immediacy and ongoing reality, not a future event. Qohelet is not asking a philosophical question but expressing outrage. The question is not rhetorical in the sense of having an obvious answer; rather, it is genuinely asked as if the answer should be different but is not.

word_study.meaning: With/alongside the fool. The preposition im suggests both simultaneity (dying at the same time) and equivalence (dying in the same manner).
word_study.significance: The preposition emphasizes that there is no distinction in death itself. The wise does not die 'better' or 'differently' than the fool — the death is identical. This complete erasure of distinction is what particularly troubles Qohelet.

cross_references.connection: Qohelet's earlier statement: 'there is no remembrance of former things; neither shall there be any remembrance of things that are to come.' This verse continues and applies that observation specifically to the distinction between wise and foolish.

The psalmist similarly reflects that 'every man at his best state is altogether vanity' and that each person passes away, leaving no lasting mark — though the psalmist's response differs from Qohelet's.
The death notices of kings often use the formulaic language 'and he slept with his fathers,' suggesting that even monarchy and achievement lead to the same end as any person.

The Lord teaches: 'Therefore, fear not to do good, my sons, for whatsoever ye sow, that shall ye also reap,' suggesting that actions have consequences that transcend mortal forgetting through divine judgment.

commentary.historical_context: The concern with legacy and remembrance was particularly acute in ancient Near Eastern cultures, where commemorative monuments, written records, and tomb inscriptions served as defenses against oblivion. Egyptian tomb inscriptions often preserved the name and deeds of the deceased, and the destruction of a person's name was considered a kind of secondary death. The fear of being forgotten was real and urgent. Qohelet's assertion that even the wise are forgotten challenges one of the primary ways ancient people thought they could achieve something lasting — through the preservation of their name and memory. He is saying this defense is illusory. For a wisdom teacher in this context, this is a radical assertion. It suggests that all the monuments, records, and achievements accumulate no lasting meaning because they too will be forgotten.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mormon 9:5–6 addresses the power of God to raise the dead and bring forth records that reveal all things: 'God is not a partial God, neither a changeable being; but he is unchangeable from all eternity to all eternity. He hath taken the Zion of Enoch into his own bosom.' The Book of Mormon insists that despite human forgetting, God remembers, and divine record-keeping preserves what mortals forget.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 127:8 states: 'Therefore, dearly beloved brethren, let us cheerfully do all things that lie in our power; and then may we stand still, with the utmost assurance, to see the salvation of God, and for his arm to be revealed.' The gathering and record-keeping emphasized in Doctrine and Covenants (see D&C 21:4–5) suggests that divine remembrance counteracts human forgetting.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ordinance of sealing 'binds' relationships and records them before God in a way that transcends mortal forgetting. The temple work ensures that even if the world forgets the dead, they are remembered before God and their eternal status is preserved. This is the LDS response to Qohelet's despair about oblivion.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's resurrection ensures that His works are not forgotten — they are preserved and their consequences continue through all eternity. Moreover, Christ, when He appears in glory, will reward each person 'according to thy works' (Revelation 22:12), suggesting that nothing done in covenant with Him is forgotten by God, even if mortal memory fails. The contrast between human forgetting and divine remembrance finds its resolution in Christ, who 'knoweth all things' and 'remembereth all covenants which he hath made with the children of men' (D&C 3:1).
commentary.application: This verse challenges the modern idolatry of legacy and personal brand. In an age of social media and personal branding, the desire to be remembered, to have lasting impact, to leave a mark — these are powerful motivators. Qohelet's observation that the wise are no more remembered than the fool is deeply unsettling to contemporary ambitions. The application is not to abandon meaningful work but to reorient motivation. Work for God's purposes, knowing that God remembers even if the world forgets. Invest in family and covenants, which have significance before God regardless of whether future generations remember your name. For Latter-day Saints specifically, the temple sealing work affirms that family bonds and spiritual accomplishments are preserved eternally before God, even if mortal memory fails. This transforms work from being motivated by fear of oblivion to being grounded in covenants with the eternal God.

text_kjv: Therefore I hated life; because the work that is wrought under the sun is grievous unto me: for all is vanity and vexation of spirit.

commentary.narrative:
This is the most extreme emotional statement in the chapter and among the most striking in all wisdom literature. Qohelet does not say he was disappointed, disillusioned, or frustrated — he says he hated life. The verb sane ('to hate') is absolute and unqualified. This is not a temporary mood but a declaration of fundamental alienation. The cause is explicitly stated: the work that is wrought under the sun is grievous (ra'a, 'bad, evil, causing suffering') to him. By 'the work' (ma'aseh), Qohelet means the totality of human labor, effort, and achievement — all the striving that characterizes human existence.

What makes this work grievous? Not that it is painful or toilsome in the immediate sense, but that it is ephemeral and meaningless in light of death. The translator notes capture this precisely: 'the structural injustice of death erasing all distinctions.' This is not personal suffering or social injustice that could be remedied. It is the fundamental structure of existence: humans work, strive, and achieve, and then die, and all their distinction-making is obliterated. The concluding phrase — 'all is vanity and vexation of spirit' — introduces a new term alongside hebel. 'Vexation of spirit' (r'ut ruach, 'chasing after wind') conveys both futility and purposelessness. It is not merely that effort is transient; it is that effort appears to be aimed at something that cannot be grasped.

word_study.meaning: I hated life. The verb sane means 'to hate, to detest, to regard with aversion.' The direct object marker et- emphasizes that it is life itself (not just some aspect of life) that is hated.
word_study.significance: This formulation is extraordinary in biblical literature. The Hebrew Bible affirms life as a fundamental good — one of the opening commands in Genesis is 'be fruitful and multiply.' To say 'I hated life' is to speak in a register of despair that challenges biblical optimism about existence itself. The translator notes that this is 'the most extreme emotional statement in the chapter,' and it cannot be softened or reinterpreted. Qohelet genuinely hates life under the conditions he perceives.

word_study.meaning: Bad, evil, causing harm or suffering. In different contexts, it can refer to moral evil, physical pain, or misfortune. Here it is existential badness — the condition of existing under conditions that make all effort ultimately futile.
word_study.significance: The word ra'a is the fundamental term for 'bad' or 'evil' in Hebrew. By using it to describe the work under the sun, Qohelet is not claiming that work is morally wrong but that it is existentially bad — harmful to one's sense of meaning and purpose. This is a philosophical evil rather than a moral one.

word_study.meaning: Work, deed, labor, accomplishment. Ma'aseh refers to the visible products of human effort and also to the effort itself. The term is central to Ecclesiastes' vocabulary — it appears frequently to describe human activity under the sun.
word_study.significance: Qohelet's complaint is not merely about physical labor (which might be understood as a curse resulting from Adam's sin) but about human work and accomplishment in general. It includes intellectual work, creative work, and the pursuit of wisdom. The universal scope of the complaint is crucial.

word_study.meaning: Chasing after wind. Ruach means 'spirit, wind, breath.' R'ut derives from the verb 'to shepherd or pasture' and has come to mean 'striving after' or 'pursuing.' The phrase suggests futile, circular effort that produces nothing.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'chasing after wind' is vivid and accurate. It conveys not merely that effort is futile but that it is absurdly so — the futility is almost comic. One chases wind; one grasps for it; one never catches it. This phrase, which appears repeatedly in Ecclesiastes, captures the phenomenology of meaninglessness — the sense that one is expending energy for something that cannot be grasped or held.

cross_references.connection: Qohelet's account of his initial pursuit of wisdom and knowledge, which also led to the conclusion that increased knowledge increases grief — this verse is the emotional culmination of that trajectory.

Qohelet will later reflect on oppression and conclude that 'I praised the dead which are already dead more than the living which are yet alive; yea, better is he than both they, which hath not yet been, who hath not seen the evil work that is done under the sun.'
Job's curse upon the day of his birth, which expresses similar despair about existence itself, though Job's despair is tied to specific suffering while Qohelet's is existential.

The Lord teaches that 'that which is of God is light; and he that receiveth light, and continueth in God, receiveth more light,' suggesting a counterpoint to Qohelet's darkness about the meaning of mortal effort.

commentary.historical_context: The expression of existential despair about life itself is rare in ancient Near Eastern wisdom literature, which typically affirms life's value even while acknowledging its difficulties. Egyptian wisdom texts often address hardship but maintain confidence in the gods' order and one's place in it. Mesopotamian texts, while more pessimistic, do not typically express hatred of life itself. Qohelet's statement is distinctive and transgressive in its cultural context. It likely reflects the crisis of meaning that can arise when traditional wisdom (which promised order and reward) encounters empirical reality (death, forgetting, the erasure of distinction). In the Hellenistic context of probable composition, this kind of philosophical despair about existence would have had some parallel in Greek philosophical traditions (certain strands of Cynicism or Stoicism), but it remains unusual in Israelite literature.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 2:27 teaches that humans are 'free to choose liberty and eternal life, through the great Mediator of all men, or to choose captivity and death, according to the captivity and power of the devil.' The Book of Mormon affirms that human choices have ultimate significance — that work directed toward God's purposes is not vanity. This directly addresses Qohelet's despair by providing a framework in which mortal effort has eternal weight.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:1–19 describes the vision of degrees of glory and teaches that individuals' actions and choices have consequences that extend into eternity. This suggests that work done in mortality is not erased or rendered meaningless at death but is eternally consequential.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The endowment's emphasis on covenants, progression, and eternal family relationships implies that human effort and relationships have meaning beyond death. The work undertaken in the temple — both the ritual work and the work for the dead — is affirmed as having ultimate cosmic significance. This provides a response to Qohelet's despair: work undertaken in covenant with God is not vain.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ entered into the full depth of this despair at Gethsemane and the crucifixion. His prayer 'if it be possible, let this cup pass from me' (Matthew 26:39) reflects the human recoil from suffering and meaninglessness. His cry on the cross 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' (Matthew 27:46) expresses the darkest moment of alienation. Yet Christ's resurrection transforms the meaning of that suffering. It is not vanity; it accomplishes redemption. By entering into the human condition fully — including the despair and meaninglessness Qohelet articulates — Christ validates that despair while ultimately transcending it. The resurrection says: this is not the end; meaning is not erased.
commentary.application: This verse speaks directly to experiences of depression, meaninglessness, and the despair that can arise when confronted with mortality and the apparent futility of effort. For someone experiencing suicidal ideation or severe depression, this verse is important both as validation ('your experience of meaninglessness is not unique or crazy; it is something people of faith have articulated') and as an invitation to what comes next in Ecclesiastes and in the gospel. The application is not to dismiss Qohelet's despair as invalid or to move quickly past it. Rather, it is to hold the despair seriously while opening to the possibility that meaning exists beyond the mortal frame. For Latter-day Saints, the answer to Qohelet's despair is found in covenants, family relationships, and the work of salvation — which provide meaning that does not vanish at death. Engaging with meaningful work tied to eternal purposes (family, faith, serving others) provides a different foundation than work aimed primarily at worldly success or personal legacy.

text_kjv: Yea, I hated all my labour which I had taken under the sun: because I should leave it unto the man that shall be after me.

commentary.narrative:
Qohelet extends his hatred from life itself to the specific product of his labor. The hatred is not abstract but concrete and personal: it is directed at 'all my labour' — the accumulated work of his lifetime. The reason given is stark and simple: 'I should leave it unto the man that shall be after me.' The phrase 'the man that shall be after me' (la-adam asher yihyeh acharai) refers indefinitely to an unknown heir — not necessarily a son but simply whoever comes after. The translator notes observe: 'Inheritance forces Qohelet to confront the fact that ownership is temporary — the builder never gets to keep what he built.'

This verse introduces a theme that will recur throughout Ecclesiastes: the problem of inheritance. The Hebrew king or wealthy person accumulates property, builds, creates, and then must leave it all to an heir. Who knows if the heir will be wise or foolish, virtuous or vicious? There is no guarantee that the heir will value or steward the inheritance as the original builder intended. Even worse from Qohelet's perspective, Qohelet has no control over what happens to his labor once he releases it. The work becomes property that can be misused, squandered, or lost. This transforms the meaning of labor: one works not for the fruits of one's labor but for an unknown successor who will do what he wishes with it. This is a particularly acute problem for someone who has accumulated wealth and built an estate.

word_study.meaning: Labor, toil, effort, trouble. Amal emphasizes the exhausting, taxing aspect of work. It can refer to the work itself or its products — what one has labored to produce. The word often carries connotations of hardship or burden.
word_study.significance: Qohelet uses both ma'aseh ('work' or 'deed') and amal ('labor' or 'toil') to describe human effort. Amal appears in this verse to emphasize the burdensome, exhausting nature of the work. This is not casual activity but strenuous effort. The pathos of the verse is heightened by the recognition that this amal — this difficult, demanding work — must be relinquished.

word_study.meaning: I have labored, I am laboring. The relative clause emphasizes Qohelet as the agent of the labor — he is the one who has exerted himself.
word_study.significance: The verb amal appears both as the noun (amal = labor) and as the root of the participle amel ('one who labors'). This repetition emphasizes the identity between Qohelet and his work — he is defined by his labor, yet he must abandon it.

word_study.meaning: I must leave/release/abandon it to the person. The verb niach in the hiphil means 'to leave, abandon, set down.' The sense is not merely of transition but of relinquishment — Qohelet is forced to let go.
word_study.significance: The verb choice is significant. Anichenu is not neutral transfer but carries a sense of resignation, even violence — the forced removal of something from one's grasp. One does not willingly niach one's labors; one is compelled to do so by the fact of death.

word_study.term_english: the man that shall be after me
word_study.meaning: To the person who will be after me. The indefinite article and the future tense indicate that this heir is unknown and unknowable from Qohelet's vantage point.
word_study.significance: The anonymity of the heir is crucial to Qohelet's despair. If he knew the heir was wise and virtuous, he might derive comfort from knowing his labor would be well-used. But the heir is unknown — possibly foolish, possibly unworthy. This unknowability is part of what makes inheritance so unsatisfying. You must release your life's work to someone you cannot vet or control.

cross_references.connection: The fundamental question that opens Ecclesiastes: 'What profit hath a man of all his labour which he taketh under the sun?' This verse applies that question specifically to inheritance and the perpetuation of one's labor.

Qohelet will return to the question of labor and its fruits, introducing the idea that the ability to enjoy one's labor is a gift from God — which presupposes that ownership and control cannot be taken for granted.

Jesus's parable of the rich fool, who builds larger barns to store his wealth, only to die and leave it all behind — a direct engagement with Qohelet's concern about leaving accumulated property to an unknown heir.
Paul writes: 'For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out,' echoing Qohelet's observation that all labor must eventually be relinquished.

The Lord teaches: 'If ye love me, keep all my commandments... and him that keepeth not his commandments and him that breaketh them shall cast down from my presence,' suggesting that inheritance of heavenly things, unlike earthly inheritance, depends on the heir's worthiness.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern societies (Egyptian, Mesopotamian, and Israelite), property inheritance was a central concern. Laws governed inheritance, and wills could specify conditions or restrictions on inheritance. In Israel, the law of primogeniture (firstborn son receives a double portion) governed most inheritance. However, even with legal frameworks, the transfer of property represented a loss of control and a vulnerability. The wealthy person could not guarantee that an heir would honor the spirit of their intentions. Moreover, the historical reality was that fortunes were lost, properties squandered, and family lines diminished across generations. This created genuine anxiety among the wealthy. Qohelet's complaint is grounded in the real human experience of accumulation followed by forced relinquishment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 34:32–35 teaches that 'this life is the day for men to perform their labors' and that 'if we do not improve our time while in this life, then cometh the night of darkness wherein there can be no labor performed.' The Book of Mormon suggests that the work done in mortality continues to matter in eternity — that one does not simply abandon one's spiritual labor. Moreover, 1 Nephi 15:32–34 describes how the righteous 'shall dwell safely' with their families in heaven, suggesting that familial and spiritual inheritance can be preserved across death.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 130:18–19 teaches: 'Whatever principle of intelligence we attain unto in this life, it will rise with us in the resurrection; And if a person gains more knowledge and intelligence in this life through his diligence and obedience than another, he will have so much the advantage in the world to come.' This suggests that intellectual and spiritual labor is not lost at death — it is retained and magnified. Additionally, D&C 76 describes the inheritance of the righteous in the celestial kingdom, suggesting that the truly valuable inheritance is spiritual and eternal, not temporal.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple's emphasis on sealing families suggests that Qohelet's anxiety about unknown heirs is addressed through covenants. The sealing power ensures that family relationships are not merely broken by death but are preserved and enhanced. Moreover, the work of the temple — both for the living and for the dead — suggests that spiritual labor has permanent significance. What is done in the temple endures, not because it is recorded in the world but because it is recorded in heaven and affects the eternal status of individuals.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ, in becoming human and taking on labor and earthly life, submitted to the condition Qohelet describes. Yet Christ's labor is not left to an unknown heir. Rather, Christ's work of redemption continues through His Church and through individuals who take upon themselves His name and covenant to perform His work. The inheritance passed down through the apostolic succession and through individual disciples is not property to be squandered but a spiritual responsibility to be fulfilled. Moreover, Christ's resurrection ensures that His labor — His life, His teaching, His atonement — is not lost or rendered vain. It accomplishes eternal redemption. Christ's labor does not vanish like Qohelet's labor; it endures forever.
commentary.application: This verse confronts modern anxieties about estate planning, legacy, and the disposition of one's life's work. Parents wonder what will become of their property when passed to their children. Businesspeople worry about whether their company will continue their vision. Artists and creators fear their work will be misused or forgotten. Qohelet's observation is that you cannot ultimately control what happens to what you have built. This can be liberating or terrifying, depending on how one receives it. The practical application is twofold: (1) recognize that temporal possessions and worldly accomplishments pass to others and may not be stewarded as you would wish — this should reduce attachment to temporal things and encourage seeking eternal values; and (2) invest in spiritual work, in covenants, and in teaching values to children, which can be preserved and perpetuated through generations in ways that property cannot. For Latter-day Saints, this means that the most valuable 'labor' is not career achievement or wealth accumulation but the spiritual development of oneself and one's family, the teaching of gospel principles, and participation in the work of salvation — all of which have significance that transcends death and property transfer.

text_kjv: And who knoweth whether he shall be a wise man or a fool? yet shall he have rule over all my labour wherein I have laboured, and wherein I have shewed myself wise under the sun. This is also vanity.

commentary.narrative:
Qohelet turns from hatred of life to a more specific despair: the uncertainty of his heir. He has invested tremendous wisdom and effort into accumulating wealth and knowledge, yet he cannot control who will inherit it or what they will do with it. This is the cruelest irony—the heir may be a fool who squanders everything, or wise enough to appreciate it, but either way, the original toiler has no say in the matter. The work belongs to someone else now.

What makes this observation particularly cutting is that it exposes the illusion of control that wealth and wisdom seem to offer. Qohelet mastered his domain—he became wise, successful, and authoritative. Yet all that mastery evaporates the moment he dies. His successor will inherit not because of merit or preparation, but by accident of birth. As The Covenant Rendering notes, "the uncertainty about the heir's character adds insult to the injury of losing one's work." The verb yishlat ('will have control') emphasizes that the heir gains authority over what he did not earn, did not build, and may not even understand.

word_study.meaning: vapor, breath, mist—something visible but insubstantial, transient, unable to be grasped or retained. Not merely futility but specifically the quality of being unable to hold meaning or value over time.
word_study.significance: This is the diagnosis, not the mood. Hevel describes an ontological condition: that which seems substantial dissolves. The repetition of this word throughout Ecclesiastes (appearing 38 times) is not pessimism but precise observation of how the world actually works under the sun.

word_study.meaning: to have dominion, to control, to exercise authority. The heir does not earn this rule; it is transferred automatically.
word_study.significance: The term emphasizes power without responsibility or understanding. The heir becomes master of what he did not create. This inverts the normal relationship between effort and reward, knowledge and authority.

word_study.meaning: I applied wisdom, I acted wisely, I mastered skillfully. The reflexive form suggests intentional cultivation of wisdom as a personal achievement.
word_study.significance: Qohelet did not stumble into success—he deliberately pursued and cultivated wisdom. Yet this conscious effort cannot secure the fruits of his labor beyond his death.

cross_references.connection: The foundational question—'what profit hath a man'—returns here in the specific form of inheritance. The answer remains: under the sun, nothing is retained.
Rehoboam's inheritance of Solomon's kingdom demonstrates exactly Qohelet's fear: the successor can be a fool who destroys his predecessor's legacy through poor judgment.
Presents the opposite theological expectation—'A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children's children'—which Qohelet questions by noting the heir's character is unknown and uncontrolled.
The Book of Mormon affirms that God's works are purposeful and eternal, contrasting with Qohelet's observation that human accomplishments fade when transferred to unknown heirs.
The next verse intensifies this concern, moving from uncertainty about the heir's character to explicit injustice in inheritance.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern society, inheritance was not a matter of meritocracy but of birthright. The firstborn son inherited regardless of ability. Kings who built empires faced this dilemma acutely—their life's work would pass to a successor chosen by biology, not by fitness. The Deuteronomistic histories record numerous instances of weak heirs following strong founders (Solomon after David, various Judahite kings in succession). Qohelet, writing in the postexilic period, reflects a wisdom tradition grappling with the reality that no amount of personal achievement can guarantee continuity or wise stewardship across generations. This was not theoretical—it was the lived experience of ancient dynasties.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 29 presents a parallel anxiety: King Mosiah recognizes that his righteous reign does not ensure his successor will be righteous, so he establishes a system of judges rather than relying on hereditary monarchy. This is practical application of Qohelet's insight that wisdom and righteousness cannot be inherited—they must be chosen anew by each generation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:34-35 emphasizes that God alone possesses enduring dominion: 'I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end. All kingdoms have their set time, both to come forth and to be consumed.' Human kingdoms and accumulations are temporary; only God's order lasts.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple covenants transcend inheritance structures.
