Qohelet laments that he must leave his wealth to another and cannot know if that person will be wise or foolish; verse 6 provides the theological principle that explains this anxiety—all getting is followed by losing.

Jesus warns against storing up possessions and losing sight of what is truly valuable, teaching a wisdom aligned with Ecclesiastes: there is a time to get, but also a time to recognize the season of dying and relinquishing.

Alma teaches that the people became 'strict in observing the ordinances of God' and in their wealth they did not send away from them those who were naked or hungry—failing to recognize the appointed time to give and relinquish.

The Lord teaches principles of stewardship and warns against inordinate desire for riches; the text implies that property is held in trust, and there are appointed times for acquiring and times for releasing.

commentary.historical_context: In the post-exilic context of Ecclesiastes' composition, the Jewish community had experienced radical loss: exile, the destruction of their temple, the loss of political independence. Many had returned to rebuild, but the memory of loss—of having and then losing everything—would have been fresh and traumatic. Qohelet's assertion that 'there is a time to lose' would have offered a framework for understanding catastrophic loss not as meaningless disaster but as an appointed season within the cosmic order. For an audience recently returned from exile and engaged in rebuilding (as in Nehemiah and Ezra), the reminder that there is a time to keep and a time to cast away would have been both encouraging (rebuilding is a valid pursuit) and cautionary (do not become too attached to what you build). In the agrarian context, farmers understood losing crops to drought or pests; they understood that grain must be used and depleted to feed the family or be sold in the market. The accumulation of possessions was never permanent—tools broke, animals died, fields failed. Qohelet's wisdom reflects this lived reality of impermanence and loss.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 4:24-26 teaches that 'ye are indebted to remain humble servants to one another' and to share from your abundance. The principle implies seasons of getting wealth so that there are resources to give, and seasons of relinquishing to help others. Jacob 2:12-19 condemns the hoarding of wealth, suggesting that there is a time to keep only for proper stewardship and a time to cast away for the relief of suffering.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 51:4-9 establishes principles of property and stewardship: 'it is against the law of God, that one man should be in bondage one to another.' The text implies that property is held in trust, not as absolute possession, and that there are times when release (casting away) is more important than accumulation. D&C 56:16-17 warns against pride and covetousness, suggesting that both getting and the refusal to let go are spiritual failings when done out of season.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches the principle of covenant and eternal perspective, which provides context for Ecclesiastes' doctrine of times to keep and cast away. What appears permanent in mortality is temporary; what we truly 'keep' in an eternal sense is not physical possessions but our relationship with God and our families sealed in the covenant. The principle of sacrifice—giving up what is precious—is central to temple teaching and resonates with Ecclesiastes' wisdom about knowing when to cast away.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's incarnation and earthly ministry represent a 'time to get'—he gathers disciples, establishes community, teaches the gospel. His crucifixion represents a 'time to lose'—he relinquishes his life, his comfort, his earthly security. The resurrection transforms losing into gaining: through his self-loss, he gains eternal life and the power to redeem all humanity. Christ's teaching about storing up treasures in heaven rather than earth (Matthew 6:19-21) applies the wisdom of Ecclesiastes: there are times to work and gain in the earthly economy, but the true time to keep is when one invests in eternal things.
commentary.application: Verse 6 addresses the modern tendency to accumulate without ceasing and to cling to possessions as identity markers and security. For many, there is no 'time to lose' because losing feels like failure or diminishment. Yet Ecclesiastes insists that this season comes to all, whether through death, economic loss, theft, or the simple realization that you cannot take possessions with you. The wise course is to prepare for this season, to practice letting go during your lifetime, to give generously while you have the opportunity, and to divest yourself of the false security that possessions provide. Practically, this might mean: regularly donating clothes, books, and possessions you no longer need; giving to others who are in need; teaching children that they do not own their toys permanently but hold them in stewardship; planning for the eventual loss of health and mobility and what you can and cannot take with you. The deeper application is spiritual: to recognize that the 'time to keep' what truly matters—your relationship with God, your integrity, your love for others—is the only keeping that ultimately endures. Everything else you will eventually cast away, whether you choose to or not. The wisdom is in choosing this casting away consciously and generously, rather than having it forced upon you by circumstances. The hardest disciples to train in this wisdom may be the wealthy; to them Jesus would say, 'There is a time to get' (and you have done well), 'but now it is the time to lose. Sell what you have and give to the poor' (Mark 10:21-22). That season, when it comes, requires the greatest strength.

text_kjv: A time to rend, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak;

commentary.narrative: Verse 7 brings the poem of times toward its conclusion, shifting from physical labor and emotional states to actions of restoration and communication. The rending of garments was a foundational mourning ritual in ancient Israel—a tearing apart that expressed unbearable grief. Yet paired immediately with sewing is the restoration that follows: not the raw pain itself, but the slow, deliberate work of mending that grief requires. This is not recovery in the sense of emotional healing alone, but the practical restoration of one's self and place in community. The second pair—silence and speech—moves from the physical to the verbal, yet carries equal weight in wisdom literature. Qohelet presents these not as moral absolutes but as moments: there is a time when speech would be folly, and a time when silence would be betrayal. The Covenant Rendering captures this perfectly: not simply 'keep silence' but 'be silent,' marking the active choice to refrain from words.
commentary.narrative_continued: This verse acknowledges a truth that wisdom literature across cultures recognized: the timing of one's words determines their power. Proverbs consistently teaches that the wise person knows when to speak (Proverbs 10:19; 17:28), and here Qohelet frames that knowledge as something predetermined, part of the underlying structure of time itself. The rending/sewing pair and the silence/speech pair also mirror each other structurally: both involve a tearing or breaking (of cloth, of silence) followed by a making whole (of garment, of the air with speech). Together they suggest that human life involves both dissolution and restoration, both withdrawal and engagement. The person who lives wisely must discern which moment demands which response.

word_study.meaning: To tear, rend, split. In the context of mourning, the tearing of one's garments was a prescribed ritual expression of grief and lament (Genesis 37:34; 2 Samuel 13:31). The root suggests a violent, irreversible breaking apart.
word_study.significance: The use of qara here is not primarily about clothing damage but about the ritual expression of inconsolable sorrow. It represents the moment when inner turmoil must be externalized. In wisdom literature, this action acknowledges that some griefs cannot be suppressed—they demand expression.

word_study.meaning: To sew, stitch together. The restoration of what was torn apart. While qara is violent and sudden, tafor is patient and deliberate work.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'mend' captures the sense better than 'sew'—this is restoration, not merely repair of fabric. It represents the slow work of returning to wholeness after grief has run its course. In covenant theology, this echoes the restoration promised after trials and afflictions.

word_study.meaning: To be silent, to refrain from speech. The root carries the sense of staying quiet or holding back words. Not silence of ignorance, but silence of restraint.
word_study.significance: Hashat is an active choice, not mere absence. This is significant because it frames wisdom not as passive avoidance but as the disciplined exercise of judgment about when to withhold speech. The Covenant Rendering's 'be silent' better captures this active dimension.

word_study.meaning: To speak, utter words, communicate. The most common verb for speech in Biblical Hebrew. In wisdom contexts, it often carries the weight of consequence—words are never neutral in Proverbs and Ecclesiastes.
word_study.significance: The pair hashat/dabber (silence/speech) frames communication as a skill requiring judgment about timing and appropriateness. The verb form here implies both the right to speak and the responsibility that comes with it.

cross_references.connection: In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise.' Qohelet's 'time to keep silence' echoes Proverbs' teaching that restraint of speech is a mark of wisdom.
Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise.' Qohelet adds nuance: there is a proper time for silence, implying also a proper time for speech—wisdom knows both.
Amnon tears his garments in rage and shame. The rending gesture that Qohelet names as part of life's rhythm is depicted throughout Hebrew narrative as an expression of extreme emotion.
Be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.' The New Testament echoes the ancient wisdom about the timing and restraint of speech as essential to understanding.

Reproving betimes with sharpness, when moved upon by the Holy Ghost; and then showing forth afterwards an increase of love.' The timing of both silence and speech—knowing when to speak and when to show love—is framed as essential to righteous communication.

commentary.historical_context: The tearing of garments was a highly codified mourning practice in the ancient Near East. Archaeological evidence and textual records from Mesopotamia and Egypt show that ritual tearing was not incidental but central to grief expression. In Israel specifically, the practice was so bound up with authentic grief that false mourning (without the torn garment) was seen as inauthentic. The reference to 'a time to rend' thus validates the legitimacy of grief as part of the human experience—it is not something to transcend but to live through. The silence/speech pair reflects the ancient world's acute awareness that words carried weight and consequence. In oral cultures especially, speech was not simply transmission of information but an act with power—it could bless or curse, bind or break. Qohelet's juxtaposition acknowledges that both speaking and restraint are necessary human functions, and wisdom consists in knowing which moment demands which response.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 31:23-25 addresses the Zoramites' empty worship and pride in their speech, suggesting that 'a time to keep silence' may be necessary when words become vessels for pride rather than truth. The Book of Mormon also emphasizes that speech should be used to edify (D&C 121:43), implying that silence can sometimes be more faithful than speech.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 63:64 counsels: 'Cease to find fault one with another; cease to sleep longer than is needful; retire to thy bed early, that ye may not be weary; arise early that your bodies and your minds may be invigorated.' While focused on rest, this teaching embodies the same principle as Ecclesiastes 3:7—that there is a time for different modes of living, and wisdom lies in recognizing the appropriate time for each.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The garments worn in the temple represent covenantal wholeness. The pair of 'tearing and sewing' echoes symbolically the covenant cycle—the tearing represents the breaking of the natural man or the dissolution of former understanding, while the sewing represents the making whole through covenantal binding. The Endowment teaches that mourning and restoration are both part of the covenant journey.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus exemplified both elements of this verse: He wept at the death of Lazarus (John 11:35), expressing grief through tears as Qohelet allows for tearing; yet He also knew when to be silent before His accusers (Isaiah 53:7, Matthew 26:63), demonstrating the wisdom of knowing when speech would be futile or when silence honors a higher purpose. The rending of the temple veil (Matthew 27:51) can be read as a cosmic tearing that makes way for a new kind of wholeness—the atonement as both tearing apart of the old covenant form and sewing together of a new and everlasting covenant.
commentary.application: Modern members often carry unspoken tension between the injunction to 'be honest' and the wisdom that 'not every truth needs to be spoken.' Verse 7 reframes this as a matter of timing rather than contradiction. There are relationships where one's grievances, however valid, should remain unspoken until the 'time to speak' arrives—and conversely, there are moments when silence in the face of injustice becomes complicity. Practically: (1) Discern the season. Is this a time for words or for letting wounds mend? (2) Recognize that tearing happens; it is part of life, not a failure of faith. Sometimes emotions must break open before they can be restored. (3) Practice the discipline of silence—not suppression, but the active restraint that comes from knowing your words' true weight. (4) In family or Church settings, ask: 'Is this my time to speak, or is this someone else's time to be silent and listen?' The most overlooked wisdom may be learning to speak when others would stay silent, and to stay silent when others would speak.

text_kjv: A time to love, and a time to hate; a time of war, and a time of peace.

commentary.narrative: The poem of times reaches its conclusion with a final pair of antitheses that sweep across the entire spectrum of human relational and political existence. 'A time to love' and 'a time to hate' is the most radical pairing Qohelet offers—it directly challenges the assumption that love is always and universally good, and that hate is always and universally evil. Instead, Qohelet frames both as legitimate responses to particular moments. There are times when love is the appropriate human response; there are also times when hatred—understood as the complete rejection of, or necessary separation from, a person, practice, or power—is demanded by the nature of the moment. This is not an endorsement of hatred as a virtue, but a recognition that there are moments when love would be moral cowardice and when the refusal to hate would be complicity with evil.
commentary.narrative_continued: The final pair—'a time for war and a time for peace'—extends the same logic to the political and social realm. Just as individuals must sometimes hate and sometimes love, societies must sometimes wage war and sometimes maintain peace. The poem ends not with 'peace' but with 'shalom'—a word that in Hebrew encompasses not merely the absence of conflict but the presence of wholeness, rightness, and well-being. This closing word may be deliberate: the reader is left not with an image of perpetual peace as the highest good, but with shalom as the fullest human condition, which sometimes requires the season of war to establish or restore it. The Covenant Rendering's placement of war and peace also holds these in equipoise—neither is presented as the default state or the ultimate goal. Like all the times before, both war and peace have their season, their necessity, their moment when they are 'fitting' (as verse 11 will say, yafeh).
commentary.narrative_continued_2: That Qohelet chooses to end the poem here—with war and peace, love and hate—is structurally significant. The poem began with birth and death, the boundaries of individual life. It moved through labor, harvest, building, and tearing down—the substance of daily work and survival. It touched on dancing, mourning, laughter, and weeping—the emotional weather of existence. Now it reaches outward to the relational (love/hate) and political (war/peace) dimensions. The arc suggests that all these times, from the most intimate to the most collective, operate under the same principle: there is a proper time for each, and wisdom consists in recognizing it.

word_study.meaning: To love, to desire, to be fond of. In Hebrew, ahab can apply to love between humans, love of God, or love of things. It expresses both emotional attachment and volitional commitment.
word_study.significance: Ahab is not mere sentiment; it is a response that involves the whole person—emotion, will, and action. That Qohelet pairs it with hate suggests both are modes of response to the world, both legitimate at their proper time. In covenant theology, ahab describes Israel's response to God (Deuteronomy 6:5), making this verse a subtle claim that sometimes fidelity to covenant may require not love but clear rejection.

word_study.meaning: To hate, to detest, to reject. In Biblical Hebrew, sana is not merely emotional but implies a deliberate stance of opposition or refusal.
word_study.significance: The pairing of sana with ahab is provocative. Wisdom literature elsewhere counsels against hatred (Proverbs 8:13 condemns pride and arrogance), but Qohelet makes space for it as a legitimate response at a particular time. This is not endorsement of hatred as a virtue, but acknowledgment that there are times when the refusal to hate—to refuse to stand against evil or injustice—would itself be a failure of wisdom.

word_study.meaning: War, battle, conflict. From the root lchem ('to fight, to do battle'). Denotes organized armed conflict between groups.
word_study.significance: Milchama is a concrete reality in the ancient Near East, not an abstraction. Qohelet's inclusion of it acknowledges that conflict is not incidental to human experience but structural. His point is not to glorify war but to recognize that there are moments when peaceful coexistence is no longer possible and when the time for war has arrived.

word_study.meaning: Peace, wholeness, well-being, completeness. Shalom encompasses far more than merely the absence of conflict; it denotes the presence of order, prosperity, and flourishing in all relationships.
word_study.significance: That the poem ends on shalom rather than 'war' is significant. The word carries within it the fullest vision of human flourishing. By closing with shalom, Qohelet leaves the reader with an image not of resignation to cycles of conflict but of the deeper peace that encompasses and transcends temporary seasons of war. Shalom is also central to Israel's covenant vision (Isaiah 2:4; Micah 4:3)—it represents the eschatological goal toward which history moves.

cross_references.connection: Verse 8 is the climactic pair in a poem that establishes the principle that opposites have their proper seasons. Each pair illuminates the others.

The fear of the LORD is to hate evil: pride, and arrogancy, and the evil way, and the froward mouth, do I hate.' Wisdom itself hates evil, suggesting that Qohelet's 'time to hate' has moral legitimacy when directed toward what is genuinely destructive.

O daughter of Babylon, who art to be destroyed; happy shall he be, that rewardeth thee as thou hast served us.' The Psalms contain expressions of justified hatred against oppressors, supporting the notion that hate has its proper season in covenant response.

Think not that I am come to send peace on earth: I came not to send peace, but a sword.' Jesus acknowledges that His mission will bring conflict—there is a 'time for war' in the metaphorical sense of the spiritual struggle that His gospel initiates.

Prophecy about wars to come. The Doctrine and Covenants acknowledges that war is a reality in human history, confirming the ancient wisdom that there are times when peace gives way to conflict as part of the pattern of mortal existence.

commentary.historical_context: The ancient Near Eastern world that produced Ecclesiastes knew war as an inescapable reality. Qohelet was likely written during the Persian period (after 539 BCE) or the early Hellenistic period, times of relative peace following centuries of conflict. Yet the echo of past wars and the uncertainty of future peace would have been vivid in communal memory. Qohelet's inclusion of war/peace as legitimate times reflects not moral relativism but realism: the prosperity of peace, however desirable, cannot be maintained by denying or refusing to engage in conflict when it becomes necessary. The phrase about love and hate occurs in a culture where tribal, family, and national loyalty could demand not just preference but active opposition to outsiders. However, love within the community (ahab) and measured hostility toward threats (sana) were both understood as operating within a framework of justice and necessity. Qohelet's pairing suggests that both are dimensions of the human condition under heaven, and wisdom is not to eliminate one but to discern its proper season.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 48:18-20 describes Moroni's preparation for war: 'And it came to pass that he had entrenched himself with his army into the borders of the land Bountiful, to defend his people against the Lamanites.' The Book of Mormon wrestles constantly with the question of righteous warfare—when does the 'time for war' arrive? Moroni's character suggests that the time for war comes when peaceful alternatives have been exhausted and innocent life must be protected.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 98:23-48 addresses the Church's approach to war and persecution, counseling patience and multiple attempts at peace before warfare becomes appropriate. The passage echoes Qohelet's wisdom: there is a time for peace, and wisdom requires exhausting it before the time for war arrives. Yet the revelation also implies that the time for war can come.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment presents the pattern of conflict and resolution—the opposition of light and darkness, the struggle between good and evil, culminating in the victory of truth and the establishment of peace (shalom). This cyclical pattern, with both conflict and peace having their place in the divine plan, aligns with Qohelet's insight that both times are necessary and have their season.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ embodies both the 'time to love' and the 'time to hate' in redemptive ways. His love is exemplified in His universal compassion and willingness to die for all humanity. His 'hatred' (in the sense of implacable opposition) is directed toward sin, hypocrisy, and the powers of darkness (Revelation 2:6 speaks of hating the deeds of the Nicolaitans). His ministry began in relative peace but culminated in His crucifixion—a kind of cosmic war between light and darkness. The Atonement can be read as occurring at the intersection of all these times: it is the ultimate act of love (John 3:16), the definitive taking of a stand against evil, and the sacrifice through which lasting peace (shalom) is purchased for all who accept it. His resurrection represents not merely the end of conflict but the establishment of true shalom—the restoration of all things.
commentary.application: This verse challenges modern sensibilities that often see love and hate, war and peace, as moral absolutes rather than responses appropriate to particular circumstances. For Latter-day Saints navigating family conflict, this might mean: (1) Recognize that some relationships may require a season of necessary distance (hate in the sense of clear boundary-setting) to preserve one's own integrity. Not all relationships can be healed; some must be released. (2) Understand that 'peace at any cost' is not the highest good—there are times when standing for truth requires conflict. (3) In matters of doctrine or morality, discern when the time calls for direct opposition rather than tolerance. (4) In prayer and patriarchal guidance, ask: 'Am I in a season of loving embrace, or is this a season requiring clear separation?' (5) On a broader scale, support the principle that national defense and even military action can be legitimate when the 'time for war' arrives—when peaceful alternatives have been exhausted and innocent lives are at stake. The hard wisdom here is that peace without justice is not shalom, and sometimes the path to true peace requires the difficult season of war.

text_kjv: What profit hath he that worketh in that wherein he laboureth?

commentary.narrative: Having reached the end of the magnificent poem detailing twenty-eight times and seasons under heaven, Qohelet does not linger in appreciation. Instead, he immediately returns to the haunting question that opened his entire argument in verse 1:3—almost identically the same words, now functioning as a pivot back to reality. The poem has been beautiful, even profound, but it has not answered the fundamental question: if all these times are divinely ordained and cyclical, what lasting benefit does human effort produce? The repetition of this question is not accidental; it serves to strip away any illusion that the poem itself represents progress or advancement in Qohelet's understanding. He has not solved the problem through poetic description; he has only clarified it. The Covenant Rendering's 'What lasting gain does the worker have from his toil?' captures the specific concern—it is about permanence, about surplus, about whether human striving adds anything that persists.
commentary.narrative_continued: The Hebrew word yitron (profit, surplus, gain) refers to something left over, something gained beyond mere subsistence. It is not asking whether people can survive through work—clearly they can and must. Rather, it asks whether work produces something of lasting value, something that remains after the worker is gone. This is the cutting edge of Qohelet's argument: you can work through all the seasons, responding appropriately to each time, and at the end you will have... what? The cycle continues; others will rend garments and sew them, speak and keep silence, love and hate, wage war and make peace. Your personal contribution vanishes into the endless repetition. The poem was meant to describe a pattern, but its very regularity becomes Qohelet's indictment: if everything is predetermined to happen in its season, what does your effort matter? This is not mere pessimism; it is a logical question about causation and meaning under conditions of endless recurrence.

word_study.meaning: Surplus, profit, advantage, that which remains over. From the root yatar ('to remain, to be left over'). Refers to gain beyond basic maintenance—something of lasting value.
word_study.significance: Yitron appears eight times in Ecclesiastes (1:3; 2:11, 2:13; 3:9; 5:9; 7:12; 10:10, 10:11) and nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible. It is Qohelet's key term for the fundamental question driving the entire book. The word carries an economic overtone—profit in the commercial sense—but extends to existential profit. The question is not merely 'Will I be fed?' but 'Will my life add something to the universe that will endure?'

word_study.meaning: One who makes, does, works, creates. From the root asah ('to make, to do, to work'). The qal active participle describes one actively engaged in labor.
word_study.significance: Oseh ties this verse to the creation narrative, where God asah ('made') the heavens and earth. Humans also asah—they make and do—but with what lasting effect? The word encompasses all forms of productive activity, from manual labor to artistic creation to building civilizations.

word_study.meaning: To toil, to labor, to exert oneself. Amel emphasizes the strain, effort, and weariness that work entails. It is not light activity but strenuous, costly exertion.
word_study.significance: The repetition of this root—yitron (profit from work) and amel (the toil involved)—sets up the central tension: we expend significant energy (amel) but what surplus (yitron) results? The word carries overtones of the curse pronounced after Eden: 'In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread' (Genesis 3:19). Work is not merely activity; it is costly expenditure of life-force.

cross_references.connection: What profit hath a man of all his labour which he taketh under the sun?' This is the identical question, establishing that Qohelet has not moved beyond the fundamental problem even after describing the poem of times.

Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that I had laboured to do: and, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit; and there was no profit under the sun.' Qohelet's later reflection confirms that even extraordinary achievement produces no lasting yitron.
In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread.' The original curse of labor, from which Qohelet cannot escape even through wisdom—labor remains toilsome and ultimately futile.

Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.' Paul's answer to Qohelet: labor is not futile if it is in the Lord, if it serves purposes beyond the immediate visible result.

Wherefore, he that doeth the works of righteousness shall receive his reward, even peace in this world, and eternal life in the world to come.' The Restoration offers what Qohelet cannot see from purely secular perspective—that righteous work does produce lasting gain when understood in covenant and eternal context.

commentary.historical_context: Qohelet's question arises from a moment of genuine philosophical crisis in the ancient Near East. The older wisdom tradition assumed that righteous action produced proportional blessing (the doctrine of retribution: good deeds yield good results, evil deeds yield punishment). But by the Persian and Hellenistic periods, this assumption was under strain. The righteous suffered, the wicked prospered, and the cycle of history seemed indifferent to individual moral effort. Qohelet is wrestling with this empirical challenge to older wisdom: if the universe operates in cycles beyond human control, what is the moral or existential justification for striving? This question would have resonated acutely in a period when Jewish cultural autonomy was limited and when individuals could see that their efforts, however sincere, barely registered against historical forces larger than themselves.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 9:28 criticizes those who 'suppose that they are wise and they hearken not unto the counsel of God, for they set it aside, supposing they know of themselves.' This echoes Qohelet's dilemma: human wisdom operating purely under the sun, without reference to God's larger purposes, cannot find lasting meaning. The Book of Mormon consistently argues that yitron (profit, gain) is only permanent when understood in light of the plan of salvation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 6:7 promises: 'Behold, you have been entrusted with these things, but with a covenant and an oath that you shall observe and keep all my commandments.' The Doctrine and Covenants reframes Qohelet's anxiety: your work does have lasting value when it is covenantal work, when it participates in God's eternal purposes rather than operating independently.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that mortality itself is not purposeless but part of a larger divine plan. The endowment presents work and toil in their proper cosmic context: the trials and labors of mortality are real, but they participate in an eternal progression that renders them meaningful. What seems futile 'under the sun' gains meaning when understood as part of the ascent through the temple toward exaltation.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ directly addresses Qohelet's question through His Atonement. Christ's labor on the cross might have seemed, from a worldly perspective, the ultimate futility—a righteous person executed, His work apparently nullified by His death. Yet His 'labor' produces infinite and eternal gain: the redemption of all souls, the conquest of death itself, the restoration of all things. In this sense, Christ's work answers Qohelet's question not through philosophical argument but through redemptive reality. His yitron ('profit') is the salvation of the world. This suggests to believers that their own labor, when aligned with Christ's redemptive purposes, similarly acquires permanent value.
commentary.application: Verse 9 confronts the modern reader with a question that many would rather avoid: 'Am I really making a lasting difference through my work and effort?' For Latter-day Saints, this verse invites four practices: (1) Distinguish between the futility Qohelet describes (work pursued purely for personal advancement or survival) and work that participates in God's purposes (family building, covenant keeping, service in the Church, raising children in righteousness). The difference between futile and meaningful work is not primarily in the activity itself but in its relationship to eternal purpose. (2) Accept that from a purely mortal, 'under the sun' perspective, Qohelet is right—much of what we build will pass away, and our personal contribution to history will be forgotten. This is not cause for despair but for reorientation. (3) Seek yitron (lasting gain) through investments in people, in covenant relationships, and in spiritual development rather than through accumulation of material goods or social status. (4) In moments of burnout or frustration with work, remember Qohelet's question not as proof of futility but as an invitation to reconnect your daily labor to larger purposes. If your work produces no yitron at all, consider whether you need to shift how you think about it—or whether you need to change it altogether.

text_kjv: I have seen the travail, which God hath given to the sons of men to be exercised in it.

commentary.narrative: Qohelet's response to his own unanswerable question is to observe (literally, 'I have seen') the nature of the burden God has placed upon human beings. The word translated as 'travail' is inyan, which can mean 'burden,' 'occupation,' 'business,' or 'affair'—a term redolent with ambiguity. It is not entirely negative (not mere suffering) nor entirely positive (not pure opportunity). Rather, it is the complex, demanding reality that constitutes human existence. God has deliberately given this to humanity—not as punishment alone, but as the defining structure of mortal existence. Qohelet's observation is that humans are 'exercised in it,' which could mean 'occupied with it' (suggesting busyness that fills time) or 'afflicted by it' (suggesting that the burden itself produces suffering). The Covenant Rendering's 'to occupy them' captures the sense well: God has given humans a complex set of tasks and challenges that serve to structure and fill their time.
commentary.narrative_continued: This verse reprises the language of 1:13, where Qohelet was 'given' (the same root, natan) the task of seeking understanding. Here he moves from his own experience of being given a task (to investigate everything under the sun) to the universal human condition: all humans are given an inyan—an occupation or burden. The verse suggests that this is not accidental or incidental to existence; it is built in. God does not merely allow humans to toil; He actively 'gives' them the inyan to occupy them. There is something almost paradoxical about this: God deliberately structures human life with burdens that keep us occupied, challenges that fill our time, work that demands our attention and energy. Why? One possible reading is that God does this to prevent despair or meaninglessness—if humans were simply idle, the awareness of mortality and futility might overwhelm them. Instead, they are given tasks that require focus and engagement. Another reading is that the inyan itself is part of the test or trial of mortality: can humans maintain meaning, faith, and righteousness while burdened with real concerns and limited perspective?

word_study.meaning: Burden, occupation, business, affair, matter of concern. A word carrying both the sense of serious engagement and of weighted difficulty. Reprises the same term from 1:13.
word_study.significance: Inyan is not the typical word for mere 'work' (melachah) or 'labor' (avodah). It specifically denotes a burden or concern that occupies one's attention. In modern Hebrew it simply means 'subject' or 'matter,' but in Biblical Ecclesiastes it carries the sense of something heavy that must be carried. The Covenant Rendering's use of 'burden' captures this weight.

word_study.meaning: To give, to place, to set, to put. The most common verb for giving in Biblical Hebrew. Implies an act of deliberate bestowal.
word_study.significance: That Qohelet emphasizes 'given' (natan) rather than merely describing what humans naturally do is crucial. God actively gives the inyan to humans. This is not something they choose or create; it is divinely assigned. This raises the theological question: why would God deliberately burden His creations? The answer emerges in verse 11—the burden comes with a corresponding gift.

word_study.meaning: Sons of men, children of Adam, humanity. A collective term emphasizing the universal human condition, often used to indicate the frailty and limitation of human existence as contrasted with God's power.
word_study.significance: By using 'sons of men' rather than merely 'people' or 'humans,' Qohelet invokes the genealogical reality—all humans are descendants of Adam, all inheritors of the mortal condition. The phrase carries overtones of limitation and dependence.

word_study.meaning: To be occupied with, to be afflicted by, to be distressed by. The root anat can mean both 'to afflict' and 'to be occupied/engaged.' The text carries both overtones simultaneously.
word_study.significance: This is the crux of ambiguity in the verse. Does God give humans the burden so that they are 'occupied' with it (neutrally), or so that they are 'afflicted' by it? The answer is likely both—the occupation itself becomes an affliction when one recognizes its futility. This captures Qohelet's paradox: even as he admits that the inyan keeps humans engaged and occupied, it also weighs upon them with the recognition that their efforts will not produce lasting gain.

cross_references.connection: And I gave my heart to seek and search out by wisdom concerning all things that are done under heaven: this sore travail hath God given to the sons of men to be exercised therewith.' The identical phrase 'inyan...natan...bnei ha-adam' appears here, creating an inclusio that binds chapters 1 and 3.

And unto Adam he said, Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife, and hast eaten of the tree...In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread.' The divine burden of labor is assigned to Adam and his descendants as a consequence of the Fall.

The days of our years are threescore years and ten...and the strength thereof be labour and sorrow.' The Psalmist similarly observes that human life is marked by labor and sorrow as the dominant experiences.
Behold, there are many called, but few are chosen. And why are they not chosen?' The D&C takes up the question of why God assigns certain burdens and trials—to test and refine the faithful.
Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.' While Qohelet observes the burden, the New Testament offers comfort that God cares for those bearing it.

commentary.historical_context: The ancient Near Eastern worldview, particularly in Mesopotamian thought, included the concept that humans were created to 'bear the burden of the gods'—literally to labor and serve divine purposes. Qohelet operates within this cultural framework but interrogates it philosophically. He accepts that God has given humans a burden to occupy them, but he questions whether this serves any ultimate purpose for those burdened. The Persian period context in which Ecclesiastes was likely written saw Jewish people under foreign rule, their political autonomy severely limited. Individual effort to shape one's circumstances was constrained by forces larger than oneself. In this context, Qohelet's observation that humans are burdened with tasks that occupy them but produce no lasting gain would have resonated acutely. People were occupied with rebuilding the Temple, with maintaining religious practice, with daily survival—but could these efforts generate lasting, meaningful change?

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mosiah 7:29-30 records King Benjamin's reflection on divine justice: 'I say unto you that if ye should render all the thanks which your whole souls have power to render unto him, he doth still bless you; and therefore I call upon you to render your thanks unto him.' The Book of Mormon suggests that the inyan ('burden') given to humans is paired with a corresponding responsibility to offer thanksgiving. The burden is not purposeless; it creates the occasion for covenant response.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:39 teaches: 'I gave unto them their agency; and by the power of their agency they refer themselves unto me, and I quicken all things both which are spiritual and temporal; and my voice do I send forth into all the earth.' The Doctrine and Covenants explains why God gives humans burdens: agency requires engagement with real, demanding circumstances. The inyan is the context within which moral choice becomes genuine.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Latter-day Saint temple endowment specifically teaches that mortal life, with all its burdens and challenges, is not incidental but central to the plan of salvation. The trials and work of mortality are presented as necessary stages through which the covenant people must pass. The 'inyan' is not punishment but structure—the context within which growth and progression become possible.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the ultimate figure who was 'given' a burden by the Father. In Gethsemane, He explicitly prays about this divine assignment: 'O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt' (Matthew 26:39). Christ accepts the inyan—the immense burden of the Atonement—that God has given Him to occupy Him and through which to redeem all humanity. His response transforms the meaning of the burden: what could have been mere futile toil becomes redemptive work of infinite consequence. In this sense, Christ shows that a burden given by God and received with faith and obedience can produce the eternal yitron (profit, gain) that Qohelet could not find through worldly observation alone.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, verse 10 offers both realism and comfort. (1) Realism: Your life is deliberately structured with burdens and challenges. These are not accidents or signs that something has gone wrong. God 'gives' the inyan—the complex weight of mortal existence—as part of the design. Accept this rather than spending energy resisting it. (2) Reframe the burden: What Qohelet sees as futile busyness can be reframed as the context for meaningful choice. You are 'occupied' with real tasks—raising children, building community, developing your talents, serving others. These are not distractions from some higher reality; they are the substance of mortal covenant life. (3) Look beyond 'under the sun' perspective: Qohelet observes that work produces no lasting gain from a purely terrestrial viewpoint. But if you understand your inyan as part of God's purposes—as the arena in which you develop character, prove faithfulness, and grow in love—then the burden becomes meaningful. (4) In moments of burnout or frustration, remember that God has deliberately given this burden to you. This is not punishment for failure but assignment for growth. The question is not 'Why do I have this burden?' but 'How can I bear it faithfully, and what is God teaching me through it?'

text_kjv: He hath made every thing beautiful in his time: also he hath set the world in their heart, so that no man can find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end.

commentary.narrative: Verse 11 is widely recognized as the theological center of Ecclesiastes and one of the most profound statements in the entire Hebrew Bible. It arrives as a kind of turning point in Qohelet's argument, offering not a solution to his dilemma but a deepening of it—and in that deepening lies a strange wisdom. The verse makes three interlocking claims. First: God has made everything yafeh be-itto—'fitting in its time,' or 'beautiful at its moment.' Each of the twenty-eight activities from the poem of times (rending, sewing, keeping silence, speaking, loving, hating, warring, peacing) has a time when it is right, when it is beautiful. The word yafeh means not merely aesthetically beautiful but appropriate, fitting, proper—each action has a moment of rightness. This is Qohelet's attempt to rescue some meaning from the cycles: though patterns repeat and individual effort produces no lasting surplus (yitron), each moment has its own intrinsic appropriateness. There is beauty in the timing itself.
commentary.narrative_continued: Second, God 'has also placed eternity (ha-olam) in the human heart (be-libbam).' This is the most theologically significant phrase in Ecclesiastes. Human beings carry within them an awareness of or longing for something beyond the present, something transcendent and permanent. The Hebrew word olam can mean 'eternity,' 'perpetuity,' 'the ages,' 'the world-order'—something vast and enduring. Some scholars have emended it to elem ('hiddenness' or 'ignorance'), which would yield 'God has placed ignorance in human hearts.' But the TCR rightly retains olam because the tension between having eternity in one's heart and being unable to grasp it is precisely Qohelet's philosophical point. Humans are built with an appetite for the permanent, the infinite, the eternal. Yet the third claim immediately undercuts the comfort that might come from this recognition: 'mi-beli asher lo yimtsa ha-adam' ('yet the human being cannot discover/find') 'et ha-ma'aseh asher asah ha-Elohim me-rosh ve-ad sof' ('the work that God has done from beginning to end').
commentary.narrative_continued_2: This is the unbearable paradox that defines the human condition according to Qohelet: we are built with an awareness of eternity, a capacity to long for the transcendent and permanent, yet we are denied the ability to comprehend the totality of God's work. We can perceive individual times and seasons (rending, sewing, loving, hating, warring, peacing), but we cannot see the whole tapestry. We are creatures stretched between two infinities—infinite awareness (eternity in the heart) and infinite ignorance (inability to see from beginning to end). This is not a problem to be solved by wisdom or hard work; it is the structure of existence itself. What might have seemed like despair in earlier verses now appears as something else: not resignation but recognition of the proper place of human understanding within a vaster divine order. The beauty of each moment, the awareness of eternity planted within the human heart, and the acceptance of our limited perspective together form a kind of wisdom—not the wisdom of having figured everything out, but the wisdom of having learned to live well within the constraints of mortality.
commentary.narrative_continued_3: The Covenant Rendering captures this perfectly: 'He has made everything fitting in its time. He has also placed eternity in the human heart—yet no one can discover what God has done from beginning to end.' The dash creates a syntactical space for the reader to hold both truths: yes, there is fitting beauty in each moment; and yes, we are nevertheless unable to grasp the whole. This is not contradiction but paradox—and it is the foundation on which genuine wisdom rests.

word_study.meaning: Beautiful, fair, comely, fitting, appropriate, becoming. Aesthetically and/or ethically pleasing. Can denote both visual beauty and the appropriateness of an action at its proper time.
word_study.significance: Yafeh is not mere decoration; it implies that something is right, fitting, proper at its moment. When Qohelet says God 'hath made everything beautiful in his time,' he means that each of the times in the poem has its own propriety and fittingness. The difficult logic is: if everything is beautiful in its time (even tearing, even hating, even war), then there is a rightness to reality as it unfolds, even if individuals cannot perceive the larger pattern that makes it right.

word_study.meaning: In its time, at its proper season, at its moment. The preposition be ('in') plus the construct form of et ('time') creates the phrase 'in its time' or 'in his/her/its time'—the appointed moment.
word_study.significance: The phrase be-itto appears multiple times in the poem (3:2-8) and is central to Qohelet's vision of a universe structured by times. Everything is beautiful be-itto—not absolutely, not all the time, but in its proper season. This suggests a kind of divine order, even if humans cannot perceive the totality.

word_study.meaning: To give, to place, to set, to put. The same verb used in verse 10 for God giving humans the inyan ('burden'). Here God 'places' eternity in the human heart.
word_study.significance: God does not merely allow humans to be aware of eternity; He actively places it within them. This is a constitutive feature of human nature, not an accident. Humans are designed with this tension between temporal limitation and eternal awareness.

word_study.meaning: Eternity, perpetuity, the ages, the world-order, the cosmos. Can refer to distant time in the past or future, to enduring permanence, or to the vast structure of existence itself. Commonly used in the phrase le-olam va-ed ('forever and ever').
word_study.significance: This is the most contested word in Ecclesiastes 3:11 and arguably in all of Ecclesiastes. The TCR retains olam because the philosophical tension it creates is central to Qohelet's meaning: humans carry within them an awareness of the eternal, the permanent, the 'ages' beyond their individual lives. Some scholars emend to elem ('darkness, ignorance, hiddenness'), which would mean God put ignorance in human hearts—a reading that fits with Qohelet's emphasis on human ignorance. However, the retained olam is more philosophically rich: it suggests that humans are built for transcendence even though they cannot achieve it. We yearn for what we cannot grasp.

word_study.meaning: To find, to discover, to come upon, to perceive, to understand. The basic verb for discovery or knowledge acquisition.
word_study.significance: The negation 'lo yimtsa' ('will not find/discover') is emphatic. The human being cannot matsa—cannot discover or comprehend—the ma'aseh asher asah ha-Elohim ('the work that God has done'). This is not a failure of effort or wisdom; it is a structural limitation built into the human condition.

word_study.meaning: Work, deed, action, labor, creation. The product or process of making or doing. In theological contexts, often refers to God's creative and providential work.
word_study.significance: God's ma'aseh is the totality of His creative and sustaining work—'from beginning to end' (me-rosh ve-ad sof). Humans cannot see the whole work, only their own small part in it. This echoes Genesis 1:1-2:3, where God's ma'aseh is surveyed by God Himself, who declares it 'very good' after each stage. Humans, unlike God, cannot step back and see the whole.

word_study.meaning: From beginning to end, from start to finish, the totality of a process or sequence. Rosh ('head, beginning') and sof ('end, finish') bracket the entire span.
word_study.significance: This phrase emphasizes the totality that humans cannot grasp. We see individual moments (times for rending, sewing, speaking, silence, etc.), but we cannot see the beginning and end of God's work together—we cannot see why these moments matter within the larger pattern of His purposes.

cross_references.connection: Establishes the theme of cyclical time and the problem of vanity. Verse 11 addresses this by suggesting that while cycles repeat, each moment has intrinsic beauty if viewed rightly.
Thy word is settled in heaven...all things are thy servants.' The Psalmist similarly recognizes that God's order is permanent and all-encompassing, though humans experience only fragments of it.

For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.' Paul echoes the idea that God's work can be perceived, yet a full understanding 'from beginning to end' remains beyond human capacity.

For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.' Paul's description of partial human knowledge parallels Qohelet's point: we can see moments but not the whole.

And the light shineth in darkness, and the darkness comprehendeth it not; nevertheless, the day shall come when you shall comprehend even God, being quickened in him and by him.' The Restoration promises that what Qohelet describes as permanent human limitation—inability to comprehend God's work—is a temporary condition; eventually the righteous shall comprehend fully.

commentary.historical_context: Ecclesiastes was likely written in the Persian or early Hellenistic period, when Jewish culture encountered Greek philosophy and the question of meaning and purpose in human existence became more acute. The concept of olam ('eternity,' 'the ages') was familiar from earlier Hebrew thought but took on new philosophical weight in dialogue with Greek ideas about the eternal and the temporal. The tension Qohelet articulates—between human capacity to perceive transcendence and human inability to comprehend the whole—reflects the existential crisis of a period when older certainties (that righteous action yields proportional blessing, that history moves toward clear goals) were being questioned by lived experience. The beautiful poetry of the times in verses 2-8 can be read as Qohelet's attempt to find some aesthetic meaning in a universe that seems indifferent to human moral effort. If not meaning in the sense of progress or lasting gain, then at least beauty in the fittingness of each moment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 12:33-35 explicitly teaches the limitation of human knowledge: 'Now there is a death which is called a temporal death...and there is a spiritual death which is the second death, which shall be pronounced upon all those who die in their sins...Now we see that death comes upon all mankind; yea, the temporal death shall cause all mankind to fall from before the presence of the Lord, save it were through the redemption which comes through Christ and his resurrection.' The Book of Mormon acknowledges Qohelet's truth—humans cannot see the full arc of God's purposes—while adding that Christ provides the perspective that Qohelet lacked: redemptive knowledge of the end from the beginning.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:22-24 records that Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon beheld a vision and 'saw the celestial kingdom of God, and the glory thereof, were exceedingly great and glorious'; 'And this greater priesthood administereth the gospel and holdeth the key of the mysteries of the kingdom.' The Doctrine and Covenants suggests that while Qohelet's observation about human limitation remains true for the natural man, the Lord reveals mysteries to those who receive the priesthood and the gospel. What Qohelet could not find out—the work God has done from beginning to end—is partially revealed through continuing revelation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Latter-day Saint temple endowment presents a symbolic journey through creation, the fall, and redemption that offers something like what Qohelet describes as impossible: the ability to see 'from the beginning to the end' of God's work, at least in miniature and symbolically. The temple teaches that mortal life, with all its times of rending and sewing, loving and hating, is part of a divine plan whose beauty and fittingness become visible when understood within the covenant framework.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ is the one who sees 'from the beginning to the end' (Revelation 1:8, 21:6—'I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end'). What Qohelet identified as impossible for humans—comprehending God's work me-rosh ve-ad sof ('from beginning to end')—Christ embodies. Furthermore, Christ demonstrates what Qohelet means by God making 'everything beautiful in his time': His entire ministry can be understood as unfolding through proper times—the time for teaching, the time for withdrawal to prayer, the time for miracles, the time for passion. The Atonement itself is, in a sense, God's vindication of the principle that everything has its fitting time. Christ's death, which appeared to be defeat, was actually the appointed moment for redemption. His resurrection vindicated the rightness of the cross at its appointed time.
commentary.application: Ecclesiastes 3:11 invites a profound reorientation of how we understand our place in time and meaning. (1) Accept the reality of limitation: You will not, in mortality, be able to comprehend God's work 'from beginning to end.' You cannot see why your life, with all its varied times and seasons, matters in the ultimate pattern. This is not a sign of spiritual failure but a feature of the mortal condition. (2) Recognize eternity in your heart: Even though you cannot comprehend the whole, you carry within you an awareness of something beyond the present—a capacity to long for permanence, to sense the transcendent, to believe in purposes larger than yourself. This awareness is not false longing; it is the truest thing about you. (3) Embrace the beauty of the present moment: Since you cannot see the whole, learn to see and honor the beauty and fittingness of this moment, this time, this season. There is 'a time to every purpose under heaven,' and your task is not to transcend your time but to live it fully and faithfully. (4) In prayer and priesthood guidance, seek incrementally greater knowledge: While full knowledge of God's purposes remains beyond you, the Lord offers increasing understanding through the Spirit, through scripture, through the teachings of His prophets, and through personal revelation. Trust that what needs to be known for your salvation will be made known, even if the ultimate comprehension awaits the next life. (5) In moments of confusion or suffering, remember that your inability to see why this trial matters does not mean it has no meaning. God has appointed this time as fitting and beautiful in ways you may only understand later.

text_kjv: I know that there is no good in them, but for a man to rejoice, and to do good in his life.

commentary.narrative: After the profound paradox of verse 11—that humans carry eternity in their hearts yet cannot comprehend God's work—Qohelet offers what has been called an 'enjoyment passage,' the second explicit endorsement of joy in Ecclesiastes. The verse is puzzling in its grammar (what does 'no good in them' refer to?), but its meaning is clear enough: given the impossibility of understanding the totality of God's purposes, the one legitimate good available to humans is to rejoice (simchah) and to do good (la'asot tov) during their lives. The Covenant Rendering clarifies: 'I know that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice and to do good during their lives.' The comparison is not to some other, superior good that is available but rejected; rather, this is the best that can be achieved under the sun, given the constraints of mortality and human limitation.
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase 'in his life' (be-chayav) is crucial. Qohelet is not recommending that one delay joy and goodness to some hypothetical afterlife or future state; he insists that this is the good to be pursued now, 'in his life,' while one is alive. This is not shallow hedonism—the phrase includes both simchah ('joy, gladness, celebration') and la'asot tov ('to do good'). Joy alone would be mere pleasure-seeking; goodness alone might be burdensome moralism. Together they form a human response that is both engaged and meaningful: to find delight in existence and to act toward others' well-being. The verse suggests that once Qohelet has accepted the permanent limitation of human understanding (verse 11), the proper response is not despair but a kind of wise contentment: to find what genuine goods are available within the human condition and to pursue them with full commitment.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: This verse appears again (with slight variations) at 2:24, 5:18, 8:15, and 9:7-9, creating a refrain that structures the entire book. Each time Qohelet affirms enjoyment and goodness, he does so in full awareness of the futility question. The recurring affirmation suggests that for Qohelet, wisdom is not about solving the problem of futility but about living well and faithfully despite it. This is not the wisdom of having comprehended everything (which is impossible); it is the wisdom of knowing what goods are truly available and worthwhile.

word_study.meaning: To rejoice, to be glad, to celebrate, to take delight. A comprehensive word for emotional and festive joy. Often used in contexts of celebration and thanksgiving.
word_study.significance: Simach is not frivolous pleasure but genuine gladness and celebration. In the Psalms and in narratives of Israel's worship, simach is the appropriate response to God's goodness and presence. That Qohelet chooses this word (rather than a weaker term like 'contentment' or 'satisfaction') suggests that he is recommending genuine joy, not mere resignation.

word_study.meaning: To do good, to act rightly, to perform beneficial actions. Tov ('good') can mean both moral goodness (doing what is right) and material good (experiencing wellbeing). The phrase encompasses both dimensions.
word_study.significance: The ambiguity of tov is productive. 'Do good' could mean perform righteous actions, or it could mean 'do yourself good' (experience good things). Qohelet likely intends both: pursue moral integrity and also allow yourself to experience wellbeing. The two are not opposed; together they constitute a worthy human response to existence.

word_study.meaning: Life, lifetime, living, vitality. The plural form chayim emphasizes the fullness and extent of one's life.
word_study.significance: Chayim is finite—'in his life' means during the span of mortal existence. This is the only opportunity to rejoice and do good. There is no assumption of afterlife reward; the good is here, now, in the present life. This urgency (carpe diem, but not in a frivolous sense) is characteristic of Qohelet's practical wisdom.

cross_references.connection: There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour.' This is the first enjoyment passage, establishing the refrain that Qohelet returns to throughout the book.
Behold that which I have seen: it is good and comely for one to eat and to drink, and to enjoy the good of all his labour.' The principle is reaffirmed with slight variation.

Then I commended mirth, because a man hath no better thing under the sun, than to eat, and to drink, and to be merry.' The refrain again, emphasizing that within the limits of 'under the sun,' joy and goodness are the best available.

Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart...Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest all the days of the life of thy vanity.' The final endorsement of enjoyment, now paired explicitly with love and human relationships.

Charge them that are rich in this world...that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate.' The New Testament echoes Qohelet's combination of joy and goodness as the proper human response.

Wherefore, let all men beware how they take my name in their lips...And in nothing doth man offend God, or against none is his wrath kindled, save those who confess not his hand in all things, and obey not his commandments.' The Doctrine and Covenants teaches that receiving God's goodness with gratitude and doing good to others is central to the covenant life.

commentary.historical_context: The enjoyment passages in Ecclesiastes may reflect the influence of Greek philosophical schools on Jewish thought during the Hellenistic period. The Epicurean tradition (often misunderstood as mere hedonism) actually taught that the good life consisted of simple pleasures—food, drink, friendship, and freedom from fear. Qohelet's affirmation of simchah ('joy') and la'asot tov ('doing good') aligns with this wisdom while remaining rooted in Hebrew covenant thinking. The book may also reflect the experience of Jews living under Persian or Hellenistic rule, where individual political agency was limited and where the question 'What good can I actually achieve?' became urgent. The answer: you can rejoice faithfully, you can act with integrity, and these are genuine goods, even if you cannot reshape the world or escape mortality.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 37:16 teaches: 'Now ye may suppose that this is foolishness in me; but behold I say unto you, that by small and simple things are great things brought to pass.' The Book of Mormon encourages the same posture that Qohelet models: not grand schemes that might produce 'lasting gain' on a historical scale, but faithful, consistent doing of good in one's life and relationships. This is real and meaningful, even if not historically monumental.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:33 counsels: 'Wherefore, be not weary in well-doing, for ye are laying the foundation of a great work. And out of small things proceedeth that which is great.' While the Doctrine and Covenants adds eschatological perspective (that small good works do ultimately build toward Zion and eternal purposes), it endorses Qohelet's emphasis on consistent goodness in daily life.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that the greatest gifts are relational and spiritual rather than material or historical. The work of the temple is fundamentally about covenant relationship with God and with family—the precise arena in which Qohelet recommends that we rejoice and do good. The Endowment teaches that mortal life, with all its limitations, is sanctified by covenant and by faithful response to our relationships and obligations.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus Christ embodies the principle of verse 12 perfectly: He rejoiced in His life and ministry (Luke 10:21 records that 'Jesus rejoiced in spirit'), and He spent His entire earthly ministry doing good—healing the sick, feeding the hungry, teaching the truth, forgiving sinners. He did not attempt to 'fix' the Roman political order or establish an earthly kingdom (despite the expectations of many). Instead, He focused on the genuine goods available: authentic relationships, spiritual transformation, and love made manifest. His own suffering and death did not negate His earlier affirmations of life's goodness; rather, they were expressions of ultimate commitment to goodness and love. The Resurrection vindicates that this is the proper human response: to rejoice and to do good, trusting that God's purposes encompass and redeem even our finite efforts.
commentary.application: Ecclesiastes 3:12 is one of the most liberating verses in scripture for those struggling with perfectionism, world-weariness, or the sense that their efforts 'don't matter.' (1) Accept limitation: You will not cure all disease, end all injustice, or reshape the world in your lifetime. Your efforts will not produce lasting, cosmic gain. This is not failure; it is the human condition. (2) Recognize the genuine good available to you: In this moment, with these people, in these relationships, you can choose joy and goodness. This is not trivial. A parent's consistent love for a child, a friend's faithful presence, a worker's integrity in their daily task, a member's faithful service—these are real and lasting goods, even if invisible to history. (3) Combine joy and goodness: Neither frivolous pleasure-seeking nor grim duty-bound moralism, but rather the integration of both. Find delight in what you do. Be joyful in your service, whether in family, church, or community. (4) Do it now, 'in his life': Don't delay. Qohelet's repeated emphasis on 'in his life' creates urgency about the present moment. This is your one life; rejoice and do good in it now. (5) In moments when you feel that your work is 'in vain' (raising children who leave home, teaching a class that won't remember, serving in a calling that will be reassigned), remember that the good is not in the cosmic outcome but in the faithful present action. That is enough. It is everything.

text_kjv: For that which befalleth the sons of men befalleth beasts; even one thing befalleth them: as the one dieth, so dieth the other; yea, they have all one breath; so that a man hath no preeminence above a beast: for all is vanity.

commentary.narrative:
This verse represents Qohelet's most philosophically unsettling claim: human and animal mortality are identical. He has spent the first two chapters exploring human achievement, wisdom, and pleasure; now he confronts the reader with the ultimate leveler—death. The Hebrew word miqreh ('occurrence, fate') appears three times, emphasizing that what befalls humans and beasts is not merely similar but echad ('one, the same'). This is not poetic hyperbole but empirical observation: both die, both return to silence, both cease to act or think. The phrase 'one breath' (ruach echad) points to the common biological animation—the life-force that moves through all living creatures. When that breath departs, the king and the ox are identically inert.

Yet Qohelet is not denying human dignity or the image of God; he is performing a radical thought experiment. Genesis 1 grants humans dominion over animals. But what does dominion mean when death makes all dominion irrelevant? The 'no preeminence' (motar...ayin—literally, 'the advantage...is nothing') directly challenges the implied hierarchy of creation. This creates an uncomfortable tension: Scripture elsewhere affirms human worth, yet here Qohelet observes that in the face of mortality, that worth becomes invisible, ineffectual. The conclusion—'all is vanity' (hevel)—is not despair but realism. Everything that humans achieve, accumulate, and pride themselves on is ultimately as insubstantial as breath or vapor in the wind.

The modern reader must resist two temptations: first, to dismiss this as nihilism; second, to spiritualize it into religious comfort. Qohelet is not saying human life has no meaning. He is saying that meaning cannot be found in the things we typically pursue—power, wealth, status—because death erases the distinctions these things create. The ancient reader, familiar with Egyptian and Mesopotamian wisdom literature, would have recognized this as the voice of honest observation pushing back against the triumphalism of empire and hierarchy.

word_study.meaning: Occurrence, fate, what happens by chance or providence. The root qrh suggests 'to meet with' or 'to encounter.' In Ecclesiastes, miqreh is the neutral event that befalls all—not divine punishment or reward, but the universal human condition.
word_study.significance: The repetition of miqreh three times in this verse emphasizes the universality and inevitability of the shared fate. Unlike the yitron (profit/advantage) language elsewhere in Ecclesiastes, miqreh does not suggest human activity earning a return; it simply names what comes to pass. This term undercuts the entire project of human striving, because striving cannot change the miqreh.

word_study.meaning: Wind, breath, spirit, the animating principle of life. In Genesis 2:7, ruach is what makes humans 'living souls.' Here it means the vital breath—the physical respiration and life-force that animates all creatures. The Covenant Rendering clarifies that this is biological breath, not the theological 'spirit' that might survive death.
word_study.significance: Qohelet deliberately uses the term that designates both humans and animals—suggesting a common life principle. When the ruach departs, both human and beast become equally lifeless corpses. This is his most biologically reductive moment, refusing to invoke metaphysical distinctions that cannot be empirically verified.

word_study.meaning: Advantage, remainder, superiority, profit. The root ytr means 'to be left over' or 'to exceed.' In Ecclesiastes 1:3, Qohelet asks 'What profit (yitron) has a man from all his labor?' Here motar carries the same weight: what remains to humans that animals lack?
word_study.significance: The answer is: nothing. This is the most direct contradiction of human exceptionalism in the biblical wisdom corpus. Yet it serves a rhetorical purpose: by denying false grounds for human superiority (immortality, perpetual achievement, lasting legacy), Qohelet clears space for a more honest basis for human worth—one that does not rest on denied mortality.

word_study.meaning: Vapor, breath, worthlessness, futility. The root suggests wind or air—something with no substance, no permanence, no weight. In Ecclesiastes, hevel is the book's central diagnosis: all human striving dissipates like breath into thin air.
word_study.significance: Hevel returns as the judgment. Not 'all is evil' or 'all is meaningless' in the modern sense, but 'all is ephemeral, insubstantial.' This includes the human sense of superiority over animals. Before the grave, such distinctions evaporate.

cross_references.connection: God grants humans dominion over animals, establishing a hierarchy. Qohelet's claim that humans have 'no preeminence' above beasts directly challenges the functional significance of this dominion when death erases all distinctions.
The judgment on humanity: 'Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.' Qohelet extends this death sentence universally to all living things, not merely humans.
The opening question—'What profit hath a man of all his labour?'—finds its sharpest answer here: no profit, no advantage, when death equalizes all.

Qohelet previously reflected on the superiority of wisdom over foolishness, only to observe that 'one event happeneth to them all'—wise and fool die alike. Verse 19 extends this leveling principle to all creatures.

The psalmist grapples with the same paradox: 'Man that is in honour understandeth not; he is like the beasts that perish.' This wisdom psalm echoes Qohelet's observation without Qohelet's radical tone.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, the hierarchy of human rule over animals was foundational to royal ideology and creation mythology. Egyptian, Mesopotamian, and Hittite texts regularly depicted the king as the apex of creation, appointed by gods to rule over subordinate realms. The great kings of antiquity carved their dominion into stone—conquest narratives, tribute lists, animal hunts rendered in reliefs. Qohelet's observation that this hierarchy becomes invisible in death would have struck the ancient reader as radically subversive, especially if read in a court context (as Ecclesiastes appears to have been written). The language of 'one fate' (miqreh echad) echoes the observation of prophetic literature about the universality of death, but Qohelet makes it empirically matter-of-fact rather than theologically laden. Ancient tomb texts from Egypt and Mesopotamia often grapple with the same anxiety: despite royal power and wealth, the coffin awaits all. Qohelet is not original in this observation, but he is unusually blunt.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 40:11-14 addresses the fate of the spirit after death, teaching that spirits are received into a state of happiness or misery according to their deeds. This directly answers the question Qohelet cannot answer empirically in verse 21. The Book of Mormon affirms what Qohelet admits he cannot verify: that the human spirit does ascend and account for its works. Moroni 10:34 similarly teaches that all things are created and made to bear record of God, suggesting a teleology and purpose that Qohelet, observing only 'under the sun,' cannot perceive.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 93:29-30 teaches that the elements are eternal and that all things are organized by law. This provides a framework for understanding Qohelet's observation: the 'one breath' and the dust are not random but part of an organized cosmos. D&C 88:15-16 expands this: 'The light which is in all things, which giveth life to all things.' The ruach that animates all creatures participates in this universal light. The Doctrine and Covenants thus supplies metaphysical grounding for Qohelet's empirical observations.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Restoration teaches that mortality is not the end of human distinction. The temple endowment teaches that humans are co-creators with God, with capacity for eternal progression—a far more exalted view of human preeminence than Genesis 1 alone provides. Yet the temple also begins in a garden of innocence before the fall, acknowledging the equality and nakedness of all souls before God. Qohelet's leveling of human and animal in death is a reminder that terrestrial achievement, titles, and honors have no weight in the eternities; only covenant and righteousness matter.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's incarnation and mortality directly address Qohelet's observation. In assuming human flesh—subject to hunger, pain, and death—the Son of God temporarily shared the fate Qohelet describes: one breath, one death, one dust. Yet the Resurrection inverts the conclusion: human beings do have preeminence, not because of earthly achievement but because of redemption. Where Qohelet sees only the grave, Christ reveals the grave as a passage. The 'no advantage' of verse 19 becomes, in the Atonement, the greatest advantage: the restoration of human dignity beyond death, earned not through striving but through faith in the One who conquered death.
commentary.application: For the modern covenant member, this verse serves as a spiritual memento mori—a confrontation with mortality that strips away false securities. We accumulate wealth, titles, credentials, and follower counts as though these establish permanent distinction. Qohelet reminds us that all these perish.
